Module 1: C and Integer Representations

Module 1 Overview

In Module 1: C and Integer Representations, we will cover the C programming language and how data is represented at the hardware level. We begin by learning the basics of C, a language that maps almost directly to hardware instructions. From there, we explore how numbers are stored inside a computer, including hexadecimal and binary representation, byte ordering, and bitwise operations. The second half of the module focuses on integer data: how signed and unsigned integers are encoded in memory, how integer arithmetic works, and what happens when values overflow their fixed-size containers.

By the end of this module, you will have a solid foundation in both C programming fundamentals and the integer representations that underlie all computation.

Learning objectives

At the end of this learning module, you will be able to:

  1. Explain the basic syntax of C, including functions and command line arguments
  2. Convert between binary, hexadecimal, and decimal numbering systems
  3. Interpret byte ordering (big-endian vs. little-endian) in memory
  4. Use bitwise operators, bit flags, and masking techniques
  5. Compare and contrast signed and unsigned integer representations
  6. Explain Two's Complement encoding for signed integers
  7. Describe type casting and conversion between signed and unsigned integers
  8. Explain integer arithmetic and identify when overflow occurs

Learning activities

You are expected to do the following tasks in order to achieve the above objectives:

  1. Complete the reading listed below
  2. Read Lessons 1 to 11 and complete the embedded practice problems
  3. Take the module quiz
  4. Review additional resources on the Module 1 Summary page

Reading

  • Bryant & O'Hallaron: Chapter 2
  • Matthews: Chapters 0 - 4

If you have questions, you can post them in the course lobby or send your instructor an email.

Module 1: C and Integer Representations

Lesson 1: C Language Basics

Introduction

History of C and C++

The C language was the original precursor to the C++ language. C was developed in the early 1970s by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Laboratories of AT&T. C++ was later developed by Bjarne Stroustrup, beginning in 1979, and was originally named "C with Classes." It added classes and many other language features on top of a C-like foundation. Both languages have gone through many revisions since then and remain important in systems, embedded, and performance-sensitive software.

C++ and C Are Closely Related

If you are coming from a C++ background you will find much of C syntax familiar. However, modern C++ is not a strict superset of C: the languages have diverged, and some valid C programs are not valid C++ programs. For this course, use gcc for C code so the compiler parses the source as C and uses the normal C toolchain. Some simple C programs may also compile with g++, but that should not be relied on.

What This Summary Is

This is just a brief description of what a C++ coder needs to know in order to write C code. So this is NOT a tutorial on writing C as a beginner. I'm assuming students have taken CS162 and know how to at least program in C++. You can find plenty of tutorials on C on the internet. A widely available and authoritative reference is The C Programming Language by Brian W. Kernighan and Dennis M. Ritchie.

Input/Output

One of the largest differences between C and C++ is how IO is handled. For the C language, to get input from the keyboard and send output to the terminal, you will need to use the C standard IO library. This is included by using the line:

#include <stdio.h>

Note the use of .h on the end of the library name. This is used for including all standard libraries.

printf

For the C language, use the printf function to print to the terminal. It takes a variable list of arguments but the first argument is always a literal string called a format string. The rest of the arguments are variables of any size or type. These are inputs for the formatted string.

Both C and C++ functions can be designed to take a variable number of arguments. This is something they don't teach you in CS161/162, as it isn't done often. If you want to know more about this, here is a resource you can consult. Tutorialspoint: C - Variable Arguments

Below is an example of using printf. We have two variables that need to be printed: a string for a name and an int for an age.

  printf("Name: %s age: %d\n", name, age);

If the name is Kayla and the age is 23, this will print:

Name: Kayla age: 23

Followed by a new line.

The percent sign starts the beginning of a format specifier. Each format specifier will be replaced by the value of a variable in the list of variables following the format string. For our example, the variable name is first in the list of variables, and so the first format specifier is replaced by the value of name. Likewise, the second format specifier is replaced by the value of the second variable age. The specifier's type needs to match the variable's type or a compiler error is generated.

The letters/numbers that follow the % indicate the type of value and optionally other information, such as number of decimal places to print, column width, etc. Each type is indicated by one or two letters. In our example, the letter 's' represents a string (C-String as there is no 'string' class in C) and the 'd' represents a signed integer.

Using printf can be more complex sometimes than using the IO stream library. For more information on printf, see Tutorialspoint: C library function - print() [link opens in new tab]. You can also do your own search for printf on Google to see many examples of using printf.

scanf

In the C language, the scanf function is used to input data from the keyboard. It also takes a variable list of arguments but the first argument is always a format string. The rest of the arguments are variables of any size or type.

Basically, the format string indicates the type(s) of input that is to be entered and in what order. The variable list is the variables to copy into. The variable list is similar to printf in that the order of the variables must be in the same order as the format specifiers in the format string.

The one difference is that each variable has to be passed by reference. For primitive types, use the address-of operator (&) in front of the variable name to pass its address. For arrays (or C-style strings which are arrays), there is no need for the address-of operator as arrays are already passed by reference.

Below is an example of using scanf. We want to pick up from the keyboard two values: a string for a name and an int for an age.

char name[200];
int age;
int main() {	
    printf("Enter name followed by a space then an age\n");
    // note the & on the age but not on the name variable
    scanf("%s %d", name, &age);  
    
    printf("name %s age %d\n", name, age);

    return 0; 
}

The format specifiers for scanf are basically the same as the printf specifiers at least for common types of variables. For more information on scanf, here is a link: Tutorialspoint: C library function - scanf() Again, you can also do your own search for scanf on Google to see many examples of using scanf.

Compiling and Running Programs

The C compiler on the Linux system is gcc. So make sure you are using this compiler instead of g++. C language source code files end in .c not in .cpp though header files still end in .h .

The same options as g++ that are not C++ centric (such as setting the version of C++) will work with gcc. Later in the course I will be introducing some new options for gcc that you will need for your programming labs.

For example, a basic command line for compiling C code would be:

gcc hello.c -o hello

The -o option does what it does in C++. It changes the name of the program to whatever follows; without this, it has the name a.out similar to g++.

Once you compile you can just run the program as you would any program.

./prog

We will go into more details of compiling in gcc when we talk about object code in Module 3.

structs

The C language has structs. You define structs the same way you do in C++. For example:

struct Employee
{
    char name[200];
    double pay;
};

But you need to add the keyword struct any time you need to use the name of the struct in a declaration. For example:

struct Employee emp;

It also is needed when listing parameters:

void addEmployee(struct Employee emp)

You won't need it when using the variable itself, just whenever you need to declare it or use it in a parameter list.

OR

Structs can be defined like this, and then you don't need to say "struct" everywhere:

typedef struct
{
    char name[200];
    double pay;
} Employee;

Even better would be:

typedef struct
{
    char* name; // dynamically allocate based on string length
    double pay;
} Employee;

Passing Parameters by Reference

While the address-of operator & does exist in C, it cannot be used to create reference parameters as in C++. To pass something by reference, pass the address of the variable and then use a pointer to change the value inside a function.

For example, the following code works in C++:

void changeEmployee(Employee &emp)
{
   ....
   emp.pay = 100.00;
}

...
  changeEmployee(emp);
...


But in the C language, you will need to pass the address instead and use a pointer inside the function:

void changeEmployee(struct Employee* emp)
{
   ....
   emp->pay = 100.00;
}

...
  changeEmployee(&emp);
...

For primitive data types, you'll need to dereference the pointer to use it in the function:

void addEmployee(struct Employee array[], int* count)
   {
	     int size = *count;
	      ....
	     (*count)++;
	     ....
   }

Using Constants

The const keyword does exist but it is not used as much as it is in C++. In C, const variables cannot be used as array sizes or in other constant expressions (unlike in C++), so it is more common to use the #define pre-processor directive instead. So instead of:

const int MAX_STR=100;

You can use:

#define MAX_STR 100

Use of String Data

C does not have a string class. This is the moment you've been preparing for: from here on, you will use null-terminated character arrays (known as "C-strings") for all string data. If you need string manipulation functions like strlen, strcpy, or strcmp, include the string library:

#include <string.h>

Dynamic Memory

Another important area of differences is handling dynamic memory. There are no new or delete operators in C. Memory allocation is done via several functions, the most popular being malloc. So to allocate space for an Employee struct on the heap, use:

struct Employee *emp = (struct Employee*) malloc(sizeof(struct Employee));

This will create one struct Employee on the heap. Note that malloc returns a pointer of type void*. In C, void* implicitly converts to any other pointer type, so the cast is optional (though required if compiling as C++). Many C programmers omit the cast because it can mask a missing #include <stdlib.h>.

To free up the memory, you will need to use the function free:

free(emp);

The functions malloc and free are available in the C standard library. You will need to include this library.

#include <stdlib.h>

Booleans

There is no built-in type called bool with its values of true and false. However, you can include the standard boolean library that will give you this type:

#include <stdbool.h>

You can also use an int variable and use the defined constants TRUE and FALSE for values. Just use the define preprocessor in a header file and then you can use these in your code:

// main.h
    #define TRUE 1
    #define FALSE 0  // you can also use !TRUE here
    
    
    // main.c
    int quit = FALSE;
    ....
    while(!quit)   
    ...

Typecasting

The newer C++ type-safe casting operators do not exist in C. So use the C typecasting operator () for typecasting.

double pay2 = (double) pay1;

Using Command Line Arguments

You can pass in input to a C/C++ program by way of command line arguments. This is similar to Bash shell scripts where you can include a space separated list of arguments after the name of the program:

./hello Frank Martin 30 5.25

Note that if you wanted the name Frank Martin to be one argument, then you need to put it in double quotes:

./hello "Frank Martin" 30 5.25

So how does your program pick up the arguments? You start by using a different header for your main function that includes an int as the first parameter and a pointer to a pointer to a char, or char**, as the second parameter.

int main(int argc, char** argv)

They are typically called argc and argv but you can call them whatever you want to. Just don't change the order or the type of these parameters.

argv is the arguments as an array of C-Strings and argc is the number of arguments (including the program name). You can access a particular C-String by using indexing. The first, or 0 index, is the name of the program. The second, or 1 index, is the 1st argument and so on.

printf("program name: %s\n", argv[0]);
    printf("1st argument: %s\n", argv[1]);
      .....

You can use argc in a for loop to go through the list of arguments and print them.

Note that the arguments are C-Strings so if you need them as integer types or floating point types, you can use the functions atof() for floating point types and atoi() for integer types.

int inum = atoi(argv[2]);
float fnum = atof(argv[3]);

You may need to include stdlib.h to use these functions.

I should point out that command line arguments are not just a feature of C alone; you can use command line arguments in C++.

Summary Table of Differences

This is a list of differences between C and C++. This is not a comprehensive list; it's only those features you might run into in this class.

C++ C
Has OOP concepts: classes and objects. Doesn't have any OOP features.
Exception handling is a mechanism built into the language. Exception handling is not built in but handled through libraries.
Has operator and function overloading Doesn't have these features.
Parameters can be passed by reference. Strictly pass by value (except for arrays). Use pointers to make parameters pass by reference.
Enumerations (enum types) built into language Has enum types, but they are essentially integer constants (no type safety).
string type available (via a string class) Use char arrays to implement strings (C-Strings)
boolean type (bool) built into the language Include the stdbool.h library. Or use #define constants TRUE and FALSE.
functions with default arguments Doesn't have this at all.
use of namespaces Doesn't have this at all.
file extension: .c++ or .cpp file extension: .c
IO: io stream library (iostream)
>> and << get, getline ...		 IO: standard io library (stdio.h)
printf, scanf, fprintf, sprintf ...
dynamic memory: new and delete dynamic memory: malloc(), free(), calloc(), etc.
no need to use the struct keyword except in defining structs need to use struct when declaring a variable or in a parameter list.
typecasting: can use () or type-safe casting which gives more control over conversions. typecasting: can only use ()

Module 1: C and Integer Representations

Lesson 2: Hexadecimal Numbers

NOTE: This is a summary of chapter 2, section 2.1 in the textbook.

Numeric Representation: Hexadecimal Numbers

Binary numbers are a bit unwieldy to read. Instead of trying to display binary information in binary digits, a more compact numbering system related to binary is used to display binary numbers. This is the hexadecimal system.

The hexadecimal system is a numeric system with 16 digits. The digits are represented by the digits 0 to 9 and the letters A to F. The letters are needed to add the extra digits past 9 that a decimal system doesn't have. 'A' represents the equivalent of the decimal number 10, 'B' represents the equivalent of decimal 11, and so on.

Each hexadecimal digit can be directly translated into a set of 4 binary digits. Below is a table of each hex digit and its corresponding 4 binary digits:

Hex Digit Binary Number
0 0000
1 0001
2 0010
3 0011
4 0100
5 0101
6 0110
7 0111
8 1000
9 1001
A (10) 1010
B (11) 1011
C (12) 1100
D (13) 1101
E (14) 1110
F (15) 1111

Since translating between hexadecimal and binary is an exact one-digit to four-digit translation, it's easy to convert between the two numbering systems. For example, if a hex number is:

   98A3F

then, the binary equivalent is obtained by substituting each hex digit for its equivalent 4 bit binary number:

    9    8    A    3    F
  1001 1000 1010 0011 1111

So, the equivalent binary number is 10011000101000111111. Note that the hex number only requires 5 digits, and the binary number requires 20 digits. This makes for a more compact representation in hex and is the reason why it is common to display binary data as hex digits.

Although this is rarely done, you can translate hex numbers into decimal numbers. This is not an exact digits-to-digits translation. To go from hex to decimal, use the formula:

    decimal = h(n)*16n + h(n-1)*16(n-1) +...+ h(1)*16 + h(0)

where h(n) is the nth hex digit (replace any letter digit with its decimal equivalent and start n at 0). For example, our number above in decimal is:

   dec = 9*164 + 8*163 + 10*162 + 3*16 + 15
   dec = 589824 + 32768  + 2560    + 48   + 15
   dec = 625215

As I said, this does not often need to be done, and if you need the decimal equivalent, feel free to find a calculator that does the conversion for you (or a web page; there are plenty of them on the internet).

Two hex digits represent one byte. Since much of memory is stored in one-byte increments, you will often see hex numbers written in groups of two to represent one byte per group. For our example (where we need to pad out with a zero the first group to make two digits):

   09 8A 3F

In C/C++ language, to indicate that a literal number is a hex number, use 0x or 0X in front of the number: 0x098A3F.

Here's an example of a small program that uses hex syntax for arithmetic:

  #include <stdio.h> // this is how we are able to call printf

  int main(){

    int hex1 = 0x1A; // 16 + 10 = 26
    int hex2 = 0xFF; // 15*16 + 15 = 255

    printf("hex1 in decimal is: %d\n", hex1); // the %d directive prints signed integers in decimal
    printf("hex2 in decimal is: %d\n", hex2);
    printf("The sum in hex is: 0x%x\n", hex1 + hex2); // the hex directive is %x (or %X if you want UPPERCASE LETTERS)

    return 0;
  }

Hex Color Codes

A lot of people's first introduction to writing numbers in hex isn't decompiling code or low-level system programming but dealing with color in art programs. For computers, color is generally represented as "24-bit color depth," which means that we're using 24 bits to represent the full RGB color. 

We do this by splitting the 24 bits into 8 bits for red, 8 bits for green, and 8 bits for blue.

Now, what numbers can you represent with 8 bits? 0 – 255!

And if you use two digits of hex, what numbers can you represent? Well, that's 0x00, which is 0 through 0xFF, which is

15*16 + 15

or 255.

So, in order to represent a 24-bit color, we can just write a hex number with six digits! Pure black is then 0x000000, pure white is 0xFFFFFF, and something like teal is 0x39a78e. If you've never played with hex representations of colors, check out Color Hex [link opens in new tab].

Module 1: C and Integer Representations

Lesson 3: Numeric Representation

Information Storage

In this summary we will be covering the binary representation of data within a computer system. Data includes numbers, symbols (letters, digits, etc), graphics, audio, and other data. Throughout this course, we will concentrate on numeric data.

No matter what type of data, all data is represented by binary digits or bits. A bit can be one of two values: 0 or 1. Bits are stored in memory in a sequence of cells. Each 8 cells (1 byte) is addressable as a whole by the system. Therefore, the smallest unit of addressable memory is one byte (8 bits).

With the exception of one-byte data values, data is stored across multiple cells. We will talk about how this is done in the lecture on byte ordering.

The bit pattern is the series of bits across many cells that represent one data value. Since a user is not likely to know binary, this bit pattern will need to be translated into the actual value (numbers, letters, etc) that the user can understand. This is typically done in hardware.

from bit pattern to number
Address Contents of Cell Data Value User Sees

...

...

...

200

10100101

3237

201

00001100

202

00000000

203

00000000

204

11110100

...

....

.....

....

Word and Data Sizes

The word size of a computer system is the size of a pointer. This is the number of bits needed to represent all addresses in memory. For a 64-bit architecture (system design), this means an address is represented by 64 bits. Because of this, the address size limits the maximum possible addressable memory locations. For a 32-bit architecture, this was about 4 billion, preventing 32-bit systems from having memory storage larger than 4 Gigabytes. Now, with the word size of most computer systems being 64-bit, the limitation on memory storage is 16 exabytes or about 1019 bytes. This is a huge amount of memory (it's about 4 billion times bigger than 4G memory) and will take quite a while before we will need to increase word size to increase memory.

Previously, the word size was also the given size of an int type on the system, but starting with 64-bit architecture, the int type is no longer the word size.

In C/C++ languages, all simple or primitive data types have a fixed size associated with them. The size depends on the word size of the architecture.

Datatypes like int can be different byte lengths on different architectures, and the sizeof() operator can be used to compensate for that:

int a[100];
int n_elements = sizeof(a) / sizeof(int);

Below is a table of the most common data types and their sizes for the 64-bit architecture (this is a portion of figure 2.3 in the textbook)

Type Size in Bytes
char (signed) 1
short 2
int 4
long 8
char* 8
float 4
double 8

Some things to note: char * is a pointer that holds an address, so it needs to be the word size, which, for a 64-bit architecture, is 8 bytes (64/8 = 8).

There are signed and unsigned versions of integer numbers. The signed versions can represent both positive, zero, and negative. The unsigned versions can only represent positive and zero. They are typically the same size but have different ranges of values. We'll talk at length about signed and unsigned integer types later in this module (Lessons 7–11). Floating point number types (float and double) are always signed types. We'll talk about floating point representation in Module 2.

Module 1: C and Integer Representations

Lesson 4: Byte Ordering

Numeric Representation: Byte Ordering

Byte order is the order in which a multi-byte data type is stored in memory. These are stored as a consecutive set of bytes that are laid out from some low address to a high address, with the lowest address representing the "address" of this data.

There are two ways to lay out the bit pattern of a value across several bytes. One way is to make the most significant byte (the leftmost byte of the bit pattern) be stored starting at the high address. This is called little endian, and I won't get into why it's called this (the textbook talks about this weird name). The other way is to store the most significant 8 bits at the low address. This is called big endian.

For an example of byte ordering, if we are storing an integer, we need 4 consecutive bytes in memory. Note that for brevity, we will be showing each byte as a two-digit hex number. For example, if we have the hex number 0x12345678 to store, the bytes will be stored in 'big endian' as:

  address ->  200  201  202  203
              12    34   56   78

For little endian, the bytes will be stored:

  address ->  200  201   202 203
               78   56   34   12

See the diagrams below for an illustration of the above.

Aside: Most computers you will work with are little-endian (x86 and most ARM deployments). Some commercial and embedded systems are still big-endian or bi-endian, so code that handles external binary formats should not assume one fixed byte order.

On the other hand, bit transmissions on the Internet are basically big-endian. So often, bits being sent between network cards need to be re-arranged when they are eventually stored in the host's memory.

For more information on the history of byte ordering, you can optionally read On Holy Wars and a Plea for Peace [link opens in a new tab].

The byte order usually doesn't affect programmers unless you are working across multiple bytes at the bit pattern level. This is pretty rare; you might run into this issue if you are doing very low-level or machine code level programming.

Byte ordering can be an issue when communicating data from one machine to another over a network connection. For more information about this, check the Wikipedia entry for Endianness [link opens in new tab].

Aside: If you print out a little-endian machine's byte-ordered value in the order of increasing addresses (which is how a char array is stored), each byte will be written in reverse order. If you want to see the actual bit pattern of a number in the right order on a 'little endian' machine, you can change the 'showbytes' function to print out the char bytes from len-1 to 0:

for (i = len-1; i >= 0; i--) 
 

This will save you some time in deciphering the number in that you don't have to first reverse the hex digits to get the actual bit pattern from the printout.

This showbytes.c code file has this function in it. 

#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

typedef unsigned char * byte_pointer;

void show_bytes(byte_pointer start, size_t len)
{
   int i;
   for(i=0; i<len; i++)
       printf(" %.2x", start[i]);
   printf("\n");
}



void show_int(int x)
{
    show_bytes((byte_pointer) &x, sizeof(int));
}

void show_float(float x)
{
    show_bytes((byte_pointer) &x, sizeof(float));
}

void show_pointer(void *x)
{
   show_bytes((byte_pointer) &x, sizeof(void *));
}

void test_show_bytes(int val)
{
   int ival = val;
   float fval = (float) val;
   int *pval = &ival;
   
   show_int(ival);
   show_float(fval);
   show_pointer(pval);
  
}


int main()
{
    const char *sval = "12345";
   //int i =-23432;

   //test_show_bytes(i);   
    show_bytes((byte_pointer) sval, strlen(sval)+1);
    return 0;
}

Module 1: C and Integer Representations

Lesson 5: Bitwise Operations

NOTE: This is a summary of chapter 2, section 2.1 in the textbook.

Bitwise Operators

Students are familiar with boolean operators && for AND and || for OR operations. These work at the numeric level in that they interpret a conditional or number to be 1 (TRUE) or 0 (FALSE).

There are boolean operators that work on the bit pattern itself. These are called bit-wise boolean operators because they perform boolean operations to each bit one at a time as opposed to the entire number. The following is a table of these bit-wise boolean operators:

Operator Name Example
& bit-wise AND 1010   &   1001   => 1000
| bit-wise OR 1010   |   1001   => 1011
~ complement or negation ~ 1011   => 0100
^ eXclusive OR 1010   ^   1001   => 0011

Note that each binary operator compares each bit with the corresponding bit in the same position. For bit-wise AND, if both bits are 1 then the result is 1 otherwise it is 0. For bit-wise OR, if both bits are 0 then the result is 0 otherwise it is 1. For exclusive OR, if both bits are the same the result is 0, otherwise the result is 1. The complement or negation operator flips the bit's value. If the bit is 1 then the result is 0; if the bit is 0 the result is 1.

Note that the bit-wise & and | use only one symbol instead of two. This is a common mistake, so be aware of it.

Shift Operators

Another set of bit-wise operators are bit shift operators. These will move the bit pattern over by some given amount of positions for a given number.

The left shift operator ( num << i ) moves each bit in num to the left by i amount. For example, if num=10010011 and i=2, the resulting value will be:

 10010011 => 01001100

Note that all left bits that don't fit into the number are just ignored, and the new right bits are filled with 0's.

The right shift operator ( num >> i) will shift the bit pattern of num by i amount to the right. For example, if num is an unsigned char equal to 10010011 and i=2:

 10010011 => 00100100

For all integers, the rightmost bits are ignored. For unsigned integers, the bits on the left are filled in with 0's. This is called a logical shift. For signed integers, the C standard says the behavior is implementation-defined, but most compilers on x86 perform an arithmetic shift, filling the left side with whatever the original leftmost bit is (1 or 0). So, for our example, if num above is a signed char:

 10010011 => 11100100

Another example:

 01100010 => 00011000

Note that the bit that is filled in is whatever the leftmost bit happens to be. We'll discuss why this is so later in this module (Lesson 9) when we talk about how signed integers are represented in memory.

Module 1: C and Integer Representations

Lesson 6: Bit Flags and Masking

NOTE: This is a summary of chapter 2, section 2.1 in the textbook.

Numeric Representation: Bit Flags and Masking

One area you might need to use bit-wise operators is when working with bit flags. A bit flag (or bit field) is a (typically unsigned) integer where each bit represents an attribute that can be on or off. If the ith attribute is on, the ith bit will be one; if the ith attribute is off, the ith bit will be zero.

For example, let's say we have some settings for a motor. We can make an 8-bit flag where each represents a setting as listed in the table below (note that position goes from right to left):

Bit Position Setting
1st position (right-most) Turn on motor
2nd position Slow Speed
3rd position Medium Speed
4th position Fast Speed
5th position Reverse Motor
6th thru 8th position Not Used - reserved for future use.

An example of a bit flag for this motor is one where we want it turned on and moving at a medium speed in reverse. The bit flag would look like:

00010101 // motor on, medium speed on, reverse on - all else off

Determining the bit in a bit flag

To determine whether a setting is on or off, we need to determine what the bit at the ith location is. One way is to set up a mask. This is a number where all positions are 0 except the ith position, which is set to 1. Let's say we want to determine if the motor is running at medium speed. Our mask would look like this:

00000100

The mask to find the ith bit can be built by setting the mask value to 1 and then left shifting this mask (i-1) places over. Note that the first position is 0, second position is 1, and so on. So, in our example, the medium speed is in the 3rd position:

00000001 << 2 -> 00000100

Bit-wise ANDing the mask to the number gives a result that is dependent only on the ith bit. The other bits will end up being 0 because 0 ANDed with any bit results in 0. So, with our example, we get:

  00010101 & 00000100 -> 00000100

Note that if the medium speed was not turned on:

00010001 & 00000100 -> 00000000

So, only the medium speed setting determines whether the result is zero or non-zero. This can be tested for in your code.

If, after you have obtained the masked results, you need to pass back a 1 for on and a 0 for off, you can use the right shift operator (>>) to move the 1 bit to the right-most bit. Just shift by the position minus 1 of the bit:

00000100 >> 2 -> 00000001
 

Turning on or off a bit in a bit flag

For turning a bit on or off, typically you would set up a set of constants to use (more convenient than remembering the decimal number needed for each setting). In our example, we would have them defined at the top of the file:

#define MOTOR_ON 1 // mask for 1st bit - 2^0
#define SPEED_LOW 2 // mask for 2nd bit - 2^1
#define SPEED_MEDIUM 4 // mask for 3rd bit - 2^2
#define SPEED_HIGH 8 // mask for 4th bit - 2^3
#define REVERSE 16 // mask for 5th bit - 2^4

Note these create a set of pre-defined masks for each setting. To turn on a bit (or a series of bits), OR the bit flag with the corresponding constant (or set of constants):

// turns on the high speed bit_flag = bit_flag | SPEED_HIGH // turns on the motor and the low speed bit_flag = bit_flag | MOTOR_ON | SPEED_LOW

To turn off a bit, take the complement of the constant and AND it with the bit flag:

  // turns off motor and low speed bit_flag = bit_flag & ~MOTOR_ON & ~SPEED_LOW

Here is a full example:

#include <stdio.h>

  #define MOTOR_ON     1   // mask for 1st bit - 2^0
  #define SPEED_LOW    2   // mask for 2nd bit - 2^1
  #define SPEED_MEDIUM 4   // mask for 3rd bit - 2^2
  #define SPEED_HIGH   8   // mask for 4th bit - 2^3
  #define REVERSE      16  // mask for 5th bit - 2^4

  void print_menu() {
      printf("\nBit Flag Menu:\n");
      printf("1. Toggle MOTOR_ON\n");
      printf("2. Toggle SPEED_LOW\n");
      printf("3. Toggle SPEED_MEDIUM\n");
      printf("4. Toggle SPEED_HIGH\n");
      printf("5. Toggle REVERSE\n");
      printf("0. Exit\n");
  }

  void print_bit_flag(int bit_flag) {
      printf("\nCurrent Bit Flag: %d\n", bit_flag);
      printf("MOTOR_ON: %s\n", (bit_flag & MOTOR_ON) ? "ON" : "OFF");
      printf("SPEED_LOW: %s\n", (bit_flag & SPEED_LOW) ? "ON" : "OFF");
      printf("SPEED_MEDIUM: %s\n", (bit_flag & SPEED_MEDIUM) ? "ON" : "OFF");
      printf("SPEED_HIGH: %s\n", (bit_flag & SPEED_HIGH) ? "ON" : "OFF");
      printf("REVERSE: %s\n", (bit_flag & REVERSE) ? "ON" : "OFF");
  }

  int main() {
      int bit_flag = 0;
      int choice;

      do {
          print_bit_flag(bit_flag);
          print_menu();
          printf("Enter your choice: ");
          scanf("%d", &choice);

          switch (choice) {
              case 1:
                  bit_flag ^= MOTOR_ON;
                  break;
              case 2:
                  bit_flag ^= SPEED_LOW;
                  break;
              case 3:
                  bit_flag ^= SPEED_MEDIUM;
                  break;
              case 4:
                  bit_flag ^= SPEED_HIGH;
                  break;
              case 5:
                  bit_flag ^= REVERSE;
                  break;
              case 0:
                  printf("Exiting...\n");
                  break;
              default:
                  printf("Invalid choice. Please try again.\n");
          }
      } while (choice != 0);

      return 0;
  }

Module 1: C and Integer Representations

Lesson 7: Integer Data Types

NOTE: This is a summary of chapter 2, sections 2.2 and 2.3 in the textbook.

Integer Representation: Integer Data Types

As mentioned earlier, there are two categories of integer types: signed and unsigned. The unsigned integer types can only represent positive and zero values. The signed integer types can represent positive, zero and negative values.

Signed values are said to have a sign (positive or negative) and a magnitude (ie. the size of the value). For example, -5 has a sign of - or negative and a magnitude of 5.

Below is a table of ranges for several unsigned and signed types. This is an abridged version from Figure 2.10 for 64-bit architecture. For unsigned, the minimum value is always 0.


Data Type Minimum Maximum
[signed] char -128 127
unsigned char 0 255
short -32,768 32,767
unsigned short 0 65,535
int -2,147,483,648 2,147,483,647
unsigned int 0 4,294,967,295

There are some facts to note. For signed, the max and min magnitudes are about 1/2 of what their unsigned counterparts are. Also note that for signed, the min is one bigger in magnitude than the max. We'll talk about why when we discuss signed encoding later.

Module 1: C and Integer Representations

Lesson 8: Unsigned Integer Encoding

NOTE: This is a summary of chapter 2, sections 2.2 and 2.3 in the textbook.

Integer Representation: Unsigned Integer Encoding

The encoding of how to represent unsigned int in memory is straightforward. The bit pattern is interpreted as a binary number which is then translated to a decimal when displayed to the screen.

For a given size w bits, the maximum value of an unsigned numeric type is given by the formula:

UMAX = 2w - 1 

The minimum value (UMIN) for unsigned is always 0.

Literal numbers (1, 0xa23, etc) are not always treated as signed: C chooses the first integer type that can represent the value (based on the literal's base and size). If you need to force an unsigned literal, use u or U after the number.

127556u or 0x2A234U

Module 1: C and Integer Representations

Lesson 9: Signed Integer Encoding

NOTE: This is a summary of chapter 2, sections 2.2 and 2.3 in the textbook.

Signed Integers: Two's Complement

Unsigned numbers are easy to come up with an encoding scheme since all we need is a magnitude to represent a number. For a signed number we need not only a magnitude but we need to indicate a sign as well. This is more of a challenge.

Some very straightforward encodings create added complexity when being designed in hardware. One straightforward way to encode signed numbers is to reserve the left-most bit as a sign bit. If this bit was 0 the number was positive; if it was 1 the number was negative. This is called sign magnitude encoding scheme.

It looks good at first, however, there are several problems with using this encoding. There are two possible zeros (one with all 0's and one with a 1 followed by all 0's) which makes checking for zero in hardware (a very common task) overly complex. It also makes doing arithmetic more complex.

To see this, first let's talk about how you would add a negative number to another number. The steps are:

  • Take all negative numbers and get the complement of each. A complement of a binary number is where each bit is changed to its opposite (0 goes to 1 and 1 goes to 0). For sign magnitude you would also need to ignore the leftmost bit.
  • Add the numbers together.
  • If there is a carry out of the left-most column (which is the next-to-left-most column), re-add this to the result.

The above introduces quite a bit of complexity. Getting the complement takes an extra step as well as adding back in the carry at the end.

So two other encoding schemes were invented: ones' complement and two's complement. In ones' complement, negative numbers were stored as their complement in memory. This gets rid of one extra step in that there is no need to calculate the complement. However, the leftmost carry needed to be added back into the number.

It was an improvement, however, this still had the problem of having two zeros to contend with and one extra step of adding the 1 back in at the end.

Two's complement encoding scheme was invented to compensate for the ones' complement difficulties. It is the same as ones' complement except that negative numbers are stored as their complement plus 1 (again, positives are kept the same). This encoding got rid of the extra zero and extra step at the end. In fact, you can just add numbers, both positive and negative, and it will work just fine as long as there is no overflowing of the range. Note that the left-most carry bit is ignored (it's actually added into the negative number from the start).

A significant motivation for the adoption of two's complement representation for negative numbers was that the same addition hardware that correctly added unsigned integers would work correctly for positive and negative signed integers as well. Most of today's computer systems use two's complement for signed integers.

Note that in order to distinguish positive from negative, the upper range positive numbers that start with a 1 are now treated as negative numbers. This is why signed positive numbers have roughly half the range of unsigned positive numbers. For every bit missing from the left, there is a 1/2 reduction in range of numbers that can be represented by the remaining bits. Also note that the negative zero now represents the maximum negative number in the range. This gives the negative range one extra value over the positive range.

The table below uses 4-bit numbers to show the bit pattern for each given number. Note that the negative magnitudes get smaller as the underlying bit pattern gets larger. With this scheme, the largest bit pattern: 1111 is actually -1. This is always true for other-sized two's complement numbers.

Value Bit Pattern
7 0111
6 0110
5 0101
4 0100
3 0011
2 0010
1 0001
0 0000
-1 1111
-2 1110
-3 1101
-4 1100
-5 1011
-6 1010
-7 1001
-8 1000

Next, we will look at how to convert between the bit pattern stored in memory and the actual decimal value. Although the examples are using a 4-bit size, the methods will work with any w-bit size type.

Finding the Value from Two's Complement

To find out the actual value of a two's complement bit pattern:

  1. Find unsigned representation for all bits but the leftmost bit
  2. Minus the leftmost bit (this is the sign bit) times 2w-1 from the sum.

For example (we are working with w=4):

 1011 
     1. 011 -> 2+1=3
     2. sign bit is 1 so 1*2(4-1) = 1*8 = 8
          -8 + 3 = -5.

Another example (we are working with w=4):

 1101 
     1. 101 -> 4+1=5
     2. sign bit is 1 so 1*2(4-1) = 1*8 = 8
          -8 + 5 = -3.

Find Two's Complement from Value

To find two's complement (in size w) from a given number:

  1. Find the bit pattern of the magnitude in w bits. If the number is positive, then this is the two's complement number.
  2. For a negative, take the complement of the bit pattern (flip 0's to 1's and 1's to 0's).
  3. Do binary addition by adding 1. Ignore any carry from the leftmost bit.

For example:

     to find -6 start with bit pattern: 0110
     take the complement:  1001
     add one to this:      1001 + 0001 = 1010
     so the bit pattern for -6 is 1010

The formulas for maximum and minimum signed integers of size w are:

TMAX = 2w-1 - 1
TMIN = -2w-1

Note that there is one less positive number than negative number. This is not too much of a problem unless you are negating the TMIN value (there's no corresponding negation value). What this means is that negating a number might actually cause an overflow to occur.

Module 1: C and Integer Representations

Lesson 10: Type Casting

NOTE: This is a summary of chapter 2, sections 2.2 and 2.3 in the textbook.

Converting Between Unsigned and Signed

When typecasting (changing from one type to another type), the computer keeps the equivalent bit pattern and just changes how the bits are interpreted. This can lead to several problems.

When going from same-sized (number of bits) signed to unsigned, if the signed value is guaranteed to be positive there is no problem as the bit pattern is the same for positive numbers between signed and unsigned. However, if the signed number turns out to be negative the result will be a positive number not even in the same ballpark. For small negative numbers, the result ends up being a very large positive number.

Even with positive values, the results may be wrong if going from an unsigned to a signed. Remember that even though the range for signed is exactly the same size, half of that range has been assigned to the negative numbers, so the positive numbers top out lower. So if the number is larger than TMAX, there will be overflow with incorrect results. In fact, the positive number is interpreted as a negative number because the leftmost bit is 1.

Typecasting From Smaller to Larger: Expanding Numbers

Changing numbers from smaller to larger sizes requires expanding the number by adding bits to the left of the smaller number to create a larger number. For unsigned numbers, this is done by adding zeros. This is called zero extension.

For signed numbers, the left bits are filled in with whatever the left-most bit of the original smaller number was. This is called sign extension and is similar to the right shift's arithmetic shift. This is done to preserve the sign and magnitude of negative values.

Typecasting from Larger to Smaller: Truncation

For changing a larger number to a smaller number, the leftmost bits get ignored. This is called truncation. This works well with values that fit into the new smaller size since the sign and magnitude are preserved for signed numbers. However, this becomes a garbage value if the value doesn't fit into the smaller range. We'll talk about this condition, called overflow, in the next lecture.

Implicit Typecasting with Mixed Signed and Unsigned Values

When doing arithmetic or doing comparisons, the compiler does implicit typecasting when there is a mixture of signed and unsigned values. If any operands are unsigned then all other operands are typecasted to an unsigned value. This has weird unpredictable results when doing math or doing comparisons. It is recommended not to allow the compiler to make a decision about typecasting, especially when doing comparisons (see textbook for some interesting effects).

Module 1: C and Integer Representations

Lesson 11: Integer Arithmetic

NOTE: This is a summary of chapter 2, sections 2.2 and 2.3 in the textbook.

Section 2.3: Integer Arithmetic

I have to admit that I was expecting this section to discuss how arithmetic is performed in hardware, but it seems like the authors decided this wasn't as important. The section seems to be more about one consequence of doing arithmetic: overflow. Overflow occurs when the full integer result cannot fit within the size limits of the data type.

I guess the reason might be that the underlying mechanism of doing arithmetic tends not to have an effect on software developers until overflow occurs. So knowing about overflow, when it happens and how to detect it, is more important from a programmer's perspective than how arithmetic is performed in hardware.

Overflow In Unsigned Addition

In order to hold the sum of two unsigned numbers of w bits, the resulting size needs to be 1 bit more or w+1 bits. For example, if you are using two 8-bit numbers, the sum might need 9 bits to prevent overflow. This represents a range that is twice the range of the two numbers.

For example, the maximum for 8-bit unsigned is 255. Adding two 255 numbers together gives a sum of 510 which will fit in a 9 bit range where the maximum number is 511. Basically, the maximum overflow from addition only requires one more bit to hold the results without overflow.

When overflow occurs, the leftmost bits are ignored. This will cause the sum value to become smaller than either of the two operands (this is proven mathematically in the textbook, so I won't prove it here). This gives us a good way to detect if an overflow has occurred by checking the sum against either of the two operands to see if the sum is smaller. A sum of two positive numbers (remember this is unsigned) is always going to be larger unless overflow occurs.

Overflow in Signed Addition

Addition for two signed integers also needs at least 1 extra bit to fit any sum. Again, this is based on the largest value possible being added to itself (see unsigned). However, overflow can only occur when the two operands have the same sign (either positive or negative). If x and y are both negative, this is called negative overflow. If x and y are both positive, this is positive overflow.

When negative overflow occurs, the sum is guaranteed to be positive. When positive overflow occurs, the sum is guaranteed to be negative. Note that under no normal circumstances (no overflow) can the sum be positive if both operands are negative and negative when both operands are positive. This allows the checking for overflow with signed addition.

WARNING: The above methods are guaranteed to detect overflow. However, using this method: 
if(x == (sum-y))
         // this is okay
else
         // this is overflow 
turns out not to work for overflow detection because this can be true even if there is overflow.

Two’s Complement Negation

The negation of a signed number is changing the sign of the number while keeping its magnitude. There is no equivalent to negation in unsigned numbers.

For the range of signed numbers, remember that there is one extra negative value than positive value. This has an effect on TMIN because there is no positive value with the same magnitude: TMAX is one smaller. So TMIN ends up being its own negation (ie. the value does not change). Try this code out to see for yourself (remember to include limits.h header):

int min = INT_MIN;
int nmin = -min;
printf("%d %d\n", min, nmin);

I guess the takeaway is that the negation of a negative number isn't guaranteed to be positive in code. If this is very important then checking for TMIN before negating should be done.

Overflow in Multiplication

For multiplication, both signed and unsigned need 2*w bits. For example, if we are multiplying two 8-bit numbers, the result may need 16 bits to fit in memory without overflow. This is much more severe than with addition, making multiplication more prone to overflow problems.

When overflow occurs, the left-most bits are truncated (ignored), and only the least significant bits are preserved. This turns out to be equivalent to taking the modulo of 2w. Signed numbers are treated the same except that the resulting modulo number is converted to two's complement, causing the resulting sign to be unpredictable. In general, there's no real pattern for detecting multiplication overflow. However, unlike addition, where x = y - sum doesn't work even when there is overflow (see warning above), the formula:

mult = x*y;
    if ( x == 0 || mult/x == y)
       // this is okay
    else
       // this is overflow

is guaranteed to work (see problem 2.35 in the textbook for details).

Multiply and Divide by Powers of 2

Right and left bit shifting can do more than move bits around. It can multiply or divide by a power of 2. In fact, this is the compiler's favorite way to do this, as it is much faster than actually multiplying and dividing. We'll talk more about this when we get to Chapter 3.

The left shift operator does multiplication:

num << i => num*2i

The right shift operator does division:

num >> i => num/(2i)

Whether right shift performs arithmetic or logical shift on signed numbers is implementation-defined in C, but virtually all compilers on x86 use arithmetic shift for signed types. Note that for negative numbers, arithmetic right shift rounds toward negative infinity (floor division), whereas C's / operator truncates toward zero. For example, -7 >> 1 gives -4, but -7 / 2 gives -3.

Note that going outside the range of the type will cause overflow for the left shift operator (multiplication). And the division is integer division; the fractional part is truncated.

Module 1: C and Integer Representations

Module 1 Summary

Wrap up

In this module, we covered the C programming language and integer data representation. Compared to other high-level languages, C maps almost directly into hardware instructions, making code potentially more efficient. C also provides a minimal set of abstractions, which is why it remains the language of choice for systems programming. We then studied how integers are stored in memory, including signed and unsigned representations, type casting between them, and the arithmetic operations that can be performed on integer data.

Key Takeaways

  • C is prevalent in critical applications such as operating systems (Windows, Linux, FreeBSD/macOS), web servers, web browsers, and mail servers. Understanding C is essential for understanding how software interacts with hardware.
  • Data inside a computer is stored as sequences of bits. Hexadecimal provides a convenient shorthand for binary, and byte ordering (big-endian vs. little-endian) determines how multi-byte values are laid out in memory.
  • Bitwise operators allow you to manipulate individual bits within a value, which is fundamental to tasks like masking, setting flags, and low-level hardware control.
  • Integer representation comes in two forms: signed (using Two's Complement) and unsigned. The finite word sizes used to represent integer data determine what values can be represented and the behavior of different operations.
  • Overflow occurs when the full integer result cannot fit within the size limits of the data type. Recognizing and handling overflow is a common challenge in systems programming.

Module 2: Floating Point

Module 2 Overview

In Module 2: Floating Point, we will explore how computers represent numbers that have fractional parts. Unlike integers, which can be represented exactly in binary, floating point numbers require an approximation scheme that trades off range, precision, and efficiency. We will study the dominant standard (IEEE 754) and also examine an alternative representation called posits.

This module contains 6 lessons:

  1. Lesson 1: Fractional Binary Numbers — How to represent fractions in binary using a radix point, and converting between binary and decimal fractions.
  2. Lesson 2: IEEE 754 Floating Point Encoding Scheme — The structure of IEEE 754: sign bit, exponent field, and fraction (mantissa) field for single and double precision.
  3. Lesson 3: Floating Point Examples — Worked examples encoding and decoding IEEE 754 floating point values, including normalized, denormalized, and special values.
  4. Lesson 4: Floating Point Rounding — The four IEEE rounding modes (round-to-even, round toward zero, round down, round up) and why round-to-even is the default.
  5. Lesson 5: Floating Point Operations — How addition, multiplication, and other operations work on floating point numbers, and the precision and overflow problems that can arise.
  6. Lesson 6: Posit Number System — An alternative to IEEE 754 developed by John Gustafson, featuring variable-length regime bits and tapered precision.

Learning Objectives

At the end of this learning module, you will be able to:

  1. Represent fractional numbers in binary using a radix point
  2. Encode and decode IEEE 754 floating point values in both single precision (32-bit) and double precision (64-bit) formats
  3. Identify and explain the three categories of IEEE 754 values: normalized, denormalized, and special values (infinity, NaN)
  4. Apply the four IEEE rounding modes and explain why round-to-even is preferred
  5. Recognize precision loss, overflow, and other problems that arise in floating point arithmetic
  6. Describe the posit number system and compare it with IEEE 754 representation

Learning Activities

You are expected to do the following tasks in order to achieve the above objectives:

  1. Read Lessons 1 through 6 and complete the embedded practice problems
  2. Read the sections below
  3. Participate in Discussion 2
  4. Take Quiz 2
  5. Complete Assignment 1 (due at the end of this module)
  6. Review additional resources on the Module 2 Summary page

Module 2: Floating Point

Lesson 1: Fractional Binary Numbers

NOTE: This is a summary of Chapter 2, sections 2.1 to 2.4 in the textbook.

Introduction

In this summary, we will look at floating point numbers. We will start by looking at how floating point is represented as binary numbers. Then, we will discuss how they are represented in computer memory. Other topics covered are rounding floating point numbers and problems encountered in doing floating point operations.

In C/C++, there are only two commonly used floating point types: float, which is 32 bit, and double, which is 64 bit. The float type is considered to be single-precision, and the double type is considered to be double-precision. Precision is how many digits there are in a floating point number; the more digits, the higher the precision.

Section 2.4.1: Fractional Binary Numbers

Fractional binary numbers have similar notation to decimal numbers. Basically, the fractional part is separated by a period:

  1011.101, 0.1101, 0.0001

the digits after the decimal point are calculated by using 1/2n in place of 2n starting at 1/2 for the first digit after the decimal. So, for the number 1011.101:

   1*23 + 0*22 + 1*21 + 1*20 + 1*1/21 + 0*1/22 + 1*1/23

   8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11
   1/2 + 0 + 1/8 = 5/8 = .625

   so 1011.101 is 11.625 in decimal

Fractional binary numbers can be represented in scientific notation the same as decimal:

   1011.101  =>  1.011101 x 23

Note that technically only the mantissa part (the digits to the left of the 23 part) is binary; the base and exponent are typically written in decimal to prevent confusion.

From Fractional Binary to Fully Decimal Number

The above isn't quite in decimal format. To go from fractional binary to full decimal, we need to convert the mantissa to decimal and then multiply by the 2 base exponent part. For example:

    1.0011 x 213
    1.0011 => 1*20 + 1*2-3 + 1*2-4 = 1.1875
    1.1875 x 213 = 9728
    9.728 x 103

Module 2: Floating Point

Lesson 2: IEEE 754 Floating Point Encoding Scheme

NOTE: This is a summary of chapter 2, sections 2.4.2 to 2.4.5 in the textbook.

IEEE 754 Floating Point Encoding Scheme

Floating Point numbers are stored in a series of bit fields where each field is a part of the bit pattern. The fields represent parts of the floating point number when written in scientific notation. An example of scientific notation would be:

  -1.1101 x 23

There are three parts of this number above that are of interest to floating point encoding:

  • minus (-):    The sign of the number.
  • 1.1101:    The significand (also known as the mantissa). This is between 1 and less than but not equal to 2 or 0 and less than but not equal to 1.
  • 3: The exponent, which can be positive or negative (or zero).

These three parts are all that need to be stored in memory in order to reproduce the floating point number.

Each of the three parts above is stored in a separate field of the bit pattern. Starting from the left-most bit:

  • 1 bit:    This is the sign bit field.
  • 8 (single) or 11 (double) bits:    This is the exponent field.
  • 23 (single) or 52 (double) bits:    This is the significand field.

The sign bit field is pretty straightforward. If the bit is 1 the number is negative; if the bit is 0 the number is positive. We will discuss the other two parts in detail below.

There are three categories (or cases) that are treated differently. These are normalized cases, which are normal numbers that are not at the smallest exponent; denormalized cases, which are normal numbers at the smallest exponent; and special cases, which are abnormal numbers, such as infinity or 'not a number.' Which case applies depends on the exponent's value. We'll describe how to determine each case in the following sections.

Normalized Cases

This section will discuss normalized cases. A normalized case is where the exponential field is neither all zeros nor all ones. These are the most common cases.

Exponent Field in Normalized Cases

The exponential field is in biased format. What this means is the actual number stored is calculated by taking the exponent of the number and adding a bias number. Keep in mind that the exponent of the number can be both positive and negative.

The bias number is chosen so that adding it to any possible exponent within the range for that field always results in a positive number. The bias can also be calculated by this formula:

 2k-1 − 1

where k is the number of bits in the exponent field.

If we take the positive range to be roughly equal to the negative range, the single-precision will have a range of −126 to +127 (exponents smaller than -126 are denormalized cases; we'll talk about this later). A bias of 127 will keep exponents within the positive range for the bit pattern, so there is no need for a signed bit for the exponent. The exponent bit field ranges from 1 to 254 for single precision.

For double precision with a range of −1022 to +1023, the bias number is 1023, and the exponent field can have a range of 1 to 2046.

Note that neither an all one pattern (255) nor an all zero pattern (0) is included. These are the other cases discussed below.

As an example, if we have an exponent of -12 for a single-precision float, the bit pattern stored in the exponent field will be equivalent to the decimal number 127 + (-12) = 115. This pattern is 01110011.

Another example: if the exponent is 120, then the bit pattern will be equivalent to the decimal value 127 + 120 = 247, which is the pattern 11110111.

An aside: Unlike two's complement, a bit pattern that is high end is positive, and one that is low end is negative. Here, the leftmost bit is 0 for negative exponents and 1 for positive exponents. A +1 exponent is 10000000, a zero exponent is 01111111, a -1 exponent is 01111110 and so on. So, the left-most bit determines the sign inversely from the sign bit for the number.

Significand in Normalized Cases

The significand field is not the straight bit pattern produced by the significand in binary. To allow for 1 bit of extra precision, the 1 in front of the decimal is ignored because, for a normalized case, it is always there. So the significand 1.0111001 for single-precision will be stored as:

   01110010000000000000000

Note that the bit pattern starts from the left-most bit and extends to the right (0's are added to the end).

So when going from bit pattern to significand, you will need to remember to put the one back in front of the number. So if we have 10001110..0, then the significand is 1.1000111.

Since the significand always has a 1 in front, the above scheme does not work with very tiny numbers or zero. The next section talks about another scheme for representing these types of numbers.

Denormalized Cases

This section will discuss denormalized cases. A denormalized case is where the exponential field is all zeros. These are numbers that are zero or very close to zero.

Zero

One denormalized case is zero. This can be two bit patterns: all 0's (positive zero) or 1 followed by 0's (negative zero). Yes, there are two zeros in this encoding scheme. If you remember, two's complement was created to get rid of the two zeros, which hardware engineers found to be a problem. However, IEEE 754 was mainly designed with numerical analysis in mind, where having two zeros is actually an asset. By allowing for positive and negative zeros, one can tell in what direction the calculations reached zero. So, what was a liability for hardware engineers is an asset for numerical analysis programmers.

If you want to know more about the decisions that led to IEEE 754, read An Interview with the Old Man of Floating-Point, a condensed version of an interview with one of the original designers of the IEEE 754 standard, William Kahan. 

Non-zero

For denormalized cases where the exponent is zero but the significand is non-zero, these represent numbers smaller than 1.0 x 2 -126 for single-precision or 1.0 x 2 -1022 for double-precision. Technically, the exponent itself is left at -126 (or -1022). In this case, the significand is interpreted as the actual significand without an implied 1. This allows for a gradual decrease to zero, known as "gradual underflow," rather than an abrupt cutoff at 1.0 x 2-126. For example, if the significand is:

   00000000000000000000001

This is interpreted as .00000000000000000000001 x 2-126 (note the lack of a leading 1). This equals 2-149, which is about 1.4 x 10-45 in decimal — this is the smallest positive value representable in single-precision (about 5 x 10-324 for double precision, which is 2-1074). Note that at these sizes, the precision is greatly reduced, and these values would be subject to serious round-off errors.

Special Cases

This section will discuss special cases. A special case is where the exponential field is all ones. There are two special cases: one case when the significand is all zeros and one where it is non-zero.

Infinity

When the significand is all zeros, the value is taken to be infinity. This is a valid number in floating point and is printed as inf in console output. It can result from a divide by zero or from overflow. This is why you don't get a divide-by-zero error with floating point numbers like you do with integers.

The sign bit can be both 1 or 0. If the sign bit is zero, we have positive infinity. If the sign bit is one, we have negative infinity.

Not a Number (NaN)

When the significand is non-zero (has at least one 1 bit in it somewhere), this is a NaN (Not a Number) result. This represents a value that is the result of an impossible calculation, such as taking the square root of a negative number. This is usually printed as NaN or nan on most systems.

There are two types of NaN's: quiet NaN and signaling NaN. The quiet NaN does not throw an exception when generated; a signaling NaN might, depending on the system state. A signaling NaN has a zero as the left-most bit but has at least one 1 in the significand (otherwise, it would be infinity). A quiet NaN has a 1 as the left-most bit. Keep in mind the significand is not a value, so the hardware will fill in the bit field with whatever information it would like to keep track of. This is hardware-dependent, so this may vary depending on the hardware architecture you are using. The above works for Intel architecture.

Module 2: Floating Point

Lesson 3: Floating Point Examples

Floating Point Examples

Here are worked floating point examples in single-precision and double-precision. These show going from the memory's bit pattern to a fractional binary number (or a special case) and vice versa. This lesson is intended as a reference you can come back to when working through problems.

Methodology: Bit Pattern to Value (Decoding)

When given a 32-bit pattern representing an IEEE 754 single-precision float, follow these steps:

  • Step 1: Identify the sign bit (bit 31, the leftmost bit). If it is 1, the number is negative; if 0, positive.
  • Step 2: Extract the 8-bit exponent field (bits 30–23). Convert it to a decimal value. If the field is neither all zeros nor all ones, compute E = exponent_field − 127 (the bias). This is the normalized case.
  • Step 3: Extract the 23-bit fraction field (bits 22–0). For a normalized number, the significand is M = 1.fraction (there is an implicit leading 1). For a denormalized number (exponent field all zeros), the significand is M = 0.fraction and the exponent is E = −126.
  • Step 4: Compute the value: value = (−1)S × M × 2E.

For special cases: if the exponent field is all ones (255), the value is either ±infinity (fraction all zeros) or NaN (fraction nonzero).

Normalized Examples: Bit Pattern to Value

Example 1: A negative normalized number

(Spaces between the fields are for clarity.)

    1 01101111 01101100000000000000000

Step 1: Sign bit = 1, so this is a negative number.

Step 2: The exponent field is 01101111. Converting: 0×128 + 1×64 + 1×32 + 0×16 + 1×8 + 1×4 + 1×2 + 1×1 = 64 + 32 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 111. (You can also use a calculator.) E = 111 − 127 = −16.

Step 3: The fraction bits are 01101100000000000000000, so the significand is M = 1.011011.

Step 4: The value is:

    −1.011011 × 2−16

Keep in mind that 2 and −16 are decimal; the significand part is in binary.

Example 2: A small positive normalized number

    0 00000001 00000000000000000000000

Step 1: Sign bit = 0, so this is positive.

Step 2: The exponent field is 00000001 = 1. E = 1 − 127 = −126. This is the smallest normalized exponent.

Step 3: The fraction bits are all zeros, so M = 1.0.

Step 4: The value is:

    +1.0 × 2−126 ≈ 1.175 × 10−38

This is the smallest positive normalized single-precision value.

Example 3: A negative number with many fraction bits

    1 10000011 10110110100000000000000

Step 1: Sign bit = 1 — negative.

Step 2: Exponent field = 10000011 = 131. E = 131 − 127 = 4.

Step 3: Fraction bits = 10110110100000000000000. The significand is M = 1.101101101.

Step 4: The fractional binary value is:

    −1.101101101 × 24

Shifting the binary point 4 places right: −11011.01101. Converting to decimal: −(16 + 8 + 2 + 1 + 0.25 + 0.125 + 0.03125) = −27.40625.

Example 4: A moderately large positive number

    0 10010100 01000000000000000000000

Step 1: Sign bit = 0 — positive.

Step 2: Exponent field = 10010100 = 148. E = 148 − 127 = 21.

Step 3: Fraction bits = 01000000000000000000000. M = 1.01.

Step 4: The value is 1.01 × 221. In decimal: 1.25 × 2,097,152 = 2,621,440.0.

Denormalized Examples

Example 5: A denormalized number

    0 00000000 01011100000000000000000

Step 1: Sign bit = 0 — positive.

Step 2: The exponent field is all zeros. This is a denormalized case. The exponent is fixed at E = −126 (not −127).

Step 3: No implicit leading 1. The significand is M = 0.01011100000000000000000 = 0.010111.

Step 4: The value is:

    +0.010111 × 2−126

This can also be written as 1.0111 × 2−128.

Example 6: Smallest positive denormalized number

    0 00000000 00000000000000000000001

Step 1: Positive. Step 2: Denormalized, E = −126. Step 3: M = 0.00000000000000000000001 = 2−23.

Step 4: Value = 2−23 × 2−126 = 2−149 ≈ 1.4 × 10−45.

This is the smallest positive value representable in single precision.

Example 7: Largest denormalized number

    0 00000000 11111111111111111111111

Step 1: Positive. Step 2: Denormalized, E = −126. Step 3: M = 0.11111111111111111111111 = 1 − 2−23.

Step 4: Value = (1 − 2−23) × 2−126 ≈ 1.175 × 10−38.

Notice this is just barely below the smallest normalized value (1.0 × 2−126), demonstrating the smooth transition between denormalized and normalized numbers. There is no gap.

Special Cases Example

Example 8: A NaN value

    0 11111111 10011100000000000000000

Step 1: Sign bit = 0. Step 2: Exponent field = 11111111 (all ones) — this is a special case.

Since the fraction field is nonzero, this is a NaN (Not a Number). Furthermore, the leftmost fraction bit is 1, making it a quiet NaN (a signaling NaN would have a 0 as the leftmost fraction bit with at least one other bit set).

Methodology: Value to Bit Pattern (Encoding)

To encode a decimal value as an IEEE 754 single-precision float:

  • Step 1: Determine the sign bit. If the number is negative, the sign bit is 1; otherwise 0. Work with the magnitude from here on.
  • Step 2: Convert the magnitude to binary scientific notation: 1.xxxx × 2E. This means expressing it as a binary number between 1 (inclusive) and 2 (exclusive) times a power of 2.
  • Step 3: Compute the exponent field = E + 127 (the bias). Verify it is between 1 and 254 (otherwise the number requires denormalization or is out of range).
  • Step 4: The fraction field is the bits after the leading 1 in the significand, padded with trailing zeros to fill 23 bits.

Encoding Examples: Value to Bit Pattern

Example 9: Encoding +1.0001 × 230

    +1.0001 × 230

Step 1: Positive, so sign bit = 0.

Step 2: Already in binary scientific notation: 1.0001 × 230.

Step 3: Exponent field = 30 + 127 = 157. In binary: 10011101.

Step 4: Drop the leading 1. Fraction field = 00010000000000000000000 (23 bits).

Assembling the fields:

    0 10011101 00010000000000000000000

Example 10: Encoding −6.5

Step 1: Negative, so sign bit = 1. Work with magnitude 6.5.

Step 2: Convert 6.5 to binary: 6 = 110, 0.5 = .1, so 6.5 = 110.1. Normalize: 1.101 × 22.

Step 3: Exponent field = 2 + 127 = 129 = 10000001 in binary.

Step 4: Fraction field = 10100000000000000000000.

Assembling:

    1 10000001 10100000000000000000000

Example 11: Encoding 0.1 (an inexact representation)

Step 1: Positive, sign bit = 0. Work with 0.1.

Step 2: Convert 0.1 to binary by repeatedly multiplying by 2:

    0.1 × 2 = 0.2  → 0
    0.2 × 2 = 0.4  → 0
    0.4 × 2 = 0.8  → 0
    0.8 × 2 = 1.6  → 1
    0.6 × 2 = 1.2  → 1
    0.2 × 2 = 0.4  → 0   (pattern repeats: 0011 repeating)

So 0.1 in binary is 0.00011 (the 0011 pattern repeats infinitely). This means 0.1 cannot be represented exactly in binary floating point. Normalizing: 1.1001100110011... × 2−4.

Step 3: Exponent field = −4 + 127 = 123 = 01111011.

Step 4: Fraction field = 10011001100110011001101 (23 bits, rounded at the end).

    0 01111011 10011001100110011001101

The stored value is approximately 0.100000001490116..., not exactly 0.1. This is a fundamental limitation of binary floating point and the root cause of many surprising rounding behaviors in programs.

Example 12: Encoding a very small denormalized number

Suppose we want to encode the value 2−140.

Step 1: Positive, sign bit = 0.

Step 2: The value is 1.0 × 2−140. But E = −140 is below the minimum normalized exponent of −126, so this requires denormalization.

Step 3: For a denormalized number, the exponent field is all zeros, and E is fixed at −126. We must express the value as M × 2−126 where M = 0.fraction. Since 2−140 = 2−14 × 2−126, the significand is 0.00000000000001 (a 1 in the 14th bit position).

Step 4: Fraction field = 00000000000001000000000.

    0 00000000 00000000000001000000000

Note the reduced precision: the fraction only has 23 − 14 = 9 significant bits remaining for any additional detail.

Double Precision Examples

Double precision works the same way but with an 11-bit exponent (bias = 1023) and 52-bit fraction. There are 64 bits total: 1 sign + 11 exponent + 52 fraction.

Example 13: Decoding a double-precision bit pattern

    0 10000000011 1011000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000

Step 1: Sign bit = 0 — positive.

Step 2: Exponent field = 10000000011 = 1027. E = 1027 − 1023 = 4.

Step 3: Fraction begins with 1011, the rest are zeros. M = 1.1011.

Step 4: Value = 1.1011 × 24 = 11011.0 in binary = 16 + 8 + 2 + 1 = 27.0.

Example 14: Encoding −0.75 in double precision

Step 1: Negative, sign bit = 1. Magnitude = 0.75.

Step 2: 0.75 = 0.11 in binary = 1.1 × 2−1.

Step 3: Exponent field = −1 + 1023 = 1022 = 01111111110 (11 bits).

Step 4: Fraction = 1000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000 (52 bits, only the first bit is 1).

    1 01111111110 1000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000

Special Values Reference Table

The following table summarizes the special bit patterns in single precision:

    Value   Sign  Exponent     Fraction
    -----   ----  --------     --------
    +0       0    00000000     00000000000000000000000
    −0       1    00000000     00000000000000000000000
    +∞       0    11111111     00000000000000000000000
    −∞       1    11111111     00000000000000000000000
    NaN      x    11111111     (any nonzero fraction)

Here x means the sign bit can be either 0 or 1. For NaN, if the leading fraction bit is 1, it is a quiet NaN; if 0 (with at least one other fraction bit set), it is a signaling NaN.

Module 2: Floating Point

Lesson 4: Floating Point Rounding

Consider a single precision 32-bit IEEE-754 floating-point number. With 32 bits available, we have 232 possible bit configurations. Think of these 232 bit configurations as "breadcrumbs" that can be placed on the real number line from -∞ to +∞. We can view the IEEE-754 floating-point standard as a system for placing those "breadcrumbs" on the real number line.

(Note that the breadcrumbs are not actually evenly spaced, as this diagram might suggest. The IEEE-754 standard places breadcrumbs that are closer to zero closer together and breadcrumbs that are further from zero further apart.)

Any floating-point calculation is likely to produce a result that, mathematically speaking, would want to fall between two adjacent breadcrumbs. However, the computer can only produce results consisting of bit configurations, so it will have to choose one of the two breadcrumbs that surround the mathematical result. Because of this, the results produced by the computer will almost always be mathematically wrong (for this not to be the case, the mathematical result would have to land exactly on top of a breadcrumb), and this difference between the mathematical result and what the computer can actually produce is referred to as roundoff error.

In fact, IEEE 754 requires that the hardware compute the correctly rounded result. Internally, the floating-point unit uses extra precision bits (called guard, round, and sticky bits) to determine which breadcrumb is closest to the exact mathematical result, even though the exact result itself is not representable. The default rounding mode always picks the nearest breadcrumb. But there are situations where the mathematical result falls exactly halfway between two breadcrumbs, and the hardware needs a tie-breaking rule. This is where different rounding modes come in.

The floating-point unit supports four rounding modes:

  • towards +∞: always pick the breadcrumb that is closest to +∞

  • towards -∞: always pick the breadcrumb that is closest to -∞

  • towards 0: always pick the breadcrumb that is closest to 0

  • towards even (default): pick the nearest breadcrumb; when exactly at the midpoint, pick the breadcrumb whose rightmost bit is 0

The towards even rounding mode is the default. Some explanation of it is necessary here. As you go along the number line in either direction, breadcrumbs whose rightmost bit is 0 always alternate with breadcrumbs whose rightmost bit is 1.

Therefore, any mathematical result will always fall between a breadcrumb whose rightmost bit is 0 and one whose rightmost bit is 1. The idea behind this rounding mode is that sometimes a mathematical result will be rounded up towards +∞ and sometimes down towards −∞. The hope is that upwards and downwards roundoff errors will cancel each other out, producing a more accurate result. Clearly, this is only a hope, and that hope may not always come true.

Concrete Rounding Examples in Decimal

Before looking at binary, let us build intuition by rounding decimal numbers to one decimal place. Suppose the exact result of some computation is 2.35 and we must round to one decimal place. The two nearest representable values are 2.3 and 2.4, and 2.35 falls exactly at the midpoint.

  • Toward +∞: 2.4 (round up toward positive infinity)
  • Toward −∞: 2.3 (round down toward negative infinity)
  • Toward 0: 2.3 (round toward zero, which is downward for a positive number)
  • Toward even: 2.4 (the digit in the last kept place would be 4, which is even)

Now consider 2.45 rounded to one decimal place. The two nearest values are 2.4 and 2.5, and 2.45 is exactly at the midpoint.

  • Toward +∞: 2.5
  • Toward −∞: 2.4
  • Toward 0: 2.4
  • Toward even: 2.4 (the digit in the last kept place is 4, which is even — so we round down)

Notice that round-to-even only differs from the other modes when the value is exactly at the midpoint between two representable values. When the value is clearly closer to one side, all four modes agree (except toward +∞ and toward −∞ may differ in direction).

Binary Rounding Examples

Now let us look at rounding in binary, which is what the hardware actually does. Suppose our floating point format has 3 fraction bits (so the significand looks like 1.xxx). We need to round values that have more than 3 fraction bits down to exactly 3.

Below the midpoint: round down

Consider the value 1.00101. This falls between the representable values 1.001 and 1.010. The dropped bits are 01, which is below the midpoint (the midpoint would be 10). All rounding modes round toward the closer value:

    1.00101 → 1.001   (rounded down; the dropped bits 01 are below the midpoint)

Above the midpoint: round up

Consider the value 1.00111. Again between 1.001 and 1.010. The dropped bits are 11, which is above the midpoint. All modes round toward the closer value:

    1.00111 → 1.010   (rounded up; the dropped bits 11 are above the midpoint)

Exactly at the midpoint: round-to-even decides
