Consider the value 1.00110. The dropped bits are 10, which is exactly the midpoint between 1.001 and 1.010. Now round-to-even looks at the last kept bit:

    1.001|10  →  last kept bit is 1 (odd), so round up to make it 0 (even)
    Result: 1.010

Now consider 1.01010. This is exactly at the midpoint between 1.010 and 1.011. The dropped bits are 10:

    1.010|10  →  last kept bit is 0 (even), so round down to keep it even
    Result: 1.010

In both midpoint cases, round-to-even chose the result whose last fraction bit is 0. This is the key rule: at an exact midpoint, choose the value whose least significant kept bit is 0.

Guard, Round, and Sticky Bits

When the floating point hardware computes an arithmetic result (such as an addition or multiplication), the exact result typically has more bits than fit in the fraction field. The hardware cannot keep all of these extra bits, but it keeps three extra bits beyond the fraction field to determine the correct rounding direction:

  • Guard bit (G): the first bit beyond the fraction field
  • Round bit (R): the second bit beyond the fraction field
  • Sticky bit (S): the logical OR of all remaining bits beyond the round bit

The sticky bit is crucial: it tells us whether there is any nonzero information beyond the first two extra bits, without needing to store all those bits individually.

These three bits determine the rounding direction under round-to-even:

    GRS = 0xx  →  below midpoint  →  round down (truncate)
    GRS = 100  →  exactly at midpoint  →  round to even
    GRS = 101, 110, or 111  →  above midpoint  →  round up

Example: Adding with guard, round, and sticky bits

Suppose we have a 3-fraction-bit system and want to compute 1.001 + 0.0101. First, align the exponents by shifting the smaller number right:

      1.001  (this is 1.001 × 20)
    + 0.0101 (this is 1.01 × 2−2, shifted right by 2)
    --------
      1.0111

The exact result is 1.0111. With 3 fraction bits, we keep 1.011 and the extra bits are: G=1, R=0, S=0. This is GRS = 100 — exactly at the midpoint. The last kept bit is 1 (odd), so round-to-even rounds up:

    1.011 + 0.001 = 1.100

The correctly rounded result is 1.100.

Why Round-to-Even Is the Default

Consider what happens if we always round up at the midpoint (as many people learn in grade school). Over many operations, every midpoint case adds a small positive error. These errors accumulate, introducing a systematic upward bias. After thousands of operations, the result can be significantly too high.

Similarly, always rounding toward zero introduces a systematic bias that makes positive results too small and negative results too large (in magnitude, too small).

Round-to-even is statistically unbiased: at midpoint cases, it rounds up half the time (when the last kept bit is odd) and rounds down half the time (when the last kept bit is already even). Over many operations, the positive and negative rounding errors tend to cancel out, producing more accurate accumulated results. This is why IEEE 754 chose it as the default.

The other three modes — toward +∞, toward −∞, and toward 0 — still exist because they are useful for interval arithmetic, where a programmer computes both an upper bound (rounding toward +∞) and a lower bound (rounding toward −∞) to determine the range of possible results. This technique is used in scientific computing to rigorously bound the error in a computation. In C, the rounding mode can be changed at runtime using the fesetround() function from <fenv.h>.

Practical Impact: Accumulated Rounding Error

Here is a simple C program that demonstrates how rounding errors accumulate:

    float sum = 0.0f;
    for (int i = 0; i < 10000000; i++) {
        sum += 0.1f;
    }
    printf("Expected: 1000000.0, Got: %f\n", sum);

The output will not be 1000000.0. It will be something like 1000000.125 or a similar value, depending on the system. The reason is twofold: first, 0.1 cannot be represented exactly in binary (as we saw in Lesson 3), so every addition introduces a small error; second, as sum grows large, the small value 0.1f loses more and more of its significant bits when aligned to sum's exponent, compounding the error.

This is not a bug in the hardware — it is the inevitable consequence of finite precision arithmetic. Understanding rounding is essential for writing software that produces reliable numerical results.

Computers must necessarily represent numbers as bits. But bits are not numbers, and getting bits to act like numbers cannot be perfectly accomplished. Computer scientists have gotten close, but perfection is impossible. It's necessary for any competent programmer to understand the ways in which bits do not act like numbers and to make sure that this does not cause incorrect results in the software they write.

Module 2: Floating Point

Lesson 5: Floating Point Operations

Floating Point Operations

Floating point operations suffer from two problems: loss of precision and overflow. Loss of precision is usually caused by rounding, and overflow is caused by the exponent being out of the range for the floating point type used.

Loss of precision when rounding on floating point numbers creates a peculiar behavior compared to integers. It almost seems like the results are breaking some mathematical laws. But keep in mind that mathematical laws assume infinite precision, whereas a computer has only finite precision.

How Floating Point Addition Works Internally

To understand why precision loss happens, it helps to know what the hardware actually does when it adds two floats. The process has four steps:

  • Step 1: Align the exponents. The number with the smaller exponent has its significand shifted right until both numbers share the same exponent. Bits shifted off the right end are lost (though the guard, round, and sticky bits from Lesson 4 capture some of this).
  • Step 2: Add the significands. With both numbers now aligned to the same exponent, the hardware adds (or subtracts) the significands as fixed-point numbers.
  • Step 3: Normalize the result. If the result is not in the form 1.xxxx × 2E, the hardware shifts the significand and adjusts the exponent.
  • Step 4: Round. The result is rounded to fit the fraction field, using the rounding mode (typically round-to-even).

The alignment step (Step 1) is where precision gets lost: when you add a large and small number, the small number's significant bits get shifted off the right end. This is the root cause of non-associativity.

Non-Associativity of Addition

For exact real-number arithmetic, addition and multiplication are commutative and associative. Floating point arithmetic is commutative for addition in typical cases, but not always associative because intermediate rounding changes results. For example, two expressions below should give the same answer mathematically, but due to how rounding works, they don't (NOTE: 1e10 is the C format for 1 × 1010):

    (3.14 + 1e10) - 1e10  = 0.0
     3.14 + (1e10 - 1e10) = 3.14

For the first expression, 3.14 is much smaller than 1 × 1010 so the bits that represent 3.14 are effectively rounded out of existence during the alignment step. Then, the resulting 1 × 1010 is subtracted from itself to give 0. In the second expression, we are doing the subtraction first to get 0 and adding this to 3.14 to get 3.14.

More Precision Loss Examples

Small values vanishing entirely

In single precision, the significand has 23 fraction bits, giving about 7 decimal digits of precision. If two numbers differ by more than about a factor of 224 (≈ 1.7 × 107), the smaller number's bits are completely shifted away during alignment:

    float a = 1.0f;
    float b = 1.0e-8f;
    printf("%d\n", (a + b) == a);   // prints 1 (true!)

The value 1.0e-8 is so much smaller than 1.0 that adding it to 1.0 produces exactly 1.0 in single precision. The small value is below the precision threshold — it has no effect whatsoever.

Summation order matters

When summing a large array of small numbers, the order of addition matters. If you accumulate into a large running sum, each small number may lose precision when aligned to the sum's exponent. A better strategy is to sort the numbers by magnitude and sum from smallest to largest, or to use pairwise summation or Kahan summation (a technique that tracks the lost low-order bits in a separate compensation variable).

    // Naive summation: small values may be lost as sum grows large
    float sum = 0.0f;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        sum += small_values[i];

    // Better: sort ascending so small values are added to other small values first
    sort(small_values, n);   // ascending order
    float sum = 0.0f;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        sum += small_values[i];

Overflow

Multiplication can behave well except in cases where overflow occurs during the calculations. Overflow for floating point is when a result is beyond the range of an exponent for that type. For single precision, this is a number larger than about 2128 (or about 3.4 × 1038). For double precision, this is about 21024 (or about 1.8 × 10308).

When an intermediate operation overflows, that operation produces infinity (and raises the overflow flag), and subsequent operations continue using that infinity. So the expression (1e20*1e20)*1e-20 ends up +inf but the expression 1e20*(1e20*1e-20) ends up being 1e20.

Underflow

Underflow is the opposite problem: a result is too small to represent as a normalized number. When this happens, the result enters the denormalized range, where it gradually loses precision (fewer and fewer significant bits). Eventually, if the result becomes smaller than the smallest denormalized value, it rounds to zero.

    float x = 1.0e-38f;
    printf("x       = %e\n", x);           // normalized
    printf("x/2     = %e\n", x / 2);       // denormalized, losing precision
    printf("x/256   = %e\n", x / 256);     // denormalized, fewer significant bits
    printf("x/2^50  = %e\n", x * powf(2, -50));  // underflows to 0.0

The gradual transition through denormalized numbers (rather than an abrupt jump to zero) is one of the important design features of IEEE 754. It ensures that a - b == 0 if and only if a == b, even for very small values.

Multiplication and Precision

Multiplication can also lose precision, though it is usually less dramatic than addition of differently-scaled numbers. When you multiply two significands that each have 23 fraction bits, the exact product has up to 46 fraction bits. This must be rounded back to 23 bits. However, since both operands contribute proportionally to the result, you do not lose entire operands the way you can with addition — the relative error from rounding a multiplication is at most one unit in the last place (1 ulp).

Floating Point Comparison Pitfalls

Due to rounding, two computations that should give the same result mathematically often produce slightly different floating point values. This makes direct equality comparison unreliable:

    // BAD: may fail even when a and b are "equal" up to rounding
    if (a == b) { ... }

    // BETTER: use an epsilon-based comparison
    if (fabs(a - b) < 1e-6) { ... }

The appropriate value of epsilon depends on the magnitude of the values being compared and the precision requirements of the application. For single-precision floats, an epsilon of around 1e-6 to 1e-7 is common for values near 1.0. For values that may be much larger or smaller, a relative epsilon is more appropriate:

    // Relative comparison
    if (fabs(a - b) < epsilon * fabs(a)) { ... }

Never use == to compare floating point results unless you have a specific reason to believe the values are exactly equal (for example, when comparing against 0.0 for a value you explicitly set to 0.0).

IEEE 754 Correctness Guarantee

Despite all these precision issues, IEEE 754 provides a very strong guarantee: every basic arithmetic operation (+, −, ×, ÷, and square root) must produce the correctly rounded result. This means the hardware must compute the result as if the operation were performed with infinite precision and then rounded to the target format using the current rounding mode.

This guarantee makes floating point arithmetic deterministic: the same inputs will always produce the same output on any compliant hardware. The rounding errors are not random — they are completely predictable and reproducible. This is what makes it possible to reason about and bound the errors in floating point computations.

Rounding and overflow are problems that need to be addressed when doing numerical analysis in programs. There is actually a whole branch of computational science on mitigating these problems in code that the textbook doesn't go into.

Floating Point Typecasting

Typecasting between floating point types and between floating point and integers has problems stemming from both overflow and rounding. This is discussed below:

  • int to float: There's no overflow possible, but since the significand is smaller than the integer's bit pattern (23 vs 32 bits), the integer number may be rounded to another integer number. I should point out that some integers can't be represented exactly in floating point representation. For example: 
        int n = 123456789;
    float f = (float)n;
    printf("%f\n", f);   // prints 123456792.000000

    The value 123456789 requires 27 significant bits, but a float only has 24 bits of significand (23 fraction + 1 implicit). So the value is rounded to the nearest representable float, which is 123456792.

  • int or float to double: Because of the greater range and precision (32 vs. 52 bits for the significand), an integer can be represented exactly in a double (but see below for why you may not want to use a double to represent integer-only values). A float likewise can fit into a double. In fact, many programmers use only doubles for floating point if there's no good reason to do otherwise (such as saving memory space or a library needs floats).
  • double to float: The value can overflow to + or - infinity since the range is smaller. Also, it may be rounded to zero because the precision is smaller. So doing this is not a very desirable thing to do unless it can't be helped. Sometimes, third-party libraries force programmers to use floats.
  • float or double to int: The value will be rounded toward zero. This is called truncation since it just cuts off the decimal part without any rounding being done. This may not be very desirable. For example: 
        printf("%d\n", (int)3.9f);    // prints 3 (truncated toward zero)
    printf("%d\n", (int)(-3.9f)); // prints -3 (truncated toward zero)

    Furthermore, when going from a double to an int, the value may overflow. Casting a value outside the range of int (such as (int)1e20f) is undefined behavior in C — the result is unpredictable and the program may crash or produce garbage.

Although it might be okay to represent integer-only values as doubles, there is a downside to this. Floating point circuitry is very complex and known to be much slower than integer circuitry, so there might be a performance hit. To increase range, you can use unsigned versions of int for twice the range, or you can use a long, which gives you 64-bit range in signed. This represents all positive integers up to about 9×1018. Unsigned long will increase this to about 1×1019. Also, depending on the version of C and compiler you are using, there might be even larger integer types, but these might not be portable to other compilers.

The biggest benefit is that all integers are represented between the maximum and minimum in an integer type. Floating point types have 'gaps' where some integers can't be represented. Just because the range on a double is roughly 10308 doesn't mean every integer in that range is representable. A double can represent every integer exactly only up to 253 in magnitude (about 9×1015); beyond that, representable values skip integers. So do use an integer type for integers whenever possible; it is better suited for integers than floating point (unless greater range is imperative and having gaps in representation is acceptable).

Module 2: Floating Point

Lesson 6: The Posit Number System

Introduction: Why Posits?

Throughout this module we have studied IEEE 754, the standard that has dominated floating point arithmetic since 1985. While IEEE 754 is enormously successful, it has well-known limitations:

  • Wasted bit patterns: IEEE 754 dedicates many bit patterns to NaN values. For 32-bit floats, there are over 16 million distinct NaN encodings — bit patterns that all mean the same thing ("not a number"). Those bit patterns could instead represent useful numeric values.
  • Uniform precision distribution: IEEE 754 distributes its precision roughly uniformly across all exponent ranges. However, in practice most computations involve values near 1.0, where more precision would be most useful.
  • Inconsistent special cases: Signed zeros (+0 and -0), multiple NaN values, and denormalized numbers add complexity to both hardware and software.

In 2017, computer scientist John L. Gustafson proposed an alternative called the posit number system. Posits are designed to deliver better accuracy for the same number of bits, eliminate redundant representations, and simplify the special-case logic that IEEE 754 requires.

Posit Format: Posit<n, es>

A posit is characterized by two parameters:

  • n — the total number of bits
  • es — the maximum number of exponent bits

We write this as Posit<n, es>. For example, Posit<8, 2> is an 8-bit posit with up to 2 exponent bits.

A posit number is divided into four fields, read left to right:

  | sign | regime | exponent | fraction |
  |  1   | variable | 0 to es | remaining bits |

The key innovation is the variable-length regime field. Because the regime can expand or shrink, the exponent and fraction fields adjust in size accordingly. This gives posits their characteristic tapered precision: values near 1.0 get a short regime, leaving more bits for the exponent and fraction (high precision), while very large or very small values get a long regime, consuming bits that would otherwise go to the fraction (lower precision, but greater range).

The Sign Bit

The leading bit is the sign bit, just like IEEE 754:

  • 0 = positive (or zero)
  • 1 = negative

However, unlike IEEE 754 where the sign bit is simply a flag, in posits a negative value is stored as the two's complement of its positive encoding. So to decode a negative posit, you first take the two's complement of the entire bit string to get the positive version, then decode that, and finally negate the result.

The Regime Field

The regime is a variable-length field that immediately follows the sign bit. It consists of a run of identical bits terminated by the opposite bit (or by the end of the number if no opposite bit fits).

There are two cases:

  • A run of 1s terminated by a 0 (or end of number): If the run contains k ones, the regime value is k - 1.
  • A run of 0s terminated by a 1 (or end of number): If the run contains k zeros, the regime value is -k.

Examples of regime fields and their values:

  Regime bits    Run length    Regime value
  -----------------------------------------
  0001           3 zeros       -3
  001            2 zeros       -2
  01             1 zero        -1
  10             1 one          0
  110            2 ones         1
  1110           3 ones         2
  11110          4 ones         3

Note that the terminating bit (the opposite bit) is part of the regime field but is not counted in the run length. If the run extends to the end of the number with no terminating bit, we simply count all the identical bits.

The Useed Value

The regime field contributes a factor of useed raised to the regime value. The useed is defined as:

  useed = 2^(2^es)

For different values of es:

  es = 0:  useed = 2^(2^0) = 2^1  = 2
  es = 1:  useed = 2^(2^1) = 2^2  = 4
  es = 2:  useed = 2^(2^2) = 2^4  = 16
  es = 3:  useed = 2^(2^3) = 2^8  = 256

The useed acts as a "super-exponent" that allows posits to cover a huge dynamic range. With es = 2, each step of the regime multiplies or divides the value by 16.

The Exponent Field

After the regime (and its terminating bit), the next es bits form the exponent field. If fewer than es bits remain in the number, the exponent is padded with trailing zeros on the right. The exponent is interpreted as an unsigned integer e, and it contributes a factor of 2^e to the value.

The Fraction Field

Any remaining bits after the exponent form the fraction field. Just like IEEE 754 normalized values, there is an implicit leading 1. So if the fraction bits are fff...f, the fraction value is 1.fff...f in binary. If there are no fraction bits remaining, the fraction value is simply 1.0.

Putting It All Together

The value of a positive posit is:

  value = useed^regime  *  2^exponent  *  (1 + fraction)

Or equivalently, since useed = 2^(2^es):

  value = 2^(regime * 2^es + exponent)  *  (1 + fraction)

For a negative posit, take the two's complement first, decode as above, then negate.

Special Values

Posits have exactly two special bit patterns:

  • Zero: all bits are 0. For example, in Posit<8, 2>: 0000 0000 = 0.
  • NaR (Not a Real): only the sign bit is 1, all other bits are 0. For example, in Posit<8, 2>: 1000 0000 = NaR.

There is no positive or negative infinity, no signed zero, and no NaN. The single NaR value replaces all of these. This is a deliberate design choice: instead of silently propagating NaN through a long computation, any undefined operation produces NaR, which is a single, unambiguous value.

Worked Example 1: Decoding a Posit<8, 2> Value

Let us decode the Posit<8, 2> bit pattern 0 110 01 10 step by step.

Step 1: Identify the sign bit

  Bit pattern:  0  110  01  10
                ^
  Sign bit = 0  -->  positive

Step 2: Extract the regime

  Remaining bits:  1 1 0 0 1 1 0
                   ^^^^^
  We read from the left: 1, 1, 0
  This is a run of two 1s terminated by a 0.

  Run length k = 2
  Regime value  = k - 1 = 2 - 1 = 1

  The regime field consumed 3 bits: "110"

Step 3: Extract the exponent

  Remaining bits after regime:  0 1 1 0
  es = 2, so we take the next 2 bits: "01"

  Exponent (unsigned) = 01 in binary = 1

Step 4: Extract the fraction

  Remaining bits after exponent:  1 0
  Fraction bits = "10"

  Fraction value = 1.10 in binary = 1 + 0.5 = 1.5
  (Remember the implicit leading 1)

Step 5: Compute the value

  Parameters:
    es = 2
    useed = 2^(2^2) = 2^4 = 16
    regime value = 1
    exponent = 1
    fraction = 1.5

  value = useed^regime  *  2^exponent  *  fraction
        = 16^1          *  2^1          *  1.5
        = 16             *  2            *  1.5
        = 48

  The Posit<8, 2> bit pattern 0 110 01 10 represents the value 48.

Worked Example 2: Encoding a Decimal Value as Posit<8, 2>

Let us encode the decimal value -3.5 as a Posit<8, 2>.

Step 1: Handle the sign

  The value is negative, so:
    sign bit = 1
  We will encode the magnitude 3.5 first, then take the two's complement.

Step 2: Determine the regime

  We need:  useed^regime * 2^exponent * fraction = 3.5
  With es = 2, useed = 16.

  Try regime = 0:
    useed^0 = 16^0 = 1
    So we need:  2^exponent * fraction = 3.5
    Since exponent can be 0..3 (2 bits), and fraction >= 1.0:
      With exponent = 1: 2^1 * fraction = 3.5  -->  fraction = 1.75
      fraction = 1.75 = 1.11 in binary. This works!

  Regime value = 0 --> regime bits = "10" (one 1, terminated by 0)

Step 3: Encode the exponent

  Exponent = 1 = "01" in binary (2 bits since es = 2)

Step 4: Encode the fraction

  Fraction = 1.75
  Remove the implicit leading 1:  0.75 = 0.11 in binary
  Fraction bits = "11"

  Remaining bits for fraction: 8 - 1(sign) - 2(regime) - 2(exponent) = 3 bits
  We have 2 fraction bits, padded to fill: "110"
  (The third bit is 0 since there are no further fractional bits.)

Step 5: Assemble the positive encoding

  sign  regime  exponent  fraction
    0     10      01        110

  Positive encoding: 0 10 01 110 --> wait, that's 9 bits!

  Let's recount. We have 8 bits total:
    1 sign + 2 regime + 2 exponent + 3 fraction = 8 bits.

  Positive encoding:  0  10  01  110
  As 8 bits:          01001110

Step 6: Apply two's complement for the negative value

  Positive encoding:   01001110
  Bitwise complement:  10110001
  Add 1:             + 00000001
                     ----------
  Two's complement:    10110010

  So Posit<8, 2> encoding of -3.5 is:  10110010

Step 7: Verify

  Start with:  10110010
  Sign bit = 1 --> negative. Take two's complement:
    Complement:  01001101
    Add 1:       01001110
  Now decode 01001110:
    Sign = 0 (positive)
    Regime: "10" --> one 1, terminated by 0 --> regime = 0
    Exponent: "01" --> e = 1
    Fraction: "110" --> 1.110 in binary = 1 + 0.5 + 0.25 = 1.75
    Value = 16^0 * 2^1 * 1.75 = 1 * 2 * 1.75 = 3.5
    Negate: -3.5.  Correct!

Comparison with IEEE 754

Here is a side-by-side comparison of the key differences between IEEE 754 and posits:

Property IEEE 754 Posit<n, es>
Field structure Fixed-size sign, exponent, fraction Fixed sign, variable-length regime, then exponent, then fraction
Special values +0, -0, +Inf, -Inf, NaN (millions of bit patterns) Only two: 0 (all zeros) and NaR (sign bit only)
Precision distribution Roughly uniform across all exponent ranges Tapered: highest precision near 1.0, less at extremes
Wasted bit patterns Many (all the distinct NaN encodings) None — every bit pattern except 0 and NaR represents a unique real number
Signed zero Yes (+0 and -0 are distinct) No — there is exactly one zero
Denormalized numbers Yes (gradual underflow) Not needed — the regime provides smooth scaling near zero
Dynamic range (for same bit width) Large Can be larger, depending on es
Hardware support Universal — supported by all modern CPUs and GPUs Limited — experimental hardware and software implementations

Precision Near 1.0

One of the most cited advantages of posits is their accuracy for values near 1.0. When a value is close to 1.0, the regime is short (just "10" for regime value 0), leaving the maximum number of bits for the exponent and fraction. This is exactly the range where most everyday computations concentrate, which means posits tend to produce more accurate results than IEEE 754 floats of the same bit width for typical workloads.

No Wasted Bit Patterns

In IEEE 754 single precision, the exponent field 11111111 with a nonzero fraction encodes NaN. Since the fraction has 23 bits, there are 2^23 - 1 = 8,388,607 distinct NaN patterns for positive NaN and the same for negative NaN, totaling over 16 million wasted bit patterns. In posits, every single bit pattern (except 0 and NaR) maps to a distinct real number. No bits are wasted.

Limitations of Posits

Despite their advantages, posits are not yet a replacement for IEEE 754 in practice:

  • Hardware support: IEEE 754 is implemented in every modern CPU, GPU, and DSP. Posit hardware is still in the research and prototype stage. Software emulation of posits is much slower than native IEEE 754 operations.
  • Variable-length fields: The variable-length regime makes hardware design more complex. Extracting the regime requires a leading-zero or leading-one count, and the shifting logic to separate the exponent and fraction fields adds latency.
  • Ecosystem and tooling: Decades of libraries, compilers, debugging tools, and numerical analysis have been built around IEEE 754. The posit ecosystem is still in its early stages.
  • Tapered precision is a trade-off: While posits give more precision near 1.0, they give less precision for very large or very small values. Applications that need uniform precision across a wide range may not benefit.
  • No infinity: IEEE 754's infinity values can be useful for signaling overflow in a controlled way. Posits use NaR instead, which is less granular (you cannot distinguish overflow from an undefined operation).

Summary

The posit number system represents a thoughtful rethinking of how computers can represent real numbers. By introducing variable-length regime bits, posits achieve tapered precision that concentrates accuracy where it matters most. They eliminate the wasted bit patterns and inconsistent special cases of IEEE 754. However, the lack of hardware support and the maturity of the IEEE 754 ecosystem mean that posits remain primarily a research topic for now. Understanding posits gives us a deeper appreciation of the design trade-offs in numeric representation and prepares us to evaluate future developments in computer arithmetic.

Module 2: Floating Point

Module 2 Summary

Wrap Up

In this module we studied floating point representation — how computers store and manipulate numbers that have fractional parts. We began with fractional binary numbers and built up to the full IEEE 754 encoding scheme, examining how sign, exponent, and fraction fields work together to represent an enormous range of values. We explored rounding modes and the arithmetic pitfalls that arise from finite precision. Finally, we looked at the posit number system as a modern alternative to IEEE 754.

Key Takeaways

  • Fractional binary numbers use a radix point, with bit positions to the right representing negative powers of 2 (1/2, 1/4, 1/8, etc.).
  • IEEE 754 is the dominant standard for floating point. A value is encoded using three fields: a sign bit, a biased exponent, and a fractional mantissa with an implicit leading 1 (for normalized values).
  • Special values in IEEE 754 include positive/negative infinity (exponent all 1s, fraction all 0s) and NaN (exponent all 1s, fraction nonzero). Denormalized numbers (exponent all 0s) allow representation of values very close to zero.
  • Rounding is unavoidable because most real numbers cannot be represented exactly. The default mode, round-to-even, minimizes statistical bias over many operations.
  • Precision loss is a fundamental limitation: floating point addition is not associative, and small numbers added to large numbers may be lost entirely. Overflow and underflow are also concerns.
  • Posits (Posit<n, es>) offer an alternative to IEEE 754 with variable-length regime bits, tapered precision (more precision near 1.0, less at extremes), no NaN, no wasted bit patterns, and a single special value (NaR) for undefined results.

Additional Resources

Floating Point (Video Lecture from Carnegie Mellon University)

PositHub — Resources and community for the posit number system

Beating Floating Point at its Own Game: Posit Arithmetic — John Gustafson's paper introducing posits

Module 3: x86-64 Assembly Fundamentals

Module 3 Overview

In Module 3: x86-64 Assembly Fundamentals, you will learn to write x86-64 assembly programs by hand. This is something that most students have not encountered in their previous programming experience, and it is one of the most important topics in computer systems.

We start by examining the build process and writing your first assembly program using the GNU tools as and ld. From there, we cover registers, data movement and addressing modes, the data section and labels, arithmetic operations, logical and shift operations, stack operations, and the Linux syscall interface for bare read, write, and exit. Each topic follows a "write it by hand first, then see how gcc does it" approach: you write a working assembly program, then compare it with gcc -S output to understand what the compiler generates.

Learning objectives

At the end of this learning module, you will be able to:

  1. Describe the four-stage build process and the role of the compiler, assembler, and linker
  2. Use as and ld to assemble and link hand-written assembly programs
  3. Write Makefiles to automate the assembly and linking of single-file and multi-file projects
  4. Use gcc -S and objdump -d to examine compiler-generated assembly
  5. Identify x86-64 registers, their sub-register names, and their typical roles
  6. Write programs that use the .data, .rodata, and .bss sections with RIP-relative addressing
  7. Use the mov and lea instructions with all addressing modes
  8. Write programs using arithmetic instructions (add, sub, imul, idiv) and logical/shift instructions
  9. Use push, pop, and manual stack manipulation for temporary storage
  10. Use the Linux x86-64 syscall convention to perform bare read, write, and exit operations
  11. Write a complete assembly program that reads input, computes a result, and prints output

Learning activities

You are expected to do the following tasks in order to achieve the above objectives:

  1. Complete the reading listed below
  2. Read Lessons 1 to 10, work through the hand-written assembly examples, and complete the embedded practice problems
  3. Take the module quiz
  4. Review additional resources on the Module 3 Summary page

Reading

  • Bryant & O'Hallaron: Chapter 3, sections 3.1 - 3.5
  • Dive into Systems: Chapters 6 & 7
  • Course _start Assembly Syntax Reference

If you have questions, you can post them in the course lobby or send your instructor an email.

Module 3: x86-64 Assembly Fundamentals

Lesson 1: The Build Process and Your First Assembly Program

From Source Code to Executable

The term "building" software is often used interchangeably with compiling, as in "compile and run your code." But compiling is actually just one step in a four-stage pipeline. Understanding each stage matters because in this module you will work with these stages individually.

  • Stage 1: Preprocessing — A preprocessor handles directives (lines starting with #). For #include, the contents of the header file are pasted into the source. For #define, the symbol is substituted throughout the file.
  • Stage 2: Compiling — The compiler translates preprocessed C into assembly code, a human-readable representation of machine instructions. This stage does the heavy lifting: parsing, type-checking, and optimizing. If you stop here with gcc -S, you get a .s text file for each .c file.
  • Stage 3: Assembling — The assembler (as) converts the .s file into an object file (.o). This is nearly machine code but with some unresolved references. Stop here with gcc -c.
  • Stage 4: Linking — The linker (ld) combines all .o files plus library code into a final executable containing pure machine code.

Two Paths to an Executable

With gcc, all four stages happen behind the scenes in a single command:

$ gcc -o myprogram myprogram.c

But there is another path — the one we will use for the rest of this module. You write assembly by hand in a .s file, then use the assembler and linker directly:

$ as -o myprogram.o myprogram.s
$ ld -o myprogram myprogram.o

The as command assembles your .s file into an object file. The ld command links it into a runnable executable. No compiler involved — you are the compiler.

Your First Assembly Program

Here is the smallest possible x86-64 Linux program. It does nothing but exit with a status code:

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        mov $60, %rax
        mov $42, %rdi
        syscall

Let's break this down line by line:

  • .text — This directive tells the assembler that what follows is executable code.
  • .global _start — This makes the label _start visible to the linker. The linker needs to know where your program begins, and by convention that label is _start.
  • _start: — A label. It marks a location in the code that can be referred to by name.
  • mov $60, %rax — Load the value 60 into register %rax. On Linux, syscall number 60 is exit.
  • mov $42, %rdi — Load 42 into %rdi. This is the exit status code — the value the program returns to the shell.
  • syscall — Transfer control to the Linux kernel to execute the system call.

Build and run it

Save the above as smallest.s, then:

$ as -o smallest.o smallest.s
$ ld -o smallest smallest.o
$ ./smallest
$ echo $?
42

The echo $? command prints the exit status of the last program. You should see 42. Congratulations — you just wrote, assembled, linked, and ran a program with no compiler at all.

Exit codes as output: Until we learn how to print text, we will use the program's exit code (checked with echo $?) as a convenient way to verify our programs produce the right answer. Exit codes are limited to 0–255 (values are taken mod 256), but that is enough for now.

gcc Comparison: return 42;

Now let's see how gcc handles the same idea. Write this C program:

int main() {
    return 42;
}

Compile it with optimization to keep the output readable:

$ gcc -Og -S return42.c
$ cat return42.s

You will see something like:

main:
        movl    $42, %eax
        ret

(Plus some assembler directives we can ignore for now.) Notice the differences:

  • gcc uses main: as the entry point. The C runtime provides the actual _start and calls main for you.
  • gcc returns the value in %eax (the 32-bit portion of %rax) and uses ret to return to the caller. The C runtime then calls exit with that value.
  • Our hand-written program used _start and invoked the exit syscall directly. There is no caller to return to.

Throughout this module, we will follow this pattern: write it by hand first, then see how gcc does the same thing. This way you understand both the raw machine and the compiler's conventions.

Module 3: x86-64 Assembly Fundamentals

Lesson 2: Writing Makefiles

Why Makefiles?

In Lesson 1 we built programs by typing as and ld commands manually at the terminal. For a single source file, that is perfectly manageable. But as programs grow to multiple source files — as we will see in Lesson 9, where a program is split across main.s, readInt.s, and writeInt.s — re-typing the assembler and linker commands for every file after every change becomes tedious and error-prone. You might forget to reassemble a file you edited, or mistype a flag, and then spend twenty minutes debugging a problem that does not actually exist in your code.

Make is a build automation tool that solves this problem. You describe the build process once in a file called a Makefile, and from then on a single command — make — does all the work for you.

What Make Does

Make reads a file called Makefile (or makefile) in the current directory. This file describes which files depend on which, and the shell commands needed to build them. When you type make, it checks the modification timestamps of all the files involved and only rebuilds what has changed. If you edit one .s file out of five, Make will reassemble just that one file and re-link the final executable — skipping the four files that have not changed. For large projects, this saves a tremendous amount of time.

Basic Syntax

A Makefile consists of rules. Each rule has three parts:

target: prerequisites
	recipe
  • The target is the file to be built (or a name for an action).
  • The prerequisites (also called dependencies) are the files that the target depends on. If any prerequisite is newer than the target, Make will run the recipe.
  • The recipe is one or more shell commands that build the target from the prerequisites.
Tab requirement: The recipe lines must be indented with a literal TAB character, not spaces. This is the single most common Makefile syntax error. If Make complains about "missing separator," check that your editor is inserting a real tab. In vim, a tab is the default. In nano, press Ctrl-I or the Tab key. In VS Code, check the status bar for "Spaces" vs. "Tabs" and switch if needed.

A First Makefile

Let's write a Makefile for the smallest exit program from Lesson 1. Recall that building it by hand requires two commands:

$ as -o smallest.o smallest.s
$ ld -o smallest smallest.o

Here is a Makefile that automates this:

smallest: smallest.o
	ld -o smallest smallest.o

smallest.o: smallest.s
	as -o smallest.o smallest.s

clean:
	rm -f smallest smallest.o

.PHONY: clean

How it works

When you type make with no arguments, Make builds the first target in the file — in this case, smallest. It sees that smallest depends on smallest.o, so it checks the rule for smallest.o. That rule depends on smallest.s. If smallest.s is newer than smallest.o (or if smallest.o does not exist), Make runs as -o smallest.o smallest.s. Then, if smallest.o is newer than smallest, Make runs ld -o smallest smallest.o.

The clean rule has no prerequisites — it simply removes the build products. You run it with make clean. The .PHONY: clean line tells Make that clean is not an actual file; without this, if a file named clean happened to exist in the directory, Make would see that it is "up to date" and skip the rule.

Variables

If you decide to switch assemblers or add flags, you would have to change every recipe line. Makefile variables (also called macros) let you define a value once and use it everywhere:

AS = as
LD = ld

smallest: smallest.o
	$(LD) -o smallest smallest.o

smallest.o: smallest.s
	$(AS) -o smallest.o smallest.s

You define a variable with NAME = value and reference it with $(NAME). Now if you want to add a flag — say, -g for debug symbols — you change one line (AS = as -g or, better, add an ASFLAGS variable) instead of editing every recipe.

Automatic Variables

Make provides several automatic variables that refer to parts of the current rule. The three most useful are:

  • $@ — the target of the current rule.
  • $< — the first prerequisite.
  • $^ — all prerequisites, separated by spaces.

Using these, our rules become more concise and less repetitive:

AS = as
LD = ld

smallest: smallest.o
	$(LD) -o $@ $^

smallest.o: smallest.s
	$(AS) -o $@ $<

In the first rule, $@ expands to smallest (the target) and $^ expands to smallest.o (all prerequisites). In the second rule, $@ expands to smallest.o and $< expands to smallest.s (the first — and only — prerequisite). The advantage of automatic variables becomes clear when you have many similar rules: you write the pattern once, and the filenames fill themselves in.

Pattern Rules

When a project has many .s files, writing a separate rule for each .o file is tedious. A pattern rule uses the % wildcard to match any stem:

%.o: %.s
	$(AS) -o $@ $<

This tells Make: "for any file ending in .o, if there is a corresponding file ending in .s, build the .o by running the assembler." The % matches the same string on both sides — so main.o depends on main.s, readInt.o depends on readInt.s, and so on. You write one rule, and it handles all of them.

A Multi-File Makefile

Here is a complete Makefile for a project with three source files — main.s, readInt.s, and writeInt.s — foreshadowing the multi-file programs we will build in Lesson 9:

AS = as
LD = ld
ASFLAGS = -g

OBJS = main.o readInt.o writeInt.o

program: $(OBJS)
	$(LD) -o $@ $^

%.o: %.s
	$(AS) $(ASFLAGS) -o $@ $<

clean:
	rm -f program $(OBJS)

.PHONY: clean

A few things to note:

  • The ASFLAGS = -g variable adds the -g flag for debug symbols. This will be essential in Lesson 10 when we use GDB to step through our programs.
  • The OBJS variable lists all the object files. It is used in both the link rule and the clean rule, so adding a new source file means changing just one line.
  • The pattern rule %.o: %.s handles all three .s–to–.o compilations.
  • Typing make builds the program target. Typing make clean removes all generated files.

Makefiles for C Programs

Makefiles are not specific to assembly — they are used for C, C++, and many other languages. Here is the equivalent Makefile for a C program:

CC = gcc
CFLAGS = -Wall -g

myprogram: myprogram.o
	$(CC) -o $@ $^

%.o: %.c
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c -o $@ $<

clean:
	rm -f myprogram *.o

.PHONY: clean

The structure is identical. The only differences are the tool names (gcc instead of as/ld), the flag variable (CFLAGS instead of ASFLAGS), the file extension (.c instead of .s), and the -c flag that tells gcc to compile without linking. The concepts — targets, prerequisites, recipes, variables, pattern rules — are exactly the same.

Common Conventions

Most Makefiles follow a few widely adopted conventions:

  • all as the default target. If a Makefile builds more than one program, the first rule is typically named all and lists all the programs as prerequisites: 
    all: program1 program2

program1: program1.o
	$(LD) -o $@ $^

program2: program2.o utils.o
	$(LD) -o $@ $^
    Since all is the first target, typing make builds everything.
  • clean for removing generated files. Every Makefile should have a clean target that deletes all object files and executables, returning the directory to a source-only state.
  • .PHONY for non-file targets. Any target that does not correspond to a real file — such as clean or all — should be declared .PHONY so that Make does not confuse it with a file of the same name.

Putting It All Together

Here is the workflow you will use throughout this module and the rest of the course:

  1. Write your assembly source files (.s files).
  2. Write a Makefile (or copy and adapt one from a previous project).
  3. Run make to build.
  4. Test your program.
  5. Edit a source file to fix a bug or add a feature.
  6. Run make again — it rebuilds only what changed.
  7. When finished, run make clean to remove generated files.

This cycle — edit, make, test — is the standard development loop in systems programming. It works the same way whether you are writing assembly, C, or C++.

Module 3: x86-64 Assembly Fundamentals

Lesson 3: Registers, Data Types, and the CPU Environment

What a Processor Has to Work With

A processor is a remarkably simple machine. It has a tiny amount of fast storage called registers — just 16 general-purpose registers on x86-64, totaling 128 bytes. Everything the CPU does involves moving data between these registers and main memory, and performing arithmetic or logical operations on register contents.

The key components of the processor state are:

  • Register file — 16 general-purpose 64-bit registers for integer data and addresses.
  • Program counter (%rip) — holds the address of the next instruction to execute.
  • Condition code registers — single-bit flags set by arithmetic operations, used for branching (covered in Module 4).
  • Floating point / vector registers — a separate bank of 16 XMM/YMM registers for floating point math (covered later).
  • Main memory — a large byte-addressable array that holds code, data, and the stack.

The 16 General-Purpose Registers

Each of the 16 registers is 64 bits (8 bytes) wide. You can also access smaller portions of each register using different names. This is a legacy of the x86 architecture growing from 16-bit to 32-bit to 64-bit over the decades.

64-bit32-bit16-bit8-bitTypical use
%rax%eax%ax%alReturn value
%rbx%ebx%bx%blCallee-saved
%rcx%ecx%cx%cl4th argument
%rdx%edx%dx%dl3rd argument
%rsi%esi%si%sil2nd argument
%rdi%edi%di%dil1st argument
%rbp%ebp%bp%bplBase pointer
%rsp%esp%sp%splStack pointer
%r8%r8d%r8w%r8b5th argument
%r9%r9d%r9w%r9b6th argument
%r10%r10d%r10w%r10bCaller-saved
%r11%r11d%r11w%r11bCaller-saved
%r12%r12d%r12w%r12bCallee-saved
%r13%r13d%r13w%r13bCallee-saved
%r14%r14d%r14w%r14bCallee-saved
%r15%r15d%r15w%r15bCallee-saved

The "Typical use" column reflects the System V AMD64 calling convention used on Linux. We will cover calling conventions in detail in Module 4. For now, just note that %rax is where return values go, %rdi is the first argument, and %rsp is the stack pointer.

AT&T Syntax

There are two common syntaxes for x86 assembly: Intel and AT&T. We use AT&T syntax, which is what gcc and the GNU assembler (as) produce by default. The key conventions are:

  • Register names are prefixed with %: %rax, %rdi, etc.
  • Immediate (constant) values are prefixed with $: $42, $0xFF.
  • In two-operand instructions, the source comes first and the destination comes second: mov $5, %rax means "move 5 into %rax."
  • Instructions have a size suffix indicating the data width:
SuffixNameSizeC type
bByte1 byte (8 bits)char
wWord2 bytes (16 bits)short
lLong / Double word4 bytes (32 bits)int
qQuad word8 bytes (64 bits)long, pointers

For example, movq moves 8 bytes, movl moves 4 bytes, and movb moves 1 byte. When the size is obvious from context (e.g., you are writing to %eax, which is 32 bits), the suffix can sometimes be omitted, but it is good practice to include it.

Hand-Write: Registers in Action

Let's write a program that uses several registers and does some arithmetic. We will add two numbers and exit with the result:

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        mov $200, %rax
        mov $100, %rbx
        add %rbx, %rax        # %rax = 200 + 100 = 300
        mov %rax, %rdi         # exit code = 300
        mov $60, %rax          # syscall number for exit
        syscall

Build and run:

$ as -o registers.o registers.s
$ ld -o registers registers.o
$ ./registers
$ echo $?
44

Wait — we computed 300 but got 44? Remember that exit codes are a single unsigned byte (0–255). The value 300 mod 256 = 44. This is a good reminder that data sizes matter in assembly. We will address this properly in Lesson 4 when we learn to print values.

gcc Comparison: Disassembly with objdump

Let's see the other direction — starting from C and examining the assembly that gcc produces. Write this C file:

long add_two(long a, long b) {
    return a + b;
}

Compile to assembly:

$ gcc -Og -S add_two.c
$ cat add_two.s

You will see gcc's output, which includes the function label and instructions using the register names from the calling convention (%rdi for the first argument, %rsi for the second).

You can also compile to an object file and use objdump to see both machine code and assembly side by side:

$ gcc -Og -c add_two.c
$ objdump -d add_two.o

The output shows each instruction's address (offset), the raw bytes of machine code in hexadecimal, and the assembly instruction. Machine instructions on x86-64 range from 1 to 15 bytes in length — this is a variable-length instruction set.

Module 3: x86-64 Assembly Fundamentals

Lesson 4: Moving Data

The Most Common Instruction

The mov instruction is the workhorse of assembly. It copies data from a source to a destination. On x86-64, many arithmetic instructions allow one memory operand, but arithmetic cannot use two memory operands at once. So most programs still spend a large fraction of their instructions moving data between memory and registers.

Three Kinds of Operands

Every instruction operand falls into one of three categories:

  • Immediate — A constant value, written with a $ prefix: $42, $0xFF, $-1.
  • Register — The contents of a register, written with a % prefix: %rax, %edi.
  • Memory — A value stored at a memory address. A register name in parentheses means "the value at the address stored in this register": (%rax) means "the value in memory at the address contained in %rax."

The mov Family

The mov instruction copies data without modifying it. Add a size suffix to specify how many bytes to move:

  • movb $0x56, %al — Move 1 byte (immediate to register)
  • movw %ax, %bx — Move 2 bytes (register to register)
  • movl $0x56, %ebx — Move 4 bytes (immediate to register)
  • movq %rax, %rcx — Move 8 bytes (register to register)
  • movw (%rcx), %bx — Move 2 bytes from the memory address in %rcx into %bx
  • movq %rax, (%rdx) — Move 8 bytes from %rax to the memory address in %rdx
Critical restriction: You cannot move directly from one memory location to another. If you need to copy memory-to-memory, you must use two instructions with a register as an intermediary:
movq (%rax), %rcx   then   movq %rcx, (%rdx)

Effective Address Computation

Memory operands can be more complex than just (%reg). The full form of a memory address in AT&T syntax is:

displacement(base, index, scale)

This computes the address: displacement + base + index × scale

Any part can be omitted. The scale must be 1, 2, 4, or 8. Some examples:

SyntaxAddress computedTypical use
(%rax)value in %raxSimple pointer dereference
8(%rax)%rax + 8Struct field access
(%rax,%rcx)%rax + %rcxBase + offset
(%rax,%rcx,8)%rax + %rcx × 8Array of 8-byte elements
200(%rbp,%r10,4)200 + %rbp + %r10 × 4Complex array indexing

For example, if %rbp holds 10 and %r10 holds 2, then 200(%rbp, %r10, 4) computes: 200 + 10 + 2 × 4 = 218.

The lea Instruction

lea stands for "Load Effective Address." Unlike mov, which loads the value at a computed address, lea loads the address itself into a register. Think of it as the assembly equivalent of C's address-of operator &.

leaq (%rax,%rcx,8), %rdx    # %rdx = %rax + %rcx * 8 (the address, not the value)

This makes lea extremely useful for two purposes: computing addresses of variables in memory, and doing quick arithmetic without a dedicated add/mul instruction.

Hand-Write: Hello, World

Let's use mov and lea to write a "Hello, world!" program. This uses the write system call (syscall number 1) which takes three arguments: file descriptor, buffer address, and byte count.

        .section .rodata
msg:    .asciz "Hello, world!\n"
msglen = . - msg - 1

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        mov $1, %rax           # syscall number: write
        mov $1, %rdi           # file descriptor: stdout
        lea msg(%rip), %rsi    # address of the string
        mov $msglen, %rdx      # number of bytes to write
        syscall

        mov $60, %rax          # syscall number: exit
        xor %rdi, %rdi         # exit code 0
        syscall

Build and run:

$ as -o hello.o hello.s
$ ld -o hello hello.o
$ ./hello
Hello, world!

Key points:

  • .section .rodata places the string in read-only data (it will not be modified at runtime).
  • .asciz creates a null-terminated ASCII string.
  • msglen = . - msg - 1 computes the printable string length at assembly time (subtracting the null terminator added by .asciz). The . symbol means "current address."
  • lea msg(%rip), %rsi uses RIP-relative addressing to load the string's address. RIP-relative addressing computes an address relative to the current instruction pointer, which is required for position-independent code on x86-64.
  • xor %rdi, %rdi is a common idiom for setting a register to zero (any value XORed with itself is zero). It is shorter and faster than mov $0, %rdi.

From write to read

The write syscall sends bytes from your program's memory to the outside world. The read syscall does the reverse: it asks the kernel to place incoming bytes into a buffer in your memory. On Linux x86-64, read is syscall number 0.

  • %rax = 0 — syscall number for read
  • %rdi = 0 — file descriptor for standard input
  • %rsi — address of the destination buffer
  • %rdx — maximum number of bytes to read
  • Return value in %rax — number of bytes actually read

This return value matters because read does not add a null terminator for us. It simply reports how many bytes it placed into memory. If we want to write those same bytes back out, we pass that returned count to write.

Hand-Write: Raw Echo with read and write

The following program reads up to 32 bytes from standard input and immediately writes back exactly the bytes it received. This is the simplest bare-syscall input/output program. For now, we assume the read succeeds; in Module 4 we will have the control flow machinery needed to check for EOF and errors.

        .section .bss
buffer: .skip 32

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        mov $0, %rax           # syscall number: read
        mov $0, %rdi           # file descriptor: stdin
        lea buffer(%rip), %rsi # address of input buffer
        mov $32, %rdx          # max bytes to read
        syscall

        mov %rax, %rdx         # byte count for write
        mov $1, %rax           # syscall number: write
        mov $1, %rdi           # file descriptor: stdout
        lea buffer(%rip), %rsi # address of data to print
        syscall

        mov $60, %rax
        xor %rdi, %rdi
        syscall

Build and run:

$ as -o raw_echo.o raw_echo.s
$ ld -o raw_echo raw_echo.o
$ ./raw_echo
hello
hello

Key points:

  • .bss reserves space for uninitialized writable data. Our buffer starts out zeroed, but read overwrites it with the bytes the user typed.
  • After the read syscall, %rax no longer holds the syscall number. It now holds the result: the number of bytes read.
  • mov %rax, %rdx reuses that returned byte count as the third argument to write, so we print exactly what was read.
  • When reading from a terminal, input is usually line-buffered: the kernel delivers the bytes after you press Enter, including the newline character.

gcc Comparison: printf("Hello")

If you write the equivalent in C and compile with gcc -Og -S:

#include <stdio.h>
int main() {
    printf("Hello, world!\n");
    return 0;
}

The generated assembly calls the C library function puts (gcc optimizes printf with a simple string to puts). Where our hand-written version used a single write syscall (7 instructions total), the gcc version calls into the C standard library, which internally does much more setup. The library approach is more portable, but now you can see what it actually comes down to at the hardware level: loading register arguments and making a system call.

Module 3: x86-64 Assembly Fundamentals

Lesson 5: The Data Section and Labels

Where Data Lives

So far, all of our values have been immediates baked directly into instructions (mov $42, %rax) or computed at runtime in registers. But real programs need to store data that persists across instructions — global variables, strings, arrays. This data lives in dedicated sections of the executable.

The Three Data Sections

An assembly program is divided into sections. The assembler and linker use these to lay out the final executable:

DirectiveSectionContents
.text or .section .textTextExecutable instructions (read-only at runtime)
.data or .section .dataDataInitialized read-write global variables
.section .rodataRead-only dataConstants, string literals (read-only at runtime)
.bss or .section .bssBSSUninitialized global variables (zero-filled at load time)

The .bss section is special: it takes up no space in the executable file on disk. The operating system simply allocates the requested amount of zero-filled memory when the program starts.

Data Directives

Inside the .data or .rodata sections, you use directives to declare values:

DirectiveSizeExample
.byte1 byte.byte 0xFF
.word2 bytes.word 1000
.long4 bytes.long 100000
.quad8 bytes.quad 5000000000
.asciistring (no null).ascii "Hello"
.ascizstring + null byte.asciz "Hello"
.space N or .skip NN zero bytes.space 100 (in .bss)

You can also declare multiple values on one line: .quad 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 allocates five consecutive 8-byte values — this is how arrays are created in assembly.

Labels

A label is a name followed by a colon that marks a location in the program. Labels in the .data section name your variables; labels in .text name your code locations (jump targets, function entry points):

        .section .data
x:      .long 10
y:      .long 25

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        # code that uses x and y

The label x: refers to the memory address where the value 10 is stored. The label _start: refers to the address of the first instruction.

RIP-Relative Addressing

To access data stored in the .data or .rodata section, you use RIP-relative addressing:

mov x(%rip), %eax       # load the 4-byte value at label x into %eax

The (%rip) part tells the assembler to encode the address as an offset from the current instruction pointer. This is the standard way to access global data on x86-64 Linux — it produces position-independent code that works regardless of where the program is loaded in memory.

To store a value back:

mov %eax, x(%rip)       # store %eax into the 4-byte location at label x

To get the address of a label (rather than the value stored there), use lea:

lea x(%rip), %rax       # %rax now holds the memory address of x

Hand-Write: Adding Two Global Variables

Let's write a program that declares two integers in .data, adds them, and exits with the result:

        .section .data
a:      .long 17
b:      .long 25

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        mov a(%rip), %eax      # load a into %eax
        add b(%rip), %eax      # %eax = a + b = 42
        mov %eax, %edi         # exit code = result
        mov $60, %rax          # syscall: exit
        syscall

Build and run:

$ as -o data1.o data1.s
$ ld -o data1 data1.o
$ ./data1
$ echo $?
42

Notice that we used .long (4 bytes) and the corresponding 32-bit register names (%eax, %edi) with the movl/addl implicit sizing. If we had used .quad (8 bytes), we would use %rax and %rdi with movq/addq.

Hand-Write: A Mutable Variable

Here is a program that reads a value, modifies it, and stores it back:

        .section .data
counter: .quad 0

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        mov counter(%rip), %rax    # load counter (0)
        add $10, %rax              # counter = 10
        add $32, %rax              # counter = 42
        mov %rax, counter(%rip)    # store back (optional here, but shows the pattern)
        mov %rax, %rdi
        mov $60, %rax
        syscall

This pattern — load from memory, operate in registers, store back to memory — is the fundamental rhythm of assembly programming.

gcc Comparison: Global Variables

Consider this C program:

int x = 17;
int y = 25;

int main() {
    return x + y;
}

Compile with gcc -Og -S and you will see that gcc puts x and y in a data section and accesses them with the same x(%rip) pattern. The main difference is that gcc adds type metadata (e.g., .size, .type) and uses .globl to make the symbols visible. The actual instructions for loading and adding the values look very similar to what we wrote by hand.

Module 3: x86-64 Assembly Fundamentals

Lesson 6: Arithmetic Operations

Computing with Values

Up to this point, we have mostly moved data around. Now we will discuss the instructions that actually compute new values. All arithmetic instructions require a size suffix (b, w, l, q) and store their result into the destination operand, overwriting what was there.

Arithmetic Instruction Reference

The add and sub instructions work on both signed and unsigned values. imul and idiv are for signed integers; mul and div are for unsigned.

InstructionEffectDescription
add S, D D + S → D Adds S to D. Result stored in D.
sub S, D D − S → D Subtracts S from D. Note: this is D minus S, not S minus D.
imul S, D D × S → D Signed multiply. Two-operand form: result goes in D.
idiv S %rdx:%rax / S → %rax
%rdx:%rax mod S → %rdx		 Signed divide. Takes one operand; divides the 128-bit value %rdx:%rax by S. Quotient in %rax, remainder in %rdx. You must sign-extend %rax into %rdx with cqto first.
inc D D + 1 → D Increment by one. Equivalent to x++ in C.
dec D D − 1 → D Decrement by one. Equivalent to x-- in C.
neg D −D → D Arithmetic negation. Same as x = -x in C.

Division in Detail: idiv and cqto

Division is more complex than the other operations because it uses implicit operands. The idiv instruction always divides the 128-bit value formed by %rdx:%rax (high bits in %rdx, low bits in %rax) by the single operand. Before using idiv, you must sign-extend %rax into %rdx using cqto (Convert Quad to Oct):

# Compute 17 / 5
mov $17, %rax          # dividend
cqto                   # sign-extend %rax into %rdx:%rax
mov $5, %rcx
idiv %rcx              # %rax = 3 (quotient), %rdx = 2 (remainder)
Common mistake: Forgetting cqto before idiv. If %rdx contains leftover data from a previous computation, you will get a wrong answer or a floating-point exception. Always use cqto (or cltd for 32-bit division) immediately before idiv.

Hand-Write: (a + b) * c

Let's compute an expression using data from the .data section:

        .section .data
a:      .long 3
b:      .long 7
c:      .long 6

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        mov  a(%rip), %eax     # %eax = 3
        add  b(%rip), %eax     # %eax = 3 + 7 = 10
        imull c(%rip), %eax    # %eax = 10 * 6 = 60
        mov  %eax, %edi        # exit code = 60
        mov  $60, %rax
        syscall
$ as -o arithmetic.o arithmetic.s
$ ld -o arithmetic arithmetic.o
$ ./arithmetic
$ echo $?
60

Hand-Write: Division with Remainder

This program divides 100 by 7 and exits with the remainder:

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        mov $100, %rax         # dividend
        cqto                   # sign-extend into %rdx:%rax
        mov $7, %rcx           # divisor
        idiv %rcx              # %rax = 14 (quotient), %rdx = 2 (remainder)
        mov %rdx, %rdi         # exit with remainder
        mov $60, %rax
        syscall
$ echo $?
2

gcc Comparison: The lea Trick

We introduced lea in Lesson 4 as a way to compute addresses. But gcc frequently uses lea for pure arithmetic, because the address-computation hardware is fast and can do addition and multiplication by small constants in a single instruction.

For example, if gcc needs to compute x * 5 (where x is in %rdx), it might generate:

leaq (%rdx, %rdx, 4), %rdx    # %rdx = %rdx + %rdx * 4 = %rdx * 5

Recall the address formula: base + index × scale. Here the base is %rdx, the index is also %rdx, and the scale is 4, giving x + x*4 = x*5. This is faster than using imul.

Similarly, x * 3:

leaq (%rdx, %rdx, 2), %rdx    # %rdx = %rdx + %rdx * 2 = %rdx * 3

And x * 2 + 10:

leaq 10(%rdx, %rdx), %rdx     # %rdx = 10 + %rdx + %rdx = 2*x + 10

Note that for lea the size suffix applies only to the destination. The source always uses 64-bit registers.

Module 3: x86-64 Assembly Fundamentals

Lesson 7: Logical and Shift Operations

Bit-Level Operations

In Module 1 you learned about bitwise operations in C: &, |, ^, ~, <<, >>. Assembly provides the same operations as instructions. These are essential for tasks like masking bits, setting flags, and fast multiplication/division by powers of two.

Logical Instruction Reference

InstructionEffectDescription
not D ~D → D Bitwise NOT (flip every bit). One operand.
and S, D D & S → D Bitwise AND. Useful for masking bits.
or S, D D | S → D Bitwise OR. Useful for setting bits.
xor S, D D ^ S → D Bitwise XOR. xor %rax, %rax is the standard idiom for zeroing a register.

Shift Instruction Reference

InstructionEffectDescription
shl k, D / sal k, D D << k → D Shift left by k bits. Fills with zeros on the right. shl and sal are identical.
shr k, D D >> k → D (logical) Logical shift right. Fills with zeros on the left. For unsigned values.
sar k, D D >> k → D (arithmetic) Arithmetic shift right. Fills with copies of the sign bit. For signed values.

The shift amount k can be an immediate value or the register %cl (the low byte of %rcx). It cannot be any other register — this is a hardware restriction.

Hand-Write: Bit Manipulation

This program demonstrates extracting the low byte with and and multiplying by 8 with shl:

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        mov $0x1234, %rax
        and $0xFF, %rax        # extract low byte: %rax = 0x34 = 52
        shl $3, %rax           # multiply by 8:  %rax = 52 * 8 = 416
        # 416 mod 256 = 160
        mov %rax, %rdi
        mov $60, %rax
        syscall
$ echo $?
160

The and $0xFF operation masks off everything except the lowest 8 bits — this is the assembly equivalent of x & 0xFF in C. Shifting left by 3 is equivalent to multiplying by 23 = 8.

Hand-Write: Swap Without a Temporary

The classic XOR swap trick works in assembly too:

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        mov $10, %rax          # a = 10
        mov $25, %rbx          # b = 25
        xor %rbx, %rax         # a = a ^ b
        xor %rax, %rbx         # b = a ^ b (now b = original a = 10)
        xor %rbx, %rax         # a = a ^ b (now a = original b = 25)
        mov %rax, %rdi         # exit with a = 25
        mov $60, %rax
        syscall
$ echo $?
25

In practice you would just use mov with a spare register, but this demonstrates how XOR works at the instruction level.

gcc Comparison

When you write bitwise operations in C, gcc translates them directly to the corresponding assembly instructions:

C expressiongcc output (typical)
x & 0xFFandl $255, %eax
x | 0x80orl $128, %eax
x ^ yxorl %edx, %eax
x << 3sall $3, %eax
x >> 1 (signed)sarl $1, %eax
x >> 1 (unsigned)shrl $1, %eax

Notice that gcc chooses sar vs shr based on whether the C variable is signed or unsigned. This is exactly what you learned in Module 1 about logical vs. arithmetic right shift.

Module 3: x86-64 Assembly Fundamentals

Lesson 8: The Stack, Push, and Pop

What is the Program Stack?

The program stack (or "call stack") is a region of memory that the program uses for temporary storage: local variables, saved register values, return addresses, and function arguments that don't fit in registers. It is the backbone of function calls.

The stack is a LIFO (Last In, First Out) data structure, like a stack of plates. You push a value onto the top and pop a value off the top. The "top" of the stack is always the address stored in the stack pointer register, %rsp.

The Stack Grows Downward

On x86-64 (and most modern architectures), the stack grows toward lower memory addresses. This is counterintuitive at first:

  • Pushing a value decreases %rsp (moves it to a lower address).
  • Popping a value increases %rsp (moves it to a higher address).

If you imagine memory as a vertical diagram with low addresses at the bottom and high addresses at the top, the stack grows downward from the top of the address space.

push and pop

The push instruction does two things in one:

  1. Subtract 8 from %rsp (make room for a 64-bit value)
  2. Write the operand to the memory address now pointed to by %rsp

In other words, pushq %rax is equivalent to:

subq $8, %rsp
movq %rax, (%rsp)

The pop instruction reverses this:

  1. Read the value at (%rsp) into the destination operand
  2. Add 8 to %rsp

So popq %rax is equivalent to:

movq (%rsp), %rax
addq $8, %rsp
Note: In normal 64-bit code, push and pop are typically used with 64-bit (8-byte) values. There are also 16-bit forms (such as pushw / popw), but there is no 32-bit push / pop form in x86-64 mode. The System V ABI requires the stack to be aligned to 16-byte boundaries before a call instruction.

Manual Stack Manipulation

Sometimes you need more stack space than push/pop provides — for instance, to allocate room for several local variables at once. You can do this by directly adjusting %rsp:

# Allocate 32 bytes of local variable space
sub $32, %rsp

# Use the space via offsets from %rsp
movq $10, (%rsp)         # first local (bytes 0-7)
movq $20, 8(%rsp)        # second local (bytes 8-15)
movq $30, 16(%rsp)       # third local (bytes 16-23)
movq $40, 24(%rsp)       # fourth local (bytes 24-31)

# Deallocate when done
add $32, %rsp

This is exactly what compilers do to create space for local variables. We will see this pattern in detail in Module 4 when we cover function stack frames.

Hand-Write: Using the Stack for Temporary Storage

Here is a complete program that uses push and pop to save and restore register values. It computes two results, saves the first on the stack while computing the second, then retrieves it:

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        # Compute first result: 5 + 7 = 12
        mov $5, %rax
        add $7, %rax           # %rax = 12
        push %rax              # save 12 on the stack

        # Compute second result: 10 + 20 = 30
        mov $10, %rax
        add $20, %rax          # %rax = 30

        # Now %rax = 30 and the stack holds 12
        pop %rbx               # %rbx = 12 (restored from stack)
        add %rbx, %rax         # %rax = 30 + 12 = 42

        mov %rax, %rdi
        mov $60, %rax
        syscall
$ echo $?
42

Without the stack, we would have needed a third register to hold the intermediate result. With only 16 registers, the stack provides essentially unlimited temporary storage — at the cost of being slower than register access.

Hand-Write: Stack-Based Local Variables

This program allocates space for two local variables on the stack, stores values, reads them back, and computes a result:

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        sub $16, %rsp          # allocate 16 bytes for 2 locals

        movq $17, (%rsp)       # local1 = 17
        movq $25, 8(%rsp)      # local2 = 25

        mov (%rsp), %rax       # load local1
        add 8(%rsp), %rax      # %rax = local1 + local2 = 42

        add $16, %rsp          # deallocate locals

        mov %rax, %rdi
        mov $60, %rax
        syscall
$ echo $?
42

gcc Comparison: Function Prologue and Epilogue

When gcc compiles a function at -O0 (no optimization), it generates a standard pattern called the prologue and epilogue. You can see this yourself by compiling a simple function:

$ cat simple.c
int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }

$ gcc -O0 -S -o simple.s simple.c
$ cat simple.s     # look for the add: label

The generated assembly will follow this pattern:

# Prologue (at function entry)
pushq   %rbp               # save old base pointer
movq    %rsp, %rbp          # set base pointer to current stack top
subq    $16, %rsp           # allocate space for local variables

# ... function body ...

# Epilogue (at function exit)
leave                       # equivalent to: movq %rbp, %rsp; popq %rbp
ret                         # return to caller

The leave instruction is a shorthand that restores %rsp and %rbp in one step. We will cover the full calling convention — including why %rbp is saved and what ret does — in Module 4.

With optimization enabled (-Og or higher), gcc often skips the prologue/epilogue for simple "leaf" functions that don't call other functions, since it can keep everything in registers.

Module 3: x86-64 Assembly Fundamentals

Lesson 9: Putting It All Together

A Complete Program

In this capstone lesson we combine everything from Module 3 — the build process, registers, data movement, the data section, arithmetic, logical operations, and the stack — into a complete, working assembly program. We also introduce readInt and writeInt, two helper routines that let our programs read and print integer values.

I/O Helper Routines: readInt and writeInt

Up to now, our only output mechanism has been the exit code (limited to 0–255). For real programs, we need to read input from the keyboard and print results to the screen. Writing I/O from scratch requires parsing ASCII digits — doable but tedious. Instead, we will use two pre-written helper routines:

  • readInt — Reads a line from standard input, parses the decimal digits into a 64-bit integer, and returns the value in %rax.
  • writeInt — Takes an integer in %rdi, converts it to decimal ASCII, and writes it to standard output followed by a newline.

These are provided as separate .s files (readInt.s, writeInt.s). To use them, you assemble each file separately and link them all together:

$ as -o readInt.o readInt.s
$ as -o writeInt.o writeInt.s
$ as -o myprogram.o myprogram.s
$ ld -o myprogram myprogram.o readInt.o writeInt.o

What the Helpers Are Hiding

The kernel only provides byte-oriented primitives. A bare read syscall copies bytes from file descriptor 0 into a buffer and returns a byte count in %rax. A bare write syscall copies bytes from a buffer to file descriptor 1. That means if the user types 42 and presses Enter, the kernel gives us the ASCII bytes '4', '2', and '\n' — not the integer value 42.

readInt and writeInt are small layers on top of those raw syscalls:

  • readInt performs a raw read, then converts decimal ASCII digits into a binary integer in %rax.
  • writeInt converts a binary integer into ASCII digits in a buffer, then performs a raw write.

So when you call these helpers, you are not avoiding syscalls — you are reusing them through a cleaner interface.

In your source file, you declare them as external symbols:

        .extern readInt
        .extern writeInt

Then you can call them like functions: put arguments in the right registers and use call.

Multi-File Assembly

To make a label visible to other files, use .global:

.global myfunction      # other files can call myfunction

To use a label defined in another file, use .extern:

.extern readInt         # readInt is defined elsewhere

The linker resolves these references when combining the .o files into a final executable.

The call and ret Instructions (Preview)

To call a function, use the call instruction. It pushes the return address onto the stack and jumps to the target label. The ret instruction pops the return address and jumps back. We will cover functions in full detail in Module 4, but we need call now to use our I/O helpers.

call readInt            # call the readInt function; result in %rax
call writeInt           # call writeInt; value to print should be in %rdi
Stack alignment: The System V AMD64 ABI requires %rsp to be 16-byte aligned at the point of a call instruction (see §3.2.2). Since call pushes an 8-byte return address, %rsp will be 8 bytes off from 16-byte alignment at the entry of the called function. The callee's prologue (e.g., push %rbp) often restores 16-byte alignment for local stack usage. In a _start program, the kernel sets the initial %rsp to a 16-byte aligned value (per the ABI §3.4, "Initial Stack and Register State"), so you can call functions directly at the start of the program. But if you push one 8-byte value and then want to make another call, you must add another 8 bytes of padding (or reserve 16 bytes total) before that call.

Echo Program: Read and Print One Integer

Let's start simple — read a number and print it back:

        .extern readInt
        .extern writeInt

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        call readInt           # read integer into %rax
        mov %rax, %rdi         # move result to %rdi (argument for writeInt)
        call writeInt          # print it

        mov $60, %rax
        xor %rdi, %rdi
        syscall
$ ./echoInt
42
42

Complete Program: Read Two Integers, Compute, and Print

Now let's build a program that reads two integers, adds them, multiplies the sum by 3, and prints the result. This uses everything from the module:

        .extern readInt
        .extern writeInt

        .section .data
result: .quad 0

        .section .rodata
prompt1: .asciz "Enter first number: "
p1len = . - prompt1 - 1
prompt2: .asciz "Enter second number: "
p2len = . - prompt2 - 1
label:   .asciz "Result: "
lablen = . - label - 1

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        # Print prompt 1
        mov $1, %rax           # write syscall
        mov $1, %rdi           # stdout
        lea prompt1(%rip), %rsi
        mov $p1len, %rdx
        syscall

        # Read first number
        call readInt
        push %rax              # save first number on stack

        # Keep %rsp 16-byte aligned before the next call
        sub $8, %rsp

        # Print prompt 2
        mov $1, %rax
        mov $1, %rdi
        lea prompt2(%rip), %rsi
        mov $p2len, %rdx
        syscall

        # Read second number
        call readInt
        add $8, %rsp           # discard alignment padding
        mov %rax, %rbx         # %rbx = second number

        # Compute: (first + second) * 3
        pop %rax               # restore first number from stack
        add %rbx, %rax         # %rax = first + second
        imul $3, %rax, %rax    # %rax = sum * 3

        # Store result
        mov %rax, result(%rip)

        # Print label
        push %rax              # save result (call may clobber %rax)
        mov $1, %rax
        mov $1, %rdi
        lea label(%rip), %rsi
        mov $lablen, %rdx
        syscall

        # Print result
        pop %rdi               # restore result into %rdi (argument for writeInt)
        call writeInt

        # Exit
        mov $60, %rax
        xor %rdi, %rdi
