        syscall
$ ./compute
Enter first number: 10
Enter second number: 4
Result: 42

What this program uses from the module

  • Sections: .data for mutable storage, .rodata for string constants, .text for code
  • Data directives: .quad, .asciz, computed lengths with . - label - 1 when using .asciz
  • Registers: %rax, %rbx, %rdi, %rsi, %rdx, %rsp
  • Data movement: mov, lea, RIP-relative addressing
  • Arithmetic: add, imul (three-operand form)
  • Stack: push/pop to save values across function calls
  • System calls: direct write and exit syscalls in the main program; readInt/writeInt themselves are built on top of raw read/write
  • Multi-file linking: .extern, call, ret

gcc Comparison: The C Equivalent

The equivalent C program would be:

#include <stdio.h>
int main() {
    int a, b;
    printf("Enter first number: ");
    scanf("%d", &a);
    printf("Enter second number: ");
    scanf("%d", &b);
    int result = (a + b) * 3;
    printf("Result: %d\n", result);
    return 0;
}

If you compile this with gcc -Og -S, you will see calls to printf and scanf, which internally make the same write and read system calls our program uses directly for prompts and indirectly through readInt/writeInt — but with thousands of lines of library code in between for formatting, buffering, and error handling. Our hand-written version does the same job in about 30 instructions.

What's Next

In Module 4, we will add control flow (comparisons, branches, loops, switch statements) and functions (calling conventions, stack frames, recursion). By the end of that module, you will be able to write assembly programs as complex as anything you would write in C.

Module 3: x86-64 Assembly Fundamentals

Lesson 10: Debugging with GDB

Why You Need a Debugger

So far, our main debugging tool has been echo $? — running the program and checking the exit code. This works for tiny programs, but it is painfully limited. If a 50-line assembly program produces the wrong answer, all echo $? tells you is what the answer was, not where things went wrong.

GDB (the GNU Debugger) lets you pause your program at any point, inspect every register and memory location, and step through instructions one at a time. It is the single most important tool for understanding what your assembly code is actually doing.

Building with Debug Symbols

For GDB to show you source-level information (label names, line numbers), you need to include debug symbols when you assemble. Add the -g flag:

$ as -g -o program.o program.s
$ ld -o program program.o

If you are using gcc instead:

$ gcc -g -nostdlib -o program program.s

Without -g, GDB still works, but you will only see raw addresses instead of label names — much harder to navigate.

Starting GDB

Launch GDB with your executable as the argument:

$ gdb ./program

You will see a welcome message and then the (gdb) prompt. Your program is not running yet — GDB has loaded it but is waiting for your instructions.

GNU gdb (Ubuntu 12.1-0ubuntu1) 12.1
...
Reading symbols from ./program...
(gdb)

Essential Commands

Here are the commands you will use constantly. You can abbreviate most of them to their first letter or two.

Setting Breakpoints

A breakpoint tells GDB to pause execution when it reaches a specific location. You can break on a label name or an address:

(gdb) break _start
Breakpoint 1 at 0x401000: file program.s, line 5.
(gdb) break myfunction
Breakpoint 2 at 0x401030: file program.s, line 20.

You can also break at a specific line number:

(gdb) break program.s:12

Running the Program

The run command starts execution. The program runs until it hits a breakpoint, crashes, or finishes:

(gdb) run
Starting program: /home/user/program

Breakpoint 1, _start () at program.s:5
5               push %rbp

Now the program is paused at the first instruction of _start.

Stepping Through Instructions

Once paused, you can execute one instruction at a time:

  • stepi (or si) — Execute the next single machine instruction. If the instruction is a call, step into the called function.
  • nexti (or ni) — Execute the next single machine instruction. If the instruction is a call, execute the entire called function and stop after it returns (step over).
(gdb) stepi
6               call readInt
(gdb) nexti
7               mov %rax, %rdi

Use stepi when you want to see what happens inside a function call. Use nexti when you trust the function and just want to get past it.

Continuing and Quitting

  • continue (or c) — Resume running until the next breakpoint or program exit.
  • quit (or q) — Exit GDB. If the program is still running, GDB will ask for confirmation.

Inspecting State

The real power of GDB is in inspecting what your program is doing.

Registers

View all general-purpose registers:

(gdb) info registers
rax            0xa                 10
rbx            0x0                 0
rcx            0x0                 0
rdx            0x0                 0
rsi            0x0                 0
rdi            0x0                 0
rbp            0x7fffffffe3a0      0x7fffffffe3a0
rsp            0x7fffffffe398      0x7fffffffe398
...
rip            0x401005            0x401005 <_start+5>

View a single register:

(gdb) print $rax
$1 = 10
(gdb) print/x $rax
$2 = 0xa

The /x format prints in hexadecimal. Other useful formats: /d (signed decimal), /u (unsigned decimal), /t (binary).

Examining Memory

The x (examine) command reads memory at a given address. The syntax is x/NFU address, where:

  • N = number of units to display
  • F = format (x hex, d decimal, c character, s string, i instruction)
  • U = unit size (b byte, h halfword/2 bytes, w word/4 bytes, g giant/8 bytes)

Examples:

# Show 8 bytes in hex starting at the address in %rsp
(gdb) x/8xb $rsp
0x7fffffffe398: 0xa0    0xe3    0xff    0xff    0xff    0x7f    0x00    0x00

# Show 4 quad-words (8 bytes each) at the top of the stack
(gdb) x/4xg $rsp
0x7fffffffe398: 0x00007fffffffe3a0      0x0000000000000001
0x7fffffffe3a8: 0x00007fffffffe5b2      0x0000000000000000

# Show a string at a label
(gdb) x/s &prompt1
0x402000:       "Enter first number: "

# Disassemble instructions at the current location
(gdb) x/5i $rip
=> 0x401005 <_start+5>:  call   0x401080 <readInt>
   0x40100a <_start+10>: push   %rax
   0x40100b <_start+11>: mov    $0x1,%eax
   0x401010 <_start+16>: mov    $0x1,%edi
   0x401015 <_start+21>: lea    0xfe4(%rip),%rsi

Walkthrough: Debugging the Compute Program

Let's debug the "compute" program from Lesson 9 step by step. Recall that it reads two integers, adds them, multiplies the sum by 3, and prints the result.

$ as -g -o compute.o compute.s
$ as -o readInt.o readInt.s
$ as -o writeInt.o writeInt.s
$ ld -o compute compute.o readInt.o writeInt.o
$ gdb ./compute

Step 1: Set breakpoints and run

Rather than stepping through the prompt-printing and I/O code one instruction at a time, we set breakpoints at the interesting points — right after each readInt call and at the arithmetic section:

(gdb) break _start
Breakpoint 1 at 0x401000: file compute.s, line 19.
(gdb) break compute.s:27
Breakpoint 2 at 0x401023: file compute.s, line 27.
(gdb) break compute.s:45
Breakpoint 3 at 0x401052: file compute.s, line 45.
(gdb) run
Starting program: /home/user/compute

Breakpoint 1, _start () at compute.s:19
19              mov $1, %rax

Step 2: Run to the first read and check the result

We use continue to skip ahead to breakpoint 2, which is just after the first readInt call. GDB will print the prompt and wait for our input along the way:

(gdb) continue
Continuing.
Enter first number: 10

Breakpoint 2, _start () at compute.s:27
27              push %rax

Now check what readInt returned:

(gdb) print $rax
$1 = 10

Good — %rax holds 10 as expected.

Step 3: Run to the arithmetic and step through it

(gdb) continue
Continuing.
Enter second number: 4

Breakpoint 3, _start () at compute.s:45
45              pop %rax

Now we are at the computation section. Let's step through it one instruction at a time with nexti:

(gdb) nexti
46              add %rbx, %rax
(gdb) print $rax
$2 = 10
(gdb) print $rbx
$3 = 4

The first number was restored from the stack into %rax, and the second number is in %rbx. After the add:

(gdb) nexti
47              imul $3, %rax, %rax
(gdb) print $rax
$4 = 14

After the imul:

(gdb) nexti
(gdb) print $rax
$5 = 42

The computation is correct: (10 + 4) × 3 = 42.

Step 4: Let it finish

(gdb) continue
Continuing.
Result: 42
[Inferior 1 (process 12345) exited normally]
(gdb) quit

This workflow — set breakpoints at the interesting locations, continue between them, and nexti through the tricky parts — is how you will typically use GDB in practice.

Quick Reference

CommandShortDescription
break <label>bSet a breakpoint at a label or address
runrStart (or restart) the program
stepisiExecute one instruction (step into calls)
nextiniExecute one instruction (step over calls)
continuecResume execution until next breakpoint
info registersi rShow all general-purpose registers
print $regpPrint the value of a register or expression
print/x $regp/xPrint in hexadecimal
x/NFU addrExamine memory (N units, Format, Unit size)
disassembledisasShow disassembly of the current function
info breakpointsi bList all breakpoints
delete Nd NDelete breakpoint number N
layout asmSwitch to TUI mode showing assembly
layout regsSwitch to TUI mode showing registers + assembly
quitqExit GDB

Tips

  • Pressing Enter with no command repeats the last command. This is especially useful with stepi — just keep pressing Enter to step one instruction at a time.
  • layout asm opens a split-screen view that shows the assembly code with an arrow pointing to the current instruction. layout regs adds a register display at the top. Press Ctrl-x a to exit TUI mode.
  • Watchpoints: watch $rax will pause the program whenever %rax changes. Useful for tracking down where a value gets corrupted. (Note: register watchpoints are slow — GDB must single-step internally since hardware watchpoints only work on memory addresses. For small programs this is fine.)
  • Conditional breakpoints: break _start if $rdi == 5 pauses only when the condition is true.
Connection to picoCTF: Many of the discussion exercises use picoCTF challenges that require reading assembly, setting breakpoints, and inspecting memory in GDB. The commands in this lesson — especially break, run, stepi, info registers, and x — are exactly what you will use in those exercises.

Module 3: x86-64 Assembly Fundamentals

Module 3 Summary

Wrap up

In this module, you wrote x86-64 assembly programs by hand using the as and ld toolchain, and compared your programs with the output of gcc -S. You progressed from a 3-line exit program to complete programs that use bare read/write syscalls, compute results using arithmetic and stack operations, and print output.

Key Takeaways

  • The build process has four stages: preprocessing, compiling, assembling, and linking. You can write assembly directly in .s files and use as and ld to bypass the compiler entirely.
  • Makefiles automate the build process. A Makefile specifies targets, prerequisites, and recipes so that make only rebuilds files whose dependencies have changed. Pattern rules (%.o: %.s) and automatic variables ($@, $<, $^) keep Makefiles concise even for multi-file projects.
  • x86-64 processors have 16 general-purpose registers, each accessible at 64-bit, 32-bit, 16-bit, or 8-bit widths. AT&T syntax uses % for registers, $ for immediates, and size suffixes (b/w/l/q).
  • The mov instruction copies data between registers and memory but cannot move memory-to-memory. The lea instruction computes addresses and is also used for fast arithmetic.
  • Global data lives in .data (read-write), .rodata (read-only), and .bss (zero-initialized) sections. Data is accessed using RIP-relative addressing: label(%rip).
  • Arithmetic instructions (add, sub, imul, idiv) and logical/shift instructions (and, or, xor, shl, shr) operate on registers and memory. Division uses implicit %rdx:%rax operands and requires cqto for sign extension.
  • Linux syscalls use %rax for the syscall number and return value. For bare byte I/O, read (0) reads from stdin into a buffer, and write (1) writes bytes from a buffer to stdout.
  • The program stack grows downward. push/pop and manual sub/add on %rsp provide temporary storage. Multi-file programs use .global/.extern and link with ld.

Module 4: x86-64 Assembly - Control, Functions, and Data

Module 4 Overview

In Module 4: x86-64 Assembly — Control, Functions, and Data, you will continue writing assembly programs by hand while learning how the processor handles control flow, function calls, and structured data. This module builds directly on the fundamentals from Module 3.

We begin with condition codes, comparisons, and jump instructions, then use them to implement if statements, loops, and switch statements. Next, we write functions in assembly: learning the calling convention, the stack frame layout, recursive function calls, and how to wrap bare read/write syscalls inside reusable functions. We also look at how arrays and structs are laid out in memory, examine buffer overflow vulnerabilities and their defenses, and conclude with floating point operations. Each topic follows the "write it by hand first, then see how gcc does it" approach.

Learning objectives

At the end of this learning module, you will be able to:

  1. Explain how condition codes are set by cmp and test, and use them with set and jump instructions
  2. Write assembly programs that implement if statements, loops, and switch statements
  3. Write assembly functions using the System V AMD64 calling convention (call, ret, argument registers)
  4. Distinguish the System V function calling convention from the Linux syscall convention, and write simple syscall wrapper functions
  5. Identify the components of a stack frame and explain the function prologue/epilogue
  6. Explain callee-saved vs. caller-saved registers and use them correctly in hand-written functions
  7. Write recursive assembly functions
  8. Describe how arrays and structures are laid out in memory, including alignment and padding
  9. Explain buffer overflow attacks and the defenses against them (ASLR, stack canaries, NX bit)
  10. Describe how floating point values are handled using XMM registers and SSE2 instructions

Learning activities

You are expected to do the following tasks in order to achieve the above objectives:

  1. Complete the reading listed below
  2. Read Lessons 1 to 9, work through the hand-written assembly examples, and complete the embedded practice problems
  3. Take the module quiz
  4. Review additional resources on the Module 4 Summary page

Reading

  • Bryant & O'Hallaron: Chapter 3, sections 3.6 - 3.11
  • Dive into Systems: Chapters 6 & 7

Module 4: x86-64 Assembly - Control, Functions, and Data

Lesson 1: Condition Codes, Comparisons, and Jumps

How the CPU Makes Decisions

High-level languages have if, while, and for. The CPU has none of these. Instead, it has condition codes (single-bit flags set by arithmetic operations) and jump instructions that branch based on those flags. All control flow in assembly — every if, every loop, every switch — is built from these two primitives.

The Four Condition Code Flags

The CPU maintains four condition code flags that are updated automatically by most arithmetic and logical instructions:

FlagNameSet when...
CFCarry FlagThe operation produced a carry out of (or borrow into) the most significant bit. Indicates unsigned overflow.
ZFZero FlagThe result of the operation is zero.
SFSign FlagThe result is negative (most significant bit is 1).
OFOverflow FlagThe operation caused a two's complement (signed) overflow.

These flags are set as a side effect of instructions like add, sub, and, xor, etc. The lea instruction does not set condition codes (it is an address computation, not an arithmetic operation).

Setting Flags Without Storing a Result: cmp and test

Often you want to compare two values without changing either one. Two special instructions do this:

InstructionComputesDescription
cmp S, DD − S (result discarded)Subtracts S from D, sets flags, but does not store the result. Used to compare two values.
test S, DD & S (result discarded)Bitwise AND of S and D, sets flags, but does not store the result. Used to test individual bits.
Operand order matters for cmp: cmp %rbx, %rax computes %rax - %rbx. The flags reflect the relationship of the second operand to the first. So after cmp %rbx, %rax, a "jump if greater" instruction checks whether %rax > %rbx. This is confusing — think of it as "compare %rax against %rbx."

The set Instructions

The set family reads the condition flags and stores a 0 or 1 in a single-byte register:

InstructionConditionDescription
sete D / setz DZF = 1Equal / zero
setne D / setnz DZF = 0Not equal / not zero
sets DSF = 1Negative
setns DSF = 0Non-negative
setg D~(SF^OF) & ~ZFGreater (signed)
setge D~(SF^OF)Greater or equal (signed)
setl DSF^OFLess (signed)
setle D(SF^OF) | ZFLess or equal (signed)
seta D~CF & ~ZFAbove (unsigned greater)
setae D~CFAbove or equal (unsigned)
setb DCFBelow (unsigned less)
setbe DCF | ZFBelow or equal (unsigned)

The destination must be a single-byte register (e.g., %al, %cl, %r8b).

Jump Instructions

Jump instructions change the program counter (%rip) to a target label, either unconditionally or based on condition flags:

InstructionConditionDescription
jmp label(always)Unconditional jump
je label / jz labelZF = 1Jump if equal / zero
jne label / jnz labelZF = 0Jump if not equal / not zero
js labelSF = 1Jump if negative
jns labelSF = 0Jump if non-negative
jg label~(SF^OF) & ~ZFJump if greater (signed)
jge label~(SF^OF)Jump if greater or equal (signed)
jl labelSF^OFJump if less (signed)
jle label(SF^OF) | ZFJump if less or equal (signed)
ja label~CF & ~ZFJump if above (unsigned)
jae label~CFJump if above or equal (unsigned)
jb labelCFJump if below (unsigned)
jbe labelCF | ZFJump if below or equal (unsigned)

Jump targets can be direct (a label name, like jmp loop_start) or indirect (an address stored in a register, like jmp *%rax). Indirect jumps are used in switch statements.

Hand-Write: Compare and Branch

This program compares two values and branches based on the result:

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        mov $1, %rax
        mov $2, %rbx
        cmp %rbx, %rax        # compute %rax - %rbx (sets flags)
        jne less               # jump if not equal (1 != 2, so we jump)
        mov $0, %rdi           # this line is skipped
        jmp finish
less:
        mov $10, %rdi          # we land here
finish:
        mov $60, %rax
        syscall
$ echo $?
10

After cmp %rbx, %rax, the flags reflect %rax - %rbx = 1 - 2 = -1. Since the result is not zero, ZF = 0, so jne (jump if not equal) takes the branch.

gcc Comparison: int max(int a, int b)

Consider this C function:

int max(int a, int b) {
    if (a > b)
        return a;
    return b;
}

Compiled with gcc -Og -S, you get something like:

max:
        cmpl    %esi, %edi     # compare a (edi) vs b (esi)
        movl    %esi, %eax     # assume b (default return)
        cmovgl  %edi, %eax     # if a > b, overwrite with a
        ret

Here gcc uses cmovg (conditional move if greater) instead of a jump. Conditional moves avoid branch misprediction penalties and are preferred by the compiler for simple two-way choices. We will see conditional moves again in Lesson 2.

Module 4: x86-64 Assembly - Control, Functions, and Data

Lesson 2: If Statements

Branching in Assembly

In C, you write if (condition) { ... } else { ... }. In assembly, this becomes a compare-and-jump pattern. The general strategy is:

  1. Evaluate the condition using cmp or test
  2. Use a conditional jump to skip over one branch
  3. Use an unconditional jmp to skip the other branch

Hand-Write: Positive, Zero, or Negative

This program checks whether a value is positive, zero, or negative, and exits with a different code for each case:

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        mov $-5, %rax          # value to test (try changing this)

        cmp $0, %rax
        jg positive            # jump if %rax > 0
        je is_zero             # jump if %rax == 0

negative:
        mov $1, %rdi           # exit code 1 = negative
        jmp done

is_zero:
        mov $2, %rdi           # exit code 2 = zero
        jmp done

positive:
        mov $3, %rdi           # exit code 3 = positive

done:
        mov $60, %rax
        syscall
$ echo $?
1

With %rax = -5, neither jg (jump if greater than 0) nor je (jump if equal to 0) fires, so execution falls through to the negative label. Try changing $-5 to $0 or $7 and verify the exit code changes.

The pattern

Notice the structure. The C equivalent would be:

if (x > 0)      goto positive;
if (x == 0)     goto is_zero;
/* fall through to negative */

Assembly "if statements" are really just conditional gotos. The jmp done after each case prevents falling through into the next case.

Inverted Conditions

A common pattern that gcc uses is to invert the condition. Instead of "jump to the then-branch if true," the compiler writes "jump past the then-branch if false." This avoids an extra unconditional jump:

# C: if (a == 0) { result = -1; }
        cmp $0, %eax
        jne skip_if            # jump PAST the body if NOT equal
        mov $-1, %eax          # this is the if-body
skip_if:
        ...

When reading compiler output, watch for these inverted conditions — a jne right after a comparison that checks for equality means "skip if the equality test fails."

gcc Comparison: Division by Zero Check

Consider this C function:

int divide(int a, int b) {
    int ans = 0;
    if (b == 0) {
        ans = -1;
    } else {
        ans = a / b;
    }
    return ans;
}

Compiled with gcc -Og -S:

divide:
        movl    $-1, %eax      # assume ans = -1 (b == 0 case)
        testl   %esi, %esi     # test b against itself (sets ZF if b == 0)
        je      .L1            # if b == 0, jump to return
        movl    %edi, %eax     # %eax = a
        cltd                   # sign-extend %eax into %edx:%eax
        idivl   %esi           # %eax = a / b
.L1:
        ret

Key observations:

  • gcc uses testl %esi, %esi to check if b is zero. This is equivalent to cmpl $0, %esi but is one byte shorter.
  • The condition is not inverted here: je jumps when b == 0, skipping the division. The compiler initialized %eax to -1 first, so if the jump is taken, -1 is already in the return register.
  • Notice cltd before idivl — this is the 32-bit version of cqto that sign-extends %eax into %edx:%eax.

Conditional Move: cmov

For simple two-way choices, modern CPUs offer conditional move instructions. A cmov copies a value only if the condition flags match:

cmp %esi, %edi
cmovgl %edi, %eax     # if edi > esi (signed), move edi into eax

Conditional moves can be more efficient than branching for simple two-way choices. Instead of jumping over code, the CPU computes both values and selects one, avoiding any penalty from guessing the wrong branch direction (a topic we will cover in detail in Module 8). gcc uses cmov whenever the two branches are simple assignments.

The condition suffixes for cmov are the same as for j instructions: cmove, cmovne, cmovg, cmovl, etc.

Module 4: x86-64 Assembly - Control, Functions, and Data

Lesson 3: Loops

Loops Are Just Conditional Jumps

Assembly has no built-in loop construct. Every loop is implemented with a backward jump: compare, and if the condition holds, jump back to an earlier label. There are three standard patterns, corresponding to do-while, while, and for loops in C.

Hand-Write: Sum 1 to N (Do-While Pattern)

The simplest loop pattern is do-while: execute the body, then check the condition and jump back if it holds. Let's sum the integers from 1 to 10:

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        mov $0, %rax           # sum = 0
        mov $1, %rcx           # i = 1

loop:
        add %rcx, %rax         # sum += i
        inc %rcx               # i++
        cmp $11, %rcx          # compare i to 11
        jl loop                # if i < 11, repeat

        mov %rax, %rdi         # exit with sum
        mov $60, %rax
        syscall
$ echo $?
55

The sum 1+2+...+10 = 55. The loop body always executes at least once, then the condition is checked at the bottom. This corresponds to:

do {
    sum += i;
    i++;
} while (i < 11);

While Loop: Jump-to-Middle Pattern

A while loop checks the condition before each iteration. One way to implement this is the jump-to-middle pattern: start with an unconditional jump to the condition check, then loop back from there:

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        mov $0, %rax           # sum = 0
        mov $1, %rcx           # i = 1
        jmp test               # jump to condition first

loop:
        add %rcx, %rax         # sum += i
        inc %rcx               # i++

test:
        cmp $11, %rcx
        jl loop                # if i < 11, go to loop body

        mov %rax, %rdi
        mov $60, %rax
        syscall

This produces the same result (55), but if %rcx were already 11 or higher at the start, the body would never execute — just like a C while loop.

This corresponds to:

while (i < 11) {
    sum += i;
    i++;
}

For Loops

A C for loop is really just a while loop with the initialization and update made explicit:

for (init; test; update) { body; }
// is equivalent to:
init;
while (test) { body; update; }

So the assembly pattern is the same as the while loop. Our sum example is already essentially a for loop: for (int i = 1; i < 11; i++) { sum += i; }

Hand-Write: Countdown with Output

Here is a loop that counts down from 5 to 1 and exits with the final value:

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        mov $5, %rcx           # start at 5

loop:
        dec %rcx               # i--
        cmp $0, %rcx
        jg loop                # if i > 0, keep going

        # %rcx is now 0
        mov %rcx, %rdi
        mov $60, %rax
        syscall
$ echo $?
0

dec sets the condition flags, so we could also write jnz loop (jump if not zero) instead of the cmp/jg pair. Using dec + jnz is a common loop optimization.

gcc Comparison: Three Loop Forms

Here are three C functions that all compute the same sum, compiled with gcc -Og -S:

Do-While

long dowhile(long n) {
    long sum = 0;
    long i = 1;
    do {
        sum += i;
        i++;
    } while (i <= n);
    return sum;
}

gcc output (simplified):

dowhile:
        movl    $0, %eax       # sum = 0
        movl    $1, %edx       # i = 1
.L2:
        addq    %rdx, %rax     # sum += i
        addq    $1, %rdx       # i++
        cmpq    %rdi, %rdx     # compare i to n
        jle     .L2            # if i <= n, loop
        ret

While

long awhile(long n) {
    long sum = 0;
    long i = 1;
    while (i <= n) {
        sum += i;
        i++;
    }
    return sum;
}

gcc output (jump-to-middle):

awhile:
        movl    $0, %eax       # sum = 0
        movl    $1, %edx       # i = 1
        jmp     .L5            # jump to test
.L6:
        addq    %rdx, %rax     # sum += i
        addq    $1, %rdx       # i++
.L5:
        cmpq    %rdi, %rdx     # compare i to n
        jle     .L6            # if i <= n, loop
        ret

For

long forloop(long n) {
    long sum = 0;
    for (long i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        sum += i;
    }
    return sum;
}

gcc produces nearly identical code to the while version — it converts the for to a while internally.

Notice how all three versions use the same registers (%rax for sum, %rdx for i, %rdi for n). The only difference is whether the test comes before or after the body.

Module 4: x86-64 Assembly - Control, Functions, and Data

Lesson 4: Switch Statements

Jump Tables

A switch statement with many cases could be implemented as a chain of if-else checks, but that would be slow for large switches. Instead, the compiler generates a jump table: an array of code addresses, one per case value. The switch variable is used as an index into this table, and an indirect jump goes directly to the correct case code in O(1) time.

Hand-Write: A Simple Dispatch Table

Let's write a program that takes a value (0, 1, or 2), looks it up in a jump table, and exits with a different code for each case:

        .section .data
value:  .long 1                # try changing to 0 or 2

        .section .rodata
        .align 8
jump_table:
        .quad case0
        .quad case1
        .quad case2

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        movl value(%rip), %eax        # load the switch variable
        cmpl $2, %eax                 # range check
        ja default                    # if above 2, go to default

        # Look up the target address in the jump table
        lea jump_table(%rip), %rdx
        movslq %eax, %rax             # sign-extend to 64-bit index
        jmp *(%rdx,%rax,8)            # indirect jump: jump_table[value]

case0:
        mov $10, %rdi
        jmp done
case1:
        mov $20, %rdi
        jmp done
case2:
        mov $30, %rdi
        jmp done
default:
        mov $99, %rdi

done:
        mov $60, %rax
        syscall
$ echo $?
20

With value = 1, the program looks up jump_table[1], which holds the address of case1, and jumps there directly.

How the jump table works

  • The jump table is stored in .rodata (it is constant data).
  • Each entry is a .quad (8-byte address) pointing to a case label.
  • The range check (cmpl $2, %eax / ja default) catches values outside 0–2 and sends them to the default case. Using ja (unsigned above) handles negative values too, since negative values become large positive values when treated as unsigned.
  • The indirect jump jmp *(%rdx,%rax,8) reads the address from jump_table + value*8 and jumps to it.

gcc Comparison: Full Switch Example

Consider a more complex switch:

long doswitch(long x) {
    long result;
    switch (x) {
        case 0: result = 10; break;
        case 1: result = 20; break;
        case 2:
        case 3: result = 30; break;   // shared case
        case 5: result = 50; break;   // gap at case 4
        default: result = -1;
    }
    return result;
}

gcc generates a jump table with entries for cases 0 through 5. For the missing case 4, the table entry points to the default code. For the shared cases 2 and 3, both table entries point to the same code block. The compiler:

  1. Subtracts the lowest case value (if not 0) to normalize the index
  2. Performs a range check using cmp and ja
  3. Uses the result as an index into the jump table stored in .rodata
  4. Executes an indirect jump via jmp *table(,%rax,8)

When gcc Uses If-Else Instead

The compiler does not always use a jump table. If the case values are sparse (e.g., case 1, case 100, case 10000), a jump table would waste enormous amounts of memory. In that situation, gcc falls back to a chain of compare-and-jump instructions, essentially an if-else ladder. For a small number of cases (typically 3 or fewer), if-else is also used since the jump table overhead is not worthwhile.

Module 4: x86-64 Assembly - Control, Functions, and Data

Lesson 5: Writing Functions

Functions in Assembly

In C, functions are a fundamental abstraction. In assembly, there is no built-in concept of a "function" — just labels you can jump to. What makes a label into a function is convention: the calling convention defines how arguments are passed, where the return value goes, and which registers must be preserved. On Linux x86-64, this is the System V AMD64 ABI.

call and ret

Two instructions provide the mechanism for function calls:

  • call label — Pushes the address of the next instruction (the return address) onto the stack, then jumps to label. Conceptually: push [return address]; jmp label (note: push %rip is not an actual valid instruction — the hardware does this internally)
  • ret — Pops the return address from the stack and jumps to it. Conceptually: pop [into %rip] (again, pop %rip is not a valid instruction — the hardware does this internally)

The Calling Convention

The System V AMD64 ABI defines three key rules:

1. Argument Passing

The first six integer/pointer arguments are passed in registers, in this order:

Argument #Register
1st%rdi
2nd%rsi
3rd%rdx
4th%rcx
5th%r8
6th%r9

Arguments beyond the sixth are pushed onto the stack (right to left). The return value is placed in %rax.

2. Callee-Saved Registers

The called function must preserve these registers — if it uses them, it must save and restore their original values:

%rbx, %rbp, %r12, %r13, %r14, %r15

3. Caller-Saved Registers

All other registers may be clobbered by the called function. If the caller needs their values after the call, it must save them itself (typically by pushing them onto the stack before the call):

%rax, %rcx, %rdx, %rsi, %rdi, %r8, %r9, %r10, %r11

Hand-Write: A Simple Function

Let's write a function add_nums that takes two arguments and returns their sum:

        .text
        .global _start

# Function: add_nums(a, b) -> a + b
add_nums:
        push %rbp              # save old base pointer
        mov %rsp, %rbp         # set up new base pointer
        mov %rdi, %rax         # %rax = first arg (a)
        add %rsi, %rax         # %rax = a + b (return value)
        pop %rbp               # restore base pointer
        ret

_start:
        mov $17, %rdi          # first argument
        mov $25, %rsi          # second argument
        call add_nums          # result in %rax

        mov %rax, %rdi         # exit with result
        mov $60, %rax
        syscall
$ echo $?
42

The push %rbp / mov %rsp, %rbp at the start and pop %rbp / ret at the end form the prologue and epilogue. For a function this simple, the prologue is not strictly necessary, but it is the standard pattern.

Function Calls Versus Syscalls

A normal function call and a Linux syscall are related but not identical interfaces. The call instruction follows the System V AMD64 function calling convention. The syscall instruction follows the Linux kernel's syscall convention.

InterfaceArgument registersReturn registerImportant clobbers
Function call%rdi, %rsi, %rdx, %rcx, %r8, %r9%raxcaller-saved registers may be overwritten
Syscall%rdi, %rsi, %rdx, %r10, %r8, %r9%rax%rcx, %r11

For read and write, only the first three arguments are used, so the two conventions line up nicely. That makes them perfect first examples of assembly wrapper functions. If you later wrap a syscall with four or more arguments, you must remember to move the fourth argument from %rcx into %r10 before executing syscall.

Hand-Write: Reusable read / write Wrappers

We can package bare syscalls inside ordinary assembly functions. The caller uses call with the normal function convention; the wrapper translates that request into a kernel syscall. In this example, we also use a branch to avoid writing anything when read returns EOF or an error.

        .section .rodata
prompt: .asciz "Type a line: "
plen = . - prompt - 1

        .section .bss
buffer: .skip 64

        .text
        .global _start

# write_buf(fd, buf, count) -> bytes written or negative error code
write_buf:
        mov $1, %rax
        syscall
        ret

# read_buf(fd, buf, count) -> bytes read or negative error code
read_buf:
        mov $0, %rax
        syscall
        ret

_start:
        mov $1, %rdi
        lea prompt(%rip), %rsi
        mov $plen, %rdx
        call write_buf

        mov $0, %rdi
        lea buffer(%rip), %rsi
        mov $64, %rdx
        call read_buf

        cmp $0, %rax
        jle done               # 0 = EOF, negative = error

        mov %rax, %rdx
        mov $1, %rdi
        lea buffer(%rip), %rsi
        call write_buf

done:
        mov $60, %rax
        xor %rdi, %rdi
        syscall
$ ./echo_line
Type a line: hello, syscalls
hello, syscalls

Key points in this program:

  • write_buf and read_buf are leaf functions: they do not call any other functions, so they need no stack frame here.
  • The caller passes (fd, buf, count) in %rdi, %rsi, and %rdx. The wrappers only need to place the syscall number in %rax.
  • read_buf returns the number of bytes read in %rax, just like the raw syscall. The caller then moves that value to %rdx before calling write_buf.
  • syscall clobbers %rcx and %r11. That is fine here because both are caller-saved registers anyway.

Hand-Write: Recursive Fibonacci

Recursion is the real test of understanding functions, because each call creates a new stack frame. Here is recursive Fibonacci:

        .text
        .global _start

# fib(n): returns the nth Fibonacci number
# fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1, fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)
fib:
        push %rbp
        mov %rsp, %rbp
        push %rbx              # save callee-saved register

        cmp $1, %rdi           # base case: n <= 1
        jle fib_base

        # Recursive case
        mov %rdi, %rbx         # save n in callee-saved %rbx
        dec %rdi               # n - 1
        call fib               # fib(n-1), result in %rax
        push %rax              # save fib(n-1) on stack

        lea -2(%rbx), %rdi     # n - 2
        call fib               # fib(n-2), result in %rax

        pop %rcx               # restore fib(n-1)
        add %rcx, %rax         # %rax = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)
        jmp fib_done

fib_base:
        mov %rdi, %rax         # return n (0 or 1)

fib_done:
        pop %rbx               # restore callee-saved register
        pop %rbp
        ret

_start:
        mov $10, %rdi          # compute fib(10)
        call fib
        mov %rax, %rdi         # exit with result
        mov $60, %rax
        syscall
$ echo $?
55

Key points in this program:

  • %rbx is callee-saved, so fib pushes and pops it. We use %rbx to hold n across the recursive calls because we know fib won't clobber it.
  • We save fib(n-1) on the stack before calling fib(n-2) because %rax is caller-saved and will be overwritten by the second call.
  • Each recursive call creates a new stack frame. For fib(10), there will be many nested frames on the stack simultaneously.

gcc Comparison: Function Compilation

The C equivalent:

int add_numbers(int a, int b) {
    int sum = a + b;
    return sum;
}

Compiled with gcc -Og -S:

add_numbers:
        leal    (%rdi,%rsi), %eax
        ret

gcc uses lea to compute a + b directly into %eax (the 32-bit return register). No prologue or epilogue — this is a leaf function (it doesn't call other functions) and doesn't need stack space, so gcc optimizes away the frame setup entirely.

Module 4: x86-64 Assembly - Control, Functions, and Data

Lesson 6: Local Variables and the Stack Frame

When Locals Need the Stack

In Lesson 5, our simple functions kept everything in registers. But a function with many local variables, or one that needs to take the address of a local (using & in C), must store those locals on the stack. The region of the stack belonging to a single function call is its stack frame.

Anatomy of a Stack Frame

When a function is called, its stack frame is laid out (from higher to lower addresses):

  1. Return address — Pushed by the call instruction. Located at (%rsp) upon function entry.
  2. Saved %rbp — Pushed by the prologue. After mov %rsp, %rbp, %rbp points here.
  3. Saved callee-saved registers — Pushed if the function needs to use %rbx, %r12–%r15.
  4. Local variables — Allocated by sub $N, %rsp. Accessed via negative offsets from %rbp.

The Prologue and Epilogue

The standard function prologue sets up the frame:

push %rbp              # save caller's base pointer
mov %rsp, %rbp         # establish our base pointer
sub $N, %rsp           # allocate N bytes for locals

Local variables are then accessed as -8(%rbp), -16(%rbp), -24(%rbp), etc. Using %rbp as a fixed reference point means the offsets don't change even if the function pushes more values onto the stack.

The standard epilogue tears it down:

leave                  # equivalent to: mov %rbp, %rsp; pop %rbp
ret                    # pop return address and jump

The leave instruction is a convenient shorthand that restores both %rsp and %rbp in one instruction.

Hand-Write: A Function with Local Variables

Here is a function that stores its arguments and an intermediate result as local variables on the stack:

        .text
        .global _start

# compute(a, b): returns (a + b) + (b * 2)
compute:
        push %rbp
        mov %rsp, %rbp
        sub $24, %rsp          # space for 3 locals (8 bytes each)

        mov %rdi, -8(%rbp)     # local1 = a
        mov %rsi, -16(%rbp)    # local2 = b

        # Compute a + b
        mov -8(%rbp), %rax
        add -16(%rbp), %rax
        mov %rax, -24(%rbp)    # local3 = a + b

        # Compute b * 2
        mov -16(%rbp), %rax
        shl $1, %rax           # %rax = b * 2

        # Final result = local3 + (b * 2)
        add -24(%rbp), %rax

        leave
        ret

_start:
        mov $10, %rdi          # a = 10
        mov $8, %rsi           # b = 8
        call compute           # (10 + 8) + (8 * 2) = 18 + 16 = 34
        mov %rax, %rdi
        mov $60, %rax
        syscall
$ echo $?
34

In practice, this function could keep everything in registers. We use stack locals here to illustrate the pattern. The compiler generates code like this when there are too many live values for the available registers.

gcc Comparison: -O0 vs -Og

Consider:

long compute(long a, long b) {
    long sum = a + b;
    long doubled = b * 2;
    return sum + doubled;
}

At -O0 (no optimization), gcc stores every variable on the stack, producing code almost identical to our hand-written version: prologue, sub $N, %rsp, moves to/from -8(%rbp), -16(%rbp), etc.

At -Og (basic optimization), gcc keeps everything in registers and often eliminates the prologue entirely:

compute:
        leaq    (%rdi,%rsi), %rax      # sum = a + b
        leaq    (%rax,%rsi,2), %rax    # sum + b*2 = a + 3b
        ret

gcc optimized sum + doubled into (a + b) + 2b = a + 3b and computed it with two lea instructions. This is why reading -O0 output is better for learning — it maps directly to the C source — while -Og or higher shows what the optimizer does.

Leaf Functions and Inlining

A leaf function is one that does not call any other functions. The compiler can optimize leaf functions aggressively:

  • No prologue/epilogue if all locals fit in registers
  • No need to save callee-saved registers if the function doesn't use them
  • May be inlined: the function body is copied directly into the caller, eliminating the call/ret overhead entirely

This is why small helper functions in C (like max(a,b)) have essentially zero overhead at higher optimization levels.

16-Byte Stack Alignment

The System V ABI requires that %rsp be aligned to a 16-byte boundary at the point of a call instruction. Since call pushes an 8-byte return address, %rsp will be 8 bytes off from 16-byte alignment at function entry. The prologue's push %rbp restores 16-byte alignment. If you allocate stack space with sub, the amount should keep %rsp 16-byte aligned.

If you get a segfault when calling library functions, misaligned stack is a common cause.

Module 4: x86-64 Assembly - Control, Functions, and Data

Lesson 7: Arrays, Structs, and Data Alignment

Arrays in Assembly

An array in C is a contiguous block of same-sized elements. In assembly, an array is simply a sequence of values at a labeled address. To access the ith element, you compute: base_address + i × element_size.

Hand-Write: Sum an Array

This program declares an array of five 8-byte integers and computes their sum using a loop with scaled index addressing:

        .section .data
arr:    .quad 10, 20, 30, 15, 25
len:    .quad 5

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        lea arr(%rip), %r8     # %r8 = base address of array
        mov $0, %r9            # %r9 = sum = 0
        mov $0, %rcx           # %rcx = index i = 0

loop:
        cmp $5, %rcx
        jge done               # if i >= 5, exit loop
        add (%r8,%rcx,8), %r9  # sum += arr[i]
        inc %rcx               # i++
        jmp loop

done:
        mov %r9, %rdi          # exit with sum
        mov $60, %rax
        syscall
$ echo $?
100

The key instruction is add (%r8,%rcx,8), %r9. This uses the scaled index addressing mode: base + index × 8. Since each .quad is 8 bytes, %rcx serves as both the loop counter and the array index.

Structures in Memory

A C struct is laid out as contiguous fields, each at a fixed offset from the start of the struct. The compiler calculates these offsets at compile time. In assembly, struct access is just memory access with a constant displacement:

# struct { long x; long y; int z; }
# Offsets: x at 0, y at 8, z at 16
# If %rdi points to the struct:
movq (%rdi), %rax        # load x (offset 0)
movq 8(%rdi), %rbx       # load y (offset 8)
movl 16(%rdi), %ecx      # load z (offset 16)

Unions

A C union stores all fields at the same memory offset (offset 0). The total size of the union equals the size of its largest field. Only one field can hold a valid value at a time:

# union { long l; int i; char c; }
# Size: 8 bytes (size of long)
# All fields start at offset 0
movq (%rdi), %rax        # read as long
movl (%rdi), %eax        # read as int (lower 4 bytes)
movb (%rdi), %al         # read as char (lowest byte)

Data Alignment

Modern processors access memory most efficiently when data is aligned — stored at an address that is a multiple of the data's size. The rules are:

  • A 1-byte value (char) can be at any address
  • A 2-byte value (short) should be at an even address
  • A 4-byte value (int) should be at a multiple of 4
  • An 8-byte value (long, pointer) should be at a multiple of 8

To satisfy alignment, the compiler inserts padding bytes between struct fields. This can make a struct larger than the sum of its field sizes.

Alignment Walkthrough

Consider this struct:

struct example {
    char  a;       // 1 byte
    int   b;       // 4 bytes
    char  c;       // 1 byte
    long  d;       // 8 bytes
};

Without padding, this would be 1 + 4 + 1 + 8 = 14 bytes. With alignment:

OffsetFieldSizeNotes
0a1
1–3(padding)3Align b to multiple of 4
4b4
8c1
9–15(padding)7Align d to multiple of 8
16d8

Total size: 24 bytes (not 14!). Additionally, the struct's overall size is padded to a multiple of 8 (its largest field's alignment), so arrays of this struct work correctly.

Reordering Fields to Save Space

If we reorder the fields from largest to smallest:

struct example_compact {
    long  d;       // 8 bytes at offset 0
    int   b;       // 4 bytes at offset 8
    char  a;       // 1 byte at offset 12
    char  c;       // 1 byte at offset 13
    // 2 bytes padding to reach multiple of 8
};

Total size: 16 bytes — 8 bytes smaller! This is a practical optimization when working with large numbers of structs.

Module 4: x86-64 Assembly - Control, Functions, and Data

Lesson 8: Buffer Overflows and Security

Out-of-Bounds Memory Access

C does not perform bounds checking on array accesses. If you write past the end of a buffer, you silently overwrite whatever happens to be next in memory — other local variables, the saved base pointer, or the return address. This is a buffer overflow.

Since local variables and the return address live on the stack, overflowing a stack-allocated buffer can corrupt the return address. When the function executes ret, it jumps to the corrupted address — which could be attacker-controlled code.

Hand-Write: Overflow Demonstration

This program allocates a small buffer on the stack and deliberately writes past it, demonstrating corruption of nearby stack metadata (here, the saved base pointer):

        .text
        .global _start

_start:
        push %rbp
        mov %rsp, %rbp
        sub $8, %rsp           # allocate 8-byte buffer at -8(%rbp)

        # Fill buffer (normal)
        movq $0x41414141, -8(%rbp)     # "AAAA" in the buffer

        # Overflow! Write past the buffer into saved %rbp
        movq $0x42424242, 0(%rbp)      # overwrites saved %rbp!

        # This corrupts frame-chain state. To hijack control flow directly,
        # an overflow typically targets the saved return address at 8(%rbp).
        # We exit safely instead of returning through the corrupted frame.
        mov $0, %rdi
        mov $60, %rax
        syscall

In a real attack scenario, the attacker would overflow the buffer until they overwrite the return address with the address of their own injected code (or a useful existing code sequence).

Why gets() Is Dangerous

The classic vulnerable function is gets() from the C standard library:

char buf[64];
gets(buf);    // reads unlimited input into 64-byte buffer!

gets() reads until a newline with no maximum length. If the user types more than 64 characters, it overflows the buffer. This is why fgets() (which takes a maximum length) should always be used instead. The gets() function has been removed from the C standard as of C11.

Thwarting Buffer Overflows

Expecting programmers to avoid all buffer overflows has not worked. Modern systems use multiple defense layers:

1. Stack Randomization (ASLR)

Address Space Layout Randomization allocates the stack at a random address each time a program runs. An attacker cannot predict where their injected code will be in memory.

One countermeasure: a NOP sled — the attacker prefixes injected code with thousands of nop instructions. If the return address lands anywhere in the sled, execution slides into the payload. ASLR's randomization range is usually large enough to defeat this.

2. Stack Canaries

The compiler inserts a random canary value between the buffer and the return address. Before the function returns, it checks whether the canary has been modified. If it has, a buffer overflow occurred and the program aborts with a "stack smashing detected" error.

# gcc inserts something like:
function_entry:
        mov %fs:0x28, %rax     # load canary from thread-local storage
        mov %rax, -8(%rbp)     # place canary on stack
        ...
function_exit:
        mov -8(%rbp), %rax
        xor %fs:0x28, %rax     # compare with original
        jne __stack_chk_fail   # if different, abort!
        leave
        ret

This is enabled by default in gcc. To disable it (for educational experiments only!), use -fno-stack-protector.

3. Non-Executable Stack (NX / DEP)

Modern hardware marks the stack as non-executable. Even if an attacker overwrites the return address to point into the stack, the CPU refuses to execute instructions from that memory region. This is enforced at the hardware level (the "NX bit" in page tables).

Attackers have responded with return-oriented programming (ROP), which chains together short instruction sequences ("gadgets") already present in executable code. Defending against ROP is an active area of research.

gcc Comparison: With and Without Protection

Compile the same vulnerable program two ways:

# With protection (default)
$ gcc -o vuln vuln.c

# Without protection
$ gcc -fno-stack-protector -o vuln_unsafe vuln.c

Disassemble both with objdump -d and compare. The protected version has extra instructions to load, store, and check the canary value. The unprotected version has none — and is vulnerable to a straightforward buffer overflow attack.

Variable-Size Stack Frames

Sometimes the compiler cannot know the stack frame size at compile time — for instance, when using alloca() or variable-length arrays. In this case, gcc uses %rbp as a fixed reference point and lets %rsp change dynamically. Local variables at fixed offsets from %rbp remain accessible even as the stack grows.

Module 4: x86-64 Assembly - Control, Functions, and Data

Lesson 9: Floating Point in Assembly

NOTE: This lesson provides a summary of floating point operations in x86-64 assembly. Floating point assembly will not be heavily tested on quizzes or exams — you should understand the general concepts and register layout, but detailed instruction memorization is not required.

Separate Hardware for Floating Point

Floating point numbers use a completely separate set of registers and instructions from the integer operations we have been studying. This reflects the hardware: the CPU has dedicated floating point/vector processing units designed for high-throughput parallel arithmetic.

The architecture has evolved through several generations: MMX, then SSE ("Streaming SIMD Extensions"), and most recently AVX ("Advanced Vector Extensions"). Modern gcc on x86-64 uses SSE2 instructions by default.

Floating Point Registers

There are 16 floating point registers at three sizes:

NameSizeNotes
%mm0–%mm764 bitsLegacy MMX registers (rarely used directly)
%xmm0–%xmm15128 bitsSSE registers. Used for scalar float/double operations.
%ymm0–%ymm15256 bitsAVX registers. The XMM registers are the lower half of these.

Each XMM register can hold a single float (32 bits in the low portion), a single double (64 bits in the low portion), or multiple values for SIMD parallel operations (e.g., 4 floats or 2 doubles). We will focus on scalar (single-value) operations.

Calling Convention for Floats

Floating point arguments are passed in %xmm0 through %xmm7 (up to 8 FP arguments). These are counted separately from integer arguments. For example:

void f(float a, int b, float c)
// a -> %xmm0, b -> %edi, c -> %xmm1

The return value goes in %xmm0. All XMM registers are caller-saved.

Moving Floating Point Data

The move instructions for floating point are:

InstructionDescription
movss S, DMove single-precision (float, 4 bytes)
movsd S, DMove double-precision (double, 8 bytes)

The same memory-to-memory restriction applies: you cannot movsd from one memory location to another.

Type Conversion Instructions

InstructionDirectionDescription
cvttss2si S, Dfloat → intConvert single-precision to integer (truncate). Source: XMM or memory. Dest: integer register.
cvttsd2si S, Ddouble → intConvert double-precision to integer (truncate).
cvtsi2ss S, Dint → floatConvert integer to single-precision. Source: integer register or memory. Dest: XMM register.
cvtsi2sd S, Dint → doubleConvert integer to double-precision.

Arithmetic Operations

SingleDoubleEffectDescription
addss S, Daddsd S, DS + D → DAddition
subss S, Dsubsd S, DD − S → DSubtraction
mulss S, Dmulsd S, DS × D → DMultiplication
divss S, Ddivsd S, DD / S → DDivision
maxss S, Dmaxsd S, Dmax(S,D) → DMaximum
minss S, Dminsd S, Dmin(S,D) → DMinimum
sqrtss S, Dsqrtsd S, D√S → DSquare root

Hand-Write: Floating Point Demo

This program loads two doubles from the data section, multiplies them, converts the result to an integer, and exits with it:

        .section .data
val_a:  .double 3.5
val_b:  .double 12.0

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        movsd val_a(%rip), %xmm0      # load 3.5
        movsd val_b(%rip), %xmm1      # load 12.0
        mulsd %xmm1, %xmm0            # %xmm0 = 3.5 * 12.0 = 42.0
        cvttsd2si %xmm0, %rdi         # convert to integer: 42
        mov $60, %rax
        syscall
$ echo $?
42

Floating Point Constants

Unlike integer instructions, most floating point instructions cannot use immediate values. Constants must be stored in memory (typically in .rodata) and loaded from there. The assembler directive .float stores a single-precision value; .double stores double-precision.

Comparisons

Floating point comparisons use ucomiss (single) and ucomisd (double). These set the same condition flags as integer cmp, so the same j instructions work:

ucomisd %xmm1, %xmm0      # compare xmm0 vs xmm1
ja label                   # jump if xmm0 > xmm1 (unsigned comparison)

The parity flag (PF) is set when either operand is NaN, which can be tested with jp (jump if parity).

Bitwise Operations on Floats

There are a few bitwise operations available for floating point: xorps/xorpd (XOR) and andps/andpd (AND). The most common use is zeroing a register:

xorpd %xmm0, %xmm0        # set %xmm0 to 0.0

gcc Comparison

Here is a C function and what gcc -Og -S produces:

double afunct(double ad, int count, double bd) {
    double sd = ad * bd;
    double res = sd * count;
    return res;
}
afunct:
        mulsd   %xmm1, %xmm0          # sd = ad * bd
        cvtsi2sd %edi, %xmm1          # convert count to double
        mulsd   %xmm1, %xmm0          # res = sd * count
        ret

Notice that ad is in %xmm0, bd is in %xmm1 (floating point arguments), and count is in %edi (integer argument). The compiler converts count to double before multiplying.

Module 4: x86-64 Assembly - Control, Functions, and Data

Module 4 Summary

Wrap up

In this module, you wrote assembly programs with control flow, functions, and structured data — completing the full arc from a 3-line exit program in Module 3 to recursive functions, syscall wrappers, and complex data structures. You also examined buffer overflow vulnerabilities and floating point operations.

Key Takeaways

  • Condition codes (CF, ZF, SF, OF) are set by arithmetic and comparison instructions. The cmp and test instructions set flags without storing a result. Jump instructions and conditional moves read these flags to implement branching.
  • All control flow — if statements, loops, and switch statements — is built from compare-and-jump patterns. Switch statements with many cases use jump tables for O(1) dispatch.
  • Functions in assembly are defined by convention, not hardware. The System V AMD64 calling convention specifies argument registers (%rdi, %rsi, ...), the return register (%rax), and which registers are callee-saved vs. caller-saved.
  • The Linux syscall convention is close to, but not identical to, the normal function calling convention. In particular, the fourth syscall argument uses %r10 instead of %rcx, and syscall clobbers %rcx and %r11.
  • A function's stack frame holds the return address, saved registers, and local variables. The prologue (push %rbp / mov %rsp, %rbp / sub) and epilogue (leave / ret) manage this frame.
  • Arrays use scaled-index addressing (base + index × size). Structs use fixed offsets with alignment padding. Reordering struct fields from largest to smallest minimizes wasted space.
  • Buffer overflows exploit C's lack of bounds checking. Defenses include ASLR (randomizing addresses), stack canaries (detecting corruption), and the NX bit (preventing code execution from the stack).
  • Floating point uses a separate set of 16 XMM registers and SSE2 instructions (movsd, addsd, mulsd, etc.). FP arguments pass in %xmm0–%xmm7, separately from integer arguments.
