Module 5: Processes, Signals, and Forking

Module 5 Overview

In Module 5: Processes, Signals, and Forking, we move from the instruction level up to the operating system level. We will study how the operating system manages running programs through processes and how it handles unexpected events through exceptional control flow.

We start by discussing control flow and exceptional control flow. The sole job of the CPU is to process one instruction after another, but sometimes events -- both hardware and software -- cause an abrupt change in that flow. We will talk about exceptions, what causes them, and how they are handled. From there, we learn about processes: what they are, how the operating system creates and manages them, and how to use system calls such as fork, exec, and wait to create and coordinate child processes. The module concludes with signal handling: how signals work as software-level exceptions, how to write signal handlers, and how to block signals safely from within your C code.

This module consolidates what were previously two separate modules (Processes and Signal Handling) into one comprehensive unit.

Learning objectives

At the end of this learning module, you will be able to:

  1. Explain control flow and exceptional control flow
  2. Define the four classes of exceptions (interrupts, traps, faults, and aborts)
  3. Describe what a process is and how processes are managed by the operating system
  4. Use fork to create child processes and predict the behavior of programs that use it
  5. Use exec to replace a process image and wait/waitpid to synchronize parent and child processes
  6. Explain how signals and signal handlers work
  7. Write signal handlers and install them using signal or sigaction
  8. Block and unblock signals from your C code using the appropriate library functions

Learning activities

You are expected to do the following tasks in order to achieve the above objectives:

  1. Complete the reading listed below
  2. Read Lessons 1 to 12 and complete the embedded practice problems
  3. Take the module quiz
  4. Review additional resources on the Module 5 Summary page

Reading

  • Bryant & O'Hallaron: Chapter 8

If you have questions, you can post them in the course lobby or send your instructor an email.

Module 5: Processes, Signals, and Forking

Lesson 1: Flow Control

NOTE: This is a summary of chapter 8, sections 8.1 to 8.4 in the textbook.

Flow Control

The sole job of the CPU is to process one instruction after another. Going from one instruction to another is called control transfer. A set of control transfers is called a flow of control or control flow.

Normal control flow is typically moving from one instruction to another along with any jumps. This is usually based on the 'state' of the internal variables. Sometimes this flow control needs to be interrupted by outside events.

For example, a hardware timer goes off at regular intervals and must be dealt with. A program had requested data from a disk and needs to be notified that the data is ready. Parent processes that create child processes must be notified when their children terminate.

In these cases the operating system makes some abrupt changes to the normal flow control of the program being run. This is called exceptional control flow (ECF). It is exceptional in that it would not be the normal flow control for the program if some event hadn't happened to interrupt this normal flow.

Module 5: Processes, Signals, and Forking

Lesson 2: Exceptions

Exceptions

The events that cause ECF to happen are called generically exceptions. An exception is an abrupt change in the control flow in response to some change in the processor’s state. The event might be directly related to the execution of the current instruction, such as a segmentation fault because the software was accessing a NULL pointer. On the other hand, the event might be unrelated to the execution of the currently running program, such as a signal that data from the disk is ready to be read by another program.

How Exceptions are Handled

When an exception happens, the hardware looks up an exception handler. This is a piece of code for managing a particular exception. Exception handlers are usually located in the operating system's code.

The start instruction for this code is stored in an exception table. The exception table is indexed by an exception number. When an exception happens, the hardware is given this number which it uses to look up which handler to run in the exception table. Exception numbers are assigned by either the operating system or by the hardware.

The hardware then transfers control flow to this handler. The handler is similar to a procedure call except the return address isn't necessarily the next instruction. Some additional processor state is also pushed onto either the program's stack or the kernel's stack.

When the handler is done, three things can happen depending on the exception. It can continue to run the program either starting at the same instruction or at the next instruction. It can also terminate the program (aborting) giving back control to the operating system.

Module 5: Processes, Signals, and Forking

Lesson 3: Classes of Exceptions

Classes of Exceptions

There are four classes of exceptions:

  • Interrupts: Interrupts occur asynchronously (basically at any time) as a result of signals from I/O devices that are external to the processor. Hardware interrupts are asynchronous in the sense that they are not caused by the execution of any particular instruction. These can happen in the middle of processing the current instruction in the CPU. The hardware signals the CPU by setting a 'pin' on the microchip that the CPU will read when it is done processing the current instruction. The hardware also sends the exception number on the system bus to let the CPU know which exception to run. Exception handlers for hardware interrupts are often called interrupt handlers.
  • Traps: This is one of three other synchronous exceptions that happen as a result of the current instruction (sometimes called the faulting instruction). Traps however are planned intentional exceptions not necessarily caused by an error.
    A system call (a call to a function that asks for a service to be performed by the operating system) is one common type of trap. System calls can be asking to access the disk, such as in a read() function, loading a new program or asking to prematurely terminate a program. In assembly code, there is the special instruction syscall that allows a program to ask for services from the operating system (the syscall number is placed in %rax before executing the instruction). This causes a trap to an exception handler that decodes the given arguments and runs the appropriate kernel routine.
  • Faults: Faults result from error conditions. They are also synchronous but might not be intentional on the part of the programmer. Control is passed to a fault handler that then tries to correct the problem. If it can do so, then it passes control to the same instruction so it can re-run. Otherwise it will stop the process (do an abort).
  • Aborts: These are also unintentional errors caused by the current instruction (so they are synchronous). But unlike faults, there is no way to recover from them and so the program is terminated. Usually these are hardware-related failures, such as a machine check exception caused by corrupted memory or a failed hardware component. (Note: integer divide by zero is technically classified as a fault, not an abort, though on Linux it typically terminates the process via SIGFPE.)

Module 5: Processes, Signals, and Forking

Lesson 4: Exceptions in Linux/x86-64 Systems

Exceptions in Linux/x86-64 Systems

In modern Linux systems, there are 256 possible exceptions. Numbers 0-31 are hardware exceptions defined by the architecture (Intel x86-64) and numbers 32-255 are interrupts and traps defined by the operating system (Linux).

The 256 exceptions are too numerous to list. Here is a short list of some common exceptions:

  • Divide Error (0) - This is classified as a fault. The kernel delivers SIGFPE, which terminates the process by default. This only works with integer arithmetic as floating point just sets the resulting value to infinity (inf) when a divide by zero is performed. Ironically, this is called a 'floating point exception' even if by default it only happens with integer math.
  • General Protection Fault (13) - This fault is triggered by segment-level protection violations such as privilege violations or certain misaligned accesses. Although the kernel delivers SIGSEGV for this exception, it is distinct from the more common Page Fault (exception 14) that produces the familiar "segmentation fault" when a program accesses invalid memory.
  • Page Fault (14) - These are pretty much recoverable so most application programmers rarely see this exception. This is when a part of memory is actually out on the disk drive instead of in main memory. A 'page' is how memory is divided.
  • Machine check (18) - Machine check is typically what is generated when hardware fails. This is always an abort (and may cause the operating system to abort).

Linux System Calls

There are hundreds of system calls in Linux. These are basically functions you can call within your C/C++ program to ask for services of the operating system. Typical ones are file I/O, managing processes (starting child processes or exiting the current process) and so on. Figure 8.10 in the textbook shows a table of some of these calls. We will discuss using some of these in future sections.

Module 5: Processes, Signals, and Forking

Lesson 5: Processes

Processes

To understand better how exceptions are handled, it helps to understand the workings of processes. According to the textbook, "A process is the instance of a program in execution". A program is a series of instructions that are run as a process (or as several processes as a program can be executed several times concurrently).

A process runs in a context which consists of the sum total of state (or information) needed to successfully run the process to completion. This state includes:

  • the program’s code and data stored in memory
  • its program stack
  • the contents of its general-purpose registers
  • its program counter
  • environment variables
  • the set of open file descriptors

When a program name is invoked at the command line (shell), the shell program creates a new process and the context needed to run the process to completion. An application program can also create a new process. This is called forking and we will talk more about this in the following sections.

How the operating system handles processes is complex. The textbook only discusses two things the operating system provides processes:

  • logical control flow.
  • address space.

For each process, these are independent from all other processes. This gives the illusion from a process's perspective that they have exclusive use of the CPU and the memory space.

Logical Control Flow

This is defined in the book as the series of PC (program counter) values that the CPU runs for just this one process. Basically it's the sequence of instructions a process is running from beginning to end. This is also abbreviated to logical flow.

A process is typically running concurrently with other processes in the system. This means that its logical flow overlaps in time with other processes. This makes it seem like these processes are running at the same time. However, if they share a CPU, only one process can run at the same time.

How does the operating system and hardware run several processes on the same CPU? This is done by interleaving the running of the processes. Each process takes turns using the CPU and memory for very short imperceptible time intervals.

Above shows an illustration of what interleaving is. There are 4 processes running on one CPU. They take turns running a portion of their instruction set before being preempted which means being suspended for a time. Each 'time slice' has one process running for a variable amount of time. How long and what process to run next is called scheduling and is decided by the operating system, which is run in between time slices.

The textbook puts more emphasis on a one-CPU system, but most modern CPUs have multiple CPUs called cores. The textbook does this for keeping the discussion simple and not having to get into the complex intricacies of scheduling on a multi-core CPU. So the picture of how programs are run is more complex than what's being presented here.

The preempting is done via a hardware interrupt that goes off every few milliseconds. This causes the currently running process to stop running (be preempted), the context is saved and the operating system's kernel is run. This is to allow the operating system to do its own tasks in-between each process (this is assuming it doesn't run in its own core). When the operating system is done it will choose another process to run and preempt itself.

Concurrent Flows

When one process's execution time overlaps another process's execution time they are said to be concurrent. Concurrency comes in two types: interleaving and parallelism. Interleaving is described as above. In today's multi-core systems, it's possible to have two processes concurrently run side-by-side (no interleaving) in two different cores. This is called parallel flows, parallel execution or running in parallel.

Private Address Space

Each process is run within a private address space that starts with 0 and goes (theoretically) to the size of the system's memory. In reality, the process is not likely to use all of this space and since portions of memory might be reserved for the operating system, it won't be able to use the full memory that the computer has to offer.

The system manages to create this illusion by mapping the program's addresses to actual physical addresses. Each program running at the same time is given a range of the actual memory addresses (usually this is 'growable' or 'shrinkable' depending on what each program needs). These are mapped starting at 0 and going to whatever the process needs. If the program needs more than the allocated memory it's given, part of the memory may be moved to disk to make room for the creation of more memory. So you can have two processes' addresses map to the same physical memory location. This is called virtual memory.

Figure 8.13 gives a much fuller view of this private address space. Note that the operating system (or its main process thread called the kernel) uses a portion of this space to store its own data, such as IO buffers the process has opened, syscall data, etc. This is inaccessible by the process itself and will throw a segmentation fault if the process tries to access it in any way.

User and Kernel Modes

Ordinary processes need to be restricted in what they can do and access while running; however, the operating system needs full access to everything. So processes can run in two modes: user mode for restricted access and kernel mode for full access. This is determined by a 'mode bit' inside a 'control register' that lets the CPU know whether the process running has access to sensitive parts of memory or can do only restricted tasks.

A process running in kernel mode can execute any instruction in the instruction set and access any memory location in the system. However, a processor in user mode is not allowed to execute privileged instructions that do things such as halt the processor, change the mode bit, or initiate an I/O operation. Nor is it allowed to directly reference code or data in the kernel area of the address space. Any such attempt results in a fatal protection fault. User programs must instead access kernel code and data indirectly via the system call interface.

Initially a process runs in user mode. It can be switched to kernel mode if an exception happens and an exception handler needs to be run. The mode bit is switched and then the exception handler is run in kernel mode. Then it is switched back to user mode to continue to run the rest of the process.

Context Switches

Every time a process needs to be switched out and in, its entire state (or 'context') needs to be switched in and out. The context of each process is kept by the kernel in its part of the memory space. An exception in hardware is used to do context switching.

Switching between processes is called scheduling and this is decided by the kernel's scheduler code.

It's not just interleaving processes on the same core that causes preemptive switching. If a process makes a system call, the process is switched out either because the operating system needs to run or because the process will be waiting on some long running action such as reading from the disk. Interrupts and other exceptions will cause processes to be switched out.

Module 5: Processes, Signals, and Forking

Lesson 6: Process Control

Process Control

This section goes over the use of some popular library functions for creating and managing processes. A process can create a separate process while it is running. The process doing the creating is called the parent process. The process being created is called the child process.

Obtaining Process ID

All processes have a unique ID called a process ID or just pid. A process can obtain its own pid by using getpid() function. It can get its parent's pid by using getppid().

// caller
   pid_t pid = getpid(); 
   // parent of caller
   pid_t ppid = getppid();

The type pid_t is currently an int type. This could change in the future.

Creating and Terminating Processes

Before we discuss creating and terminating processes, here are some states (the status of a process) that a process can be in:

  • running - currently executing or waiting to be executed.
  • stopped - suspended temporarily (signals: SIGSTOP, SIGTSTP, SIGTTIN, or SIGTTOU). While stopped the process won't be scheduled until the status changes back to running (signal: SIGCONT).
  • terminated - the process is permanently suspended and won't ever be scheduled to run. This is the result of:
    1. getting a signal (SIGKILL or SIGINT).
    2. returning from its main function.
    3. The exit() function has been called.

The main return value or the exit status number from an exit() call can be picked up by the parent program. This allows the parent program to find out how the child process was terminated.

Creating a Process Within a Process

The fork() function will create another process (a child process) within the running of another process (a parent process). The fork will create another separate process with a separate context but one where the initial values are copied from the parent's context. It actually will return twice: once in the parent process where it will return the pid of the child process. And once in the new child process where it will return a 0. PIDs are always non-zero positive numbers so this allows the following code after the fork (which will be running concurrently in each process) to tell which process it is: the child or the parent. See figure 8.15 for an example.

Because context is duplicated, variables are in separate memory spaces but files are shared (since file descriptor numbers are copied between each process).

Reaping Child Processes

When the child process terminates, it is not removed from the system. The parent process needs to reap the child process first in order to completely terminate the child process. Until the child process is reaped, it is called a zombie process.

If the parent process terminates before the child process does, the child process becomes a child of the init process (first process in the chain of processes that start running when the operating system boots up). The init process will then reap the child process.

If the parent process is a long running program (such as a daemon that runs in the background permanently) then the child may become a permanent zombie. Zombies use up resources such as memory. If enough of them are present this can slow down the system or cause it to run out of memory. It is important for long running programs to reap any child processes that have terminated.

To do this, use either the wait() function or the waitpid() function.

pid_t waitpid(pid_t pid, int* statusp, int options)

The three parameters are as follows:

  • pid - This is either the pid of the child to reap (this will only reap one child) OR -1 in which any one child in a wait set is reaped (the wait set is all child processes that have terminated unless options have changed the behavior). The pid of the reaped child is returned.
  • options - This allows for modifying the behavior of the call by passing in a pre-defined constant. You can OR (|) together several option constants to get multiple settings.
    The settings are:
    • WNOHANG - return immediately with a 0 if no child is waiting to be reaped. Otherwise the default behavior is to wait for a child to terminate.
    • WUNTRACED - suspend the executing of the calling process until a process in the wait set is terminated or stopped. The default behavior (without this flag) is to wait only for terminated processes. Adding WUNTRACED also reports stopped processes.
    • WCONTINUED - suspend until a process is terminated or a stopped process has continued.
  • statusp - This is a pointer to an integer. This is filled in by the function itself to give back information about how the process exited. There are a set of macros (these are pre-processor functions) that take the passed back int and either give further info or determine whether some state is true or false:
    • WIFEXITED(status) - True if the child terminated normally (via exit() or a return from main), regardless of what exit status was used. Use WEXITSTATUS to get the actual exit code.
    • WEXITSTATUS(status) - returns the exit status (the number put into an exit call or the return value in main). WARNING: Only the low 8 bits of the exit status are available (values 0-255). If the value is larger than 255, it is truncated to the low 8 bits (e.g., exit(256) results in a status of 0).
    • WIFSIGNALED(status) - True if terminated by a signal.
    • WTERMSIG(status) - If above is true, this will return the number of the signal that did the termination.
    • WIFSTOPPED(status) - True if the child is stopped (suspended).
    • WSTOPSIG(status) - Gets the signal number if above is true.
    • WIFCONTINUED(status) - True if child was restarted.

Note that waitpid() also picks up stopped or suspended children.

If an error has happened then waitpid() will send back a -1 and sets the errno (error code) to ECHILD. If the waitpid() was interrupted itself the error code will be EINTR.

The wait() function is as below:

pid_t wait(int *statusp);

It is a simpler version of waitpid() in that it's equivalent to:

waitpid(-1,&status,0);

In other words it will reap any child with no options (takes the default of waiting for a child to reap).

Putting Processes to Sleep

A function that can be used to suspend (or stop) the currently running process is sleep():

unsigned int sleep(unsigned int secs);

The function takes a time in seconds and returns how many actual seconds were left. This is because the process can be woken early if interrupted by a caught signal (any signal for which a handler has been installed).

Another function is the pause() function, which stops the process until it receives a signal:

int pause(void);

Loading and Running Different Processes

The fork command creates a process that runs the same code. But what if you want to run different code from another program? This is where execve() function comes in. This is a newer variation on the exec function.

The execve() function can be used to load a program and run it as a part of the process currently running. Note the current process becomes the loaded process so it no longer runs its own code. So it is said to NOT return to the same code if successful. It will return with a -1 if it is NOT successful.

int execve(const char *filename, 
     const char *argv[], const char *envp[]);

The filename is a path to the program. It can optionally take arguments to pass to the program and a set of environmental variables. Use getenv() function to get a pointer to environmental variables.

Note that if you call execve() within the program, the current program is replaced by the new program. If you want to keep the current program running, do a fork() first, and inside the child process, call the execve() function. This will keep the parent running as the current program but have the child become the new program.

You can look at the interesting example of a shell program in the textbook to see how execve() is used in code. I won't have you use execve() in labs or ask questions about it on the quiz/exam. So just basically know what it does.

Module 5: Processes, Signals, and Forking

Lesson 7: Examples of Using Fork

Examples of Using Fork to Create Child Processes

Below are some simple examples of using fork() and waitpid() to create and manage child processes. These will be helpful when doing the Module 5 lab. Note that these examples are under the Example Code submodule for Module 5.

Example 1: fork1.c

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <unistd.h>         // for fork()
#include <sys/types.h>      // for pid_t
#include <sys/wait.h>       // for waitpid()

int main()
{
   pid_t pid, ppid1, ppid2, cpid1, cpid2;
   int number = 1;
   
   pid = getpid();  //gets parent id
   // up to this point only the parent is running
   cpid1 = fork();
   
   // after this point BOTH parent and child
   // are running the SAME code below
   // However, the cpid1 number is DIFFERENT
   // in the parent and the child.
   
   if(cpid1 < 0) // error condition
   {
     // only parent exists if this happens
     printf("ERROR in forking\n");
   }
   else if(cpid1 == 0)  // this is the child
   {
     // This code will be run by the child
     // ONLY as the parent's cpid1 will not be 0.
     pid_t cpid2 = getpid(); // child's pid
     pid_t ppid2 = getppid();// parent's pid
     printf("CHILD: child's pid is %d\n",cpid2);
     printf("CHILD: parent's pid is %d\n", ppid2);
   }
   // pid > 0 so this is the parent, the pid is the child's
   else 
   {
     // This code will be run by the parent
     // ONLY as it will have non-zero returned
     pid_t ppid1 = getpid(); // parent's pid
     printf("PARENT: child's pid is %d\n", cpid1);
     printf("PARENT: parent's pid is %d\n", ppid1);
   }
   return 0;
}

Example Output (your output will have different pid numbers and might be in a different order):

PARENT: child's pid is 7491
PARENT: parent's pid is 7490
CHILD: child's pid is 7491
CHILD: parent's pid is 7490

Note that before any fork call, only the parent is running. After fork is called, there are two processes running the same code. The return value for fork is one of three things:

  • pid < 0 - This is an error where the fork couldn't be done. Assume only the parent is running at this point.
  • pid == 0 - This is what is passed back in the child process. You can use an if statement to process any code that the child needs to run.
  • pid > 0 - This is what is passed back in the parent process. In fact, the pid is the child's pid. Again, you can use an if statement to run any code that only the parent needs to run.

Note that the child's pid is available to the parent, but the child itself will need to call getpid() to get its own pid.

Control Order of Parent and Child

Since either process can be preempted at any time, this may change the order that the child and parent print to the terminal. There are some restrictions though. The order of output must match the order in which each printf() statement appears in each process. For example, the printf() statements for PARENT must be in the order shown in the code (they are only being run by the parent). However, you could have any CHILD printf() statements printed before, after or in-between any of the PARENT statements.

Figure 8.16 in Section 8.4.2 shows a technique called a process graph that you can use to determine the order that each process will do a task (print to terminal, etc). This technique will be handy for doing the Module 5 lab where you will need to determine the possible order of output to the terminal.

For example, the above has the following process graph

The printouts BETWEEN two parallel branches can be printed in any order. The printouts INSIDE one branch have to be in the order they are in. So the following output is possible:

PARENT: child's pid is 7491
CHILD: child's pid is 7491
PARENT: parent's pid is 7490
CHILD: parent's pid is 7490

because the order inside each branch is kept. However, the following output is NOT possible.

PARENT: parent's pid is 7490
PARENT: child's pid is 7491
CHILD: child's pid is 7491
CHILD: parent's pid is 7490

This is because it violates the order in the parent's branch.

Example 2: fork2.c

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <unistd.h>         // for fork()
#include <sys/types.h>      // for pid_t
#include <sys/wait.h>       // for waitpid()

int global = 10;

int main()
{
   pid_t pid, cpid1;
   int number = 1;
   
   // up to this point only the parent is running
   // global is 10 and number is 1.
   cpid1 = fork();
   // after this point BOTH parent and child
   // are running. The child inherits the 
   // variables declared before the fork
   // with their current values. However,
   // the 'number' variable is DIFFERENT
   // in each process.
   
   if(cpid1 < 0)
   {
     // only parent exists if this happens
     printf("ERROR in forking\n");
     return 0;
   }
   // these lines are run by BOTH processes in their own flow
   pid = getpid(); // gets either the child or parent pid
   printf("BEFORE: pid %d number is %d global is %d\n",pid, number, global);
   if(cpid1 == 0)  // this is the child
   {
     number = -100;
     global = -100;
   }
   else // pid > 0 so this is the parent
   {
     number = 200;
     global = 200;
   }
   sleep(1); // pause for 1 second so both processes are done running.
   
   // NOTE: this will print TWICE because two different
   // processes are going to print it.
   printf("AFTER: pid: %d number is %d global is %d\n", pid, number, global);
 
   return 0;
}

Example Output (your output may be in a different order)

BEFORE: pid 7851 number is 1 global is 10
BEFORE: pid 7852 number is 1 global is 10
AFTER: pid: 7851 number is 200 global is 200
AFTER: pid: 7852 number is -100 global is -100

This is illustrating what happens with variables. Any variable declared either as a global variable or as a local one is not shared between the two processes. Note that they do share the same values just after the fork. But when they change the value in their respective flows, the change doesn't affect the other process's values.

Example 3: fork3.c

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <unistd.h>         // for fork()
#include <sys/types.h>      // for pid_t
#include <sys/wait.h>       // for waitpid()

int main()
{
   pid_t cpid1, pid;
   
   cpid1 = fork();
   
   if(cpid1 < 0)
   {
     // only parent exists if this happens
     printf("ERROR in forking\n");
     return 0;
   }
   
   if(cpid1 == 0)  // this is the child
   {
      printf("CHILD's pid is %d\n", getpid());
      return 100;
   }
   
    // child has exited  so this is the parent
    printf("PARENT's pid is %d\n", getpid());
    int status;
    pid_t wpid = waitpid(-1, &status, 0); // taking defaults
    if(WIFEXITED(status)) 
    {
      int chstat = WEXITSTATUS(status);
      printf("PARENT: child %d exited with a status of %d\n", wpid, chstat); 
    }  
    return 0; // ONLY parent returns here
}

Example Output

PARENT's pid is 8864
CHILD's pid is 8865
PARENT: child 8865 exited with a status of 100

This is an example of using waitpid() to 'reap' a child process. Also, this picks up the child's return value in the parent, allowing for some information to be passed back to the parent.

I might point out that this method of getting information back to the parent is very limited. Only the low 8 bits of the exit status are available to the parent (values 0-255). If the return value is larger than 255, it is truncated to the low 8 bits (e.g., returning 256 results in a status of 0). There are better ways to pass information between processes, such as using shared memory via the mmap() system call, but they are beyond the scope of this course. Also, if processes need to share memory, it's much better to make them threads instead of separate processes. Threads are separate logical flows within the same process that share memory and context but have a different flow of instructions. Again, this is not something that is discussed in this course (although in my opinion they ought to).

Note that if the child terminates before the parent can get to the waitpid line, it will still be 'reaped' properly. This is because the child will be put into a 'zombie' state until the parent calls waitpid. Also, if the parent gets to the waitpid line before any child does terminate, then the program will hang until a child does terminate. Then it will 'reap' that child and go on. Which is why you need to use a while loop to 'reap' multiple children.

Example 4: fork4.c

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <unistd.h>         // for fork()
#include <sys/types.h>      // for pid_t
#include <sys/wait.h>       // for waitpid()

int main()
{
   int pid = 0;
   
   for(int i=1; i<=4; i++)
   {
     pid_t cpid = fork();
     if(cpid == 0) // this is a child
     {
        pid = getpid();
        printf("the %d child (pid %d) has been launched\n",i,pid);
        return i;
     }
   }
   
   // only parent gets this far
   int status;
   while ((pid = waitpid(-1, &status, 0)) > 0)
   {
     if (WIFEXITED(status))
       printf("child %d terminated normally with exit status=%d\n",pid, WEXITSTATUS(status));
     else
       printf("child %d terminated abnormally\n", pid);
   }
   return 0;
}

Example Output:

the 2 child (pid 9536) has been launched
the 1 child (pid 9535) has been launched
the 4 child (pid 9538) has been launched
the 3 child (pid 9537) has been launched
child 9535 terminated normally with exit status=1
child 9536 terminated normally with exit status=2
child 9537 terminated normally with exit status=3
child 9538 terminated normally with exit status=4

This is an example of launching multiple child processes and reaping them in the end. Note that I need to either return, exit or break out of the loop when in the child processes. If this isn't done, the child processes will generate their own child processes and so on. Try removing the if statement inside the for loop and see what happens.

Also, note that in order to pick up all children, I need a while loop. The way it works is if there are any child processes in a zombie state, one of them will be reaped and their information will be printed. Then waitpid is called again to pick up the next child process. If there are no child processes running or in a zombie state, waitpid will pass back a -1 and the while loop will end (since -1 is not greater than 0).

Module 5: Processes, Signals, and Forking

Lesson 8: Signals in Linux Systems

NOTE: This is a summary of chapter 8, section 8.5 in the textbook.

Signals in Linux Systems

Signals are higher-level or software-level exceptions that processes, including the operating system, can send to other processes (or to itself). These can be 'caught' by the process through a signal handler: a function that is to be called when the signal is caught by the process. If the process doesn't have a signal handler, the operating system has a default action that it takes.

The list of POSIX signals on the Signals (IPC) wiki shows all of the 31 standard signal types that can be sent in a Linux system. You don't need to memorize these signal types. Below is a list of some important signals:

  • SIGINT (2): default action: terminates
    this is sent to the foreground process running in a terminal when the user hits <ctrl> c. Also, can be sent to any user process by using the command "kill -2".
  • SIGFPE (8): default action: terminates with core dump
    Called a 'floating point exception', it is sent when dividing by 0 is attempted. Ironically, by default, floating point divide by zero isn't affected by this signal, only integers are.
  • SIGKILL (9): default action: terminates
    can send this by using the command kill -9 followed by the PID of the process. This is one of two signals that can't be overridden by a signal handler.
  • SIGSEGV (11): default action: terminates with core dump
    the infamous 'segmentation fault' when accessing invalid memory.
  • SIGALRM (14): default action: terminates
    can be used to set up a one-shot timer. The alarm() function sends this signal once after n seconds. To get repeated alarms, alarm() must be called again (e.g., from within the signal handler).
  • SIGCHLD (17): default action: ignores
    sent from a child process to its parent when the child terminates or is stopped.
  • SIGCONT (18): default action: ignores
    Sent to continue running a stopped process.
  • SIGSTOP (19): default action: stops until SIGCONT
    sent to a process to stop or suspend a process. This is NOT sent from the terminal when hitting <ctrl> z. It's typically used by the operating system, and its behavior cannot be changed by a signal handler.
  • SIGTSTP (20): default action: stops until SIGCONT
    Same as SIGSTOP except sent from a terminal. This IS sent from the terminal when hitting <ctrl> z.

We'll discuss how a process can deal with some of these in a later lesson.

Module 5: Processes, Signals, and Forking

Lesson 9: Signal Management

Signal Management

A signal is sent from the operating system to one or more processes due to some system event. The event can be a run-time error, such as divide by zero, or the user typing <ctrl> c at a terminal. Many of the signals available are low-level events that are only handled by the operating system. Processes can send signals to other processes including to themselves.

All signals are processed by the operating system (even ones sent to itself). The operating system then records the signal as pending in the process's context. For standard signals, you can think of this as a bit mask where each bit position corresponds to a signal number. Pending signals are not received by the process until the process is in a state where the kernel can deliver them.

The operating system will check first another bit flag to see if this signal has been blocked. A process can block most signals (except SIGKILL and SIGSTOP). When a signal is blocked, it cannot be received by the process and stays a pending signal until unblocked. This blocks even the default behavior. Note that blocking does not get rid of the signal; once the signal is unblocked, it is delivered to the process. If a process wants to prevent even the default behavior of the signal, it can use the signal library to ignore the signal. We'll discuss the signal library in detail in later sections.

Since there is one bit for each signal, the process can only receive one signal of a particular type at a time. If a signal of the same type is already pending, any additional signals of that type are discarded (since there is only one pending bit per signal type, signals are not queued). Signals of different types are tracked independently.

Group ID

Signals can target either a specific process or an entire process group, depending on how they are sent. For example, terminal-generated signals like <ctrl> c go to the foreground process group, while kill(pid, sig) targets one process. Each process belongs to one process group and has a process group ID (pgrp or pgid). Any child processes that a process forks are automatically put into the process's own group unless changed with process-group APIs.

To get the pgid:

#include <unistd.h>
pid_t getpgrp(void);

To set the pgid for itself or another process:

#include <unistd.h>
int setpgid(pid_t pid, pid_t pgid);

The parameters are the pid of the process and the group id of the group to put the process in. There are some special values that do something different:

  • if pid is 0: Set the current process to the given group pgid.
  • if pgid is 0: Set the group ID to the given pid.
  • if both are 0: Create a new group with the current process's current pid and put the current pid into this group.

Sending Signals

There are several ways to send a signal:

  • Sending Signals with the kill command: The kill command can be used to send not just terminate signals but any type of signal. The signal can be sent to either a specific process or it can be sent to all processes in a group.

    sending SIGKILL (signal 9) to a particular process (pid 15213, pgid 15111):
    kill -9 15213
    sending SIGKILL to all processes in a group, use a minus sign in front of the group ID: 
    kill -9 -15111
  • Sending signals with the keyboard: Both <ctrl> c and <ctrl> z send a signal to every process in the foreground's process group. So it affects not only the starting process but all of the process's children. If you want to distinguish what gets killed or stopped, you will need to provide a signal handler.
  • Sending signals with the kill() function: This function is in the C language signal library. It will send any signal (not just SIGKILL) to another process or itself: 
    #include <sys/types.h>
#include <signal.h>
int kill(pid_t pid, int sig);
    sig is the signal to send. If pid is positive, the signal is sent only to that process. if pid is zero, the signal is sent to all processes in the current process's group including the process itself. if the pid is negative, the signal is sent to all processes in the process group whose ID is the absolute value of pid (including the current process if it belongs to that group).
  • Sending Signals with the alarm() function: The alarm function in the signal library sends a SIGALRM to the process itself after n seconds. 
    #include <unistd.h>

unsigned int alarm(unsigned int secs);
    The return value is how many seconds were left on the last alarm sent or 0 if there was no previous alarm. Setting secs to 0 will cancel any pending alarms and not set any new ones. Note that this only sets one alarm not an interval of alarms sent every n seconds. There are other functions for doing this. Check out timer_create function for how to do repeated time intervals.

Receiving Signals: Signal Handlers

Whenever the kernel is about to resume user-mode execution for a process or thread (for example, after a system call or when scheduling it onto the CPU), it checks for pending unblocked signals. If a standard signal is pending and not blocked, the kernel delivers it and clears that pending bit. Standard signals are not queued, and if multiple different standard signals are pending, the delivery order is unspecified.

The process can do three things with this signal:

  1. if the SIG_IGN flag is set for this signal, it will ignore it.
  2. If there is a signal handler, it will be called.
  3. If there is no signal handler and it is not being ignored, it will do the default action for this signal: this can be terminate, stop the process or ignore the signal.

Signal Handlers

A signal handler modifies the default action for a particular signal. This is a function that is 'installed' using the signal() function from the signal library:

#include <signal.h>
typedef void (*sighandler_t)(int);

sighandler_t signal(int signum, sighandler_t handler);

It takes a signal number and a pointer to a function. A pointer to a function allows a function to be passed into another function to be called by that other function. To pass in a pointer to a function, just use the function name without any quotes around it. The function needs to have the header:

void {name}(int sig)

where {name} is replaced with the function name. the passed-in sig value is the signal number, as you can set the same handler to handle more than one signal (you need to install each one individually).

Instead of a pointer to a function, the handler argument can be one of two constants:

  • SIG_IGN: This sets the signal to be ignored completely. Works with all signals except SIGKILL and SIGSTOP.
  • SIG_DFL: This sets the signal to have the default behavior.

The signal() function returns a pointer to the previous signal handler (which may be a user-defined function, SIG_DFL, or SIG_IGN). It returns SIG_ERR on error.

Module 5: Processes, Signals, and Forking

Lesson 10: Blocking and Unblocking Signals

Blocking and Unblocking Signals

You can block signals from your C code by using a series of functions for blocking signals.

The function sigprocmask() takes an action and a bit flag ( or a mask). The mask has a 1 for every signal needed to be blocked or a 0 if the signal is not to be blocked.

#include <signal.h>
int sigprocmask(int how, const sigset_t *set, sigset_t *oldset);

The set argument is a mask with the signals' bits set to 1 that are to be affected. oldset is the current (before changing) blocking bit flag.

The how is a constant that indicates what to do with the set mask:

  • SIG_BLOCK - Just add any 1 bits to the current bit flag. This turns on blocking.
  • SIG_UNBLOCK - unset (set to 0) any 1 bits in the current bit flag. This turns off blocking.
  • SIG_SETMASK - this replaces the block bit flag with the passed-in set mask.

sigprocmask() returns 0 on OK and -1 on error.

sigprocmask() can also be used to get the current signal mask without changing anything by using SIG_UNBLOCK for the first parameter, NULL for the second parameter, and a pointer to an int for the third parameter. The third parameter will hold the current signal mask when the function is done.

Setting up set Mask

There are several other functions that can be used to create the set mask from scratch. These are used with any of the three sigprocmask actions (SIG_BLOCK, SIG_UNBLOCK, or SIG_SETMASK) to build the signal set.

The following (sigemptyset) creates an empty signal mask to be filled in by the other functions below:

int sigemptyset(sigset_t *set);

The following (sigfillset) will create a signal mask that has all signals set to one. This is useful if you want to block every signal. But remember that SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be blocked.

int sigfillset(sigset_t *set);

The following (sigaddset) will add (set to 1) a signal to the passed-in signal mask:

int sigaddset(sigset_t *set, int signum);

The following (sigdelset) will delete (set to 0) a signal from the passed-in signal mask.

int sigdelset(sigset_t *set, int signum);

All of these functions return a 0 if OK, −1 on error.

There is one more that can be useful for finding out if a signal is blocked or not:

int sigismember(const sigset_t *set, int signum);

Sends back a 1 if a member (is set to 1), a 0 if not a member (set to 0), or a −1 on error.

An Example: Blocking the SIGINT and SIGTSTP Signals

Here is a snippet of code that blocks the SIGINT and SIGTSTP signals. Afterwards this program can't be killed by using <ctrl> c OR suspended by using <ctrl> z . It can still be killed by using kill -9 though.

sigset_t mask, prev_mask; // type to use for bit mask

    sigemptyset(&mask); // make a blank bit mask
    sigaddset(&mask, SIGINT); // add SIGINT to bit mask
    sigaddset(&mask, SIGTSTP); // add SIGTSTP to bit mask

     /* Block SIGINT and SIGTSTP and save previous blocked set */
        sigprocmask(SIG_BLOCK, &mask, &prev_mask);
       ....

     /* Restore previous blocked set, unblocking SIGINT
        and SIGTSTP */
     sigprocmask(SIG_SETMASK, &prev_mask, NULL);

Module 5: Processes, Signals, and Forking

Lesson 11: Writing Signal Handlers

Writing Signal Handlers

Signal handlers are run differently than ordinary functions. There is no call located in the rest of the code to this function. Please don't call them yourself in your code. They are called from outside by the operating system while the rest of the process is running (usually this is done just when the process gets back from being preempted). A call can happen at any point in the running of your code. It can happen in the middle of processing a C code line (C code lines are usually equivalent to several machine code lines).

This causes some problems when sharing resources between signal handler and the main code in your program. For example, let's say an int type global variable called flag is being read or written to by both the handler and the main part of the program. The handler decides to write to flag at the same time the main program is reading flag. Since there may be several machine-level instructions in writing to memory, the main program may not pick up the right value.

To avoid this problem, whenever a global variable is written to and read by both the handler and the main program, use the 'volatile' keyword and the 'sig_atomic_t' type.

volatile sig_atomic_t flag;

Note that global variables that are constant and don't change don't need to be declared this way.

Also, remember that your handler is blocking the main code from running to completion. So it's suggested to keep signal handlers short and simple so they run quickly. If the main code needs to know that a signal was handled, use a global flag.

Also, there are some functions in the C standard libraries that may cause problems when called from the signal handler. Figure 8.33 in section 8.5.5 has a list of async-signal-safe functions that you can use. Note that printf() is not on the list. For output from the signal handler, you can use the write() function. Example 1 and Example 2 below show how to use it to print a message. For Example 4, I used a flag to get the main to print a signal from a child process.

Module 5: Processes, Signals, and Forking

Lesson 12: Signal Handler Examples

Signal Handler Examples

Here are some signal handler examples.

Example 1: Simple SIGINT Handler

This installs a simple handler to pick up any SIGINT signals. These are caused by hitting <ctrl> c at the terminal. Compile and run this program, then hit <ctrl> c to see what happens.

#include <unistd.h> // for sleep and write functions
#include <stdio.h>  // for printf
#include <signal.h>  // needed for the signal handling

#define MAX 10
#define STDOUT 1

void sigint_handler(int signum)
{
	char mess[100] = "\nOuch!\n";
	
	write(STDOUT, mess, 7);
}

int main(){
	int signum = SIGINT;
	
	//install signal handler for SIGINT
    signal(signum, sigint_handler);	
    
    // do some busy work
    int i =0;
    while(i < MAX)
    {
		sleep(1);
		i++;
    }
    printf("I've had enough! Goodbye!\n");
    return 0;
}

Note that I'm using the write() function within the signal handler to be on the safe side. The write function takes a file handle (1 is for standard out which means print to the terminal), an array of char, and the number of bytes to send, which is 7.

Example 2: Blocking SIGTSTP and SIGINT

This program shows how to block signals from being delivered. While signals are blocked, any signal handlers for those signals will not execute. Once the signals are unblocked, any pending signals that arrived during the blocked period will then be delivered.

#include <unistd.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <signal.h>

#define STDOUT 1

void sigint_handler(int signum) {
    char msg[] = "\nCaught SIGINT!\n";
    write(STDOUT, msg, sizeof(msg) - 1);
}

void busyWork() {
    for (int i = 5; i > 0; i--) {
        printf("  Working... %d seconds left\n", i);
        sleep(1);
    }
}

int main() {
    // Install handler for SIGINT
    signal(SIGINT, sigint_handler);

    printf("Phase 1: Signals are NOT blocked. Try Ctrl+C.\n");
    busyWork();

    // Block SIGINT and SIGTSTP
    sigset_t mask, prev_mask;
    sigemptyset(&mask);
    sigaddset(&mask, SIGINT);
    sigaddset(&mask, SIGTSTP);
    sigprocmask(SIG_BLOCK, &mask, &prev_mask);

    printf("\nPhase 2: SIGINT and SIGTSTP are BLOCKED. Try Ctrl+C now.\n");
    busyWork();

    // Restore the previous signal mask (unblock)
    printf("\nPhase 3: Unblocking signals now...\n");
    sigprocmask(SIG_SETMASK, &prev_mask, NULL);
    // Any SIGINT that arrived during Phase 2 will be delivered here

    printf("Done.\n");
    return 0;
}

Notice that during Phase 2, hitting <ctrl> c appears to do nothing. But once we restore the previous mask with SIG_SETMASK, the pending SIGINT is delivered and the handler runs. Remember: blocked signals are not lost, they are held as pending until unblocked.

Example 3: Using a global flag

This is a complete example of using a global flag to communicate between a signal handler and the main program. The handler only sets the flag (which is safe), and the main loop checks it. Note the use of volatile sig_atomic_t to ensure the compiler does not optimize away reads of the flag.

#include <unistd.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <signal.h>

volatile sig_atomic_t flag = 0;

void signal_handler(int signum) {
    if (signum == SIGINT)
        flag = 1;
    else if (signum == SIGTSTP)
        flag = 2;
}

int main() {
    // Install the same handler for both signals
    signal(SIGINT, signal_handler);
    signal(SIGTSTP, signal_handler);

    printf("Running. Press Ctrl+C to quit, Ctrl+Z to poke.\n");

    while (1) {
        sleep(1);
        if (flag == 1) {
            printf("Got a SIGINT! We'll quit now!\n");
            break;
        } else if (flag == 2) {
            printf("Got a SIGTSTP! Not quitting.\n");
            flag = 0;  // reset flag so we can detect the next one
        }
    }

    printf("Goodbye.\n");
    return 0;
}

Key points: the handler itself does nothing dangerous -- it just sets an integer. The main loop polls the flag each iteration. This pattern avoids calling printf() or other non-async-signal-safe functions inside the handler.

Example 4: Child Processes and Signals

This example demonstrates sending signals between a parent and child process. When fork() is called, the child inherits the parent's signal handlers. However, each process has its own copy of global variables, so the flag in the parent and the flag in the child are independent -- you cannot use a global variable to communicate between processes. Instead, we use kill() to send signals between them.

#include <unistd.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <sys/wait.h>

#define STDOUT 1

volatile sig_atomic_t got_signal = 0;

void handler(int signum) {
    // Use write() since it is async-signal-safe
    if (signum == SIGUSR1) {
        char msg[] = "  [Handler] Received SIGUSR1\n";
        write(STDOUT, msg, sizeof(msg) - 1);
        got_signal = 1;
    }
}

int main() {
    // Install handler for SIGUSR1 (before fork, so both processes inherit it)
    signal(SIGUSR1, handler);

    pid_t pid = fork();

    if (pid < 0) {
        perror("fork");
        exit(1);
    }

    if (pid == 0) {
        // --- Child process ---
        printf("Child (PID %d): sleeping, waiting for signal from parent...\n",
               getpid());

        // Wait for a signal from the parent
        while (!got_signal) {
            sleep(1);
        }

        printf("Child: got the signal! Sending SIGUSR1 back to parent (PID %d).\n",
               getppid());
        kill(getppid(), SIGUSR1);

        printf("Child: done.\n");
        exit(0);

    } else {
        // --- Parent process ---
        printf("Parent (PID %d): child is PID %d\n", getpid(), pid);
        sleep(2);  // give the child time to set up

        printf("Parent: sending SIGUSR1 to child...\n");
        kill(pid, SIGUSR1);

        // Now wait for the child to signal us back
        printf("Parent: waiting for child to signal back...\n");
        while (!got_signal) {
            sleep(1);
        }

        printf("Parent: got the signal back from child!\n");

        // Wait for child to finish
        waitpid(pid, NULL, 0);
        printf("Parent: child has exited. Done.\n");
    }

    return 0;
}

Trace through the code for each process:

  1. The parent installs a SIGUSR1 handler, then fork()s. Both processes now have the handler.
  2. The child sleeps, polling its got_signal flag.
  3. The parent sleeps briefly, then sends SIGUSR1 to the child via kill(pid, SIGUSR1).
  4. The child's handler fires, setting the child's copy of got_signal to 1.
  5. The child wakes up, sees the flag, and sends SIGUSR1 back to the parent via kill(getppid(), SIGUSR1).
  6. The parent's handler fires, setting the parent's copy of got_signal to 1.
  7. The parent wakes up, reaps the child with waitpid(), and both exit.

Key takeaway: after fork(), each process has its own address space. The got_signal variable is separate in each process. To communicate between processes, you must use mechanisms like signals, pipes, or shared memory.

Module 5: Processes, Signals, and Forking

Module 5 Summary

Wrap up

In this module, we moved from the instruction level to the operating system level. We discussed exceptional control flow and the four classes of exceptions. We learned about processes -- how the operating system creates, schedules, and terminates them -- and practiced using fork, exec, and wait to create and manage child processes. Finally, we studied signals: what they are, how to write signal handlers, and how to safely block and unblock them.

Key Takeaways

  • The sole job of the CPU is to process one instruction after another. Going from one instruction to the next is called a control transfer, and a sequence of control transfers is called the control flow. Exceptions are abrupt changes in the control flow triggered by some change in the processor's state.
  • In modern Linux systems, there are 256 possible exceptions. Numbers 0-31 are hardware exceptions defined by the architecture (Intel x86-64), and numbers 32-255 are interrupts and traps defined by the operating system.
  • A process is an instance of a program in execution. Each process has its own private address space and the illusion that it has exclusive use of the processor. The fork system call creates a new child process that is a copy of the parent, and the child and parent continue executing concurrently from the point of the fork.
  • The fork call returns twice: once in the parent (returning the child's PID) and once in the child (returning 0). Programs that use fork can produce different outputs on different runs because the order in which the parent and child execute is not guaranteed.
  • Signals are software-level exceptions that processes can send to other processes. A signal can be caught by installing a signal handler -- a function that the operating system calls when the signal is delivered to the process. If no handler is installed, the operating system takes a default action.
  • Signal handlers run asynchronously, outside the normal flow of the program. Because of this, signal handlers must be written carefully: they should use only async-signal-safe functions, and shared data structures should be protected by blocking signals during critical sections.

Module 6: Threads and Synchronization

Module 6 Overview

In this Module 6: Threads and Synchronization, you will learn about:

  • Threads: what they are, how they differ from processes, and why they are a fundamental building block of concurrent programs.
  • The POSIX threads (pthreads) library: how to create, manage, and join threads in C programs.
  • Race conditions: what happens when multiple threads access shared data without coordination, and why the results are unpredictable.
  • Mutexes: the primary synchronization primitive for protecting critical sections of code.
  • Condition variables and semaphores: more advanced synchronization tools for coordinating thread activity.
  • Classic concurrency problems: the Dining Philosophers problem and the Reader-Writer problem, which illustrate the challenges of concurrent programming.

Background

In earlier modules, you learned how to create new processes using fork() and how processes communicate using signals. Processes are heavyweight: each fork creates a complete copy of the address space. Threads offer a lighter-weight alternative. Multiple threads within the same process share the same address space (code, heap, global variables) but each has its own stack and set of registers. This makes threads cheaper to create and allows them to communicate through shared memory. However, shared memory introduces new problems: when multiple threads read and write the same data simultaneously, the results can be unpredictable and incorrect. This module teaches you how to write correct concurrent programs by using synchronization primitives.

Learning Objectives

At the end of this learning module, you will be able to:

  1. Explain the difference between threads and processes, including what is shared and what is private to each thread.
  2. Create and join POSIX threads using pthread_create() and pthread_join(), passing arguments and receiving return values.
  3. Identify race conditions in concurrent code and explain why they produce incorrect results.
  4. Use mutexes (pthread_mutex_t) to protect critical sections and prevent race conditions.
  5. Use condition variables (pthread_cond_t) and semaphores (sem_t) to coordinate threads that must wait for specific conditions.
  6. Describe classic concurrency problems (Dining Philosophers, Reader-Writer) and implement solutions that avoid deadlock and starvation.
  7. Identify and avoid common pitfalls in concurrent programming, including deadlock, starvation, and data races.

Learning Activities

You are expected to do the following tasks in order to achieve the above objectives:

  1. Read Lessons 1 through 6 and study the code examples carefully. Type them in and run them yourself.
  2. Compile and experiment with the provided C programs. Observe how race conditions produce different results on each run.
  3. Complete Discussion 6
  4. Take Quiz 6
  5. Review additional resources in the Module 6 Summary
Important: The code examples in this module require the pthreads library. When compiling, prefer the -pthread flag. For example: gcc -o myprogram myprogram.c -pthread

If you have questions, you can post them in the Course Lobby or send your instructor an email.

Module 6: Threads and Synchronization

Lesson 1: Threads vs. Processes

Introduction

You already know how to create a new process using fork(). When a process calls fork(), the operating system creates an entirely new process with its own copy of the address space. The parent and child processes do not share memory: changes made in one process are invisible to the other (unless you set up explicit inter-process communication like pipes or shared memory segments).

A thread is a different kind of concurrent execution unit. Threads exist within a process. A single process can contain multiple threads, and all threads within that process share the same address space. This means they share the same code, the same global variables, and the same heap memory. However, each thread has its own stack and its own set of CPU registers (including its own program counter).

What Is a Thread?

A thread is sometimes called a lightweight process. It is the smallest unit of execution that the operating system can schedule. Every process has at least one thread (the main thread), which is the thread that begins executing at main().

When you create additional threads, they begin executing a function you specify. All threads in the process run concurrently. On a multi-core CPU, threads can run truly in parallel (at the same instant on different cores). On a single-core CPU, the operating system rapidly switches between threads, giving the illusion of parallelism.

Threads vs Processes: Key Differences

Property Process (fork) Thread (pthread_create)
Address space Each process has its own copy All threads share the same address space
Code segment Copied (copy-on-write) Shared
Global variables Each process has its own copy Shared among all threads
Heap memory Each process has its own copy Shared among all threads
Stack Each process has its own Each thread has its own
Registers Each process has its own Each thread has its own
File descriptors Copied at fork time Shared among all threads
Creation cost Expensive (copy address space) Cheap (just allocate a stack)
Communication Requires IPC (pipes, signals, shared memory) Direct access to shared variables
Isolation Strong: crash in one process does not affect another Weak: a bug in one thread can corrupt data for all threads

The Thread Memory Model

The diagram below shows how memory is laid out when a process has multiple threads. Notice that the code, global/static data, and heap are shared, while each thread has its own stack.

+--------------------------------------------------+
|                  PROCESS                         |
+--------------------------------------------------+
|                                                  |
|   Code (Text) Segment        [SHARED]            |
|   (program instructions)                         |
|                                                  |
+--------------------------------------------------+
|                                                  |
|   Global / Static Data       [SHARED]            |
|   (global variables, static variables)           |
|                                                  |
+--------------------------------------------------+
|                                                  |
|   Heap                       [SHARED]            |
|   (malloc'd memory)                              |
|   grows upward -->                               |
|                                                  |
+--------------------------------------------------+
|                                                  |
|              ... free space ...                   |
|                                                  |
+--------------------------------------------------+
|                                                  |
|   Thread 3 Stack             [PRIVATE]           |
|   (local variables, return addresses)            |
|                                                  |
+--------------------------------------------------+
|   Thread 2 Stack             [PRIVATE]           |
|   (local variables, return addresses)            |
|                                                  |
+--------------------------------------------------+
|   Thread 1 Stack (Main)      [PRIVATE]           |
|   (local variables, return addresses)            |
|                                                  |
+--------------------------------------------------+

Compare this to what happens with fork():

+-------------------------+    +-------------------------+
|      PARENT PROCESS     |    |      CHILD PROCESS      |
+-------------------------+    +-------------------------+
|  Code      [OWN COPY]  |    |  Code      [OWN COPY]  |
|  Globals   [OWN COPY]  |    |  Globals   [OWN COPY]  |
|  Heap      [OWN COPY]  |    |  Heap      [OWN COPY]  |
|  Stack     [OWN COPY]  |    |  Stack     [OWN COPY]  |
+-------------------------+    +-------------------------+
  Completely separate            Completely separate
  address spaces                 address spaces

Why Use Threads?

There are several important reasons to use threads instead of (or in addition to) processes:

1. Performance and Efficiency

Creating a thread is much faster than creating a new process. With fork(), the operating system must duplicate the entire address space (even with copy-on-write optimization, there is overhead for setting up page tables). Creating a thread only requires allocating a new stack and some bookkeeping. Context switching between threads within the same process is also faster than switching between processes, because the memory mappings do not need to change.

2. Shared Memory Communication

Because threads share the same address space, they can communicate simply by reading and writing shared variables. With separate processes, you need to set up pipes, shared memory segments, message queues, or other IPC mechanisms. Thread communication is more direct, though as we will see, it requires careful synchronization.

3. Parallelism

On a multi-core system, threads allow your program to do real work in parallel. For example, if you need to process a large array, you can divide it among several threads, each working on a portion simultaneously. This can give you a significant speedup.

4. Responsiveness

In a program with a user interface, one thread can handle user input while another thread performs a long computation in the background. Without threads, the program would freeze during the computation.

When to Use Threads vs fork()

Use threads when:

  • The concurrent tasks need to share data frequently.
  • You need low overhead for creating and managing concurrent tasks.
  • The tasks are parts of the same logical program (e.g., a web server handling multiple requests).

Use fork() when:

  • You need strong isolation between concurrent tasks (a bug in one should not crash the other).
  • You want to run a completely different program (fork + exec).
  • Security is a concern and you want to limit what each task can access.

What Threads Share and What They Do Not

Let us be precise about what is shared and what is private:

Shared by all threads in a process:

  • The code (text) segment
  • Global and static variables
  • The heap (anything allocated with malloc)
  • Open file descriptors
  • Signal handlers and signal dispositions
  • The current working directory
  • User and group IDs

Private to each thread:

  • Thread ID (pthread_t)
  • Stack (local variables, function call chain)
  • CPU registers (including the program counter and stack pointer)
  • The errno variable (each thread has its own copy)
  • Signal mask (which signals are blocked)
  • Thread-specific data (set with pthread_setspecific)

A Simple Illustration

Here is a small program to demonstrate that threads share global variables but have separate stacks (local variables). We will learn the details of pthread_create and pthread_join in the next lesson; for now, just focus on the output.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <pthread.h>

int shared_global = 0;  /* shared by all threads */

void *thread_func(void *arg) {
    int local_var = 42;  /* private to this thread */
    shared_global = 100; /* modifies the shared global */

    printf("Thread: shared_global = %d\n", shared_global);
    printf("Thread: local_var = %d\n", local_var);
    printf("Thread: address of local_var = %p\n",
           (void *)&local_var);
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    int local_var = 7;  /* private to main thread */
    pthread_t tid;

    printf("Main before: shared_global = %d\n", shared_global);

    pthread_create(&tid, NULL, thread_func, NULL);
    pthread_join(tid, NULL);

    printf("Main after: shared_global = %d\n", shared_global);
    printf("Main: local_var = %d\n", local_var);
    printf("Main: address of local_var = %p\n",
           (void *)&local_var);

    return 0;
}

Compile and run:

gcc -o threads_demo threads_demo.c -lpthread
./threads_demo

Sample output:

Main before: shared_global = 0
Thread: shared_global = 100
Thread: local_var = 42
Thread: address of local_var = 0x7f2a1c000ef4
Main after: shared_global = 100
Main: local_var = 7
Main: address of local_var = 0x7ffd5a3b1c2c

Notice the following:

  • The thread changed shared_global to 100, and main can see that change (it prints 100 after the thread finishes). This confirms that global variables are shared.
  • The thread's local_var is 42, but main's local_var is still 7. Local variables live on each thread's private stack and are independent.
  • The addresses of the two local_var variables are very different, confirming they are on separate stacks.
Warning: The fact that threads share memory is both their greatest strength and their greatest danger. If two threads modify the same variable at the same time without synchronization, the results are unpredictable. We will explore this problem in detail starting in Lesson 3.

Key Takeaways

  • A thread is a lightweight unit of execution within a process.
  • All threads in a process share the same address space (code, globals, heap).
  • Each thread has its own stack and registers.
  • Threads are cheaper to create and faster to context-switch than processes.
  • Shared memory makes communication easy but introduces the risk of race conditions.
  • Use threads for concurrent tasks that need to share data; use fork() when you need isolation.

Module 6: Threads and Synchronization

Lesson 2: Creating and Joining Threads

The POSIX Threads Library (pthreads)

On Linux and other Unix-like systems, the standard library for thread programming is POSIX Threads, commonly called pthreads. To use it, include the header <pthread.h> and compile/link with -pthread (preferred on Linux). The older -lpthread form also works for many of the examples in this course.

#include <pthread.h>

All pthread functions and types begin with pthread_. The functions return 0 on success and an error number on failure (they do not set errno like many other system calls).

The pthread_t Type

Every thread is identified by a value of type pthread_t. This is an opaque type; you should not make assumptions about its internal structure. You use it to refer to a specific thread when calling functions like pthread_join().

pthread_t tid;  /* declare a thread ID variable */

Creating a Thread: pthread_create()

The function pthread_create() creates a new thread. Its signature is:

int pthread_create(pthread_t *thread,
                   const pthread_attr_t *attr,
                   void *(*start_routine)(void *),
                   void *arg);

Let us break down each parameter:

Parameter Description
thread Pointer to a pthread_t variable. On success, the new thread's ID is stored here.
attr Pointer to thread attributes (stack size, scheduling, etc). Pass NULL for default attributes. You will almost always pass NULL.
start_routine A pointer to the function the new thread will execute. This function must take a single void * parameter and return void *.
arg The argument to pass to start_routine. Use NULL if you do not need to pass anything.

The third parameter deserves special attention. The type void *(*start_routine)(void *) means "a pointer to a function that takes a void pointer and returns a void pointer." Your thread function must have exactly this signature.

A Minimal Example

#include <stdio.h>
#include <pthread.h>

void *say_hello(void *arg) {
    printf("Hello from the new thread!\n");
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t tid;

    /* Create a new thread that runs say_hello */
    pthread_create(&tid, NULL, say_hello, NULL);

    /* Wait for the thread to finish */
    pthread_join(tid, NULL);

    printf("Thread has finished. Back in main.\n");
    return 0;
}

Compile and run:

gcc -o hello_thread hello_thread.c -lpthread
./hello_thread

Output:

Hello from the new thread!
Thread has finished. Back in main.

Waiting for a Thread: pthread_join()

The function pthread_join() blocks the calling thread until the specified thread terminates. It is analogous to waitpid() for processes.

int pthread_join(pthread_t thread, void **retval);
Parameter Description
thread The thread ID of the thread to wait for.
retval If not NULL, the return value of the thread's start function is stored here. Pass NULL if you do not need the return value.
Important: If you do not call pthread_join() (and the thread is not detached), the thread's resources are not fully released when it terminates. This is similar to a zombie process. Always join your threads or detach them.

Passing Arguments to Threads

The fourth parameter to pthread_create is a void *. This is the generic pointer type in C: it can point to anything. To pass data to your thread function, you pass the address of the data, and inside the function you cast the void pointer back to the appropriate type.

Passing a Single Integer

A common pattern is to pass an integer to a thread. You must be careful: you cannot simply cast an int to a void pointer and back (this is technically undefined behavior on some platforms, though it works on most). The safe approach is to pass a pointer to the integer:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <pthread.h>

void *print_number(void *arg) {
    int *num_ptr = (int *)arg;   /* cast void* back to int* */
    printf("Thread received: %d\n", *num_ptr);
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t tid;
    int value = 42;

    pthread_create(&tid, NULL, print_number, &value);
    pthread_join(tid, NULL);

    return 0;
}

Output:

Thread received: 42

The Danger of Passing Stack Variables to Multiple Threads

When creating multiple threads in a loop, a very common mistake is to pass the address of the loop variable. Consider this BROKEN example:

/* WARNING: This code has a bug! */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <pthread.h>

#define NUM_THREADS 5

void *print_id(void *arg) {
    int *id_ptr = (int *)arg;
    printf("I am thread %d\n", *id_ptr);
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t threads[NUM_THREADS];

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; i++) {
        /* BUG: passing address of i, which changes! */
        pthread_create(&threads[i], NULL, print_id, &i);
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; i++) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], NULL);
    }
    return 0;
}

This is a race condition. The loop variable i changes as the loop progresses, and all threads receive a pointer to the same variable. By the time a thread runs and dereferences the pointer, i may have already moved to the next value. You might see output like:

I am thread 2
I am thread 3
I am thread 5
I am thread 5
I am thread 5

The correct approach is to give each thread its own copy of the argument. One way is to use an array:

/* CORRECT version */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <pthread.h>

#define NUM_THREADS 5

void *print_id(void *arg) {
    int *id_ptr = (int *)arg;
    printf("I am thread %d\n", *id_ptr);
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t threads[NUM_THREADS];
    int thread_args[NUM_THREADS];

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; i++) {
        thread_args[i] = i;  /* each thread gets its own copy */
        pthread_create(&threads[i], NULL, print_id,
                       &thread_args[i]);
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; i++) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], NULL);
    }
    return 0;
}

Now each thread has its own integer that will not change. The output (in some order) will be:

I am thread 0
I am thread 1
I am thread 2
I am thread 3
I am thread 4

(The order may vary because threads run concurrently, but each thread will correctly print its own ID.)

Passing a Struct

If you need to pass multiple values to a thread, define a struct and pass a pointer to it:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <pthread.h>

typedef struct {
    int id;
    char name[32];
    double value;
} thread_data_t;

void *worker(void *arg) {
    thread_data_t *data = (thread_data_t *)arg;
    printf("Thread %d: name=%s, value=%.2f\n",
           data->id, data->name, data->value);
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t tid;
    thread_data_t data = {1, "alpha", 3.14};

    pthread_create(&tid, NULL, worker, &data);
    pthread_join(tid, NULL);

    return 0;
}

Output:

Thread 1: name=alpha, value=3.14

Returning Values from Threads
