A thread function returns void *. You can return a value by returning a pointer. The calling thread retrieves this value through pthread_join().

Warning: Do not return a pointer to a local variable! The thread's stack is deallocated when it finishes. Use malloc to allocate the return value on the heap, or use a global/static variable. 
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <pthread.h>

void *compute_sum(void *arg) {
    int *range = (int *)arg;  /* array of two ints: start, end */
    int start = range[0];
    int end = range[1];

    /* Allocate result on the heap so it survives after return */
    long *result = malloc(sizeof(long));
    *result = 0;

    for (int i = start; i <= end; i++) {
        *result += i;
    }

    printf("Thread computed sum from %d to %d = %ld\n",
           start, end, *result);
    return (void *)result;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t tid;
    int range[] = {1, 1000000};
    void *retval;

    pthread_create(&tid, NULL, compute_sum, range);
    pthread_join(tid, &retval);

    long *sum = (long *)retval;
    printf("Main received result: %ld\n", *sum);

    free(sum);  /* free the memory allocated by the thread */
    return 0;
}

Compile and run:

gcc -o sum_thread sum_thread.c -lpthread
./sum_thread

Output:

Thread computed sum from 1 to 1000000 = 500000500000
Main received result: 500000500000

Creating Multiple Threads

Here is a complete example that creates several threads, each performing work, and then joins them all:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <pthread.h>

#define NUM_THREADS 4

void *do_work(void *arg) {
    int id = *(int *)arg;
    long sum = 0;

    /* Each thread sums a different range */
    int start = id * 250000 + 1;
    int end = (id + 1) * 250000;

    for (int i = start; i <= end; i++) {
        sum += i;
    }

    printf("Thread %d: sum of %d to %d = %ld\n",
           id, start, end, sum);

    long *result = malloc(sizeof(long));
    *result = sum;
    return (void *)result;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t threads[NUM_THREADS];
    int thread_ids[NUM_THREADS];
    long total = 0;

    /* Create all threads */
    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; i++) {
        thread_ids[i] = i;
        if (pthread_create(&threads[i], NULL, do_work,
                           &thread_ids[i]) != 0) {
            perror("pthread_create failed");
            exit(1);
        }
    }

    /* Join all threads and collect results */
    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; i++) {
        void *retval;
        pthread_join(threads[i], &retval);
        total += *(long *)retval;
        free(retval);
    }

    printf("Total sum: %ld\n", total);
    printf("Expected:  %ld\n", (long)1000000 * 1000001 / 2);

    return 0;
}

This program divides the task of summing numbers 1 through 1,000,000 among 4 threads. Each thread computes a partial sum, and main adds them together.

Compile and run:

gcc -o parallel_sum parallel_sum.c -lpthread
./parallel_sum

Sample output:

Thread 0: sum of 1 to 250000 = 31250125000
Thread 1: sum of 250001 to 500000 = 93750125000
Thread 2: sum of 500001 to 750000 = 156250125000
Thread 3: sum of 750001 to 1000000 = 218750125000
Total sum: 500000500000
Expected:  500000500000

Error Handling

The pthread functions return 0 on success and an error number (positive integer) on failure. They do not return -1 and set errno like many POSIX functions. You should check the return value:

int ret = pthread_create(&tid, NULL, my_func, NULL);
if (ret != 0) {
    fprintf(stderr, "pthread_create failed: %s\n",
            strerror(ret));
    exit(1);
}

Include <string.h> to use strerror().

Compiling with pthreads

You must link the pthreads library when compiling. Either of these works:

gcc -o myprogram myprogram.c -lpthread
gcc -o myprogram myprogram.c -pthread

The -pthread flag (without the "l") is actually preferred on Linux because it sets both the compiler and linker flags correctly. Both will work for the examples in this course.

Key Takeaways

  • pthread_create() creates a new thread that begins executing a specified function.
  • pthread_join() waits for a thread to finish and retrieves its return value.
  • Thread functions must have the signature void *func(void *arg).
  • Pass arguments via the void* parameter; cast to the correct type inside the thread function.
  • Be careful when passing addresses of loop variables; give each thread its own copy.
  • Return values from threads using malloc'd memory; do not return pointers to local variables.
  • Always compile with -lpthread or -pthread.

Module 6: Threads and Synchronization

Lesson 3: Race Conditions

Introduction

In Lesson 1, we learned that threads share the same address space, including global variables and heap memory. In Lesson 2, we learned how to create threads and pass data to them. Now we encounter the fundamental problem of concurrent programming: race conditions.

A race condition occurs when two or more threads access shared data at the same time, and at least one of them modifies it. The final result depends on the unpredictable order in which the threads execute, which is determined by the OS scheduler and can vary from run to run.

A Motivating Example: The Shared Counter

Consider a simple task: two threads each increment a shared counter 1,000,000 times. You would expect the final value to be 2,000,000. Let us see what actually happens.

/* race_condition.c - demonstrates a race condition */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <pthread.h>

#define ITERATIONS 1000000

int counter = 0;  /* shared global variable */

void *increment(void *arg) {
    for (int i = 0; i < ITERATIONS; i++) {
        counter++;   /* this is NOT atomic! */
    }
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t t1, t2;

    pthread_create(&t1, NULL, increment, NULL);
    pthread_create(&t2, NULL, increment, NULL);

    pthread_join(t1, NULL);
    pthread_join(t2, NULL);

    printf("Expected: %d\n", 2 * ITERATIONS);
    printf("Actual:   %d\n", counter);

    return 0;
}

Compile and run this several times:

gcc -o race race_condition.c -lpthread
./race
./race
./race

You will get different results each time! Here is what typical output might look like:

Expected: 2000000
Actual:   1247832

Expected: 2000000
Actual:   1389241

Expected: 2000000
Actual:   1156903

The actual value is always less than 2,000,000 and varies from run to run. This is a race condition in action.

Why Does This Happen?

The statement counter++ looks like a single operation in C, but it is actually three separate operations at the machine level:

  1. Read the current value of counter from memory into a register.
  2. Modify the value by adding 1 in the register.
  3. Write the new value from the register back to memory.

This is called a read-modify-write sequence. The problem is that a thread can be interrupted (by the OS scheduler) between any of these steps. Consider this scenario with two threads:

Suppose counter = 5

Thread A:                    Thread B:
---------                    ---------
1. Read counter (5)
                             1. Read counter (5)
2. Add 1 (6)
                             2. Add 1 (6)
3. Write 6 to counter
                             3. Write 6 to counter

Result: counter = 6 (should be 7!)

Both threads read the value 5, both add 1 to get 6, and both write 6 back. One increment is completely lost! This is called a lost update.

This happens because the read-modify-write sequence is not atomic. An atomic operation is one that completes entirely without any possibility of interruption. The individual read, add, and write are each atomic, but the three-step sequence as a whole is not.

The Concept of a Critical Section

A critical section is a section of code that accesses shared data and must not be executed by more than one thread at a time. In our counter example, the line counter++ is a critical section.

More formally, a critical section is any code where:

  • A shared resource (variable, file, data structure) is being accessed, AND
  • At least one thread is writing to (modifying) that resource.

To prevent race conditions, we must ensure mutual exclusion: only one thread can be in the critical section at a time. We will learn how to achieve this using mutexes in Lesson 4.

Non-Deterministic Behavior

One of the most frustrating aspects of race conditions is that they cause non-deterministic behavior. The program does not always produce the same output for the same input. Whether a race condition manifests depends on:

  • How the OS scheduler happens to interleave the threads
  • The number of CPU cores on your machine
  • System load from other processes
  • Timing variations at the microsecond level

This means:

  • A buggy program might appear to work correctly during testing and fail in production.
  • Adding a print statement can change the timing enough to make the bug disappear (the Heisenbug phenomenon).
  • Running under a debugger changes timing and may hide the bug.
  • The bug might appear on one machine but not another.
Key insight: Race conditions are among the hardest bugs to find and fix. A program with a race condition is incorrect even if it sometimes produces the right answer. "It works on my machine" is not evidence of correctness.

A More Detailed Example

Let us expand our example to make the race condition more visible. This version prints each thread's contribution and shows the final discrepancy:

/* race_detailed.c */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <pthread.h>

#define ITERATIONS 1000000
#define NUM_THREADS 4

int counter = 0;

void *increment(void *arg) {
    int id = *(int *)arg;
    int local_count = 0;

    for (int i = 0; i < ITERATIONS; i++) {
        counter++;
        local_count++;
    }

    printf("Thread %d: incremented %d times\n",
           id, local_count);
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t threads[NUM_THREADS];
    int ids[NUM_THREADS];

    printf("Starting %d threads, each incrementing %d times\n",
           NUM_THREADS, ITERATIONS);
    printf("Expected final counter: %d\n\n",
           NUM_THREADS * ITERATIONS);

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; i++) {
        ids[i] = i;
        pthread_create(&threads[i], NULL, increment, &ids[i]);
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; i++) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], NULL);
    }

    printf("\nActual final counter: %d\n", counter);
    printf("Lost updates: %d\n",
           NUM_THREADS * ITERATIONS - counter);

    return 0;
}

Sample output:

Starting 4 threads, each incrementing 1000000 times
Expected final counter: 4000000

Thread 0: incremented 1000000 times
Thread 2: incremented 1000000 times
Thread 1: incremented 1000000 times
Thread 3: incremented 1000000 times

Actual final counter: 2641873
Lost updates: 1358127

Notice that each thread correctly performed 1,000,000 increments (as counted by its local variable), but more than a million updates were lost due to the race condition. The exact numbers will differ each time you run the program.

It Is Not Just Counters

Race conditions can occur with any shared data, not just integer counters. Here are other common scenarios:

  • Linked list operations: Two threads inserting into a linked list simultaneously can corrupt the list structure, causing lost nodes or infinite loops.
  • Bank account transfers: Reading a balance, checking if sufficient, and deducting must be done atomically.
  • Array updates: Two threads writing to the same array index.
  • File operations: Two threads writing to the same file descriptor.
  • Checking then acting: Thread A checks if a resource is available, but Thread B grabs it before A can act.

A Linked List Race Condition

Consider two threads both trying to insert at the head of a linked list:

/* Shared linked list head */
node_t *head = NULL;

/* Thread A and Thread B both do this: */
void insert(int value) {
    node_t *new = malloc(sizeof(node_t));
    new->data = value;
    new->next = head;   /* Step 1: read head */
    head = new;          /* Step 2: update head */
}

If both threads execute Step 1 before either executes Step 2, both new nodes will point to the old head. Then whichever thread writes to head last will win, and the other thread's node will be lost (a memory leak and data loss).

Initial state: head --> [C] --> [D] --> NULL

Thread A: new_a->next = head  (new_a --> [C])
Thread B: new_b->next = head  (new_b --> [C])
Thread A: head = new_a         (head --> [A] --> [C] --> [D])
Thread B: head = new_b         (head --> [B] --> [C] --> [D])

Result: Node A is lost! head --> [B] --> [C] --> [D]

Identifying Race Conditions

To identify potential race conditions in your code, ask these questions:

  1. Is there any data that is accessible by more than one thread?
  2. Is at least one thread writing to (modifying) that data?
  3. Can the accesses happen simultaneously (without synchronization)?

If the answer to all three is yes, you have a potential race condition.

Note: If all threads only read shared data (and no one writes), there is no race condition. Multiple readers are safe. The problem arises when at least one writer is present.

What Does the C Standard Say?

The C11 standard (and later) formally defines a data race as undefined behavior. This means the compiler is allowed to assume your program is free of data races. If your program has one, the compiler might optimize your code in ways that make the bug even worse. For example, the compiler might reorder instructions, cache values in registers indefinitely, or eliminate "redundant" reads. This is another reason why race conditions must be fixed with proper synchronization, not with tricks like adding volatile keywords.

Can We Fix This Without Synchronization?

You might be tempted to try fixes like:

  • Making the variable volatile: This tells the compiler not to cache the variable in a register, but it does NOT make the read-modify-write atomic. It does not prevent race conditions.
  • Using a temporary variable: This does not help because the fundamental problem is the non-atomic read-modify-write.
  • Adding sleep() calls: This might change timing but does not guarantee correctness.

The only correct solution is to use proper synchronization primitives. We will learn about the most important one, the mutex, in the next lesson.

Key Takeaways

  • A race condition occurs when multiple threads access shared data concurrently and at least one writes to it.
  • The statement counter++ is three machine-level operations (read, modify, write) and is not atomic.
  • Race conditions cause non-deterministic behavior: different results on every run.
  • A critical section is code that accesses shared data and must be executed by only one thread at a time.
  • Race conditions can affect any shared data structure, not just counters.
  • The C standard defines data races as undefined behavior.
  • Volatile, sleep, and other tricks do not fix race conditions. Proper synchronization is required.

Module 6: Threads and Synchronization

Lesson 4: Mutexes

Introduction

In Lesson 3, we saw that race conditions occur when multiple threads access shared data without coordination. The solution is to enforce mutual exclusion: only one thread can execute the critical section at a time. The primary tool for achieving mutual exclusion in pthreads is the mutex (short for "mutual exclusion").

A mutex is like a lock on a door. Before entering the critical section, a thread must lock the mutex. If another thread already holds the lock, the requesting thread blocks (waits) until the lock is released. When a thread is done with the critical section, it unlocks the mutex, allowing another waiting thread to proceed.

The Mutex API

The pthreads library provides the following functions and types for working with mutexes:

Function / Type Purpose
pthread_mutex_t The mutex data type
PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER Static initializer for a mutex (used for global/static mutexes)
pthread_mutex_init(&mutex, attr) Initialize a mutex at runtime (used for local/dynamic mutexes). Pass NULL for attr to get default behavior.
pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex) Acquire the lock. Blocks if already locked by another thread.
pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex) Release the lock. Another waiting thread can now acquire it.
pthread_mutex_destroy(&mutex) Free resources associated with the mutex. Call when done with it.

Initializing a Mutex

There are two ways to initialize a mutex:

Static Initialization (for global or static mutexes)

/* Simple and preferred for global mutexes */
pthread_mutex_t lock = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;

This is the easiest approach when the mutex is declared at global scope.

Dynamic Initialization (for local or heap-allocated mutexes)

pthread_mutex_t lock;
pthread_mutex_init(&lock, NULL);  /* NULL = default attributes */

Use this when the mutex is a local variable or when you need to set special attributes. When using dynamic initialization, you must call pthread_mutex_destroy() when you are done with the mutex.

Locking and Unlocking

The basic pattern for protecting a critical section is:

pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);    /* acquire the lock */

/* ... critical section ... */
/* only one thread at a time can be here */

pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);  /* release the lock */

When a thread calls pthread_mutex_lock():

  • If the mutex is unlocked, the thread acquires it immediately and continues.
  • If the mutex is locked by another thread, the calling thread blocks (sleeps) until the mutex becomes available.

When a thread calls pthread_mutex_unlock():

  • The mutex is released. If any threads are waiting on this mutex, one of them is woken up and acquires it.
Rule: A mutex must be unlocked by the same thread that locked it. It is an error for one thread to unlock a mutex that was locked by a different thread.

Fixing the Race Condition

Let us fix the counter program from Lesson 3 by adding a mutex:

/* fixed_counter.c - race condition fixed with a mutex */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <pthread.h>

#define ITERATIONS 1000000

int counter = 0;
pthread_mutex_t lock = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;

void *increment(void *arg) {
    for (int i = 0; i < ITERATIONS; i++) {
        pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);    /* enter critical section */
        counter++;
        pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);  /* leave critical section */
    }
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t t1, t2;

    pthread_create(&t1, NULL, increment, NULL);
    pthread_create(&t2, NULL, increment, NULL);

    pthread_join(t1, NULL);
    pthread_join(t2, NULL);

    printf("Expected: %d\n", 2 * ITERATIONS);
    printf("Actual:   %d\n", counter);

    return 0;
}

Compile and run:

gcc -o fixed fixed_counter.c -lpthread
./fixed
./fixed
./fixed

Output (every time):

Expected: 2000000
Actual:   2000000

The answer is now correct every time. The mutex ensures that only one thread can execute the counter++ line at a time, preventing the read-modify-write interleaving we saw in Lesson 3.

A Complete Example with Dynamic Initialization

Here is a more complete example using dynamic initialization and proper cleanup:

/* mutex_dynamic.c */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <pthread.h>

#define NUM_THREADS 4
#define ITERATIONS 500000

typedef struct {
    int counter;
    pthread_mutex_t lock;
} shared_data_t;

void *increment(void *arg) {
    shared_data_t *data = (shared_data_t *)arg;

    for (int i = 0; i < ITERATIONS; i++) {
        pthread_mutex_lock(&data->lock);
        data->counter++;
        pthread_mutex_unlock(&data->lock);
    }

    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t threads[NUM_THREADS];
    shared_data_t shared;

    /* Initialize shared data */
    shared.counter = 0;
    pthread_mutex_init(&shared.lock, NULL);

    /* Create threads */
    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; i++) {
        pthread_create(&threads[i], NULL, increment, &shared);
    }

    /* Join threads */
    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; i++) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], NULL);
    }

    printf("Expected: %d\n", NUM_THREADS * ITERATIONS);
    printf("Actual:   %d\n", shared.counter);

    /* Clean up */
    pthread_mutex_destroy(&shared.lock);

    return 0;
}

Output:

Expected: 2000000
Actual:   2000000

Protecting Multiple Operations

Sometimes the critical section involves more than one line of code. You must hold the lock for the entire sequence of operations that must be atomic. For example, transferring money between two accounts:

/* Both accounts share the same mutex */
pthread_mutex_lock(&bank_lock);
if (accounts[from] >= amount) {
    accounts[from] -= amount;
    accounts[to] += amount;
}
pthread_mutex_unlock(&bank_lock);

You would not want to lock and unlock around each individual line, because another thread could see an inconsistent state where money has left one account but not yet arrived in the other.

Performance Implications

Mutexes add overhead. Every lock and unlock operation requires atomic CPU instructions and potential context switches. If you lock and unlock very frequently (like locking for every single counter increment in a tight loop), the overhead can be significant.

Here are some strategies to manage performance:

Minimize Time in the Critical Section

Do as little work as possible while holding the lock. Move any computation that does not need shared data outside the critical section:

/* Slower: unnecessary work inside lock */
pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);
result = expensive_calculation(input);
shared_array[index] = result;
pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);

/* Faster: only the shared access is inside the lock */
result = expensive_calculation(input);
pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);
shared_array[index] = result;
pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);

Accumulate Locally, Then Update Shared Data Once

/* Slow: lock/unlock 1,000,000 times */
void *increment_slow(void *arg) {
    for (int i = 0; i < ITERATIONS; i++) {
        pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);
        counter++;
        pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);
    }
    return NULL;
}

/* Faster: lock/unlock only once */
void *increment_fast(void *arg) {
    int local_sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < ITERATIONS; i++) {
        local_sum++;
    }
    pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);
    counter += local_sum;
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);
    return NULL;
}

The second version is much faster because each thread accumulates its count in a private local variable and only acquires the lock once at the end.

Deadlock

A deadlock occurs when two or more threads are each waiting for a lock held by the other, so none of them can make progress. This is a permanent state: the program hangs forever.

Example of Deadlock

pthread_mutex_t lock_a = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;
pthread_mutex_t lock_b = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;

void *thread1(void *arg) {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&lock_a);     /* holds A */
    sleep(1);  /* simulate some work */
    pthread_mutex_lock(&lock_b);     /* waits for B */

    /* ... critical section ... */

    pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock_b);
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock_a);
    return NULL;
}

void *thread2(void *arg) {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&lock_b);     /* holds B */
    sleep(1);  /* simulate some work */
    pthread_mutex_lock(&lock_a);     /* waits for A */

    /* ... critical section ... */

    pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock_a);
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock_b);
    return NULL;
}

Here, Thread 1 holds lock_a and waits for lock_b. Thread 2 holds lock_b and waits for lock_a. Neither can proceed. The program is deadlocked.

Thread 1:  holds lock_a  ---waits for--->  lock_b
                                              |
                                         held by
                                              |
Thread 2:  holds lock_b  ---waits for--->  lock_a
                                              |
                                         held by
                                              |
                                          Thread 1  (circular!)

Four Conditions for Deadlock

All four of these conditions must be true simultaneously for deadlock to occur:

  1. Mutual exclusion: At least one resource is held in a non-shareable way.
  2. Hold and wait: A thread holds one resource while waiting for another.
  3. No preemption: Resources cannot be forcibly taken from a thread.
  4. Circular wait: There is a circular chain of threads, each waiting for a resource held by the next.

Preventing Deadlock

The most practical way to prevent deadlock is to break the circular wait condition by always acquiring locks in a consistent, global order:

/* SAFE: both threads lock in the same order (A first, then B) */

void *thread1(void *arg) {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&lock_a);     /* lock A first */
    pthread_mutex_lock(&lock_b);     /* then lock B */
    /* ... critical section ... */
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock_b);
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock_a);
    return NULL;
}

void *thread2(void *arg) {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&lock_a);     /* lock A first (same order!) */
    pthread_mutex_lock(&lock_b);     /* then lock B */
    /* ... critical section ... */
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock_b);
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock_a);
    return NULL;
}

If all threads always acquire locks in the same order, the circular wait cannot form, and deadlock is impossible.

Common Mutex Mistakes

Here are some common mistakes to avoid:

  • Forgetting to unlock: If a thread returns or exits without unlocking a mutex, other threads will wait forever.
  • Locking twice without unlocking: Calling pthread_mutex_lock on a mutex you already hold causes undefined behavior (for the default mutex type, this typically causes the thread to deadlock, blocking forever waiting for itself to release the lock). With PTHREAD_MUTEX_ERRORCHECK type, an error code is returned instead.
  • Using different mutexes: Two threads must lock the same mutex to achieve mutual exclusion. If thread A locks mutex_1 and thread B locks mutex_2, they are not coordinating at all.
  • Unlocking a mutex you do not hold: Only the thread that locked a mutex should unlock it.
/* BUG: forgot to unlock in the error case! */
pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);
if (error_condition) {
    return NULL;  /* OOPS! mutex is still locked forever */
}
/* ... do work ... */
pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);

/* FIXED: unlock before returning */
pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);
if (error_condition) {
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);  /* unlock first! */
    return NULL;
}
/* ... do work ... */
pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);

trylock: Non-Blocking Lock Attempt

Sometimes you want to attempt to acquire a lock without blocking. The function pthread_mutex_trylock() does this:

int ret = pthread_mutex_trylock(&lock);
if (ret == 0) {
    /* lock acquired successfully */
    /* ... critical section ... */
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);
} else {
    /* lock is held by someone else */
    /* do something else instead of waiting */
}

This is useful in situations where a thread has other work it could do instead of blocking.

Key Takeaways

  • A mutex enforces mutual exclusion: only one thread can hold it at a time.
  • Protect every critical section with pthread_mutex_lock() and pthread_mutex_unlock().
  • Initialize with PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER for global mutexes or pthread_mutex_init() for dynamic ones.
  • Always unlock the mutex when leaving the critical section, including error paths.
  • Deadlock occurs when threads form a circular chain of lock dependencies. Prevent it by always acquiring locks in a consistent order.
  • Minimize time spent holding a lock for better performance.
  • When done, call pthread_mutex_destroy() on dynamically initialized mutexes.

Module 6: Threads and Synchronization

Lesson 5: Condition Variables and Semaphores

Introduction: Why Mutexes Alone Are Not Enough

Mutexes solve the problem of ensuring only one thread accesses shared data at a time. But there is another common pattern that mutexes alone cannot handle efficiently: one thread needs to wait for a specific condition that another thread will make true.

Consider the producer-consumer problem: a producer thread generates data and places it in a buffer, while a consumer thread removes data from the buffer and processes it. The consumer must wait when the buffer is empty, and the producer must wait when the buffer is full.

With only a mutex, the consumer would have to do something like this:

/* Busy waiting - WASTEFUL! */
while (1) {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);
    if (count > 0) {
        /* consume an item */
        pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);
        break;
    }
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);
    /* spin and try again... wastes CPU! */
}

This is called busy waiting (or spinning). The consumer constantly locks and unlocks the mutex, checking the condition over and over, wasting CPU cycles. What we need is a way for the consumer to sleep until the producer signals that data is available. This is exactly what condition variables provide.

Condition Variables

A condition variable allows a thread to block until a particular condition is true, and allows another thread to signal when that condition has changed. Condition variables are always used together with a mutex.

The Condition Variable API

Function / Type Purpose
pthread_cond_t The condition variable data type
PTHREAD_COND_INITIALIZER Static initializer for a condition variable
pthread_cond_init(&cond, attr) Initialize dynamically. Pass NULL for default attributes.
pthread_cond_wait(&cond, &mutex) Atomically release the mutex and block until signaled. When it returns, the mutex is re-acquired.
pthread_cond_signal(&cond) Wake up one thread waiting on this condition variable.
pthread_cond_broadcast(&cond) Wake up all threads waiting on this condition variable.
pthread_cond_destroy(&cond) Free resources associated with the condition variable.

How pthread_cond_wait() Works

The function pthread_cond_wait(&cond, &mutex) does three things atomically:

  1. Releases the mutex (so other threads can make progress).
  2. Puts the calling thread to sleep, waiting on the condition variable.
  3. When the thread is woken up (by a signal or broadcast), it re-acquires the mutex before returning.

The fact that steps 1 and 2 are atomic is critical. If they were not, another thread could signal the condition between the unlock and the sleep, and the signal would be lost.

The Correct Pattern

You must always use condition variables with a while loop, not an if statement:

pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex);
while (condition_is_not_true) {
    pthread_cond_wait(&cond, &mutex);
}
/* condition is now true, and we hold the mutex */
/* ... do work ... */
pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex);

Why a while loop instead of if? Two reasons:

  • Spurious wakeups: The POSIX standard allows pthread_cond_wait to return even if no one signaled. This is rare but possible. The while loop handles this by rechecking the condition.
  • Stolen wakeups: If multiple threads are waiting and one is woken up, another thread might acquire the mutex first and consume the resource before the woken thread gets to run. The while loop handles this by rechecking.
Critical rule: Always check the condition in a while loop, never with just an if statement. This is one of the most common mistakes in concurrent programming.

Producer-Consumer with Condition Variables

Here is a complete implementation of the bounded-buffer producer-consumer problem using condition variables:

/* producer_consumer.c */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <pthread.h>

#define BUFFER_SIZE 5
#define NUM_ITEMS 20

int buffer[BUFFER_SIZE];
int count = 0;       /* number of items in buffer */
int in_index = 0;    /* next position to insert */
int out_index = 0;   /* next position to remove */

pthread_mutex_t mutex = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;
pthread_cond_t not_full = PTHREAD_COND_INITIALIZER;
pthread_cond_t not_empty = PTHREAD_COND_INITIALIZER;

void *producer(void *arg) {
    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_ITEMS; i++) {
        int item = i + 1;  /* produce an item */

        pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex);

        /* Wait while buffer is full */
        while (count == BUFFER_SIZE) {
            printf("Producer: buffer full, waiting...\n");
            pthread_cond_wait(&not_full, &mutex);
        }

        /* Insert item into buffer */
        buffer[in_index] = item;
        in_index = (in_index + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
        count++;
        printf("Producer: produced item %d (count=%d)\n",
               item, count);

        /* Signal consumer that buffer is not empty */
        pthread_cond_signal(&not_empty);

        pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex);
    }
    return NULL;
}

void *consumer(void *arg) {
    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_ITEMS; i++) {
        pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex);

        /* Wait while buffer is empty */
        while (count == 0) {
            printf("Consumer: buffer empty, waiting...\n");
            pthread_cond_wait(&not_empty, &mutex);
        }

        /* Remove item from buffer */
        int item = buffer[out_index];
        out_index = (out_index + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
        count--;
        printf("Consumer: consumed item %d (count=%d)\n",
               item, count);

        /* Signal producer that buffer is not full */
        pthread_cond_signal(&not_full);

        pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex);
    }
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t prod_thread, cons_thread;

    pthread_create(&prod_thread, NULL, producer, NULL);
    pthread_create(&cons_thread, NULL, consumer, NULL);

    pthread_join(prod_thread, NULL);
    pthread_join(cons_thread, NULL);

    printf("All items produced and consumed.\n");
    return 0;
}

Compile and run:

gcc -o prodcons producer_consumer.c -lpthread
./prodcons

Sample output (abbreviated):

Producer: produced item 1 (count=1)
Producer: produced item 2 (count=2)
Producer: produced item 3 (count=3)
Consumer: consumed item 1 (count=2)
Consumer: consumed item 2 (count=1)
Producer: produced item 4 (count=2)
Producer: produced item 5 (count=3)
Producer: produced item 6 (count=4)
Producer: produced item 7 (count=5)
Producer: buffer full, waiting...
Consumer: consumed item 3 (count=4)
...
All items produced and consumed.

Notice how the producer blocks when the buffer is full and the consumer blocks when it is empty. The condition variables handle the coordination efficiently without busy waiting.

Understanding the Flow

Let us trace through the key interactions:

  1. The producer locks the mutex, checks if the buffer is full. If not, it inserts an item and signals not_empty to wake the consumer if it was sleeping.
  2. The consumer locks the mutex, checks if the buffer is empty. If so, it calls pthread_cond_wait(&not_empty, &mutex), which atomically releases the mutex and puts the consumer to sleep.
  3. When the producer signals not_empty, the consumer wakes up. pthread_cond_wait re-acquires the mutex before returning. The consumer then re-checks the condition (while loop), finds the buffer is not empty, and consumes the item.

Signal vs Broadcast

pthread_cond_signal wakes up one waiting thread. pthread_cond_broadcast wakes up all waiting threads.

Use signal when:

  • Only one waiting thread can make progress at a time (e.g., there is exactly one item available, so only one consumer should wake up).

Use broadcast when:

  • The condition change might allow multiple waiters to proceed.
  • Different threads are waiting for different conditions on the same condition variable.
  • You are unsure which waiting threads can proceed.

When in doubt, use broadcast. It is less efficient (wakes up threads that may just go back to sleep) but always correct. Using signal incorrectly can cause threads to sleep forever.

Semaphores

A semaphore is another synchronization primitive, older than condition variables. A semaphore maintains an integer counter that can be incremented and decremented atomically. It is useful for controlling access to a resource with a limited number of instances.

To use semaphores on Linux, include <semaphore.h>.

The Semaphore API

Function / Type Purpose
sem_t The semaphore data type
sem_init(&sem, pshared, value) Initialize an unnamed semaphore. pshared=0 for threads in the same process. value is the initial count.
sem_wait(&sem) Decrement the counter. If the counter is 0, the thread blocks until it becomes positive. Also called "P" or "down".
sem_post(&sem) Increment the counter. If threads are waiting, one is woken up. Also called "V" or "up".
sem_destroy(&sem) Free resources associated with the semaphore.

How Semaphores Work

Think of a semaphore as a counter with special rules:

  • sem_wait: "I want to use a resource." If the counter is greater than 0, decrement it and proceed. If the counter is 0, block until someone posts.
  • sem_post: "I am done with a resource." Increment the counter. If anyone is waiting, wake one up.

A semaphore initialized to 1 behaves like a mutex (a "binary semaphore"). A semaphore initialized to N allows up to N threads to access a resource simultaneously.

Using a Semaphore as a Mutex

#include <stdio.h>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <semaphore.h>

sem_t sem;
int counter = 0;

void *increment(void *arg) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000000; i++) {
        sem_wait(&sem);    /* like pthread_mutex_lock */
        counter++;
        sem_post(&sem);    /* like pthread_mutex_unlock */
    }
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t t1, t2;

    sem_init(&sem, 0, 1);  /* initial value 1 = binary semaphore */

    pthread_create(&t1, NULL, increment, NULL);
    pthread_create(&t2, NULL, increment, NULL);

    pthread_join(t1, NULL);
    pthread_join(t2, NULL);

    printf("Counter: %d\n", counter);

    sem_destroy(&sem);
    return 0;
}

Producer-Consumer with Semaphores

Semaphores can elegantly solve the producer-consumer problem. We use three semaphores:

  • empty: counts empty slots (initialized to BUFFER_SIZE)
  • full: counts full slots (initialized to 0)
  • mutex: binary semaphore for mutual exclusion (initialized to 1)
/* prodcons_sem.c - Producer-Consumer with semaphores */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <semaphore.h>

#define BUFFER_SIZE 5
#define NUM_ITEMS 20

int buffer[BUFFER_SIZE];
int in_index = 0;
int out_index = 0;

sem_t empty_slots;  /* counts empty positions */
sem_t full_slots;   /* counts filled positions */
sem_t mutex;        /* binary semaphore for mutual exclusion */

void *producer(void *arg) {
    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_ITEMS; i++) {
        int item = i + 1;

        sem_wait(&empty_slots);  /* wait for an empty slot */
        sem_wait(&mutex);        /* enter critical section */

        buffer[in_index] = item;
        in_index = (in_index + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
        printf("Producer: produced %d\n", item);

        sem_post(&mutex);        /* leave critical section */
        sem_post(&full_slots);   /* signal a full slot */
    }
    return NULL;
}

void *consumer(void *arg) {
    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_ITEMS; i++) {
        sem_wait(&full_slots);   /* wait for a full slot */
        sem_wait(&mutex);        /* enter critical section */

        int item = buffer[out_index];
        out_index = (out_index + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
        printf("Consumer: consumed %d\n", item);

        sem_post(&mutex);        /* leave critical section */
        sem_post(&empty_slots);  /* signal an empty slot */
    }
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t prod, cons;

    sem_init(&empty_slots, 0, BUFFER_SIZE);
    sem_init(&full_slots, 0, 0);
    sem_init(&mutex, 0, 1);

    pthread_create(&prod, NULL, producer, NULL);
    pthread_create(&cons, NULL, consumer, NULL);

    pthread_join(prod, NULL);
    pthread_join(cons, NULL);

    sem_destroy(&empty_slots);
    sem_destroy(&full_slots);
    sem_destroy(&mutex);

    printf("Done.\n");
    return 0;
}

Compile and run:

gcc -o prodcons_sem prodcons_sem.c -lpthread
./prodcons_sem

Named vs Unnamed Semaphores

The semaphores we have used so far are unnamed semaphores, initialized with sem_init(). They exist in memory and are shared between threads in the same process (when pshared=0).

Named semaphores are created with sem_open() and have a name in the filesystem (typically under /dev/shm/ on Linux). They can be shared between different processes.

#include <fcntl.h>
#include <semaphore.h>

/* Create or open a named semaphore */
sem_t *sem = sem_open("/my_semaphore", O_CREAT, 0644, 1);

/* Use it just like an unnamed semaphore */
sem_wait(sem);
/* ... critical section ... */
sem_post(sem);

/* Close it when done */
sem_close(sem);

/* Remove it from the system (once, when no longer needed) */
sem_unlink("/my_semaphore");

Named semaphores are useful when you need synchronization between separate processes (not just threads within one process).

Condition Variables vs Semaphores

Feature Condition Variable Semaphore
Must be used with a mutex Yes (always) No (self-contained)
Maintains a count No Yes (integer counter)
Signal without waiter Signal is lost Count is incremented (remembered)
Spurious wakeups Possible (use while loop) Not applicable
Broadcast Yes (wake all waiters) No (must post N times)
Cross-process Possible but complex Easy with named semaphores

In general, condition variables with mutexes are more flexible and are the preferred approach in most pthreads programs. Semaphores are simpler for certain patterns like resource counting and are familiar from operating systems theory.

Key Takeaways

  • Mutexes alone cannot efficiently handle "wait for a condition" patterns.
  • Condition variables let a thread sleep until another thread signals that a condition has changed.
  • Always use condition variables with a mutex and a while loop around the wait.
  • pthread_cond_signal wakes one waiter; pthread_cond_broadcast wakes all waiters.
  • Semaphores maintain a counter and provide sem_wait (decrement/block) and sem_post (increment/wake).
  • A semaphore initialized to 1 works like a mutex.
  • Named semaphores can be shared between processes; unnamed semaphores are for threads within a process.

Module 6: Threads and Synchronization

Lesson 6: Classic Concurrency Problems

Introduction

Throughout the history of computer science, certain concurrency problems have become famous because they cleanly illustrate the challenges of writing correct concurrent programs. In this lesson, we will study two of the most well-known: the Dining Philosophers problem and the Reader-Writer problem. These problems appear in nearly every operating systems textbook and are frequently asked about in technical interviews.

More importantly, these problems represent real patterns that appear in actual systems. The Dining Philosophers problem models any situation where multiple processes compete for a limited set of shared resources. The Reader-Writer problem models any situation where some threads only read shared data while others need to modify it.

The Dining Philosophers Problem

Problem Description

Five philosophers sit around a circular table. Between each pair of adjacent philosophers, there is a single fork (so there are 5 forks total). Each philosopher alternates between thinking and eating. To eat, a philosopher must pick up both the fork on their left and the fork on their right. After eating, they put both forks down and resume thinking.

            [Philosopher 0]
           /               \
      (Fork 0)           (Fork 1)
        /                     \
[Philosopher 4]         [Philosopher 1]
        \                     /
      (Fork 4)           (Fork 2)
        \                     /
[Philosopher 3] ------- [Philosopher 2]
              (Fork 3)

The challenge: design a protocol so that:

  • No philosopher starves (everyone eventually gets to eat).
  • No deadlock occurs (the system does not freeze with everyone waiting).
  • Maximum concurrency is achieved (as many philosophers as possible eat simultaneously).

Each fork is a shared resource, and each philosopher is a thread.

Naive Solution (Deadlock!)

The most natural approach is for each philosopher to pick up their left fork, then their right fork, eat, and put both down. Let us implement this and see what goes wrong:

/* dining_deadlock.c - naive solution that DEADLOCKS */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <unistd.h>

#define NUM_PHILOSOPHERS 5
#define NUM_MEALS 3

pthread_mutex_t forks[NUM_PHILOSOPHERS];

void think(int id) {
    printf("Philosopher %d is thinking.\n", id);
    usleep(rand() % 500000);  /* think for a random time */
}

void eat(int id) {
    printf("Philosopher %d is EATING.\n", id);
    usleep(rand() % 500000);  /* eat for a random time */
}

void *philosopher(void *arg) {
    int id = *(int *)arg;
    int left = id;
    int right = (id + 1) % NUM_PHILOSOPHERS;

    for (int meal = 0; meal < NUM_MEALS; meal++) {
        think(id);

        /* Pick up left fork */
        printf("Philosopher %d picks up left fork %d.\n",
               id, left);
        pthread_mutex_lock(&forks[left]);

        /* Pick up right fork */
        printf("Philosopher %d picks up right fork %d.\n",
               id, right);
        pthread_mutex_lock(&forks[right]);

        eat(id);

        /* Put down forks */
        pthread_mutex_unlock(&forks[right]);
        pthread_mutex_unlock(&forks[left]);
    }
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t threads[NUM_PHILOSOPHERS];
    int ids[NUM_PHILOSOPHERS];

    srand(42);

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_PHILOSOPHERS; i++) {
        pthread_mutex_init(&forks[i], NULL);
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_PHILOSOPHERS; i++) {
        ids[i] = i;
        pthread_create(&threads[i], NULL, philosopher, &ids[i]);
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_PHILOSOPHERS; i++) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], NULL);
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_PHILOSOPHERS; i++) {
        pthread_mutex_destroy(&forks[i]);
    }

    printf("All done.\n");
    return 0;
}

If you compile and run this, it may work sometimes, but it can also deadlock. The deadlock scenario is:

  1. Philosopher 0 picks up fork 0 (left).
  2. Philosopher 1 picks up fork 1 (left).
  3. Philosopher 2 picks up fork 2 (left).
  4. Philosopher 3 picks up fork 3 (left).
  5. Philosopher 4 picks up fork 4 (left).
  6. Now every philosopher tries to pick up their right fork, but every fork is already held. Everyone is waiting for someone else. Deadlock!
Phil 0: holds fork 0, waits for fork 1
Phil 1: holds fork 1, waits for fork 2
Phil 2: holds fork 2, waits for fork 3
Phil 3: holds fork 3, waits for fork 4
Phil 4: holds fork 4, waits for fork 0    <-- circular!

This is the classic circular wait condition for deadlock.

Solution 1: Break the Symmetry (Resource Ordering)

The simplest and most elegant solution is to break the circular wait by having one philosopher pick up forks in a different order. Specifically, we have all philosophers pick up the lower-numbered fork first, then the higher-numbered fork. Since Philosopher 4's left fork is fork 4 and right fork is fork 0, this philosopher will pick up fork 0 first (the lower number) instead of fork 4.

This breaks the cycle because no circular wait can form when all threads acquire locks in a consistent global order.

/* dining_ordered.c - correct solution using resource ordering */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <unistd.h>

#define NUM_PHILOSOPHERS 5
#define NUM_MEALS 5

pthread_mutex_t forks[NUM_PHILOSOPHERS];

void think(int id) {
    printf("Philosopher %d is thinking.\n", id);
    usleep(rand() % 500000);
}

void eat(int id) {
    printf("Philosopher %d is EATING.\n", id);
    usleep(rand() % 500000);
}

void *philosopher(void *arg) {
    int id = *(int *)arg;
    int left = id;
    int right = (id + 1) % NUM_PHILOSOPHERS;

    /* Determine which fork has the lower number */
    int first, second;
    if (left < right) {
        first = left;
        second = right;
    } else {
        first = right;
        second = left;
    }

    for (int meal = 0; meal < NUM_MEALS; meal++) {
        think(id);

        /* Always pick up the lower-numbered fork first */
        printf("Philosopher %d picks up fork %d.\n", id, first);
        pthread_mutex_lock(&forks[first]);

        printf("Philosopher %d picks up fork %d.\n", id, second);
        pthread_mutex_lock(&forks[second]);

        eat(id);

        /* Put down forks (order does not matter for unlocking) */
        pthread_mutex_unlock(&forks[second]);
        pthread_mutex_unlock(&forks[first]);

        printf("Philosopher %d puts down forks.\n", id);
    }

    printf("Philosopher %d is done.\n", id);
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t threads[NUM_PHILOSOPHERS];
    int ids[NUM_PHILOSOPHERS];

    srand(42);

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_PHILOSOPHERS; i++) {
        pthread_mutex_init(&forks[i], NULL);
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_PHILOSOPHERS; i++) {
        ids[i] = i;
        pthread_create(&threads[i], NULL, philosopher, &ids[i]);
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_PHILOSOPHERS; i++) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], NULL);
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_PHILOSOPHERS; i++) {
        pthread_mutex_destroy(&forks[i]);
    }

    printf("All philosophers have finished dining.\n");
    return 0;
}

Compile and run:

gcc -o dining dining_ordered.c -lpthread
./dining

This solution will never deadlock. The key insight is that Philosopher 4, who sits between fork 4 and fork 0, picks up fork 0 first (the lower number). This means they cannot complete the circular chain.

Solution 2: Limit the Number of Diners

Another approach is to use a semaphore to ensure that at most 4 philosophers (out of 5) can attempt to pick up forks at the same time. If at most 4 try, at least one will always be able to get both forks and eat, preventing deadlock.

/* dining_semaphore.c - limit concurrent diners */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <semaphore.h>
#include <unistd.h>

#define NUM_PHILOSOPHERS 5
#define NUM_MEALS 5

pthread_mutex_t forks[NUM_PHILOSOPHERS];
sem_t seats;  /* limits concurrent diners to N-1 */

void think(int id) {
    printf("Philosopher %d is thinking.\n", id);
    usleep(rand() % 500000);
}

void eat(int id) {
    printf("Philosopher %d is EATING.\n", id);
    usleep(rand() % 500000);
}

void *philosopher(void *arg) {
    int id = *(int *)arg;
    int left = id;
    int right = (id + 1) % NUM_PHILOSOPHERS;

    for (int meal = 0; meal < NUM_MEALS; meal++) {
        think(id);

        sem_wait(&seats);  /* sit down (at most 4 at a time) */

        pthread_mutex_lock(&forks[left]);
        pthread_mutex_lock(&forks[right]);

        eat(id);

        pthread_mutex_unlock(&forks[right]);
        pthread_mutex_unlock(&forks[left]);

        sem_post(&seats);  /* stand up */
    }

    printf("Philosopher %d is done.\n", id);
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t threads[NUM_PHILOSOPHERS];
    int ids[NUM_PHILOSOPHERS];

    srand(42);

    /* Allow at most NUM_PHILOSOPHERS - 1 concurrent diners */
    sem_init(&seats, 0, NUM_PHILOSOPHERS - 1);

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_PHILOSOPHERS; i++) {
        pthread_mutex_init(&forks[i], NULL);
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_PHILOSOPHERS; i++) {
        ids[i] = i;
        pthread_create(&threads[i], NULL, philosopher, &ids[i]);
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_PHILOSOPHERS; i++) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], NULL);
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_PHILOSOPHERS; i++) {
        pthread_mutex_destroy(&forks[i]);
    }
    sem_destroy(&seats);

    printf("All philosophers have finished dining.\n");
    return 0;
}

This works because with only 4 philosophers attempting at a time around 5 forks, at least one will always be able to pick up both forks. The pigeonhole principle guarantees that deadlock cannot occur.

The Reader-Writer Problem

Problem Description

Consider a shared data structure (such as a database or a file) that is accessed by two types of threads:

  • Readers only read the data. Multiple readers can access the data simultaneously without any problem, because reading does not change the data.
  • Writers modify the data. A writer needs exclusive access: no other reader or writer should access the data while a writer is writing.

The rules are:

  1. Multiple readers can read at the same time (shared access).
  2. Only one writer can write at a time (exclusive access).
  3. No reader can read while a writer is writing.
  4. No writer can write while any reader is reading.

Using a single mutex for all access would work for correctness, but it would be too restrictive: it would prevent multiple readers from reading simultaneously, even though that is perfectly safe.

Reader-Writer Lock Concept

The idea is to maintain a count of active readers. The first reader locks out writers, and the last reader unlocks for writers. Writers need exclusive access.

+-----------+----------+----------+
| New       | Readers  | Writer   |
| request   | active   | active   |
+-----------+----------+----------+
| Reader    | Allowed  | Must     |
|           |          | wait     |
+-----------+----------+----------+
| Writer    | Must     | Must     |
|           | wait     | wait     |
+-----------+----------+----------+

Implementation Using Mutexes and a Counter

/* readers_writers.c - reader-preference solution */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <unistd.h>

#define NUM_READERS 5
#define NUM_WRITERS 2
#define NUM_READS 3
#define NUM_WRITES 3

int shared_data = 0;        /* the shared resource */
int reader_count = 0;        /* number of active readers */

pthread_mutex_t mutex = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;
pthread_mutex_t write_lock = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;

void *reader(void *arg) {
    int id = *(int *)arg;

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_READS; i++) {
        /* Entry section for readers */
        pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex);
        reader_count++;
        if (reader_count == 1) {
            /* First reader locks out writers */
            pthread_mutex_lock(&write_lock);
        }
        pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex);

        /* Reading section (multiple readers can be here) */
        printf("Reader %d reads shared_data = %d "
               "(readers active: %d)\n",
               id, shared_data, reader_count);
        usleep(rand() % 200000);

        /* Exit section for readers */
        pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex);
        reader_count--;
        if (reader_count == 0) {
            /* Last reader allows writers */
            pthread_mutex_unlock(&write_lock);
        }
        pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex);

        usleep(rand() % 300000);  /* delay between reads */
    }
    return NULL;
}

void *writer(void *arg) {
    int id = *(int *)arg;

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_WRITES; i++) {
        /* Writer needs exclusive access */
        pthread_mutex_lock(&write_lock);

        shared_data++;
        printf("Writer %d wrote shared_data = %d\n",
               id, shared_data);
        usleep(rand() % 300000);

        pthread_mutex_unlock(&write_lock);

        usleep(rand() % 500000);  /* delay between writes */
    }
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t r_threads[NUM_READERS], w_threads[NUM_WRITERS];
    int r_ids[NUM_READERS], w_ids[NUM_WRITERS];

    srand(42);

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_READERS; i++) {
        r_ids[i] = i;
        pthread_create(&r_threads[i], NULL, reader, &r_ids[i]);
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_WRITERS; i++) {
        w_ids[i] = i;
        pthread_create(&w_threads[i], NULL, writer, &w_ids[i]);
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_READERS; i++) {
        pthread_join(r_threads[i], NULL);
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_WRITERS; i++) {
        pthread_join(w_threads[i], NULL);
    }

    printf("Final shared_data = %d\n", shared_data);
    return 0;
}

Compile and run:

gcc -o rw readers_writers.c -lpthread
./rw

Reader-Preference vs Writer-Preference

The solution above has reader preference (also called the "first readers-writers problem"): as long as there is any reader active, new readers can join in, and writers must wait. This can lead to writer starvation: if readers arrive continuously, a writer might wait forever.

The opposite approach, writer preference (the "second readers-writers problem"), gives priority to writers: once a writer is waiting, no new readers are allowed to start. This can lead to reader starvation.

In practice, pthread_rwlock_t provides a built-in reader-writer lock that handles these details for you:

pthread_rwlock_t rwlock = PTHREAD_RWLOCK_INITIALIZER;

/* Reader */
pthread_rwlock_rdlock(&rwlock);
/* ... read shared data ... */
pthread_rwlock_unlock(&rwlock);

/* Writer */
pthread_rwlock_wrlock(&rwlock);
/* ... write shared data ... */
pthread_rwlock_unlock(&rwlock);

The implementation of pthread_rwlock_t varies by system, but it typically tries to balance reader and writer priorities.

Summary of Solutions

Problem Key Challenge Solution Approaches
Dining Philosophers Circular wait leading to deadlock Resource ordering (always pick up lower-numbered fork first) or limit the number of concurrent diners with a semaphore
Reader-Writer Allowing multiple readers while giving writers exclusive access Track reader count; first reader locks out writers, last reader unlocks. Or use pthread_rwlock_t.

Why These Problems Matter

These classic problems are not just academic exercises. They appear everywhere in real systems:

  • Dining Philosophers: Any system where multiple threads compete for a fixed set of resources. Database connections, network sockets, hardware devices, file locks.
  • Reader-Writer: Caching systems, databases, configuration files, shared data structures where reads are far more frequent than writes.

Understanding these problems and their solutions gives you the conceptual tools to design correct concurrent systems.

Key Takeaways

  • The Dining Philosophers problem demonstrates how naive lock acquisition can lead to deadlock.
  • Resource ordering (always acquiring locks in a consistent global order) is the most practical way to prevent deadlock.
  • Limiting the number of concurrent resource consumers (using a semaphore) is another effective deadlock prevention strategy.
  • The Reader-Writer problem shows that different types of access (read vs write) can have different concurrency requirements.
  • Reader-preference solutions can starve writers; writer-preference solutions can starve readers. The built-in pthread_rwlock_t attempts to balance both.
  • These problems represent patterns that appear throughout real-world systems programming.

Module 6: Threads and Synchronization

Module 6 Summary

Wrap Up

In this module, we covered threads, synchronization primitives, and classic concurrency problems. These are essential topics for any systems programmer. Writing correct concurrent code is one of the most challenging tasks in software engineering, and the concepts you learned here form the foundation for tackling that challenge.

The topics included:

  • Threads: what they are and how they differ from processes. Threads share the same address space (code, globals, heap) but have their own stack and registers.
  • The pthreads library: creating threads with pthread_create(), waiting for them with pthread_join(), passing arguments and returning values.
  • Race conditions: the unpredictable behavior that occurs when threads access shared data without synchronization. The read-modify-write problem.
  • Mutexes: the primary synchronization primitive for protecting critical sections and enforcing mutual exclusion.
  • Condition variables: a mechanism for threads to wait for specific conditions, enabling efficient producer-consumer patterns.
  • Semaphores: counting-based synchronization primitives, useful for resource management and as an alternative to mutexes plus condition variables.
  • Classic concurrency problems: the Dining Philosophers and Reader-Writer problems, along with solutions that prevent deadlock and starvation.

Key Concepts to Remember

  • Threads vs Processes: Threads are lightweight, share memory, and are cheap to create. Processes are isolated, have separate address spaces, and are more expensive. Use threads when tasks need to share data; use processes when you need isolation.
  • Shared state requires synchronization: If two or more threads access the same data and at least one writes to it, you must use synchronization. No exceptions.
  • counter++ is not atomic: A single line of C code can be multiple machine instructions. The read-modify-write pattern is the most common source of race conditions.
  • Mutexes enforce mutual exclusion: Lock before entering a critical section, unlock when leaving. Always unlock on every code path, including error paths.
  • Condition variables use while loops: Always check the condition in a while loop, not an if statement, to handle spurious and stolen wakeups.
  • Deadlock requires four conditions: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Break any one of these to prevent deadlock. The most practical approach is to acquire locks in a consistent global order.
  • Test concurrent code aggressively: Race conditions are non-deterministic. A program that works 99 times out of 100 is still buggy. Run tests many times and on different machines.

Common Pitfalls Checklist

Before submitting any concurrent program, check for these common mistakes:

Pitfall How to Avoid It
Forgetting -pthread when compiling Always compile with gcc -o prog prog.c -pthread
Passing the address of a loop variable to threads Use an array so each thread has its own copy of the argument
Returning a pointer to a local variable from a thread Use malloc for return values; free them after pthread_join
Accessing shared data without a lock Identify all shared variables and protect every access with a mutex
Forgetting to unlock a mutex (especially on error paths) Review every code path through the critical section
Using different mutexes for the same shared data All threads must lock the same mutex for mutual exclusion to work
Using if instead of while with pthread_cond_wait Always use a while loop to recheck the condition
Deadlock from inconsistent lock ordering Always acquire multiple locks in the same global order
Not calling pthread_join (resource leak) Always join every thread you create, or detach it

The pthreads Functions We Covered

Here is a quick reference for all the functions introduced in this module:

Category Function Purpose
Threads pthread_create() Create a new thread
pthread_join() Wait for a thread to finish
Mutexes pthread_mutex_init() Initialize a mutex
pthread_mutex_lock() Acquire the lock (blocks if held)
pthread_mutex_trylock() Try to acquire (non-blocking)
pthread_mutex_unlock() Release the lock
pthread_mutex_destroy() Free mutex resources
Condition Variables pthread_cond_init() Initialize a condition variable
pthread_cond_wait() Release mutex and sleep until signaled
pthread_cond_signal() Wake one waiting thread
pthread_cond_broadcast() Wake all waiting threads
pthread_cond_destroy() Destroy a condition variable and free its resources
Semaphores sem_init() Initialize an unnamed semaphore
sem_wait() Decrement counter (blocks if zero)
sem_post() Increment counter (wakes a waiter)
sem_destroy() Free semaphore resources
Reader-Writer Locks pthread_rwlock_init() Initialize a reader-writer lock
pthread_rwlock_rdlock() Acquire a read lock (shared)
pthread_rwlock_wrlock() Acquire a write lock (exclusive)
pthread_rwlock_unlock() Unlock a reader-writer lock (for both readers and writers)
pthread_rwlock_destroy() Destroy a reader-writer lock and free its resources
