Module 7: File I/O and Sockets Programming

Module 7 Overview

In Module 7: File I/O and Sockets Programming, we will explore how Unix systems handle input and output at the lowest level and then build on that foundation to write networked programs. Unix is built on a powerful idea: everything is a file. Whether you are reading from a disk, writing to a terminal, or communicating over a network, you interact with the same set of system calls. This module traces that idea from opening a file on disk all the way to building a working web server.

We begin with low-level file I/O using the system calls open, read, write, and close. We then examine the buffered FILE* API provided by the C standard library and learn how to work with directories and file metadata. In the second half of the module, we turn to networking. We study the TCP/IP protocol stack, learn the sockets API that lets programs communicate over a network, and progressively build more capable servers: first an echo server, then a multi-client threaded server, and finally a minimal HTTP web server that ties together file I/O, sockets, and threads.

This module is the capstone of the course. It brings together nearly every concept you have learned: C programming, system calls, processes, and threads. By the end, you will see how a few simple abstractions -- file descriptors and byte streams -- underlie all of modern networked computing.

Learning objectives

At the end of this learning module, you will be able to:

  1. Explain the Unix "everything is a file" philosophy and describe what a file descriptor represents
  2. Use the low-level I/O system calls open, read, write, and close to manipulate files
  3. Compare and contrast unbuffered I/O (file descriptors) with buffered I/O (the FILE* API)
  4. Read directory contents and query file metadata using opendir, readdir, and stat
  5. Describe the four layers of the TCP/IP model and explain what TCP provides to applications
  6. Explain the purpose of IP addresses, ports, and network byte order
  7. Implement a TCP server using the socket API: socket, bind, listen, accept
  8. Implement a TCP client using socket and connect
  9. Build a multi-client server using threads
  10. Construct a minimal HTTP web server that serves static files

Learning activities

You are expected to do the following tasks in order to achieve the above objectives:

  1. Complete the reading listed below
  2. Read Lessons 1 through 6 and work through the code examples on your own machine
  3. Take the module quiz
  4. Review additional resources on the Module 7 Summary page

Reading

  • Bryant & O'Hallaron: Chapters 10 and 11 (System-Level I/O and Network Programming)

If you have questions, you can post them in the course lobby or send your instructor an email.

Module 7: File I/O and Sockets Programming

Lesson 1: File Descriptors and Low-Level I/O

Everything Is a File

One of the most important design principles in Unix is that everything is a file. Regular files on disk, directories, terminals, pipes, and even network connections are all accessed through the same interface. A program reads from a keyboard the same way it reads from a file on disk: by calling read() on a file descriptor.

This is not just a metaphor. The kernel maintains a table of open files for each process, and every open file -- regardless of what it actually represents -- is identified by a small non-negative integer called a file descriptor. When you open a file, the kernel returns a file descriptor. When you want to read, write, or close that file, you pass the file descriptor back to the kernel.

File Descriptors

A file descriptor is simply an int. It serves as an index into a per-process table that the kernel maintains. Each entry in this table points to an entry in a system-wide open file table, which in turn points to the file's inode (the on-disk data structure that describes the file).

Every process starts with three file descriptors already open:

File DescriptorNameC ConstantPurpose
0Standard InputSTDIN_FILENOReading input (usually the keyboard)
1Standard OutputSTDOUT_FILENOWriting normal output (usually the terminal)
2Standard ErrorSTDERR_FILENOWriting error messages (usually the terminal)

These constants are defined in <unistd.h>. When you call printf("hello"), the C library ultimately calls write(1, "hello", 5) -- it writes 5 bytes to file descriptor 1 (standard output).

When you open a new file, the kernel assigns the lowest available file descriptor number. So the first file you open will typically get descriptor 3, the next gets 4, and so on.

Opening Files: open()

The open() system call opens a file and returns a file descriptor. It is declared in <fcntl.h>:

#include <fcntl.h>

int open(const char *pathname, int flags);
int open(const char *pathname, int flags, mode_t mode);

The flags argument specifies how the file should be opened. You must include exactly one of these access modes:

  • O_RDONLY -- Open for reading only
  • O_WRONLY -- Open for writing only
  • O_RDWR -- Open for both reading and writing

You can combine additional flags using the bitwise OR operator:

  • O_CREAT -- Create the file if it does not exist. When using this flag, you must provide the mode argument (e.g., 0644) to set the file's permissions.
  • O_TRUNC -- If the file exists and is opened for writing, truncate it to zero length (erase its contents).
  • O_APPEND -- Writes are appended to the end of the file.

The return value is a file descriptor on success, or -1 on error (with errno set to indicate the error).

Example: Opening a file for reading

int fd = open("data.txt", O_RDONLY);
if (fd == -1) {
    perror("open");
    exit(1);
}

Example: Creating a file for writing

int fd = open("output.txt", O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC, 0644);
if (fd == -1) {
    perror("open");
    exit(1);
}

The permission mode 0644 means the owner can read and write, and everyone else can only read. This is an octal number -- the leading zero tells the compiler it is octal.

Closing Files: close()

When you are finished with a file, you should close it:

#include <unistd.h>

int close(int fd);

Closing a file descriptor releases the kernel resources associated with the open file. It returns 0 on success and -1 on error. If your program opens many files without closing them, it will eventually run out of file descriptors.

Reading: read()

The read() system call reads bytes from a file descriptor into a buffer:

#include <unistd.h>

ssize_t read(int fd, void *buf, size_t count);

It attempts to read up to count bytes from file descriptor fd into the buffer pointed to by buf. The return value is:

  • A positive number: the number of bytes actually read. This can be less than count. This is called a short read or partial read. It happens when there are fewer bytes available than requested (for example, you are near the end of the file).
  • 0: End of file (EOF) has been reached. There is nothing left to read.
  • -1: An error occurred. Check errno for the specific error.

Because read() can return fewer bytes than you asked for, robust code must handle partial reads. Typically you call read() in a loop:

char buf[4096];
ssize_t bytes_read;

while ((bytes_read = read(fd, buf, sizeof(buf))) > 0) {
    // process bytes_read bytes in buf
}
if (bytes_read == -1) {
    perror("read");
}

Writing: write()

The write() system call writes bytes from a buffer to a file descriptor:

#include <unistd.h>

ssize_t write(int fd, const void *buf, size_t count);

It attempts to write count bytes from buf to file descriptor fd. Like read(), it can return fewer bytes than requested (a short write). The return value is:

  • A positive number: the number of bytes actually written.
  • -1: An error occurred.

To ensure all bytes are written, you should loop:

ssize_t write_all(int fd, const char *buf, size_t count) {
    size_t total = 0;
    while (total < count) {
        ssize_t written = write(fd, buf + total, count - total);
        if (written == -1) {
            perror("write");
            return -1;
        }
        total += written;
    }
    return total;
}

Error Handling: errno and perror()

When a system call fails (returns -1), it sets the global variable errno to an integer code indicating what went wrong. Common values include:

  • ENOENT -- No such file or directory
  • EACCES -- Permission denied
  • EBADF -- Bad file descriptor
  • ENOMEM -- Out of memory

The perror() function prints a human-readable error message to standard error. It takes a string prefix, appends a colon and the message corresponding to the current value of errno:

int fd = open("nonexistent.txt", O_RDONLY);
if (fd == -1) {
    perror("open");  // prints: open: No such file or directory
    exit(1);
}

You must include <errno.h> to use errno directly and <stdio.h> for perror().

Complete Example: Copying a File

Here is a complete program that copies one file to another using low-level I/O. It reads from a source file and writes to a destination file, handling partial reads and writes:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <unistd.h>

#define BUF_SIZE 4096

int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {
    if (argc != 3) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Usage: %s <source> <destination>\n", argv[0]);
        exit(1);
    }

    // Open source file for reading
    int src_fd = open(argv[1], O_RDONLY);
    if (src_fd == -1) {
        perror("open source");
        exit(1);
    }

    // Create destination file for writing
    int dst_fd = open(argv[2], O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC, 0644);
    if (dst_fd == -1) {
        perror("open destination");
        close(src_fd);
        exit(1);
    }

    // Copy loop
    char buf[BUF_SIZE];
    ssize_t bytes_read;

    while ((bytes_read = read(src_fd, buf, BUF_SIZE)) > 0) {
        // Write all bytes that were read
        char *write_ptr = buf;
        ssize_t remaining = bytes_read;

        while (remaining > 0) {
            ssize_t written = write(dst_fd, write_ptr, remaining);
            if (written == -1) {
                perror("write");
                close(src_fd);
                close(dst_fd);
                exit(1);
            }
            write_ptr += written;
            remaining -= written;
        }
    }

    if (bytes_read == -1) {
        perror("read");
    }

    close(src_fd);
    close(dst_fd);

    return 0;
}

Compile and run:

$ gcc -o filecopy filecopy.c
$ ./filecopy original.txt copy.txt

This program demonstrates several important patterns:

  • Always check return values of system calls
  • Use a loop to handle partial reads and writes
  • Clean up resources (close file descriptors) even on error paths
  • Use perror() for informative error messages

Complete Example: Reading from Standard Input

Since standard input is just file descriptor 0, we can read from the keyboard using read(). This program reads a line from the user and echoes it back:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>

int main(void) {
    char buf[256];

    write(STDOUT_FILENO, "Enter text: ", 12);

    ssize_t n = read(STDIN_FILENO, buf, sizeof(buf) - 1);
    if (n == -1) {
        perror("read");
        return 1;
    }

    buf[n] = '\0';  // null-terminate the string

    write(STDOUT_FILENO, "You typed: ", 11);
    write(STDOUT_FILENO, buf, n);

    return 0;
}

Notice that we use sizeof(buf) - 1 to leave room for the null terminator. The read() system call does not add a null terminator -- it reads raw bytes. If you want to treat the data as a C string, you must add the '\0' yourself.

Key Takeaways

  • In Unix, everything is accessed through file descriptors: regular files, terminals, pipes, and sockets.
  • open() returns a file descriptor; close() releases it.
  • read() and write() are the fundamental I/O operations. Both can return fewer bytes than requested.
  • Always check return values and handle errors with errno and perror().
  • File descriptors 0, 1, and 2 are automatically open as stdin, stdout, and stderr.

Module 7: File I/O and Sockets Programming

Lesson 2: The FILE API and Directories

Why Buffered I/O?

In Lesson 1, we used read() and write() directly. These are system calls -- each one requires a context switch from user mode to kernel mode and back. Context switches are expensive. If your program reads a file one byte at a time using read(fd, &ch, 1), it will make one system call per byte. For a 1 MB file, that is over a million system calls.

The C standard library provides a buffered I/O layer on top of file descriptors. Instead of a raw int file descriptor, you work with a FILE * pointer. Internally, the library maintains a buffer (typically 4096 or 8192 bytes). When you call fgetc(), the library does not issue a system call for every byte. Instead, it reads a large chunk into its buffer with a single read() call and then serves subsequent fgetc() requests from the buffer. This dramatically reduces the number of system calls.

The same idea applies to output. When you call fprintf(), the output is written into a buffer. The buffer is flushed (actually written to the file descriptor via write()) when it is full, when a newline is written (for line-buffered streams like stdout), or when you call fflush().

Opening and Closing Files with FILE*

The fopen() function opens a file and returns a FILE *:

#include <stdio.h>

FILE *fopen(const char *pathname, const char *mode);

The mode string specifies how the file is opened:

ModeDescription
"r"Open for reading. File must exist.
"w"Open for writing. Creates the file or truncates it to zero length.
"a"Open for appending. Creates the file if it does not exist.
"r+"Open for reading and writing. File must exist.
"w+"Open for reading and writing. Creates or truncates.

fopen() returns NULL on error. Always check:

FILE *fp = fopen("data.txt", "r");
if (fp == NULL) {
    perror("fopen");
    exit(1);
}

When finished, close the file with fclose():

fclose(fp);

This flushes any remaining buffered output and releases the underlying file descriptor.

Standard Streams

Just as every process starts with three open file descriptors (0, 1, 2), the C library provides three pre-opened FILE * streams:

  • stdin -- corresponds to file descriptor 0
  • stdout -- corresponds to file descriptor 1
  • stderr -- corresponds to file descriptor 2

Functions like printf() write to stdout. Functions like scanf() read from stdin. You can use fprintf(stderr, ...) to write error messages.

Reading and Writing with FILE*

The C library provides many functions for buffered I/O. Here are the most important ones:

Character-level I/O

int fgetc(FILE *stream);          // read one character, returns EOF on end
int fputc(int c, FILE *stream);   // write one character

Line-level I/O

char *fgets(char *buf, int size, FILE *stream);   // read a line (up to size-1 chars)
int fputs(const char *str, FILE *stream);         // write a string

fgets() reads until it encounters a newline, EOF, or has read size - 1 characters. It always null-terminates the buffer. The newline character, if read, is included in the buffer. It returns NULL on error or EOF.

Formatted I/O

int fprintf(FILE *stream, const char *format, ...);   // formatted output
int fscanf(FILE *stream, const char *format, ...);    // formatted input

These work exactly like printf() and scanf(), but operate on any FILE * stream rather than just stdout/stdin.

Block I/O

size_t fread(void *ptr, size_t size, size_t nmemb, FILE *stream);
size_t fwrite(const void *ptr, size_t size, size_t nmemb, FILE *stream);

fread() and fwrite() read and write blocks of data. The size parameter is the size of each element, and nmemb is the number of elements. They return the number of elements (not bytes) successfully read or written.

Flushing the buffer

int fflush(FILE *stream);

Forces any buffered output to be written to the underlying file descriptor. This is important when you need output to appear immediately -- for example, before calling fork() or when writing a prompt before reading input.

Complete Example: A Simple cat Clone

The Unix cat command reads files and writes their contents to standard output. Here is a simple version using the FILE* API:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

void cat(FILE *fp) {
    int ch;
    while ((ch = fgetc(fp)) != EOF) {
        fputc(ch, stdout);
    }
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {
    if (argc == 1) {
        // No arguments: read from stdin
        cat(stdin);
    } else {
        // Process each file argument
        for (int i = 1; i < argc; i++) {
            FILE *fp = fopen(argv[i], "r");
            if (fp == NULL) {
                perror(argv[i]);
                continue;
            }
            cat(fp);
            fclose(fp);
        }
    }

    return 0;
}

Notice how this program handles argc and argv. The first element argv[0] is the program name. The remaining elements argv[1] through argv[argc-1] are the command-line arguments. If no files are given, the program reads from standard input -- just like the real cat.

Reading Directories

Directories are a special kind of file. You cannot read a directory with fopen() and fgets() -- instead, you use the opendir()/readdir()/closedir() functions declared in <dirent.h>:

#include <dirent.h>

DIR *opendir(const char *name);
struct dirent *readdir(DIR *dirp);
int closedir(DIR *dirp);

opendir() opens a directory and returns a DIR * handle (or NULL on error). readdir() returns a pointer to a struct dirent for the next entry in the directory, or NULL when there are no more entries. The most important field in struct dirent is d_name, which is the name of the file.

File Metadata: stat()

To get information about a file -- its size, permissions, type, modification time -- you use the stat() system call:

#include <sys/stat.h>

int stat(const char *pathname, struct stat *statbuf);
int fstat(int fd, struct stat *statbuf);

stat() takes a pathname; fstat() takes an already-open file descriptor. Both fill in a struct stat with information about the file. Key fields include:

FieldTypeDescription
st_sizeoff_tTotal size in bytes
st_modemode_tFile type and permissions
st_mtimetime_tTime of last modification
st_nlinknlink_tNumber of hard links

The st_mode field encodes both the file type and permissions. You can test the type with macros:

  • S_ISREG(st_mode) -- Is it a regular file?
  • S_ISDIR(st_mode) -- Is it a directory?
  • S_ISLNK(st_mode) -- Is it a symbolic link? (Use lstat() for this.)

Complete Example: A Directory Lister

Here is a program that lists the contents of a directory, showing each entry's name, type, and size -- a simplified version of ls -l:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <dirent.h>
#include <sys/stat.h>
#include <string.h>

int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {
    const char *dirname = ".";   // default to current directory
    if (argc > 1) {
        dirname = argv[1];
    }

    DIR *dir = opendir(dirname);
    if (dir == NULL) {
        perror("opendir");
        exit(1);
    }

    struct dirent *entry;
    while ((entry = readdir(dir)) != NULL) {
        // Build the full path
        char path[1024];
        snprintf(path, sizeof(path), "%s/%s", dirname, entry->d_name);

        // Get file metadata
        struct stat sb;
        if (stat(path, &sb) == -1) {
            perror(path);
            continue;
        }

        // Determine type
        char type;
        if (S_ISREG(sb.st_mode)) {
            type = '-';
        } else if (S_ISDIR(sb.st_mode)) {
            type = 'd';
        } else {
            type = '?';
        }

        printf("%c  %8ld  %s\n", type, (long)sb.st_size, entry->d_name);
    }

    closedir(dir);
    return 0;
}

Compile and run:

$ gcc -o myls myls.c
$ ./myls /home/student
d      4096  .
d      4096  ..
-      1234  notes.txt
d      4096  projects
-       567  hello.c

Buffered vs. Unbuffered: When to Use Which

As a general rule:

  • Use the FILE* API (fopen, fprintf, fgets, etc.) for most file I/O. It is more convenient, more portable, and faster for small reads/writes due to buffering.
  • Use low-level I/O (open, read, write) when you need precise control over file descriptors -- for example, with pipes, sockets, or dup2() for I/O redirection. Network programming almost always uses file descriptors directly.

You can get the underlying file descriptor from a FILE * using fileno(fp), and you can wrap a file descriptor in a FILE * using fdopen(fd, mode). However, mixing buffered and unbuffered I/O on the same file is dangerous -- the buffer and the file descriptor can get out of sync.

Key Takeaways

  • The FILE* API provides buffered I/O on top of file descriptors, reducing the number of system calls.
  • fopen() / fclose() open and close buffered streams. fprintf(), fgets(), fread(), and fwrite() perform buffered reads and writes.
  • fflush() forces buffered output to be written immediately.
  • opendir() / readdir() / closedir() iterate over directory contents.
  • stat() retrieves file metadata including size, type, and permissions.
  • Use argc and argv to accept command-line arguments in your programs.

Module 7: File I/O and Sockets Programming

Lesson 3: TCP/IP and Socket Basics

From Files to Networks

In the first two lessons, we learned how to read and write files. Now we turn to a more ambitious goal: reading and writing data across a network. The good news is that Unix treats network connections as file descriptors too. Once a network connection is established, you can call read() and write() on it just as you would with a regular file. The challenge is in establishing that connection in the first place.

Before we write any networking code, we need to understand the protocols that make network communication possible.

The TCP/IP Model

The internet is organized into layers. Each layer provides services to the layer above it and uses services from the layer below it. The TCP/IP model has four layers:

LayerNameWhat It DoesExample Protocols
4 (top)ApplicationDefines the format and meaning of messages exchanged by programsHTTP, FTP, SSH, DNS, SMTP
3TransportProvides end-to-end communication between processes on different machinesTCP, UDP
2InternetRoutes packets across networks from source to destination hostIP (IPv4, IPv6)
1 (bottom)LinkMoves data across a single physical network linkEthernet, Wi-Fi

As a systems programmer, you will work primarily at the boundary between the Application and Transport layers. You write code that constructs application-level messages and hands them to TCP (or UDP) for delivery. The lower layers handle the details of routing and physical transmission.

What TCP Provides

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) provides a reliable, ordered, byte-stream connection between two processes. Let us unpack each of those properties:

  • Reliable: TCP guarantees that data arrives at the destination. If a packet is lost in transit, TCP automatically detects the loss and retransmits it. Your application does not need to worry about lost data.
  • Ordered: TCP guarantees that bytes arrive in the same order they were sent. Even if packets take different routes through the network and arrive out of order, TCP reassembles them in the correct sequence before delivering them to your application.
  • Byte stream: TCP treats data as a continuous stream of bytes, not as discrete messages. There are no message boundaries. If you write 100 bytes and then 200 bytes, the receiver might read them as one 300-byte chunk, or as three 100-byte chunks, or any other combination. It is up to the application to determine where one message ends and the next begins.

This last point is critical and a common source of bugs. You cannot assume that one write() on the sender side corresponds to one read() on the receiver side.

TCP vs. UDP

UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is the other major transport protocol. It provides a much simpler service:

PropertyTCPUDP
Reliable?Yes -- retransmits lost packetsNo -- packets can be lost
Ordered?Yes -- delivers in orderNo -- packets can arrive out of order
Connection?Yes -- requires setup (handshake)No -- just send packets
Message boundaries?No -- byte streamYes -- each send is a datagram
Overhead?Higher (headers, acknowledgments, retransmissions)Lower (minimal headers)

Use TCP when you need reliable, ordered delivery -- which is most of the time (web pages, file transfers, email, remote shells). Use UDP when low latency matters more than reliability (video streaming, online games, DNS lookups).

In this module, we will focus exclusively on TCP.

IP Addresses

An IP address identifies a host (a machine) on a network. IPv4 addresses are 32-bit numbers, conventionally written in dotted decimal notation: four decimal numbers separated by dots, where each number represents one byte (0-255).

192.168.1.100     -- a private network address
10.0.0.1          -- another private address
128.59.105.24     -- a public address (Columbia University)
127.0.0.1         -- the loopback address (localhost)

The address 127.0.0.1 is special. It always refers to the local machine. When you are developing and testing network programs, you will typically connect to 127.0.0.1 (or equivalently, localhost) so that both the client and server run on the same machine.

IPv6 addresses are 128 bits and written in hexadecimal with colons (e.g., ::1 for localhost). We will use IPv4 in this module for simplicity.

Ports

An IP address identifies a machine, but a machine can run many programs simultaneously. A port number identifies a specific process (or service) on that machine. Port numbers are 16-bit unsigned integers (0 to 65535).

A network connection is identified by a 4-tuple: (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port).

Port numbers are divided into ranges:

  • Well-known ports (0-1023): Reserved for standard services. Examples: port 80 for HTTP, port 443 for HTTPS, port 22 for SSH. On Unix, binding to these ports requires root privileges.
  • Registered ports (1024-49151): Can be used by any user. When you write a server for testing, pick a port in this range (e.g., 8080, 9000).
  • Ephemeral ports (49152-65535): Automatically assigned by the OS to clients when they make outgoing connections. You generally do not choose these.

Network Byte Order

Different machines may store multi-byte integers in different byte orders. Intel x86 processors use little-endian byte order (least significant byte first), but the internet protocols use big-endian byte order (most significant byte first). This is called network byte order.

When you send multi-byte values (like port numbers and IP addresses) over the network, you must convert them to network byte order. The following functions, declared in <arpa/inet.h>, perform the conversion:

FunctionPurpose
htons(x)Host to Network Short -- converts a 16-bit value from host to network byte order
htonl(x)Host to Network Long -- converts a 32-bit value from host to network byte order
ntohs(x)Network to Host Short -- converts a 16-bit value from network to host byte order
ntohl(x)Network to Host Long -- converts a 32-bit value from network to host byte order

On a big-endian machine, these are no-ops. On a little-endian machine (like x86), they reverse the byte order. You should always use these functions when filling in network data structures, so your code is portable.

The Socket Address Structure

To specify an IP address and port number together, we use a struct sockaddr_in (for IPv4), declared in <netinet/in.h>:

struct sockaddr_in {
    sa_family_t    sin_family;   // Address family: AF_INET for IPv4
    in_port_t      sin_port;     // Port number in network byte order
    struct in_addr sin_addr;     // IP address in network byte order
};

struct in_addr {
    uint32_t s_addr;             // IP address as a 32-bit integer
};

Here is how you fill in this structure for a server listening on port 8080 on all interfaces:

struct sockaddr_in addr;
memset(&addr, 0, sizeof(addr));          // zero out the structure
addr.sin_family = AF_INET;               // IPv4
addr.sin_port = htons(8080);             // port 8080, converted to network byte order
addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(INADDR_ANY); // listen on all interfaces

INADDR_ANY (which is 0.0.0.0) tells the server to accept connections on any of the machine's network interfaces.

Converting IP Addresses: inet_pton() and inet_ntop()

To convert between human-readable IP address strings and the binary format stored in struct in_addr, use:

#include <arpa/inet.h>

// Presentation to Network: convert string to binary
int inet_pton(int af, const char *src, void *dst);

// Network to Presentation: convert binary to string
const char *inet_ntop(int af, const void *src, char *dst, socklen_t size);

The "p" stands for "presentation" (the human-readable string) and "n" stands for "network" (the binary format).

Example: Converting an IP address string to binary

struct sockaddr_in addr;
memset(&addr, 0, sizeof(addr));
addr.sin_family = AF_INET;
addr.sin_port = htons(8080);

// Convert "127.0.0.1" to binary and store in addr.sin_addr
if (inet_pton(AF_INET, "127.0.0.1", &addr.sin_addr) != 1) {
    fprintf(stderr, "Invalid address\n");
    exit(1);
}

Example: Converting binary to a string

char ip_str[INET_ADDRSTRLEN];
inet_ntop(AF_INET, &addr.sin_addr, ip_str, sizeof(ip_str));
printf("Address: %s\n", ip_str);   // prints: Address: 127.0.0.1

The Headers You Will Need

Network programming in C requires several header files. Here is a summary:

#include <sys/socket.h>    // socket(), bind(), listen(), accept(), connect()
#include <netinet/in.h>    // struct sockaddr_in, INADDR_ANY
#include <arpa/inet.h>     // htons(), htonl(), inet_pton(), inet_ntop()
#include <unistd.h>        // close(), read(), write()
#include <string.h>        // memset()
#include <stdio.h>         // perror(), printf()
#include <stdlib.h>        // exit()

Putting It Together: Preparing an Address

Here is a complete example that sets up a socket address structure and prints it. No actual networking happens yet -- that comes in the next lesson.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <arpa/inet.h>
#include <netinet/in.h>

int main(void) {
    struct sockaddr_in server_addr;
    memset(&server_addr, 0, sizeof(server_addr));

    server_addr.sin_family = AF_INET;
    server_addr.sin_port = htons(8080);

    if (inet_pton(AF_INET, "192.168.1.100", &server_addr.sin_addr) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Invalid address\n");
        return 1;
    }

    // Print back the address to verify
    char ip_str[INET_ADDRSTRLEN];
    inet_ntop(AF_INET, &server_addr.sin_addr, ip_str, sizeof(ip_str));

    printf("Server address: %s\n", ip_str);
    printf("Server port:    %d\n", ntohs(server_addr.sin_port));

    return 0;
}

Output:

Server address: 192.168.1.100
Server port:    8080

Key Takeaways

  • The TCP/IP model has four layers: Link, Internet, Transport, and Application. We program at the Transport/Application boundary.
  • TCP provides a reliable, ordered byte stream. UDP provides an unreliable datagram service. We use TCP for most applications.
  • An IPv4 address is a 32-bit number written in dotted decimal notation. Port numbers are 16-bit unsigned integers.
  • Network byte order is big-endian. Use htons()/htonl() to convert from host to network order, and ntohs()/ntohl() for the reverse.
  • struct sockaddr_in holds an IPv4 address and port. inet_pton() and inet_ntop() convert between string and binary representations of IP addresses.

Module 7: File I/O and Sockets Programming

Lesson 4: Building a Server

The Socket Lifecycle

In the last lesson, we learned the concepts behind TCP/IP networking. Now it is time to write actual networking code. A TCP server goes through a specific sequence of system calls to accept incoming connections. This sequence is sometimes called the socket lifecycle:

  1. socket() -- Create a socket (get a file descriptor)
  2. bind() -- Assign a local address (IP + port) to the socket
  3. listen() -- Mark the socket as passive (willing to accept connections)
  4. accept() -- Wait for and accept an incoming connection (returns a new file descriptor for that connection)
  5. read() / write() -- Exchange data with the connected client
  6. close() -- Close the connection

Let us walk through each step in detail.

Step 1: socket() -- Creating a Socket

#include <sys/socket.h>

int socket(int domain, int type, int protocol);

This creates a new socket and returns a file descriptor. The arguments are:

  • domain: The address family. Use AF_INET for IPv4.
  • type: The socket type. Use SOCK_STREAM for TCP (a reliable byte stream).
  • protocol: The protocol. Use 0 to let the OS choose the appropriate protocol (TCP for SOCK_STREAM).
int server_fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
if (server_fd == -1) {
    perror("socket");
    exit(1);
}

At this point, server_fd is a file descriptor, but it is not yet associated with any address or port.

Setting SO_REUSEADDR

Before binding, it is a good practice to set the SO_REUSEADDR option. When a server closes, the port it was using enters a "TIME_WAIT" state and cannot be reused for a couple of minutes. This is annoying during development, because if you stop and restart your server, the bind() call will fail with "Address already in use." Setting SO_REUSEADDR allows the port to be reused immediately:

int opt = 1;
if (setsockopt(server_fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEADDR, &opt, sizeof(opt)) == -1) {
    perror("setsockopt");
    exit(1);
}

You should include this in every server you write.

Step 2: bind() -- Assigning an Address

int bind(int sockfd, const struct sockaddr *addr, socklen_t addrlen);

bind() associates the socket with a specific IP address and port number. We fill in a struct sockaddr_in as we learned in Lesson 3:

struct sockaddr_in addr;
memset(&addr, 0, sizeof(addr));
addr.sin_family = AF_INET;
addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(INADDR_ANY);  // listen on all interfaces
addr.sin_port = htons(8080);               // listen on port 8080

if (bind(server_fd, (struct sockaddr *)&addr, sizeof(addr)) == -1) {
    perror("bind");
    exit(1);
}

Note the cast to (struct sockaddr *). The socket API was designed before C had void *, so it uses a generic struct sockaddr as the base type. You always cast your address-family-specific structure to this type.

Step 3: listen() -- Marking as Passive

int listen(int sockfd, int backlog);

listen() marks the socket as a passive socket -- one that will be used to accept incoming connections rather than to initiate outgoing connections. The backlog argument specifies the maximum number of pending connections that can be queued before the server calls accept(). A value of 5 to 10 is typical for a simple server:

if (listen(server_fd, 5) == -1) {
    perror("listen");
    exit(1);
}
printf("Server listening on port 8080...\n");

Step 4: accept() -- Accepting a Connection

int accept(int sockfd, struct sockaddr *addr, socklen_t *addrlen);

This is where the server waits for a client to connect. accept() blocks (pauses execution) until a client connects. When a connection arrives, it returns a new file descriptor that represents the connection to that specific client. The original server_fd remains open and continues to listen for more connections.

The addr and addrlen parameters are filled in with the client's address. You can pass NULL for both if you do not care who the client is:

struct sockaddr_in client_addr;
socklen_t client_len = sizeof(client_addr);

int client_fd = accept(server_fd, (struct sockaddr *)&client_addr, &client_len);
if (client_fd == -1) {
    perror("accept");
    exit(1);
}

// Print the client's address
char client_ip[INET_ADDRSTRLEN];
inet_ntop(AF_INET, &client_addr.sin_addr, client_ip, sizeof(client_ip));
printf("Client connected from %s:%d\n", client_ip, ntohs(client_addr.sin_port));

This is the key insight of the socket API: accept() returns a new file descriptor. The listening socket (server_fd) and the connected socket (client_fd) are two different file descriptors. The server uses client_fd to communicate with the client, and server_fd to wait for more clients.

Step 5: Exchanging Data

Once you have a connected file descriptor, you can use read() and write() -- the same system calls we used for file I/O. You can also use send() and recv(), which are socket-specific versions that offer additional flags:

ssize_t send(int sockfd, const void *buf, size_t len, int flags);
ssize_t recv(int sockfd, void *buf, size_t len, int flags);

With flags set to 0, send() and recv() behave identically to write() and read(). We will use read() and write() in our examples since they reinforce the "everything is a file" concept.

Step 6: Closing the Connection

When the conversation is finished, close the client's file descriptor:

close(client_fd);

When you are done accepting connections entirely, close the listening socket too:

close(server_fd);

Complete Example: Echo Server

An echo server reads data from a client and sends it back unchanged. Here is a complete, working echo server that handles one client at a time:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <netinet/in.h>
#include <arpa/inet.h>

#define PORT 8080
#define BUF_SIZE 1024

int main(void) {
    // 1. Create socket
    int server_fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
    if (server_fd == -1) {
        perror("socket");
        exit(1);
    }

    // Allow port reuse
    int opt = 1;
    setsockopt(server_fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEADDR, &opt, sizeof(opt));

    // 2. Bind to address
    struct sockaddr_in addr;
    memset(&addr, 0, sizeof(addr));
    addr.sin_family = AF_INET;
    addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(INADDR_ANY);
    addr.sin_port = htons(PORT);

    if (bind(server_fd, (struct sockaddr *)&addr, sizeof(addr)) == -1) {
        perror("bind");
        exit(1);
    }

    // 3. Listen for connections
    if (listen(server_fd, 5) == -1) {
        perror("listen");
        exit(1);
    }
    printf("Echo server listening on port %d...\n", PORT);

    // 4. Accept a client
    struct sockaddr_in client_addr;
    socklen_t client_len = sizeof(client_addr);

    int client_fd = accept(server_fd, (struct sockaddr *)&client_addr, &client_len);
    if (client_fd == -1) {
        perror("accept");
        exit(1);
    }

    char client_ip[INET_ADDRSTRLEN];
    inet_ntop(AF_INET, &client_addr.sin_addr, client_ip, sizeof(client_ip));
    printf("Client connected from %s:%d\n", client_ip, ntohs(client_addr.sin_port));

    // 5. Echo loop: read from client, write back
    char buf[BUF_SIZE];
    ssize_t bytes_read;

    while ((bytes_read = read(client_fd, buf, sizeof(buf))) > 0) {
        // Write all bytes back to the client
        char *ptr = buf;
        ssize_t remaining = bytes_read;
        while (remaining > 0) {
            ssize_t written = write(client_fd, ptr, remaining);
            if (written == -1) {
                perror("write");
                break;
            }
            ptr += written;
            remaining -= written;
        }
    }

    if (bytes_read == -1) {
        perror("read");
    } else {
        printf("Client disconnected.\n");
    }

    // 6. Close
    close(client_fd);
    close(server_fd);

    return 0;
}

Testing the Echo Server

Compile and start the server in one terminal:

$ gcc -o echo_server echo_server.c
$ ./echo_server
Echo server listening on port 8080...

In a second terminal, connect using nc (netcat) or telnet:

$ nc localhost 8080
Hello, server!
Hello, server!
Testing 123
Testing 123

Every line you type is sent to the server, which echoes it back. Press Ctrl+C or Ctrl+D to disconnect.

You can also use telnet:

$ telnet localhost 8080
Trying 127.0.0.1...
Connected to localhost.

Understanding the Data Flow

Let us trace what happens when a client types "Hello" and presses Enter:

  1. The client sends the bytes Hello\n (6 bytes) over the TCP connection.
  2. The server's read() returns 6, placing Hello\n in the buffer.
  3. The server's write() sends those same 6 bytes back.
  4. The client receives Hello\n and displays it.

When the client disconnects (closes its end of the connection), the server's read() returns 0 (EOF), and the echo loop ends.

Limitations of This Server

This server has a major limitation: it can only handle one client at a time. After the first client connects, accept() is not called again, so additional clients must wait until the first client disconnects. In the next lesson, we will fix this with threads.

Key Takeaways

  • The server socket lifecycle is: socket(), bind(), listen(), accept(), read/write, close().
  • accept() returns a new file descriptor for each client connection. The listening socket is separate from the connected socket.
  • Always set SO_REUSEADDR on your server socket to avoid "Address already in use" errors during development.
  • Once a connection is established, read() and write() work just like file I/O -- this is the "everything is a file" principle in action.
  • Use nc (netcat) or telnet to test your server.

Module 7: File I/O and Sockets Programming

Lesson 5: Clients and Multi-Client Servers

Writing a TCP Client

In Lesson 4, we tested our server using nc. Now let us write our own client program in C. The client lifecycle is simpler than the server's:

  1. socket() -- Create a socket
  2. connect() -- Connect to a server at a given IP and port
  3. read() / write() -- Exchange data
  4. close() -- Close the connection

Notice that the client does not call bind() or listen(). It does not need to bind to a specific port -- the operating system automatically assigns an ephemeral port when connect() is called.

The connect() System Call

#include <sys/socket.h>

int connect(int sockfd, const struct sockaddr *addr, socklen_t addrlen);

connect() initiates a TCP connection to the server specified by addr. It performs the TCP three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK). It blocks until the connection is established or an error occurs. Returns 0 on success, -1 on error.

Complete Example: Echo Client

This client connects to our echo server, sends lines of text typed by the user, and prints the echoed responses:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <netinet/in.h>
#include <arpa/inet.h>

#define PORT 8080
#define BUF_SIZE 1024

int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {
    const char *server_ip = "127.0.0.1";
    if (argc > 1) {
        server_ip = argv[1];
    }

    // 1. Create socket
    int sock_fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
    if (sock_fd == -1) {
        perror("socket");
        exit(1);
    }

    // 2. Set up the server address
    struct sockaddr_in server_addr;
    memset(&server_addr, 0, sizeof(server_addr));
    server_addr.sin_family = AF_INET;
    server_addr.sin_port = htons(PORT);

    if (inet_pton(AF_INET, server_ip, &server_addr.sin_addr) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Invalid address: %s\n", server_ip);
        exit(1);
    }

    // 3. Connect to the server
    if (connect(sock_fd, (struct sockaddr *)&server_addr, sizeof(server_addr)) == -1) {
        perror("connect");
        exit(1);
    }
    printf("Connected to %s:%d\n", server_ip, PORT);

    // 4. Send and receive loop
    char send_buf[BUF_SIZE];
    char recv_buf[BUF_SIZE];

    printf("Type a message (Ctrl+D to quit):\n");

    while (fgets(send_buf, sizeof(send_buf), stdin) != NULL) {
        // Send the line to the server
        size_t len = strlen(send_buf);
        if (write(sock_fd, send_buf, len) == -1) {
            perror("write");
            break;
        }

        // Read the echo back
        ssize_t bytes_read = read(sock_fd, recv_buf, sizeof(recv_buf) - 1);
        if (bytes_read <= 0) {
            if (bytes_read == 0)
                printf("Server closed connection.\n");
            else
                perror("read");
            break;
        }

        recv_buf[bytes_read] = '\0';
        printf("Echo: %s", recv_buf);
    }

    // 5. Close
    close(sock_fd);
    printf("Disconnected.\n");

    return 0;
}

Compile and test against the echo server from Lesson 4:

$ gcc -o echo_client echo_client.c
$ ./echo_client
Connected to 127.0.0.1:8080
Type a message (Ctrl+D to quit):
Hello from the client!
Echo: Hello from the client!

The Problem with One Client at a Time

Our echo server from Lesson 4 can only handle one client. After accept() returns, the server enters the echo loop and stays there until that client disconnects. Any other clients trying to connect must wait.

For a real server, this is unacceptable. A web server might need to handle hundreds or thousands of simultaneous connections. There are several approaches to solving this problem:

  • fork() -- Spawn a child process for each client (you know this from earlier modules)
  • Threads -- Spawn a thread for each client (you know this too)
  • select() / poll() / epoll() -- Multiplex I/O in a single thread (beyond the scope of this module)

We will use threads, since you have already learned about them in the previous module. Threads are a natural fit because all threads in a process share the same address space, which makes sharing data (if needed) straightforward.

The Threaded Server Pattern

The idea is simple:

  1. The main thread runs an accept loop, calling accept() repeatedly.
  2. Each time accept() returns a new client file descriptor, the main thread spawns a new thread to handle that client.
  3. The handler thread reads from and writes to the client, then closes the connection and exits.
  4. Meanwhile, the main thread loops back to accept() and waits for the next client.

Passing the file descriptor to the thread

There is a subtle but important issue when passing the client file descriptor to a thread. Consider this incorrect approach:

// WRONG -- race condition!
while (1) {
    int client_fd = accept(server_fd, NULL, NULL);
    pthread_create(&tid, NULL, handle_client, &client_fd);
    // Problem: client_fd might be overwritten by the next accept()
    // before the thread has a chance to read it!
}

The variable client_fd lives on the main thread's stack. If the main thread loops back and calls accept() again before the new thread reads the value, the new thread will see the wrong file descriptor. This is a race condition.

The solution is to allocate memory for each file descriptor on the heap:

while (1) {
    int *client_fd = malloc(sizeof(int));
    *client_fd = accept(server_fd, NULL, NULL);
    if (*client_fd == -1) {
        perror("accept");
        free(client_fd);
        continue;
    }
    pthread_create(&tid, NULL, handle_client, client_fd);
    pthread_detach(tid);  // we won't join this thread
}

Each thread gets its own copy of the file descriptor on the heap. The thread is responsible for freeing the memory when it is done.

Complete Example: Threaded Echo Server

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <netinet/in.h>
#include <arpa/inet.h>

#define PORT 8080
#define BUF_SIZE 1024

void *handle_client(void *arg) {
    int client_fd = *(int *)arg;
    free(arg);  // free the heap-allocated file descriptor

    char client_ip[INET_ADDRSTRLEN];
    struct sockaddr_in client_addr;
    socklen_t addr_len = sizeof(client_addr);
    getpeername(client_fd, (struct sockaddr *)&client_addr, &addr_len);
    inet_ntop(AF_INET, &client_addr.sin_addr, client_ip, sizeof(client_ip));
    printf("Thread %lu handling client %s:%d\n",
           (unsigned long)pthread_self(), client_ip, ntohs(client_addr.sin_port));

    // Echo loop
    char buf[BUF_SIZE];
    ssize_t bytes_read;

    while ((bytes_read = read(client_fd, buf, sizeof(buf))) > 0) {
        char *ptr = buf;
        ssize_t remaining = bytes_read;
        while (remaining > 0) {
            ssize_t written = write(client_fd, ptr, remaining);
            if (written == -1) {
                perror("write");
                goto done;
            }
            ptr += written;
            remaining -= written;
        }
    }

done:
    printf("Client %s:%d disconnected.\n", client_ip, ntohs(client_addr.sin_port));
    close(client_fd);
    return NULL;
}

int main(void) {
    // Create socket
    int server_fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
    if (server_fd == -1) {
        perror("socket");
        exit(1);
    }

    int opt = 1;
    setsockopt(server_fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEADDR, &opt, sizeof(opt));

    // Bind
    struct sockaddr_in addr;
    memset(&addr, 0, sizeof(addr));
    addr.sin_family = AF_INET;
    addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(INADDR_ANY);
    addr.sin_port = htons(PORT);

    if (bind(server_fd, (struct sockaddr *)&addr, sizeof(addr)) == -1) {
        perror("bind");
        exit(1);
    }

    // Listen
    if (listen(server_fd, 10) == -1) {
        perror("listen");
        exit(1);
    }
    printf("Threaded echo server listening on port %d...\n", PORT);

    // Accept loop
    while (1) {
        int *client_fd = malloc(sizeof(int));
        if (client_fd == NULL) {
            perror("malloc");
            continue;
        }

        *client_fd = accept(server_fd, NULL, NULL);
        if (*client_fd == -1) {
            perror("accept");
            free(client_fd);
            continue;
        }

        pthread_t tid;
        if (pthread_create(&tid, NULL, handle_client, client_fd) != 0) {
            perror("pthread_create");
            close(*client_fd);
            free(client_fd);
            continue;
        }
        pthread_detach(tid);
    }

    close(server_fd);
    return 0;
}

Compile with the -pthread flag:

$ gcc -o threaded_echo threaded_echo.c -pthread
$ ./threaded_echo
Threaded echo server listening on port 8080...

Now you can open multiple terminals and connect multiple clients simultaneously. Each client is handled by its own thread.

File Descriptor Lifecycle in Multi-Client Servers

It is important to understand which file descriptors exist and who is responsible for closing them:

File DescriptorCreated ByUsed ByClosed By
server_fdMain thread (socket())Main thread (accept())Main thread (at shutdown)
client_fd (one per client)Main thread (accept())Handler thread (read/write)Handler thread

Each accept() call creates a new file descriptor. The handler thread owns that file descriptor and is responsible for closing it when the client disconnects. The listening socket (server_fd) stays open the entire time the server is running.

If you use fork() instead of threads, the situation is more complex: both the parent and child process have copies of the file descriptor, and both must close their copy. With threads, there is only one copy because threads share the same file descriptor table.

Using pthread_detach()

In the server above, we call pthread_detach(tid) after creating each thread. This tells the system that no other thread will call pthread_join() on this thread. When the detached thread finishes, its resources are automatically cleaned up. Without detaching (and without joining), the thread's resources would leak.

A Note on Robustness

The threaded server above is a good starting point, but a production server would need additional features:

  • Thread pool: Creating a new thread for every client is expensive. A real server would pre-create a pool of threads and assign clients to them.
  • Signal handling: The server should handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) gracefully, closing the listening socket and waiting for active clients to finish.
  • Connection limits: Without limits, an attacker could exhaust the server's resources by opening thousands of connections.

For this course, the thread-per-client model is sufficient. Understanding it is the foundation for understanding more sophisticated approaches.

Key Takeaways

  • A TCP client calls socket(), connect(), read/write, and close(). No bind() or listen() is needed.
  • To handle multiple clients, put accept() in a loop and spawn a thread for each new connection.
  • Pass the client file descriptor to the thread via a heap-allocated pointer to avoid race conditions.
  • Use pthread_detach() so thread resources are cleaned up automatically.
  • Each client connection gets its own file descriptor. The handler thread is responsible for closing it.

Module 7: File I/O and Sockets Programming

Lesson 6: From Echo Server to Web Server

Introduction

In the previous two lessons, we built echo servers and clients. An echo server is useful for learning, but it does not do anything practical. In this lesson, we will build something real: a minimal HTTP web server. This ties together everything we have learned in this module -- file I/O, sockets, and threads -- into a single program.

When you type a URL into your browser, the browser connects to a web server using TCP, sends an HTTP request, and receives an HTTP response containing the web page. Our server will handle exactly this: accept TCP connections, parse HTTP requests, read files from disk, and send HTTP responses.

HTTP Basics

HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is a text-based application-layer protocol. It follows a simple request-response pattern: the client sends a request, the server sends a response.

HTTP Request Format

An HTTP request looks like this:

GET /index.html HTTP/1.1\r\n
Host: localhost:8080\r\n
Connection: close\r\n
\r\n

The first line is the request line. It has three parts:

  • Method: GET means "retrieve this resource." Other methods include POST, PUT, DELETE, etc. We only need to handle GET.
  • Path: /index.html is the file being requested.
  • Version: HTTP/1.1 is the protocol version.

After the request line come zero or more header lines, each ending with \r\n (carriage return followed by newline). The headers end with a blank line (\r\n by itself).

For our minimal server, we only need to parse the first line to extract the method and path. We can ignore the headers.

HTTP Response Format

An HTTP response looks like this:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n
Content-Type: text/html\r\n
Content-Length: 45\r\n
Connection: close\r\n
\r\n
<html><body><h1>Hello!</h1></body></html>

The first line is the status line:

  • Version: HTTP/1.1
  • Status code: 200 means success. 404 means "not found." 500 means "internal server error."
  • Reason phrase: OK is a human-readable description of the status code.

After the status line come response headers, then a blank line, then the body (the actual content). The Content-Length header tells the client how many bytes are in the body. The Content-Type header tells the client what kind of data it is (HTML, plain text, an image, etc.).

Content Types

The Content-Type header tells the browser how to interpret the response body. Here are common types:

File ExtensionContent-Type
.htmltext/html
.csstext/css
.jsapplication/javascript
.txttext/plain
.jpgimage/jpeg
.pngimage/png

Parsing an HTTP Request

Our server needs to extract the path from the request line. Here is a function that reads the request and extracts the method and path:

// Read the HTTP request and extract the path.
// Returns 0 on success, -1 on error.
int parse_request(int client_fd, char *method, char *path) {
    char buf[2048];
    ssize_t bytes_read = read(client_fd, buf, sizeof(buf) - 1);
    if (bytes_read <= 0) {
        return -1;
    }
    buf[bytes_read] = '\0';

    // Parse the request line: "GET /path HTTP/1.1\r\n..."
    // sscanf will extract the method and path
    if (sscanf(buf, "%15s %255s", method, path) != 2) {
        return -1;
    }

    return 0;
}

This is a simplified parser. A production HTTP server would need to handle multi-packet requests, very long headers, and many edge cases. For our purposes, this works because the request line is almost always contained in the first read().

Serving a Static File

Once we know the requested path (e.g., /index.html), we need to open that file from a directory on disk, read its contents, and send them back in an HTTP response. We also need to handle the case where the file does not exist (404 Not Found).

Here is a function that determines the content type from the file extension:

const char *get_content_type(const char *path) {
    const char *ext = strrchr(path, '.');
    if (ext == NULL)        return "application/octet-stream";
    if (strcmp(ext, ".html") == 0) return "text/html";
    if (strcmp(ext, ".css") == 0)  return "text/css";
    if (strcmp(ext, ".js") == 0)   return "application/javascript";
    if (strcmp(ext, ".txt") == 0)  return "text/plain";
    if (strcmp(ext, ".jpg") == 0)  return "image/jpeg";
    if (strcmp(ext, ".png") == 0)  return "image/png";
    return "application/octet-stream";
}

Sending the Response

Here is a helper function that sends an HTTP response with headers and a body:

void send_response(int client_fd, int status_code, const char *status_text,
                   const char *content_type, const char *body, size_t body_len) {
    char header[512];
    int header_len = snprintf(header, sizeof(header),
        "HTTP/1.1 %d %s\r\n"
        "Content-Type: %s\r\n"
        "Content-Length: %zu\r\n"
        "Connection: close\r\n"
        "\r\n",
        status_code, status_text, content_type, body_len);

    write(client_fd, header, header_len);
    if (body_len > 0) {
        write(client_fd, body, body_len);
    }
}

Complete Example: Minimal Web Server

Here is the complete web server. It serves files from a directory called www in the current working directory. It uses threads to handle multiple clients.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <sys/stat.h>
#include <netinet/in.h>
#include <arpa/inet.h>

#define PORT 8080
#define BUF_SIZE 4096
#define WEB_ROOT "./www"

const char *get_content_type(const char *path) {
    const char *ext = strrchr(path, '.');
    if (ext == NULL)               return "application/octet-stream";
    if (strcmp(ext, ".html") == 0)  return "text/html";
    if (strcmp(ext, ".css") == 0)   return "text/css";
    if (strcmp(ext, ".js") == 0)    return "application/javascript";
    if (strcmp(ext, ".txt") == 0)   return "text/plain";
    if (strcmp(ext, ".jpg") == 0)   return "image/jpeg";
    if (strcmp(ext, ".png") == 0)   return "image/png";
    return "application/octet-stream";
}

void send_response(int client_fd, int status_code, const char *status_text,
                   const char *content_type, const char *body, size_t body_len) {
    char header[512];
    int header_len = snprintf(header, sizeof(header),
        "HTTP/1.1 %d %s\r\n"
        "Content-Type: %s\r\n"
        "Content-Length: %zu\r\n"
        "Connection: close\r\n"
        "\r\n",
        status_code, status_text, content_type, body_len);

    write(client_fd, header, header_len);
    if (body_len > 0) {
        write(client_fd, body, body_len);
    }
}

void send_error(int client_fd, int status_code, const char *status_text) {
    char body[256];
    int body_len = snprintf(body, sizeof(body),
        "<html><body><h1>%d %s</h1></body></html>",
        status_code, status_text);
    send_response(client_fd, status_code, status_text,
                  "text/html", body, body_len);
}

void *handle_client(void *arg) {
    int client_fd = *(int *)arg;
    free(arg);

    // Read the request
    char request[2048];
    ssize_t bytes_read = read(client_fd, request, sizeof(request) - 1);
    if (bytes_read <= 0) {
        close(client_fd);
        return NULL;
    }
    request[bytes_read] = '\0';

    // Parse the request line
    char method[16], path[256];
    if (sscanf(request, "%15s %255s", method, path) != 2) {
        send_error(client_fd, 400, "Bad Request");
        close(client_fd);
        return NULL;
    }

    printf("%s %s\n", method, path);

    // Only handle GET requests
    if (strcmp(method, "GET") != 0) {
        send_error(client_fd, 405, "Method Not Allowed");
        close(client_fd);
        return NULL;
    }

    // If path is "/", serve "/index.html"
    if (strcmp(path, "/") == 0) {
        strcpy(path, "/index.html");
    }

    // Build the file path: WEB_ROOT + path
    // Security note: a real server must prevent ".." traversal attacks
    char filepath[512];
    snprintf(filepath, sizeof(filepath), "%s%s", WEB_ROOT, path);

    // Check that the path does not contain ".."
    if (strstr(filepath, "..") != NULL) {
        send_error(client_fd, 403, "Forbidden");
        close(client_fd);
        return NULL;
    }

    // Get file info
    struct stat sb;
    if (stat(filepath, &sb) == -1 || !S_ISREG(sb.st_mode)) {
        send_error(client_fd, 404, "Not Found");
        close(client_fd);
        return NULL;
    }

    // Open and read the file
    int file_fd = open(filepath, O_RDONLY);
    if (file_fd == -1) {
        send_error(client_fd, 500, "Internal Server Error");
        close(client_fd);
        return NULL;
    }

    // Send the response header
    const char *content_type = get_content_type(filepath);
    char header[512];
    int header_len = snprintf(header, sizeof(header),
        "HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n"
        "Content-Type: %s\r\n"
        "Content-Length: %ld\r\n"
        "Connection: close\r\n"
        "\r\n",
        content_type, (long)sb.st_size);

    write(client_fd, header, header_len);

    // Send the file contents
    char buf[BUF_SIZE];
    ssize_t n;
    while ((n = read(file_fd, buf, sizeof(buf))) > 0) {
        char *ptr = buf;
        ssize_t remaining = n;
        while (remaining > 0) {
            ssize_t written = write(client_fd, ptr, remaining);
            if (written == -1) {
                break;
            }
            ptr += written;
            remaining -= written;
        }
    }

    close(file_fd);
    close(client_fd);
    return NULL;
}

int main(void) {
    int server_fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
    if (server_fd == -1) {
        perror("socket");
        exit(1);
    }

    int opt = 1;
    setsockopt(server_fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEADDR, &opt, sizeof(opt));

    struct sockaddr_in addr;
    memset(&addr, 0, sizeof(addr));
    addr.sin_family = AF_INET;
    addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(INADDR_ANY);
    addr.sin_port = htons(PORT);

    if (bind(server_fd, (struct sockaddr *)&addr, sizeof(addr)) == -1) {
        perror("bind");
        exit(1);
    }

    if (listen(server_fd, 10) == -1) {
        perror("listen");
        exit(1);
    }

    printf("Web server listening on http://localhost:%d/\n", PORT);
    printf("Serving files from %s\n", WEB_ROOT);

    while (1) {
        int *client_fd = malloc(sizeof(int));
        if (client_fd == NULL) {
            perror("malloc");
            continue;
        }

        *client_fd = accept(server_fd, NULL, NULL);
        if (*client_fd == -1) {
            perror("accept");
            free(client_fd);
            continue;
        }

        pthread_t tid;
        if (pthread_create(&tid, NULL, handle_client, client_fd) != 0) {
            perror("pthread_create");
            close(*client_fd);
            free(client_fd);
            continue;
        }
        pthread_detach(tid);
    }

    close(server_fd);
    return 0;
}

Testing the Web Server

First, create the web root directory and an HTML file:

$ mkdir www
$ cat > www/index.html <<'EOF'
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head><title>My Web Server</title></head>
<body>
<h1>It works!</h1>
<p>This page is being served by our C web server.</p>
</body>
</html>
EOF

Compile and run:

$ gcc -o webserver webserver.c -pthread
$ ./webserver
Web server listening on http://localhost:8080/
Serving files from ./www

Open a browser and go to http://localhost:8080/. You should see the HTML page rendered. You can also test with curl:

$ curl -v http://localhost:8080/
* Connected to localhost (127.0.0.1) port 8080
> GET / HTTP/1.1
> Host: localhost:8080
>
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
< Content-Type: text/html
< Content-Length: 142
< Connection: close
<
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
...

How It All Fits Together

Look at how many concepts from this module (and the entire course) come together in this one program:

  • File descriptors (Lesson 1): The server uses open(), read(), write(), and close() to read files from disk.
  • The FILE API and stat() (Lesson 2): We use stat() to get the file size for the Content-Length header, and S_ISREG() to verify we are serving a regular file.
  • TCP/IP (Lesson 3): The server communicates over TCP. Data is sent as a byte stream.
  • The socket API (Lesson 4): We use socket/bind/listen/accept to set up the server.
  • Threads (Lesson 5, and earlier modules): Each client is handled in its own thread.
  • String parsing: We parse the HTTP request to extract the method and path.
  • Memory management: We heap-allocate the client file descriptor to avoid race conditions.

This is the power of the Unix "everything is a file" philosophy. The same read() and write() calls work for disk files and network sockets. The same file descriptor abstraction unifies all I/O.

Security Considerations

Our web server includes a basic check for .. in the path to prevent directory traversal attacks (where a client requests /../../../etc/passwd to read files outside the web root). A production server would need much more robust security:

  • Canonicalize the path and verify it falls within the web root
  • Limit request sizes to prevent memory exhaustion
  • Add timeouts so slow clients cannot hold connections open forever
  • Run as an unprivileged user
  • Support HTTPS (TLS encryption)

Our server is for learning purposes only. Do not expose it to the internet.

Key Takeaways

  • HTTP is a text-based request-response protocol. A request has a method, path, and headers. A response has a status code, headers, and a body.
  • A minimal web server parses the request path, opens the corresponding file, and sends it back with appropriate HTTP headers.
  • Building a web server ties together file I/O, sockets, threads, and string parsing -- nearly every systems programming concept in this course.
  • The "everything is a file" abstraction is what makes this possible: the same read()/write() interface works for both disk files and network sockets.

Module 7: File I/O and Sockets Programming

Module 7 Summary

What We Covered

Module 7 traced a single idea -- the Unix "everything is a file" philosophy -- from opening a file on disk all the way to building a web server. Here is a summary of each lesson and its key concepts.

Lesson 1: File Descriptors and Low-Level I/O

We learned that a file descriptor is a small non-negative integer that the kernel uses to identify an open file, device, pipe, or socket. Every process starts with three open descriptors: stdin (0), stdout (1), and stderr (2). The system calls open(), read(), write(), and close() form the foundation of all I/O in Unix. We saw that read() and write() can return fewer bytes than requested (short reads/writes), and that robust code must loop to handle this.

Lesson 2: The FILE API and Directories

We learned about the C standard library's buffered I/O layer (FILE *), which wraps file descriptors in a buffer to reduce the number of system calls. Functions like fopen(), fclose(), fprintf(), fgets(), fread(), and fwrite() provide a more convenient interface for most file operations. We also learned to read directory contents with opendir()/readdir()/closedir() and to query file metadata with stat().

Lesson 3: TCP/IP and Socket Basics

We studied the TCP/IP model and its four layers (Link, Internet, Transport, Application). TCP provides a reliable, ordered byte stream between two processes. We learned about IP addresses (32-bit numbers in dotted decimal notation), ports (16-bit numbers identifying services), and network byte order (big-endian). The functions htons()/htonl()/ntohs()/ntohl() convert between host and network byte order. The struct sockaddr_in structure holds an IP address and port for socket operations.

Lesson 4: Building a Server

We built our first TCP server by walking through the socket lifecycle: socket() to create a file descriptor, bind() to assign an address, listen() to mark it as passive, and accept() to wait for connections. The critical insight is that accept() returns a new file descriptor for each client -- the listening socket and the connected socket are separate. We built a complete echo server and tested it with nc.

Lesson 5: Clients and Multi-Client Servers

We wrote a TCP client using socket() and connect(), then addressed the limitation of our single-client server by using threads. The threaded server pattern puts accept() in a loop, spawning a new thread for each connection. We learned to pass the client file descriptor via heap allocation to avoid race conditions, and to use pthread_detach() for automatic resource cleanup.

Lesson 6: From Echo Server to Web Server

We built a minimal HTTP web server that ties together every concept in the module. The server parses HTTP requests (extracting the method and path), reads files from disk using low-level I/O, determines content types, constructs HTTP responses with proper headers, and serves them over TCP sockets -- all while handling multiple clients with threads.

The Big Picture: Everything Is a File

The central theme of this module is that Unix provides a uniform interface for all I/O. Whether you are reading from a file on disk, writing to a terminal, piping data between processes, or sending bytes over a network, you use the same fundamental operations: open (or socket + accept), read, write, close.

This is what allowed us to build a web server that reads files from disk and sends them over the network using the same read() and write() calls. It is also why the skills you learned in this module -- handling file descriptors, managing partial reads/writes, understanding byte streams -- will serve you well in any systems programming context.

The Socket API at a Glance

System CallServerClientPurpose
socket()YesYesCreate a new socket (file descriptor)
bind()YesNoAssign a local address and port
listen()YesNoMark socket as passive (ready to accept)
accept()YesNoWait for and accept a client connection
connect()NoYesInitiate a connection to a server
read()/recv()YesYesReceive data
write()/send()YesYesSend data
close()YesYesClose a file descriptor

Common Pitfalls

  • Forgetting to handle partial reads/writes: Both read() and write() can transfer fewer bytes than requested. Always loop.
  • Not checking return values: Every system call can fail. Always check for -1 returns and use perror() to diagnose errors.
  • Forgetting to close file descriptors: Leaked file descriptors are a resource leak. Close them when done.
  • Forgetting network byte order: Port numbers and IP addresses in struct sockaddr_in must be in big-endian format. Use htons() and htonl().
  • Race conditions in threaded servers: Do not pass a stack variable's address to a thread. Use heap allocation.
  • Mixing buffered and unbuffered I/O: Do not use FILE * functions and raw read()/write() on the same file descriptor without care. The buffer can get out of sync.
  • Assuming message boundaries in TCP: TCP is a byte stream. One write() does not correspond to one read().

What Comes Next

The concepts in this module form the basis of virtually all networked software. Web servers, databases, chat applications, distributed systems, and cloud infrastructure all rely on the same socket API and file I/O primitives you learned here. Understanding these low-level details will make you a more effective programmer, even when you eventually work with higher-level languages and frameworks that abstract them away.

Module 8: Memory Hierarchy and Optimization

Module 8 Overview

In Module 8: Memory Hierarchy and Optimization, we explore how modern computer systems organize and access memory, and how understanding the hardware allows us to write dramatically faster code. We begin at the hardware level with random access memory (RAM) and storage technologies, then examine how the principle of locality allows systems to bridge the enormous speed gap between the CPU and main memory through caching. From there, we turn to optimization: how to measure performance, what the compiler can do for us, what it cannot, and the code-level techniques a programmer can apply to make programs run faster. The module concludes with cache-aware programming, which ties the hardware and software sides together.

This module spans eight lessons that build on each other. Understanding RAM and locality explains why caches work; understanding caches explains why certain code patterns are fast and others are slow; and understanding optimization techniques gives you the tools to exploit that knowledge in practice.

Learning Objectives

At the end of this learning module, you will be able to:

  1. Describe the basic hardware technologies used in RAM, including the differences between SRAM and DRAM.
  2. Explain the principle of locality (temporal and spatial) and identify locality in code examples.
  3. Describe the organization of memory caches, including cache lines, sets, mapping schemes (direct-mapped, set-associative, fully associative), and write policies.
  4. Explain when optimization matters and make informed decisions about whether performance gains justify the costs in code complexity and readability.
  5. Use gcc optimization flags (-O0 through -O3) effectively and understand what the compiler can and cannot optimize on its own.
  6. Measure program performance using timing tools and profilers to identify bottlenecks before attempting to optimize.
  7. Apply code-level optimization techniques such as reducing procedure calls, eliminating unnecessary memory accesses, and loop unrolling.
  8. Write cache-friendly code by choosing data access patterns and data structure layouts that exploit spatial and temporal locality.

Learning Activities

You are expected to do the following tasks in order to achieve the above objectives:

  1. Complete the reading listed below.
  2. Read Lessons 1 through 8 and complete the embedded practice problems.
  3. Compile and experiment with the provided C code examples. Try varying compiler optimization levels and measuring the performance differences.
  4. Take Quiz 8.
  5. Review additional resources on the Module 8 Summary page.

Reading
