Module 8: Memory Hierarchy and Optimization

Lesson 1: Random Access Memory (RAM)

NOTE: This is a summary of chapter 6, sections 6.1 - 6.4 in the textbook.

Random Access Memory (RAM)

Random access memory (RAM) is part of the main memory system. The main memory system consists of many parts including memory caches and virtual memory. Memory caches sit between the CPU and RAM, holding copies of recently accessed RAM data for faster access. Virtual memory extends RAM by using disk storage: when RAM is full, less-used pages are swapped to disk, and in this sense RAM acts as a fast cache for the full virtual address space backed by disk.

Main memory is not permanent data storage. When the power is turned off on the computer; all data is lost. This is called volatile memory. We'll discuss permanent storage (non-volatile) technology in later sections.

RAM Hardware

RAM memory is stored on microchips that contain a grid of cells. Each cell holds one bit of information. There are two types of RAM microchips:

  • static RAM (SRAM) - Each cell is made from six transistors. In the past, this was used in main memory but now it's only used in memory caches. It is persistent as long as electricity is flowing in the chip. It is bistable in that it can keep itself easily in two memory states and is not subject to change due to small disturbances (static electricity or leaks).
  • dynamic RAM (DRAM) - uses a capacitor and transistor to keep a state. It is much smaller than SRAM cells so it can fit more memory in the same space (higher density). However, it is not stable and needs constant refreshing of the cells to keep state.

More on SRAM

SRAM uses 6 transistors per bit arranged in a bistable circuit. "Bistable" means the circuit naturally settles into one of two stable states (representing 0 or 1) and resists small disturbances like electrical noise. As long as power is supplied, the cell holds its value indefinitely — no refresh is needed. This makes SRAM fast and reliable, with typical access times of about 1–2 nanoseconds.

The downside is cost and density. Six transistors per bit means SRAM cells are physically large, so you cannot fit much SRAM on a chip. SRAM is also more expensive to manufacture per bit than DRAM. For these reasons, SRAM is used where speed matters most and capacity requirements are small: CPU caches (L1, L2, and L3).

More on DRAM

DRAM stores each bit as a charge on a tiny capacitor, paired with a single transistor that acts as an access switch. This is much simpler than SRAM's six-transistor design, which is why DRAM achieves much higher density (more bits per chip) and lower cost per bit.

The trade-off is that capacitors leak charge over time. If the charge is not restored, the stored bit will be lost. To prevent this, the memory controller must periodically refresh every row in the DRAM — typically every few milliseconds. During a refresh, each row is read and then written back, restoring the charge on every capacitor. This refresh process consumes power and briefly makes those rows unavailable.

DRAM access times are much slower than SRAM: roughly 50–100 nanoseconds for a random access. Despite this, DRAM is used for main memory because it provides the large capacities (8–64 GB or more) that modern programs require at a reasonable cost.

SRAM vs. DRAM Summary

SRAM's are faster to access than DRAM's and are more reliable. But they are more expensive to make per byte and take up more power because of the increased amount of transistors. So they tend to be used only in small quantities in memory caches whereas DRAM's are used in the main memory.

SRAMDRAM
Transistors per bit61 (+ capacitor)
Access time~1–2 ns~50–100 ns
Needs refresh?NoYes (every few ms)
Relative cost per bitHighLow
DensityLowHigh
Primary useCPU caches (L1, L2, L3)Main memory

DRAM Structure

Each DRAM chip is broken into many supercells. Each supercell is a rectangular array of DRAM cells. To access one cell, the memory address bit pattern is broken into parts that identify a particular row and column. The 2 dimensional arrangement makes it possible to use fewer connections into each cell. The DRAM chips themselves are packaged into memory modules called DIMM's. These are placed into slots on the memory board of the computer.

How DRAM Access Works

To read data from DRAM, the memory controller performs a two-step process:

  1. Row Access Strobe (RAS): The controller sends a row address, which selects an entire row of the DRAM array. The contents of that row are copied into a row buffer (also called a sense amplifier array). This step is relatively slow because it involves charging the sense amplifiers.
  2. Column Access Strobe (CAS): The controller then sends a column address, which selects specific columns from the row buffer and sends that data back to the controller.

An important consequence of this design: if the next access is to a different column in the same row, the row is already open in the buffer and only the CAS step is needed. This is called a page hit (or row buffer hit) and is significantly faster than accessing a different row. Accessing a different row requires closing the current row, precharging, and then issuing a new RAS — a much slower operation called a page miss.

This is one reason why sequential memory access patterns are faster than random patterns: sequential accesses tend to hit the same DRAM row repeatedly, while random accesses cause frequent row switches.

The Memory Bus

The CPU communicates with memory through a memory bus, which consists of three logical parts:

  • Address bus: carries the memory address the CPU wants to read or write.
  • Data bus: carries the actual data being transferred.
  • Control bus: carries signals that coordinate the transaction (read/write commands, acknowledgments, etc.).

A typical read transaction works as follows: the CPU places an address on the address bus and signals a read request on the control bus. The memory controller receives the request, retrieves the data from DRAM (using the RAS/CAS process described above), and places it on the data bus. The CPU then reads the data from the bus. This entire round trip — across the bus, through the controller, into the DRAM, and back — is what makes memory access slow relative to CPU speed.

DDR Generations

Modern DRAM modules use DDR (Double Data Rate) technology, which transfers data on both the rising and falling edges of the clock signal, effectively doubling the data rate compared to the original single-data-rate SDRAM. Each successive DDR generation roughly doubles bandwidth over the previous one by increasing the I/O clock rate and prefetch width:

  • DDR (2000): ~1.6–3.2 GB/s bandwidth
  • DDR2 (2003): ~3.2–8.5 GB/s
  • DDR3 (2007): ~6.4–17 GB/s
  • DDR4 (2014): ~12.8–25.6 GB/s
  • DDR5 (2020): ~25.6–51.2 GB/s

You don't need to memorize these numbers, but the pattern is important: bandwidth has been growing with each generation. However, latency (measured in nanoseconds) has improved much more slowly. A DDR5 random access still takes roughly 50–100 ns, not dramatically different from DDR1. This is a key point for understanding performance.

The Processor-Memory Gap

Over the past several decades, CPU speeds have improved at a much faster rate than memory access speeds. Modern processors can execute billions of operations per second, but a single main memory access still takes on the order of 100 nanoseconds — enough time for the CPU to have executed hundreds of instructions. This growing disparity is known as the processor-memory gap (or "memory wall").

The processor-memory gap is the fundamental reason the memory hierarchy exists. Caches, prefetching, and other hardware techniques all exist to bridge this gap by keeping frequently used data close to the CPU. From a programmer's perspective, this gap is why cache optimization matters so much: a program that makes good use of the cache can run orders of magnitude faster than one that constantly waits for data from main memory. This motivates the entire rest of the module.

Module 8: Memory Hierarchy and Optimization

Lesson 2: Locality

Locality

Accessing main memory is slow and getting slower. But there are some things that can be done in hardware and software to mitigate this problem. In hardware, the use of memory caches are one of the ways to keep from accessing main memory. We'll talk about this in the next section.

In software, taking advantage of what is known as locality helps speed up the running of your programs. We'll talk about locality first in this section and then discuss how to use it in optimization later in this module.

What is Locality

Below is the locality principle. Basically it comes down to two facts about memory access patterns:

  • temporal locality: A memory location that was recently accessed will most likely be accessed again soon.
  • spatial locality: A memory location that was recently accessed will most likely have nearby memory locations accessed soon.

There are several ways computer systems can exploit locality. One way is by using memory caches; we'll discuss this in the following section. Another way is through writing software that displays both spatial and temporal locality; we'll discuss this later when we talk about optimization.

Temporal Locality Examples

Temporal locality occurs when the same memory location is accessed repeatedly over a short period of time. The most common example is a variable that is read or written inside a loop:

int sum = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    sum += a[i];  /* sum is accessed every iteration (good temporal locality) */
}

Here, the variable sum is read and written on every iteration of the loop. Because it is accessed so frequently, the hardware will keep it in the cache (or even in a register), making each access very fast. The loop counter i also exhibits excellent temporal locality for the same reason.

Spatial Locality Examples

Spatial locality occurs when memory locations near each other are accessed in close succession. The most important example is sequential array access:

/* Good spatial locality: stride-1 access */
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    sum += a[i];

Each access to a[i] is immediately followed by an access to a[i+1], which is the next location in memory. When the hardware loads a cache line containing a[i], it also loads several subsequent elements, so the next few iterations will be cache hits.

Contrast this with poor spatial locality:

/* Poor spatial locality: stride-n access (column traversal of row-major array) */
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    sum += a[i][0];  /* jumps by an entire row each time */

Here, each access jumps over an entire row of the 2D array. The elements accessed are far apart in memory, so loading a cache line for one access does not help with the next access.

Stride Patterns

The stride of an access pattern is the distance (in elements) between successive memory accesses. The most common stride patterns are:

  • Stride-1 (sequential): Each access is to the next element in memory. This gives the best spatial locality. Examples include iterating over a 1D array or traversing a 2D array row by row.
  • Stride-k: Each access skips k–1 elements. For example, accessing every other element of an array is stride-2. Accessing column 0 of a row-major 2D array with N columns is stride-N.

The general rule is: the smaller the stride, the better the spatial locality. Stride-1 access is ideal because every element loaded into a cache line gets used. Larger strides mean that most of the data brought into the cache goes unused before being evicted, wasting cache capacity and bandwidth.

Instruction Locality

Locality applies not just to data but also to instructions. When the CPU fetches instructions from memory, the same locality principles apply:

  • Temporal locality: Loops execute the same set of instructions repeatedly. The instructions in the loop body are fetched over and over, so they stay in the instruction cache.
  • Spatial locality: Instructions are stored sequentially in memory, so when the CPU fetches one instruction, the next instruction is likely in the same cache line.

This is why most CPUs have separate instruction caches and data caches (the L1 cache is typically split into L1i for instructions and L1d for data). The instruction stream has excellent locality almost by default, and a dedicated cache can exploit this without interference from data accesses.

Evaluating Locality in Code

When analyzing a program for locality, a practical approach is to look at the innermost loops and ask two questions:

  1. Does it reuse the same data? Variables that are read and written on every iteration (like accumulators, loop counters, and frequently accessed pointers) exhibit temporal locality.
  2. Does it access memory sequentially? Array accesses with stride-1 patterns exhibit spatial locality. Accesses that jump around in memory (large strides, pointer chasing through linked lists, random indexing) exhibit poor spatial locality.

Programs that have both good temporal and good spatial locality in their innermost loops tend to run much faster, because the cache can serve most of their memory requests without going to main memory.

Quantitative Example: Row-Major vs. Column-Major

Consider summing all elements of a 2D array. Here are two approaches:

/* Version 1: Row-major traversal (good locality) */
int sum = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
    for (int j = 0; j < N; j++)
        sum += a[i][j];

/* Version 2: Column-major traversal (poor locality) */
int sum = 0;
for (int j = 0; j < N; j++)
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
        sum += a[i][j];

Both versions compute the same result, but their locality properties are very different. In Version 1, the inner loop varies j, which steps through the columns of a single row — this is stride-1 access with excellent spatial locality. In Version 2, the inner loop varies i, which steps through different rows at the same column — this is stride-N access with poor spatial locality.

For large N, Version 2 can be 5–20 times slower than Version 1, even though they perform exactly the same number of additions. The difference is entirely due to cache behavior. This example foreshadows the cache-aware programming techniques we will study in Lesson 8.

Module 8: Memory Hierarchy and Optimization

Lesson 3: Memory Caches

Memory Hierarchy and Memory Caches

To better exploit locality to speed up delivery of memory data, memory is designed in layers that form a hierarchy. Figure 6.21 shows this hierarchy where levels at the top of the memory have faster access times and therefore are more desirable space to store values in. However, because of increased cost and decreased amount of space, these levels are limited in size and can't hold all the data from main memory needed to run a process. Still, they can help by storing a portion of memory that is currently being worked on. This assumes that the software being processed has good spatial and temporal locality.

Because of the restraints between size and speed (the larger the cache, the slower the access times), memory caches have become hierarchical in nature over time. The L1 cache is small (about 32 to 64 Kilobytes per core); it needs to be small in order to keep the access times short. The L2 cache is larger (up to 8 Megabytes) and holds more memory but has slower access times. There may also be an L3 cache that is even larger (up to 50 Megabytes).

In many designs (called inclusive caches), each larger cache holds a copy of everything in the smaller cache above it. Other designs use non-inclusive or exclusive policies where the levels may hold different data. The general idea is that the most frequently accessed data ends up in L1 (the fastest cache), and less recently used data migrates to L2 or L3. The larger caches serve as a backstop for data that does not fit in the smaller, faster caches above them.

How Do Caches Work

Note that we will only be discussing single-core CPUs. In modern CPUs, the cache system is much more complex. Typically, each core will have its own L1 cache(s) and possibly L2 cache but the L3 cache will be shared between cores. Also, the L1 cache is typically two caches: one for data and one for instructions. This way loading data doesn't interfere with loading instructions.

When the CPU needs to get a value at a requested address, it looks in the highest cache (L1) and goes down to the lowest cache (L3). If the value is found in one of the caches, this is called a hit. A miss is when the value is not in any cache and needs to be gotten from RAM.

Here is a very simplified example of how caches work. When a process starts running, none of the process's memory is in any of the caches. At some moment, it needs to read a portion of memory, say 1 byte at address 100. The hardware goes to main memory and loads a cache line (a fixed-size block, typically 64 bytes on modern CPUs) containing that address into the caches. The cache line would cover, say, addresses 64 to 127. This line is loaded into both L1 and L2 (we are ignoring L3 for the moment). The hardware loads an entire cache line rather than just the one byte to take advantage of spatial locality: nearby bytes are likely to be needed soon. The next time the program accesses any address within that same cache line (e.g., address 101 or 115), it will be a cache hit — no need to go back to RAM.

In reality, caches are much larger than this and so it would be inefficient to just fill up the entire cache with one block of memory. Caches are broken into cache lines which are the smallest block of memory that can be read from or written to memory. On modern x86 CPUs, cache lines are 64 bytes. Historically, cache line sizes have ranged from 32 to 128 bytes on various architectures. The process's memory is broken up into line-size portions of blocks and mapped to one or more cache lines. In the next section, we will talk about how memory is mapped to cache line(s).

Cache Mapping

There are three types of mapping schemes:

  • Direct-Mapped: Here more than one memory block is mapped to one and only one cache line. Usually this is done by using the middle bits of the first address of a memory block and finding the corresponding cache line index. Since more than one part of memory can be located in this line, there is also a corresponding tag value, typically the upper bits of the address, that is written into the cache line for CPU to determine which block of code in memory is in the cache.
    When the CPU looks for a value, it determines the index from the middle bits of the address, then it finds the cache line. It then compares the tag in the cache line to the tag from the address. If they match then this is a hit and the value is used. If the tags don't match, then it will evict the current block by overwriting it with the new memory block, updating the tag to the new block. This is known as a conflict miss.
  • Set Associative Mapping: Direct mapping causes a lot of conflict misses. To help avoid this problem, caches use set associative mapping. Here the cache is grouped into sets of cache lines. Each line can hold one chunk of memory that can be read and written to. Each set has a fixed number of lines. Set associative caches are called N-way associative caches where N is the number of lines in each set.
    • For example, instead of having one index map to one cache line, you can have one index map to 2 cache lines (2-way associative). This way if there is already a block in one cache line, the new block can be stored in the other cache line. This helps to reduce conflict misses. However, if all cache lines fill up, then the hardware has to determine which of the cache line's block of data to evict (overwrite with the new data). There are several algorithms for determining which block to evict: one is least frequently used (LFU) and another is least recently used (LRU).
  • Fully Associative Mapping: This mapping scheme does away with mapping altogether. Each memory block can be put into any cache line. This is not used much because of the huge cost of searching the entire cache to find the correct block losing the main purpose of having a cache: quick access. Typically, caches are N-way set associative.

Cache Writes

The above mapping works for both reading and writing to memory. For reading, this isn't too much of a problem but for writing, we need to decide if and when we should update main memory. Since we are trying to avoid accessing main memory, we don't want to do a write every time a value is updated (this is called write through). For example, what if the value is written to over and over again? We would be wasting time writing a value that would be written over again soon. On the other hand, we may need to read the updated value later in the running of the program so we do need to update memory at some point.

One way to avoid excessive writes to memory is to wait until a line is evicted to update main memory. This is called a write back. This requires being able to keep track of whether a value has been updated by using a dirty bit. If this is set to 1, the value will be written back to main memory.

There's also the question of what happens on a write miss (when the address being written to is not in the cache). With write-allocate (also called "fetch on write"), the cache first loads the block from the next level into the cache, then performs the write on the cached copy. This is typically paired with write-back. With no-write-allocate (also called "write around"), the write goes directly to the next level of memory without loading the block into the cache. This is typically paired with write-through.

Lesson 4: Optimization - Why and When?

NOTE: This is a summary of chapter 5, sections 5.1 - 5.6, 5.8, 5.13-5.14 and chapter 6, sections 6.6 - 6.7 in the textbook.

Introduction

The main focus of this summary is on how to optimize your code to run faster. There are other optimizations that are also important, such as memory or space optimization, but here we will concentrate on time optimization or performance.

Why Optimize and When?

We want to write programs that are readable and work correctly but we also need to write programs with good performance as well. In this section we are going to concentrate on getting programs to run faster; this is called optimization.

Some optimizing techniques cause a decrease in readability. An example is loop unrolling which causes the code to become longer and more complex. So one should decide if optimization is worth it before deciding to do it. It may not matter to the end user if a program runs 2 seconds longer. On the other hand, if the program is running 2 hours longer then optimization, however ugly it looks, will be worth it. And a programmer should never compromise correctness of the program for performance. A program is useless if it doesn't give the right output no matter how much bragging a programmer might do about how much faster it runs.

Modern compilers do a good job in optimizing code. However, a programmer can accidentally limit the compiler's ability to optimize code. A programmer can help out by writing "compiler friendly" code that helps the compiler to optimize code better.

Other methods of helping make programs run faster exist. Running programs in parallel on multi-core or multiple systems is one method. However, even if we are using several computers or cores to do the optimizing it doesn't hurt to make sure each individual program is running at optimal speed.

Using performance tools such as profilers helps the optimization process. We won't be discussing profilers in this course much but in this module's lab you will get to use a simple profiler available on the PCC Linux system called gprof. I will be covering how to use this program during this module's lecture.

We'll look at various techniques that can be used to write optimized code. These techniques may not always work. Often it's a matter of trial and error to find a technique that works.

Amdahl's Law

Amdahl's Law gives us a formula for the maximum speedup we can achieve by optimizing part of a program. Suppose a fraction α of the program's runtime is spent in some component, and we speed up that component by a factor of k. The overall speedup is:

Speedup = 1 / ((1 - α) + α/k)

For example, suppose 80% of a program's runtime is spent in a single function, and we make that function 4x faster. Then:

Speedup = 1 / ((1 - 0.8) + 0.8/4)
        = 1 / (0.2 + 0.2)
        = 1 / 0.4
        = 2.5x overall speedup

Even though we made the function 4x faster, the overall program is only 2.5x faster because the remaining 20% of the runtime is unchanged.

The key lesson from Amdahl's Law: optimizing a function that accounts for 5% of runtime can yield at most about a 1.05x overall speedup (roughly 5.26% faster), even if that function becomes infinitely fast. This is why profiling (measuring where the time is actually spent) is so important — you need to know which parts of your program dominate the runtime before deciding where to focus your optimization effort.

The Optimization Workflow

Experienced programmers follow a disciplined process when optimizing. Here is the recommended workflow:

  1. Write correct code first. Get the program working and producing the right output. Do not think about performance yet.
  2. Profile to find the hot spots. Use a profiler (like gprof or perf) or the time command to measure where the program spends its time.
  3. Optimize the hot spots. Apply optimization techniques to the functions and loops that consume the most runtime.
  4. Measure again to verify. After making changes, measure the performance again to confirm that your optimization actually helped. Sometimes a change that seems like it should be faster is not, due to compiler behavior or hardware effects.
  5. Repeat if needed. If the program is still not fast enough, go back to step 2 and profile again. The hot spots may have shifted after your first round of optimization.

The most important rule is: never optimize without measuring first. Guessing where the bottleneck is almost always leads to wasted effort on code that does not matter.

What "Hot Spots" Look Like

In practice, a small fraction of the code accounts for the vast majority of the runtime. This is sometimes called the 90/10 rule: roughly 90% of the execution time is spent in 10% of the code. The hot spots are usually:

  • Inner loops that process large data sets (e.g., iterating over every element of a large array)
  • Functions that are called millions of times (e.g., comparison functions in a sorting algorithm)
  • Sections of code with poor cache behavior (e.g., traversing large data structures with random access patterns)

These are where optimization effort should be focused. Code that runs once at startup, or a function called only a handful of times, is almost never worth optimizing.

Types of Optimization

There are several levels at which you can optimize a program, roughly ordered from highest impact to lowest:

  1. Algorithmic optimization: Choosing a better algorithm — for example, replacing an O(n²) sort with an O(n log n) sort. This typically gives the biggest wins and should always be considered first. No amount of low-level tuning can compensate for a fundamentally inefficient algorithm.
  2. Compiler optimization: Letting gcc -O2 (or -O3) do the work. The compiler can perform many transformations automatically: register allocation, instruction scheduling, function inlining, and more. This is essentially "free" performance — you just turn on the flag. We cover this in Lesson 5.
  3. Code-level optimization: Reducing unnecessary work in loops — eliminating redundant function calls, using local variables instead of repeated memory references, loop unrolling. We cover these techniques in Lesson 7.
  4. Memory-level optimization: Writing code with cache-friendly access patterns — stride-1 array traversals, loop tiling, choosing the right data layout. We cover this in Lesson 8.

When NOT to Optimize

Optimization is not always the right choice. Here are some situations where you should think twice:

  • The program already runs fast enough. If the user is satisfied with the performance, there is no reason to spend time making it faster. Engineering time is valuable.
  • It's a one-time script. If you will run the program once and never again, spending an hour optimizing code to save 30 seconds of runtime is a poor trade-off.
  • Readability would suffer greatly. If an optimization makes the code much harder to understand and maintain, the long-term cost may outweigh the short-term speed gain.
  • Correctness is at risk. Never sacrifice correctness for performance. A fast program that produces wrong results is worse than useless.

The famous quote, "premature optimization is the root of all evil" (attributed to Donald Knuth), is often misunderstood. It does not mean you should never optimize. It means you should not optimize prematurely — that is, before you know where the bottleneck is and before you have measured the impact. Optimization guided by measurement and focused on actual hot spots is not premature; it is good engineering.

Module 8: Memory Hierarchy and Optimization

Lesson 5: gcc Optimization Levels and Limitations

gcc Optimization Levels and Limitations

Probably a good place to start in optimizing your program is to make sure you use the right level of optimization when compiling with gcc. For looking at assembly code, we've been having you reduce optimization to a minimum in gcc by using the new switch -Og which also makes the code easier to run in a debugger (gdb). This is so that you can see assembly code that follows closely with your C code.

In practice you want to use the highest level of optimization that is appropriate for your project. The standard in the industry for gcc optimization level is -O2. Why not -O3? While -O3 does not introduce bugs on its own, it optimizes more aggressively in ways that can expose latent bugs in code that has undefined behavior (such as signed integer overflow or strict aliasing violations). Code that appeared to work at -O0 may break at -O3 because the optimizer is free to assume undefined behavior never happens. Additionally, -O3 tends to increase the size of the executable (due to aggressive inlining and loop unrolling), which can hurt instruction cache performance. The default for compiling in gcc is -O0 which disables optimization (the compiler still performs basic code generation, but does not attempt to optimize). This is usually a good one for doing development but you should use at least -O1 or -O2 in a production build.

gcc Optimization Blockers

When compiling code, gcc takes a conservative approach to optimizing. One example given in the textbook is the code:

void twiddle1(long *xp, long *yp)
{
  *xp += *yp;
  *xp += *yp;
}

void twiddle2(long *xp, long *yp)
{
  *xp += 2*(*yp);
}

the function twiddle1() would be a good candidate for optimization to twiddle2() (adding the value *yp twice is the same as multiplying by 2). But gcc compiles this to two adds. Why? because it is possible for xp and yp to be pointing to the same memory space. This will make the second add dependent on the outcome of the first add's results.

For example, let's say that xp and yp have the same address. At this address, the initial value is 3. For twiddle1(), xp after the first line is 6 and after the second line is 12 (note that the first line replaces xp with 6; 6+6 = 12). For twiddle2(), xp is 9 (3 + 2*3 = 9). This effect is called memory aliasing where two pointers can possibly point to the same memory location.

It's possible that xp and yp will never point to the same memory space but gcc doesn't know this at compile time. So it plays it safe and doesn't try to optimize the twiddle1() to match twiddle2(). Note that if xp and yp are not pointers, gcc will be able to optimize to one shift and then one add. So there's a slight performance downside in using pointers as parameters in this case but this may be needed to achieve pass by reference.

Another such blocker is function calls. This example is from the textbook:

long f();

   long func1()
   {
      return f() + f() + f() + f();
   }

   long func2()
   {
      return 4*f();
   }

Here f() is defined in another file. We would probably guess that gcc will most likely compile func1() to something like func2(). But it doesn't; it does four calls to f(). This again is done because it is possible for the return value between calls to f() to be different each time.

For example, if f() is defined as:

long counter = 0;
 
    long f() {
       return counter++;
    }

Then func1() is going to have a different result than func2(). gcc tends to be very conservative about making any guesses about what a function will return if the function is outside the file that is currently being compiled. Remember that the compilation step is done on each individual file without referencing any other files. This may also prevent a function from being inlined if the function is outside of the file being compiled.

Module 8: Memory Hierarchy and Optimization

Lesson 6: How to Measure Performance

How to Measure Performance

In order to understand how well our optimization is working, we need to be able to measure how fast our programs are running. The textbook defines something called cycles per element (CPE) which it then uses for its optimization example. This is fine but not necessarily available outside of the book's code.

Most optimization tools in the industry (benchmarks, profilers, etc) use CPU time. CPU time is the amount of time in seconds a CPU was processing this particular program (as opposed to other programs that were also using the CPU). This is more accurate than straight clock time as it doesn't measure the times that the program was inactive.

The time Command

In this module's lab, you can use the command time at the terminal to get CPU time. For example, if we want to know how much CPU time it takes to run a matrix multiplication program, we type at the command line:

$ time ./matmul 1000
real    0m2.341s
user    0m2.312s
sys     0m0.024s

Each line of the output means something specific:

  • real — The total wall-clock time: how long the program took from start to finish, including time spent waiting for I/O and time when other processes were using the CPU.
  • user — The CPU time spent executing your program's own code (user mode). This is the time the CPU was actually doing work for your process.
  • sys — The CPU time spent in the kernel on behalf of your program (system mode) — things like file I/O, memory allocation, and other operating system services.

The sum of user + sys gives the total CPU time. For CPU-bound programs (programs that spend most of their time computing), you will see user ≈ real, because the program is actively using the CPU almost the entire time. For I/O-bound programs (programs that spend a lot of time waiting for disk or network), you will see real >> user, because the program is idle while waiting for data.

Note that real can also be less than user + sys if the program uses multiple CPU cores, since wall-clock time measures elapsed time but CPU time is summed across all cores.

The time command is very useful for getting an overall feel for how fast your program is running, but its downside is that it doesn't say where in the code any slowdowns are. For that, we need a profiler.

Profiling with gprof

A profiler is a tool that measures how much time is spent in each function of your program. The profiler we will use is gprof, which is available on the PCC Linux system. Here is the workflow:

gcc -pg -O2 -o program program.c    # compile with profiling enabled (-pg flag)
./program                            # run the program (generates gmon.out)
gprof program gmon.out               # print the profile report

The -pg flag tells gcc to insert profiling instrumentation into the compiled code. When you run the program, it writes profiling data to a file called gmon.out. Then gprof reads that file and produces a human-readable report.

Reading a Flat Profile

The most useful part of gprof's output is the flat profile, which lists each function and how much time was spent in it. Here is an example of what it might look like:

  %   cumulative   self              self     total
 time   seconds   seconds    calls  ms/call  ms/call  name
 78.23      1.83     1.83        1  1830.00  1830.00  multiply_matrices
 12.41      2.12     0.29   100000     0.00     0.00  compute_element
  5.13      2.24     0.12        1   120.00   120.00  initialize_matrix
  2.14      2.29     0.05        1    50.00    50.00  read_input
  2.09      2.34     0.05        1    50.00    50.00  print_result

The columns you should focus on are:

  • % time: The percentage of total runtime spent in this function. This is the most important column.
  • self seconds: The actual number of seconds spent in this function (not counting functions it calls).
  • calls: How many times this function was called.

In this example, multiply_matrices takes 78% of the runtime while print_result takes only 2%. This tells you exactly where to focus your optimization effort. By Amdahl's Law (from Lesson 4), even if you made print_result infinitely fast, the overall speedup would be negligible. But making multiply_matrices even 2x faster would give a significant overall improvement.

CPE: Cycles Per Element

The textbook uses a metric called CPE (Cycles Per Element) to measure the efficiency of code that processes arrays or vectors. CPE is defined as:

CPE = (total CPU cycles) / (number of elements processed)

A lower CPE means better performance. The advantage of CPE as a metric is that it is independent of the array size: whether you process 1,000 elements or 1,000,000 elements, a well-optimized function should have roughly the same CPE. This makes it useful for comparing different implementations of the same algorithm without worrying about input size.

For example, if a function takes 4,000 cycles to process an array of 1,000 integers, its CPE is 4.0. If you optimize the function to take 2,000 cycles for the same array, the CPE drops to 2.0 — a 2x improvement. The textbook's optimization chapters use CPE extensively to track progress through successive improvements to a running example.

Benchmarking Tips

Getting reliable performance measurements requires some care. Here are some practical tips:

  • Run the program multiple times and take the minimum. The minimum runtime is closest to the program's true performance. Higher values include noise from OS scheduling, other processes, and interrupts.
  • Use large enough inputs. The runtime should be at least a few seconds. Very short runtimes are dominated by startup overhead and measurement noise.
  • Be aware of cold caches. The first run of a program (or the first run after changing the input) may be slower because the caches are empty. If you are comparing two implementations, run each one a few times to "warm up" the caches before recording the measurement.
  • Disable CPU frequency scaling if possible. Modern CPUs can change their clock speed dynamically (turbo boost, power saving modes). This can cause inconsistent measurements. On Linux, you can set the CPU governor to "performance" mode if you have the right permissions.
  • Minimize background activity. Close other programs and avoid running benchmarks while the system is under load from other tasks.

Other Useful Tools

Beyond time and gprof, there are other performance tools worth knowing about:

  • perf stat — A Linux tool that gives you access to hardware performance counters. It can report the number of cache misses, branch mispredictions, instructions per cycle, and other low-level metrics. Very useful for understanding why a program is slow, not just where.
  • valgrind --tool=callgrind — A tool that simulates a cache and records detailed information about function calls and cache behavior. The output can be visualized with kcachegrind, which shows call graphs and per-line cache miss counts.
  • valgrind --tool=cachegrind — Similar to callgrind but focused specifically on cache simulation. It reports the number of cache hits and misses for each line of source code, which is invaluable when optimizing cache behavior (as discussed in Lesson 8).

You do not need to master all of these tools for this course, but knowing they exist is valuable. In the lab, we will focus on time and gprof.

Module 8: Memory Hierarchy and Optimization

Lesson 7: How to Optimize Code

How to Optimize Code

The textbook goes through an example program for the next couple of sections. I think I'll leave it up to the student to study the example in the textbook. Remember to skip 5.7 and 5.9 through 5.12.

Below are some pointers for optimization that you should know about for the lab or final exam (optimization will be on the final):

  1. Eliminate Function Calls: Eliminate any function call inside a loop that will always return the same value each time through the loop. Also don't put these calls in the conditional and update parts of the for loop's header as well. There is no reason to keep calling the function every time through the loop if it is guaranteed to give the same value.

    A good example that the textbook talks about is strlen(). It's common to get the length of a string as an upper bound for stepping through a string's characters. Many programmers tend to put the call to strlen() inside the for loop's conditional: 
    for(int i=0; i < strlen(str); i++)
    ....
    but strlen() ends up being called N (the size of the string) amount of times only to return the same value. This is N-1 too many times. A better idea is to call it above the loop and put the value inside a local variable: 
    int size = strlen(str);
    for(int i=0; i < size; i++)
    ....
    This way there is only one function call and the value is probably going to be stored in a register for faster access. In fact, the strlen() function itself goes through the string to find the null value on the end so it is already doing N iterations. Putting it inside the for loop's conditional, it will now do N*N or N2 iterations which is very costly.
  2. Reducing Function Calls: Function calls are notoriously bad for performance. This is why whenever gcc can do so, it will 'inline' a function but, as discussed above, it isn't always able to do this due to possible 'side effects'. This is where the function might change something else outside of the function that then alters the behavior of the program.

    So think about whether a function call is necessary inside the loop if the code itself can just be written into the loop. An example from the textbook is the function get_vec_element(). This function is just basically stepping through the array one element at a time; the code for this function can just be copied into the loop for faster performance in accessing array elements (no function call mechanisms to set up and break down). This is also why doing recursion is bad for performance; it's a lot of function calls where using a loop is faster and simpler.

    Of course, you can't eliminate all function calls but do look at function calls as good candidates for optimization.
  3. Eliminate Unneeded Memory References: Try to avoid directly reading from and writing to arrays and pointers. These can't be kept in a register and so they need to be accessed from main memory, which is slow. It's best to use a local variable when possible. Local variables end up being stored in registers rather than memory references. So look at how combine4() function (figure 5.10) used the variable acc to avoid a read and write to memory. It can't avoid the read to data[i] entirely but it did cut down the number of memory references from 3 to 1. acc is an example of an accumulator which is very useful in optimizing code.
  4. Loop Unrolling: This is an interesting technique that unfortunately makes code a bit unreadable and may not always work but it's worth trying as it can boost performance under some circumstances. Sometimes gcc will use this method if it feels it's safe to do so.

    Loop unrolling involves doing two or more iterations at one time before going back to the top of the loop. For example: 
    for(int i=0; i < size; i++)
{
   sum += array[i];
}

can be transformed into

int i;
for(i=0; i < size-4; i += 5)
{
    sum += array[i];
    sum += array[i+1];
    sum += array[i+2];
    sum += array[i+3];
    sum += array[i+4];
}

for(; i < size; i++)
{
   sum += array[i];
}
    Note that the last loop is to pick up any leftover array values at the end of the array. Also, note that we need to be careful not to increment past the array size. So basically the first loop stops short of the array size and the rest is picked up in the second loop.

    This is an example of a "5 x 1" loop. The first number represents the number of iterations being done inside the for loop and the second number is the number of accumulators you are using inside the loop. Accumulators are local variables set up to hold the accumulation of results. Using more than one helps with performance as well.

    You can use any number of iterations but there usually is a point where the unrolling stops being effective. How many to use is a matter of trial and error.

    Why does this work? Well, each time you reach the top of the loop, a conditional is performed along with a jump. Although not as bad as function calls, conditional jumps are still costly. By doing more per iteration you cut down on the number of jumps needed.

    You can also help boost things but using two or more accumulators. (this is a 5 x 2 loop): 
    int sum1 = 0;
int sum2 = 0;
int i;
for(i=0; i < size-4; i += 5)
{
    sum1 += array[i];
    sum2 += array[i+1];
    sum1 += array[i+2];
    sum2 += array[i+3];
    sum1 += array[i+4];
}

for(; i < size; i++)
{
   sum1 += array[i];
}
int sum = sum1 + sum2;
    This speeds up code by making each sum independent from each other creating an opportunity for the CPU to use parallelization (or pipelining) when doing the arithmetic on each line. The trick is to alternate the use of each accumulator.
  5. Write Cache Friendly Code: (from Section 6.5 and 6.6)
    In the previous module we talked about how memory caches work and how they use locality to speed up accessing memory. You can also help in making the caches work better by thinking about locality when writing your code.

    Arrays are stored in memory in a row-wise fashion. For example, the array = {{1,3,5,7},{20,30,40,50},{100,200,300,400}} is stored in sequence as: 
    1|3|5|7|20|30|40|50|100|200|300|400

    To step through this array you need to use two for loops: 
    int n, m;
   for(int i=0; i < n; i++)
    {
      for(int j=0; j < m; j++)
      {
         ....
      }
   }
    To preserve spatial locality, ideally you want to step through the elements so that the next element is an adjacent element. This is because it is most likely to be in the memory cache increasing the hit ratio. 

    For example, if we step through the above array as: 
    int n = 4, m = 3;
    for(int i=0; i < n; i++)
    {
       for(int j=0; j < m; j++)
       {
           sum += array[j][i];
       }
    }
    Then each element is accessed in this pattern: 
    1|20|100|3|30|200|5|40|300|7|50|400
    This jumps around by one whole row-size of n. This is called a stride-n pattern. This is not good for memory caches if n is a large number. There will be a good chance that every read is a miss if the element isn't in the cache.

    If we instead set up the loops so that the outer loop iterates over rows and the inner loop over columns: 
    int n = 3, m = 4;
    for(int i=0; i < n; i++)
    {
       for(int j=0; j < m; j++)
       {
           sum += array[i][j];
       }
    }
    then the pattern is now jumping over by 1 to the next value, making this a stride-1 pattern. This is the best as it will mainly be accessing adjacent elements and therefore reduce the possibility of a cache miss.

    The textbook goes into detail on more elaborate arrays but just keep in mind that the closer the next element is, the lower the stride number and the better the cache performance.

Module 8: Memory Hierarchy and Optimization

Lesson 8: Cache-Aware Programming

NOTE: This lesson builds on the memory hierarchy concepts from Chapter 6, Sections 6.6–6.7 in the textbook, and extends the optimization techniques covered in Lessons 1–4.

Introduction: Why Cache Behavior Matters

In earlier lessons we looked at code-level optimizations such as reducing function calls, eliminating redundant memory references, and loop unrolling. These are important techniques, but they operate at the level of individual instructions. In this lesson, we focus on a different and often more impactful factor: how your program accesses memory.

Recall from our study of the memory hierarchy that modern systems have multiple levels of cache between the CPU and main memory. A typical L1 cache access takes about 1–4 CPU cycles, while a main memory access can take 100 or more cycles. That is roughly a 25–100x difference in access time. When a program repeatedly misses the cache, the CPU stalls waiting for data, and performance can degrade by orders of magnitude. The good news is that by understanding how caches work, we can write code that keeps the data we need close to the processor.

The two key principles that make caches effective are:

  • Temporal locality: If a program accesses a memory location, it is likely to access the same location again soon. Caches exploit this by keeping recently accessed data.
  • Spatial locality: If a program accesses a memory location, it is likely to access nearby locations soon. Caches exploit this by loading entire cache lines (typically 64 bytes) at a time.

Cache-aware programming means writing code that maximizes both forms of locality so that the cache can do its job effectively.

Row-Major vs. Column-Major Array Traversal

C stores two-dimensional arrays in row-major order: the elements of each row are stored contiguously in memory. This means that a[0][0] is followed immediately by a[0][1], then a[0][2], and so on. The first element of the next row, a[1][0], comes after the last element of the first row.

This storage layout has a direct consequence for cache performance. When we iterate over the array by varying the column index in the inner loop (row-by-row), we access memory sequentially. Each cache line loaded from memory provides multiple useful values, and we use all of them before moving on. This gives us excellent spatial locality.

When we instead vary the row index in the inner loop (column-by-column), we jump across entire rows with each access. If the rows are large, each access may land in a different cache line, and by the time we come back to a given row, the cache line we loaded earlier may have been evicted. This wastes the cache bandwidth and causes many more cache misses.

Example: Summing a 2D Array

Consider two ways of summing all elements of an N x N array:

Row-major traversal (cache-friendly):

/* Good: varies column index (j) in inner loop.
 * Accesses memory sequentially. */
int sum_row_major(int a[N][N]) {
    int sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++)
            sum += a[i][j];
    return sum;
}

Column-major traversal (cache-unfriendly):

/* Bad: varies row index (i) in inner loop.
 * Jumps across rows, causing cache misses. */
int sum_col_major(int a[N][N]) {
    int sum = 0;
    for (int j = 0; j < N; j++)
        for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
            sum += a[i][j];
    return sum;
}

Both functions compute exactly the same result. But for large N (say, N = 4096), the row-major version can run 5–20 times faster than the column-major version, depending on the system. The difference is entirely due to cache behavior. The row-major version has a cache miss roughly once per cache line (every 16 integers for a 64-byte cache line with 4-byte ints), while the column-major version may have a cache miss on nearly every access.

Loop Tiling (Blocking)

Sometimes the natural algorithm for a computation does not have good locality, even when we traverse arrays in row-major order. The classic example is matrix multiplication. In the standard three-nested-loop algorithm, the inner loop accesses one row of the first matrix and one column of the second matrix. The row access has good spatial locality, but the column access does not. For large matrices, the column of the second matrix will not fit in the cache, causing repeated cache misses.

Loop tiling (also called blocking) is the technique of breaking the computation into smaller blocks that fit in the cache. Instead of processing entire rows and columns, we process small sub-matrices (tiles) of size B x B, where B is chosen so that the working set of a single tile operation fits comfortably in the cache.

Example: Matrix Multiplication Without and With Blocking

Standard matrix multiply (no blocking):

/* Standard ijk matrix multiply.
 * The inner loop scans a column of b, which has poor
 * spatial locality for large matrices. */
void matmul(int n, double a[n][n], double b[n][n], double c[n][n]) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
            double sum = 0.0;
            for (int k = 0; k < n; k++)
                sum += a[i][k] * b[k][j];
            c[i][j] = sum;
        }
}

Blocked matrix multiply:

/* Blocked matrix multiply.
 * Process B x B sub-blocks so that the working data
 * fits in the cache. Typical good values for B are
 * 16, 32, or 64 depending on cache size. */
#define B 32

void matmul_blocked(int n, double a[n][n], double b[n][n], double c[n][n]) {
    for (int ii = 0; ii < n; ii += B)
        for (int jj = 0; jj < n; jj += B)
            for (int kk = 0; kk < n; kk += B)
                /* Multiply the B x B sub-blocks */
                for (int i = ii; i < ii + B && i < n; i++)
                    for (int j = jj; j < jj + B && j < n; j++) {
                        double sum = c[i][j];
                        for (int k = kk; k < kk + B && k < n; k++)
                            sum += a[i][k] * b[k][j];
                        c[i][j] = sum;
                    }
}

The blocked version processes small B x B tiles of each matrix. Within each tile, the data fits in the cache, so accesses to both a and b are served from cache rather than main memory. For large matrices (e.g., 1024 x 1024 or larger), the blocked version typically runs 2–8 times faster than the unblocked version. The optimal block size B depends on the cache size of your system; a common starting point is to choose B so that three B x B sub-matrices fit in the L1 data cache.

Structure of Arrays (SoA) vs. Array of Structures (AoS)

The way we organize our data structures also affects cache performance. Consider a program that manages a collection of particles, each with an x-coordinate, y-coordinate, z-coordinate, mass, and velocity. The natural approach in C is an Array of Structures (AoS):

/* Array of Structures (AoS) layout.
 * Each particle's fields are stored together. */
struct Particle {
    double x, y, z;
    double mass;
    double vx, vy, vz;
};

struct Particle particles[NUM_PARTICLES];

If we frequently need to iterate over all particles and access only the x-coordinates (for example, to compute an average x position), we end up loading entire 56-byte structures into cache lines when we only need the 8-byte x field. Six-sevenths of the cache capacity is wasted on fields we are not using.

An alternative is the Structure of Arrays (SoA) layout:

/* Structure of Arrays (SoA) layout.
 * Each field is stored in its own contiguous array. */
struct Particles {
    double x[NUM_PARTICLES];
    double y[NUM_PARTICLES];
    double z[NUM_PARTICLES];
    double mass[NUM_PARTICLES];
    double vx[NUM_PARTICLES];
    double vy[NUM_PARTICLES];
    double vz[NUM_PARTICLES];
};

struct Particles particles;

Now when we iterate over all x-coordinates, we access a contiguous array of doubles. Every byte loaded into the cache is a value we actually need. The SoA layout provides much better spatial locality for computations that access only a subset of fields.

When to Use Each Layout

  • Use AoS when you typically access most or all fields of each element together (e.g., processing one particle at a time with all its attributes).
  • Use SoA when you typically iterate over all elements but access only one or two fields at a time (e.g., computing the sum of all x-coordinates, or updating all velocities).

In practice, high-performance scientific computing, game engines, and data processing systems often use SoA layouts for this reason.

Avoiding Unnecessary Memory Accesses

We touched on this in Lesson 4 when discussing how to eliminate unnecessary memory references, but it bears repeating in the context of cache performance. Every write to memory through a pointer forces the value to be stored in the cache (and eventually to main memory), even if the value will be updated again immediately. By accumulating intermediate results in a local variable, we allow the compiler to keep the value in a register, avoiding repeated cache accesses entirely.

Example: Accumulating in a Local Variable

Before (repeated memory writes):

/* Bad: writes to *result on every iteration.
 * The compiler may not be able to optimize this
 * away because result could alias elements of a. */
void sum_array(double *a, int n, double *result) {
    *result = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        *result += a[i];
}

After (accumulate in a local variable):

/* Good: accumulates in a local variable that the
 * compiler can keep in a register. Only one write
 * to *result at the end. */
void sum_array(double *a, int n, double *result) {
    double sum = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        sum += a[i];
    *result = sum;
}

The improved version is not only friendlier to the cache but also removes the potential aliasing problem: the compiler cannot assume that result does not point into the array a, so it may not be able to optimize the first version on its own. By using a local variable, we make the optimization explicit and portable.

Data Alignment

A data value is naturally aligned when its memory address is a multiple of its size. For example, a 4-byte int is naturally aligned when stored at an address that is a multiple of 4, and an 8-byte double is naturally aligned at a multiple of 8.

When data is not aligned, a single value can straddle two cache lines. Accessing such a value requires loading two cache lines instead of one, which doubles the cache traffic for that access. Modern x86 processors can handle unaligned accesses in hardware, but there is still a performance penalty, especially when it causes extra cache line loads.

In most cases, the C compiler handles alignment for you. The compiler inserts padding between structure fields to ensure natural alignment. However, there are situations where alignment can be disrupted:

  • Using __attribute__((packed)) or #pragma pack to eliminate padding in structures.
  • Casting pointers to different types and accessing data through the cast pointer.
  • Using custom memory allocators that do not guarantee alignment.

Unless you have a specific reason to override the compiler's alignment (such as matching a hardware register layout or a network protocol format), it is best to let the compiler manage alignment naturally.

Example: Struct Padding and Alignment

/* The compiler may insert padding to align fields. */
struct Example {
    char  a;     /* 1 byte                            */
                 /* 3 bytes of padding                 */
    int   b;     /* 4 bytes, aligned to 4-byte boundary */
    char  c;     /* 1 byte                            */
                 /* 7 bytes of padding                 */
    double d;    /* 8 bytes, aligned to 8-byte boundary */
};
/* Total size: 24 bytes (not 14) due to padding. */

/* Reordering fields can reduce padding: */
struct ExampleBetter {
    double d;    /* 8 bytes                           */
    int    b;    /* 4 bytes                           */
    char   a;    /* 1 byte                            */
    char   c;    /* 1 byte                            */
                 /* 2 bytes of padding                 */
};
/* Total size: 16 bytes. Same data, less wasted space. */

By ordering structure fields from largest to smallest, we can minimize the amount of padding the compiler inserts, reducing the structure's memory footprint and improving cache utilization.

Practical Advice

Here is a summary of practical guidelines for writing cache-aware code:

  1. Profile first. Use tools like gprof, perf, or valgrind --tool=cachegrind to identify where your program spends its time and where cache misses are occurring. Do not guess.
  2. Focus on hot loops. The inner loops that process large data sets are where cache performance matters most. Optimizing a loop that runs ten times is not worth the effort; optimizing a loop that runs ten million times can be transformative.
  3. Prefer sequential access patterns. Traverse arrays in the order they are laid out in memory. In C, this means row-major order for 2D arrays.
  4. Use blocking for matrix and grid computations. When an algorithm must access data in patterns that do not naturally have good locality (such as accessing both rows and columns of a matrix), use loop tiling to keep the working set in the cache.
  5. Think about data layout. Choose between AoS and SoA based on your access patterns. If you iterate over a large collection and only touch one or two fields, SoA will often be faster.
  6. Accumulate in local variables. Avoid unnecessary writes to memory in tight loops. Let the compiler use registers for intermediate values.
  7. Let the compiler handle alignment. Do not disable struct padding unless you have a specific reason. Order struct fields from largest to smallest to minimize padding.
  8. Test on realistic data sizes. Cache effects are often invisible on small inputs. A matrix multiply might show no difference between blocked and unblocked versions for 32 x 32 matrices, but a dramatic difference for 1024 x 1024 matrices.

Conclusion

Cache-aware programming is one of the most practical optimization skills a systems programmer can develop. The techniques are not complicated: traverse data sequentially, keep working sets small, and choose data layouts that match your access patterns. But the performance impact can be enormous, because the gap between cache and main memory speeds is so large. By combining the code-level optimizations from Lesson 4 with the cache-aware techniques from this lesson, you can write programs that make efficient use of the entire memory hierarchy, from registers to main memory.

Module 8: Memory Hierarchy and Optimization

Module 8 Summary

Wrap Up

In this module, we studied memory from the hardware level and then used that knowledge to write faster code. We began with the underlying storage technologies — SRAM and DRAM — and saw how the enormous speed gap between the CPU and main memory motivates the entire memory hierarchy. We explored how the principle of locality allows caching to be effective, and how cache organization (direct-mapped, set-associative) determines hit rates and performance. From there, we turned to optimization: when it matters, what the compiler can do automatically, how to measure where time is actually spent, and the code-level techniques a programmer can apply. We concluded with cache-aware programming, where understanding the hardware directly translates into dramatic performance improvements.

Key Takeaways

  • The memory hierarchy is a series of storage levels (registers, L1/L2/L3 caches, main memory, disk) where each level serves as a cache for the level below. Faster levels are smaller and more expensive per byte; slower levels are larger and cheaper. Locality is what makes this hierarchy effective.
  • Locality comes in two forms: temporal (recently accessed data will likely be accessed again soon) and spatial (data near recently accessed data will likely be accessed soon). Writing code with good locality is one of the most impactful optimizations a programmer can make.
  • Caches exploit locality by storing recently used data in fast SRAM close to the CPU. Cache organization — including cache lines, sets, mapping schemes, and write policies — determines how effectively the cache can reduce average memory access time.
  • Correctness comes first. Optimization should only be pursued after a program is working correctly, and only when measurement shows that the performance improvement is meaningful. Not every program needs to be optimized.
  • The compiler is a powerful optimizer. Using gcc's optimization flags (-O1, -O2, -O3) can yield significant speedups automatically. However, the compiler must produce code that behaves identically in all cases, so it cannot make optimizations that depend on assumptions about pointer aliasing or side effects. Writing compiler-friendly code helps the compiler do its job better.
  • Measure before you optimize. Profiling tools like gprof show exactly which functions and loops consume the most time. Always profile first and focus optimization efforts on the hot spots.
  • Code-level techniques include reducing procedure calls in loops, eliminating unnecessary memory references (accumulating in registers instead), loop unrolling, and exploiting instruction-level parallelism.
  • Cache-aware programming is one of the most impactful optimizations. Traversing 2D arrays in row-major order, using loop tiling for matrix computations, and choosing data layouts that match access patterns can yield order-of-magnitude speedups by keeping data in cache.
