Module 9: Virtual Memory, Linking, and Dynamic Memory

Module 9 Overview

In Module 9, we explore how the operating system manages memory and how programs are loaded and run. We begin with virtual memory — the mechanism that gives each process its own private address space while sharing a single pool of physical memory. With that foundation in place, we examine linking: how object files are combined into executables, how shared libraries work, and why dynamic linking depends on virtual memory concepts like position-independent code and memory-mapped files. Finally, we study dynamic memory allocation — how malloc and free manage the heap, what happens under the hood, and how to avoid the common pitfalls that plague C programs. The module concludes with garbage collection, the automatic memory management approach used by languages like Java, Python, and Go.

These topics build on each other. Understanding virtual memory explains the address space within which programs are loaded and within which malloc operates. Understanding linking explains how code and data actually get placed into that address space. And understanding malloc explains how the programmer manages the heap region of that space at runtime.

Learning Objectives

At the end of this learning module, you will be able to:

  1. Explain how virtual memory works, including virtual and physical addresses, page tables, the TLB, and page faults.
  2. Describe the purpose of demand paging and swapping, and explain how the operating system manages physical memory.
  3. Explain the difference between static and dynamic linking, including the roles of the linker, symbol resolution, and relocation.
  4. Describe how shared libraries work, including position-independent code (PIC), the PLT, and the GOT.
  5. Use the malloc/free API correctly in C programs to allocate and deallocate heap memory.
  6. Explain how malloc manages the heap internally, including free lists, block structure, and allocation strategies.
  7. Identify and avoid common dynamic memory errors such as memory leaks, dangling pointers, double frees, and buffer overflows.
  8. Use Valgrind to detect memory errors including leaks, invalid reads and writes, use of uninitialized memory, and double frees.
  9. Explain the basic concepts of garbage collection, including mark-and-sweep, reference counting, and generational collection, and contrast automatic memory management with C's manual approach.

Learning Activities

You are expected to do the following tasks in order to achieve the above objectives:

  1. Complete the reading listed below.
  2. Read Lessons 1 through 5 and complete the embedded practice problems.
  3. Compile and experiment with the provided C code examples. Pay special attention to the malloc/free examples.
  4. Run your C programs under Valgrind with --leak-check=full to check for memory errors. Practice reading Valgrind output and fixing each reported issue.
  5. Take Quiz 9.
  6. Review additional resources on the Module 9 Summary page.

Reading

  • Bryant & O'Hallaron: Chapter 7 (Linking)
  • Bryant & O'Hallaron: Chapter 9 (Virtual Memory)

If you have questions, you can post them in the course lobby or send your instructor an email.

Module 9: Virtual Memory, Linking, and Dynamic Memory

Lesson 1: Virtual Memory

NOTE: This is a summary of chapter 9, sections 9.1 - 9.8 in the textbook.

Why Virtual Memory Exists

In the early days of computing, programs accessed physical memory directly. This created serious problems: a bug in one program could overwrite the memory of another program or even the operating system itself. If two programs happened to use the same memory addresses, they could not run at the same time. And if a program needed more memory than was physically available, it simply could not run.

Virtual memory solves all of these problems by introducing a layer of abstraction between the addresses a program uses and the actual physical memory hardware. With virtual memory:

  • Isolation: Each process gets its own private address space. Process A cannot see or modify Process B's memory, even by accident.
  • Sharing: The physical RAM is shared among all running processes, but each process believes it has the entire address space to itself.
  • Overcommitment: The total virtual memory used by all processes can exceed the amount of physical RAM, because the OS can use disk as overflow storage.

Virtual vs. Physical Addresses

When your C program accesses a variable, the CPU does not send the variable's address directly to the memory hardware. Instead, the CPU generates a virtual address (VA). A hardware component called the Memory Management Unit (MMU) translates this virtual address into a physical address (PA) before the memory access proceeds.

Every address you see in a C program — every pointer value, every address printed by a debugger — is a virtual address. The physical address is hidden from the programmer.

  CPU                    MMU                   Physical Memory
  +----------+      +------------+      +---------------------+
  | generates | ---> | translates | ---> |  actual RAM chips   |
  | virtual   |      | VA to PA   |      |  (DRAM)             |
  | address   |      |            |      |                     |
  +----------+      +------------+      +---------------------+

Pages

Virtual memory divides both the virtual address space and physical memory into fixed-size blocks called pages. On most systems, a page is 4 KB (4096 bytes). The virtual address space is divided into virtual pages (VPs) and physical memory is divided into physical pages (PPs), also called page frames.

At any given time, each virtual page is in one of three states:

  • Unallocated: The page has not been created by the OS. It takes up no space anywhere.
  • Cached: The page is allocated and currently stored in a physical page in RAM.
  • Uncached: The page is allocated but currently stored only on disk (it has been swapped out or has not yet been loaded).

The following diagram shows how virtual pages map to physical pages. Notice that not every virtual page is in physical memory at the same time, and that two different processes can have virtual pages that map to different physical pages:

  Process A                                    Physical Memory
  Virtual Address Space                        (Page Frames)
  +------------------+                        +------------------+
  | VP 0 (code)      | ----+                  | PP 0: A's VP 0   |
  +------------------+     |                  +------------------+
  | VP 1 (data)      | ----+------+           | PP 1: B's VP 0   |
  +------------------+     |      |           +------------------+
  | VP 2 (heap)      | ----|------|--+        | PP 2: A's VP 1   |
  +------------------+     |      |  |        +------------------+
  | VP 3 (on disk)   |     |      |  +------> PP 3: A's VP 2   |
  +------------------+     |      |           +------------------+
  |       ...         |     +------|---------> PP 0              |
  +------------------+            |           +------------------+
                                  |
  Process B                       |
  Virtual Address Space           |
  +------------------+            |
  | VP 0 (code)      | -----------+---------> PP 1              |
  +------------------+
  | VP 1 (data)      | ----------------------> PP 4             |
  +------------------+

Page Tables

The mapping from virtual pages to physical pages is stored in a data structure called the page table. Each process has its own page table, maintained by the operating system. The page table is an array of page table entries (PTEs). Each PTE contains:

  • Valid bit: Is this virtual page currently in physical memory? (1 = yes, 0 = no)
  • Physical page number (PPN): If valid, which physical page frame holds this virtual page.
  • Permission bits: Can this page be read? Written? Executed? These bits enforce memory protection.
  • Dirty bit: Has this page been modified since it was loaded from disk?
  • Reference bit: Has this page been accessed recently? (Used by the OS to make eviction decisions.)
  Page Table (one per process)
  +-------+-------+-----+-------+------+------+
  | Index | Valid | PPN | Read  | Write| Exec |
  +-------+-------+-----+-------+------+------+
  |   0   |   1   |  3  |   1   |   0  |   1  |  (code: read+execute)
  |   1   |   1   |  7  |   1   |   1  |   0  |  (data: read+write)
  |   2   |   1   |  5  |   1   |   1  |   0  |  (heap: read+write)
  |   3   |   0   | disk|   1   |   1  |   0  |  (swapped to disk)
  |   4   |   0   | --- |   -   |   -  |   -  |  (unallocated)
  +-------+-------+-----+-------+------+------+

To translate a virtual address, the hardware splits it into two parts:

  • Virtual Page Number (VPN): The upper bits, used as an index into the page table.
  • Virtual Page Offset (VPO): The lower bits (12 bits for 4 KB pages), which identify the byte within the page. The offset is the same in both the virtual and physical address.
  Virtual Address (e.g., 32-bit system with 4 KB pages):
  +-----------------------------+------------------+
  |  Virtual Page Number (VPN)  |  Page Offset (12) |
  |       (20 bits)             |     bits          |
  +-----------------------------+------------------+

  Translation:
  VPN ---> look up in page table ---> PPN

  Physical Address:
  +------------------------------+------------------+
  |  Physical Page Number (PPN)  |  Page Offset (12) |
  +------------------------------+------------------+

The TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer)

Every memory access requires an address translation, which means every memory access requires reading the page table. But the page table itself is stored in main memory! This means that without any optimization, every memory access would require two memory accesses: one to read the page table entry and one to read the actual data. This would cut performance in half.

The solution is the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB), a small, fast hardware cache inside the MMU that stores recently used page table entries. When the CPU generates a virtual address:

  1. The MMU checks the TLB for the VPN.
  2. TLB hit: The PPN is immediately available. No extra memory access needed. This is the common case.
  3. TLB miss: The MMU must read the page table from memory, get the PPN, and store the new entry in the TLB (possibly evicting an old entry).

Because programs exhibit strong locality, the TLB has a very high hit rate — typically above 99%. The TLB is what makes virtual memory practical. Without it, the performance cost of address translation would be prohibitive.

Page Faults

A page fault occurs when the CPU accesses a virtual page that is not currently in physical memory (the valid bit in the PTE is 0). Here is what happens step by step:

  1. The CPU generates a virtual address and the MMU looks up the PTE.
  2. The valid bit is 0 — the page is not in RAM. The MMU triggers a page fault exception.
  3. The CPU transfers control to the OS page fault handler.
  4. The handler determines where the page is stored on disk.
  5. If physical memory is full, the handler selects a victim page to evict. If the victim is dirty (has been modified), it is written back to disk first.
  6. The handler loads the requested page from disk into the freed physical page frame.
  7. The handler updates the page table: sets the valid bit to 1, records the new PPN.
  8. The handler returns to the faulting instruction, which now re-executes successfully because the page is in RAM.

Page faults are extremely expensive because they involve disk I/O, which is roughly 100,000 times slower than accessing RAM. This is why locality is so critical: a program with good locality will keep its working set of pages in physical memory and rarely trigger page faults.

Demand Paging

Operating systems use a strategy called demand paging: pages are loaded into physical memory only when they are actually accessed, not before. When a process first starts, none of its pages are in memory. Each first access to a new page triggers a page fault that loads that page. Over time, the process's working set — the set of pages it is actively using — accumulates in physical memory.

This is efficient because many programs have large address spaces but only use a small fraction of their pages during any given phase of execution.

Swapping

When physical memory is full and a new page needs to be loaded, the OS must swap an existing page out to disk to make room. The OS maintains a swap area (or swap partition) on disk for this purpose. The OS uses page replacement algorithms (such as LRU — Least Recently Used) to decide which page to evict. The goal is to evict pages that are unlikely to be used again soon.

If the system is constantly swapping pages in and out because the working set of all active processes exceeds physical memory, this is called thrashing. Thrashing devastates performance because the system spends most of its time doing disk I/O instead of useful computation.

Memory-Mapped Files

Virtual memory also enables memory-mapped files. The mmap() system call maps a file (or portion of a file) into a process's virtual address space. Once mapped, the process can read and write the file as if it were an array in memory. The OS handles loading pages from the file on demand (using the same page fault mechanism) and writing modified pages back to the file.

Memory-mapped files are used for:

  • Loading program code and shared libraries (the text segment is memory-mapped from the executable file).
  • Sharing memory between processes (two processes can mmap the same file).
  • Efficient file I/O for large files (avoids explicit read/write system calls).

Process Memory Layout Revisited

Now that we understand virtual memory, we can revisit the memory layout of a process with a deeper understanding. Every region in the layout below is a range of virtual addresses. The OS sets up the page table so that each region maps to appropriate physical pages (or is marked as unallocated).

  High addresses (0xFFFFFFFF on 32-bit)
  +---------------------------+
  |        Kernel space        |  (not accessible to user code)
  +---------------------------+  0xC0000000 (typical on 32-bit Linux)
  |         Stack              |  grows downward
  |            |               |
  |            v               |
  |                            |
  |          (free)            |
  |                            |
  |            ^               |
  |            |               |
  |         Heap               |  grows upward (managed by malloc)
  +---------------------------+
  |   Uninitialized data (BSS) |  global/static vars initialized to 0
  +---------------------------+
  |   Initialized data         |  global/static vars with initial values
  +---------------------------+
  |   Text (code)              |  program instructions (read-only)
  +---------------------------+
  Low addresses (0x00000000)

Each of these regions has different page permissions:

  • Text: Read and execute, but not write. The code is memory-mapped from the executable file.
  • Data and BSS: Read and write, but not execute.
  • Heap: Read and write. Grows upward as malloc requests more memory (via brk/sbrk or mmap).
  • Stack: Read and write. Grows downward as functions are called.
  • Kernel space: Not accessible to user-mode code. Any access triggers a segmentation fault.

A segmentation fault occurs when a process tries to access a virtual address that is either unallocated or that violates the permission bits in the page table entry. The MMU detects the violation and raises an exception, which the OS converts into a SIGSEGV signal that typically terminates the process.

Putting It All Together

Let us trace what happens when your C program executes int x = *ptr; where ptr holds the virtual address 0x00405024:

  1. The CPU sends the virtual address 0x00405024 to the MMU.
  2. The MMU extracts the VPN (upper 20 bits: 0x00405) and the offset (lower 12 bits: 0x024).
  3. The MMU checks the TLB for VPN 0x00405.
  4. If TLB hit: The PPN is retrieved immediately. Skip to step 6.
  5. If TLB miss: The MMU reads the page table entry for VPN 0x00405 from memory. If the valid bit is 0, a page fault occurs and the OS loads the page from disk. The TLB is updated.
  6. The physical address is formed by concatenating the PPN with the offset 0x024.
  7. The data at the physical address is read from RAM (or from the cache hierarchy) and loaded into register x.

Module 9: Virtual Memory, Linking, and Dynamic Memory

Lesson 2: Static and Dynamic Linking

Review: What the Linker Does

In Module 3 Lesson 1, we saw the build process: source files are assembled into object files (.o), and then the linker combines those object files into a single executable. But what exactly is the linker doing?

The linker has two main jobs:

  1. Symbol resolution: matching every reference to a symbol (function or variable name) with exactly one definition of that symbol.
  2. Relocation: assigning final memory addresses to each section and patching the code so that every reference points to the correct address.

In Module 3 Lesson 8, we linked multiple .o files together (main.o, readInt.o, writeInt.o). That was static linking in its simplest form. This lesson goes deeper into how the linker resolves symbols and introduces the distinction between static and dynamic linking.

Symbol Resolution

Every object file has a symbol table — a list of the symbols it defines and the symbols it references. When you write:

        .global myfunction       # this file DEFINES myfunction
        .extern readInt          # this file USES readInt (defined elsewhere)

The assembler records myfunction as a defined symbol and readInt as an undefined symbol in the object file's symbol table. The linker's job is to match every undefined symbol in every object file with exactly one definition.

If a symbol is referenced but never defined, you get the familiar error:

ld: main.o: in function `_start':
main.s:(.text+0x5): undefined reference to `readInt'

If a symbol is defined in two different object files, you may get a multiple definition error (more on this below).

Strong and Weak Symbols

The linker classifies symbols as strong or weak:

  • Strong symbols: functions and initialized global variables.
  • Weak symbols: uninitialized global variables (those in .bss or declared with .comm).

The resolution rules are:

  1. Multiple strong symbols with the same name → error (multiple definition).
  2. One strong symbol and one or more weak symbols with the same name → the strong symbol wins.
  3. Multiple weak symbols with the same name → the linker picks one (usually the largest).

Rules 2 and 3 can cause subtle bugs. For example, if two C files both declare int x; (uninitialized), the linker may silently merge them into one variable, and both files unknowingly share the same memory. This is one reason to use static for file-scoped variables in C.

Modern GCC note: Since GCC 10 (2020), the default is -fno-common, which places uninitialized globals in .bss as strong definitions instead of COMMON/weak symbols. With this default, two files that both declare int x; will produce a multiple definition error at link time — which is actually safer. The classic weak-symbol behavior described above still applies when using the -fcommon flag or the .comm assembler directive.

Viewing Symbol Tables

You can inspect a file's symbol table with nm:

$ nm main.o
                 U readInt
                 U writeInt
0000000000000000 T _start

T means the symbol is defined in the text section (a strong symbol). U means it is undefined (referenced but not defined here). Other common codes: D = initialized data, B = BSS (uninitialized data), W = weak.

For more detail, objdump -t shows the full symbol table with sizes and section information.

Static Linking

In static linking, the linker copies all needed code and data from the input object files (and static libraries) into one self-contained executable. This is what we have been doing with ld:

$ ld -o program main.o readInt.o writeInt.o

A static library (.a file) is simply an archive of .o files. When you link against a static library, the linker pulls in only the object files that contain symbols your program actually references.

Pros and Cons

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Self-contained: the executable has everything it needsLarge binary: every program gets its own copy of library code
Fast startup: no runtime symbol resolution neededNo shared updates: to fix a library bug, you must relink every program
Portable: runs on any compatible system without needing libraries installedWastes memory: if 10 programs use the same library, 10 copies are in RAM

Dynamic Linking and Shared Libraries

A shared library (also called a dynamic library) is a .so file ("shared object") on Linux. Instead of being copied into the executable at link time, the library is loaded into memory at runtime and shared among all programs that use it.

When you compile a C program normally, gcc uses dynamic linking by default:

$ gcc -o hello hello.c          # dynamically linked (default)
$ gcc -static -o hello hello.c  # statically linked

The size difference is dramatic:

$ gcc -o hello hello.c
$ ls -l hello
-rwxr-xr-x 1 user user 16696 hello

$ gcc -static -o hello_static hello.c
$ ls -l hello_static
-rwxr-xr-x 1 user user 900424 hello_static

The statically linked version is over 50× larger because it includes the entire C library.

Inspecting Dynamic Dependencies

You can see which shared libraries an executable depends on with ldd:

$ ldd hello
    linux-vdso.so.1 (0x00007ffd3b1f2000)
    libc.so.6 => /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6 (0x00007f2a1c600000)
    /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 (0x00007f2a1c82d000)

The key entries are:

  • libc.so.6 — the C standard library (printf, malloc, etc.)
  • ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 — the dynamic linker itself, responsible for loading shared libraries at program startup

Pros and Cons

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Small executables: library code is not duplicatedStartup cost: the dynamic linker must resolve symbols at load time
Shared memory: one copy of the library serves all processesDependency: the program won't run if a required .so is missing
Easy updates: fix a bug in the library and all programs benefitVersion conflicts: different programs may need different library versions

PLT and GOT: How Dynamic Calls Work

When your program calls a function from a shared library (like printf), the call doesn't jump directly to printf's code — the address isn't known until runtime. Instead, the call goes through two data structures:

  • The PLT (Procedure Linkage Table) — a small array of code stubs in your executable, one per external function.
  • The GOT (Global Offset Table) — a table of addresses that gets filled in by the dynamic linker.

Here is the high-level flow:

  1. Your code calls printf, which actually jumps to the PLT entry for printf.
  2. First call: The PLT entry jumps to the dynamic linker, which looks up the real address of printf in the shared library, writes it into the GOT, and then jumps to printf.
  3. Subsequent calls: The PLT entry reads the (now filled-in) address from the GOT and jumps directly to printf. No dynamic linker involved.

The first call to each function pays a one-time lookup cost. After that, calls go through the GOT with only one extra level of indirection — very fast.

  Your code              PLT                    GOT                 libc.so
  +----------+     +-----------+         +------------+      +------------+
  | call printf--> | PLT stub  |--read-->| GOT entry  |      |            |
  +----------+     | for printf|         | (address)  |--->  | printf()   |
                   +-----------+         +------------+      +------------+
                         |
                   (first call only:
                    invokes dynamic
                    linker to fill GOT)

You don't need to memorize the mechanics of lazy binding. The key idea is: dynamic function calls go through an extra table (the GOT), and the first call to each function is slightly slower than subsequent calls.

Creating a Shared Library

To build a shared library from C source:

$ gcc -shared -fPIC -o libmymath.so mymath.c

The -fPIC flag generates position-independent code, which is required for shared libraries (the library may be loaded at any address). The -shared flag tells the linker to produce a .so instead of an executable.

To link against it:

$ gcc -o program program.c -L. -lmymath

And to run it (since the library is not in a standard path):

$ LD_LIBRARY_PATH=. ./program

Summary

Static LinkingDynamic Linking
When linking happensBuild time (by ld)Load time / run time (by ld-linux)
Library format.a (archive of .o files).so (shared object)
Executable sizeLarge (contains library code)Small (just references)
Memory usageEach process has its own copyShared across processes
UpdatesMust relink to pick up fixesJust replace the .so file
Toolsld, arld, ldd, LD_LIBRARY_PATH

Module 9: Virtual Memory, Linking, and Dynamic Memory

Lesson 3: Dynamic Memory Allocation

NOTE: This is a summary of chapter 9, sections 9.9 - 9.11 in the textbook.

The Heap

In the previous lesson, we saw the memory layout of a process. The heap is the region of virtual memory that sits between the initialized data segment and the stack. Unlike the stack, which is managed automatically by function calls and returns, the heap is managed explicitly by the programmer through library functions.

The top of the heap is tracked by a pointer called brk (the "break"). When a program needs more heap space, the OS moves brk upward using the brk() or sbrk() system calls. In practice, you almost never call these directly. Instead, you use the malloc family of functions, which call brk/sbrk (or mmap for large allocations) internally.

  +---------------------------+
  |         Stack              |  (grows downward)
  |            |               |
  |            v               |
  |                            |
  |        (unmapped)          |
  |                            |
  |            ^               |
  |            |               |
  |         Heap               |  (grows upward)
  +------ brk pointer --------+  <-- top of heap
  |   [allocated] [free] ...   |
  +---------------------------+
  |   Data segments            |
  +---------------------------+
  |   Text (code)              |
  +---------------------------+

The malloc/free API

The C standard library provides four functions for dynamic memory allocation, all declared in <stdlib.h>:

  • malloc(size_t size) — Allocates size bytes of uninitialized memory. Returns a pointer to the beginning of the allocated block, or NULL if the request fails.
  • free(void *ptr) — Deallocates the block of memory pointed to by ptr. The pointer must have been returned by a previous call to malloc, calloc, or realloc.
  • calloc(size_t count, size_t size) — Allocates memory for an array of count elements, each of size bytes, and initializes all bytes to zero.
  • realloc(void *ptr, size_t size) — Resizes a previously allocated block to size bytes. May move the block to a new location (the old pointer becomes invalid). Returns a pointer to the new block.

Here is a basic example of proper usage:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

int main() {
    // Allocate an array of 10 integers
    int *arr = (int *)malloc(10 * sizeof(int));
    if (arr == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }

    // Use the allocated memory
    for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
        arr[i] = i * i;
    }

    // Print the values
    for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
        printf("arr[%d] = %d\n", i, arr[i]);
    }

    // Free the memory when done
    free(arr);
    arr = NULL;  // Good practice: set pointer to NULL after freeing

    return 0;
}

Important rules:

  • Always check the return value of malloc. It returns NULL if allocation fails.
  • Always free memory that you allocate, when you are done with it.
  • Never use memory after freeing it.
  • Never free the same pointer twice.
  • Only free pointers returned by malloc/calloc/realloc — never free a stack variable or a string literal.

How malloc Works Internally

Understanding what happens inside malloc helps you write better code and debug memory problems. The malloc implementation maintains a data structure called the free list: a linked list of all available (free) blocks of memory on the heap.

Block Structure

Each block on the heap — whether allocated or free — has a header that stores metadata. The header typically contains:

  • Size of the block (including the header itself).
  • Allocated bit: indicates whether this block is currently in use (1) or free (0). This bit is often stored in the lowest bit of the size field, since block sizes are always multiples of 8 (or 16) and the lowest bits would otherwise be zero.
  A heap with three blocks (one free between two allocated):

  +--------+------------------+--------+------------------+--------+------------------+
  | Header | Payload          | Header | (free space)     | Header | Payload          |
  | size=32| (user data)      | size=64| (available)      | size=16| (user data)      |
  | alloc=1|                  | alloc=0|                  | alloc=1|                  |
  +--------+------------------+--------+------------------+--------+------------------+
  ^                           ^                            ^
  |                           |                            |
  ptr returned              free block                   ptr returned
  by malloc                 (on free list)               by malloc

  Header detail:
  +-------------------------------------------+---+
  |          Block size (in bytes)             | A |  <-- A = allocated bit (0 or 1)
  +-------------------------------------------+---+
    31 ..................................... 1   0

When malloc returns a pointer to the user, it points to the payload — the usable memory just after the header. The user never sees the header. When free is called, the implementation uses the pointer to find the header (by subtracting the header size) and marks the block as free.

Blocks may also include optional padding at the end to satisfy alignment requirements. On most 64-bit systems, malloc returns addresses aligned to 16-byte boundaries. This means block sizes are always rounded up to multiples of 16.

Allocation Strategies

When malloc needs to find a free block to satisfy a request, it searches the free list. There are several strategies for choosing which free block to use:

  • First Fit: Search the free list from the beginning and use the first block that is large enough. This is fast but tends to leave many small fragments near the beginning of the list.
  • Next Fit: Like first fit, but start the search from where the last search left off (instead of from the beginning). This spreads allocation more evenly across the heap but can have worse fragmentation than first fit in practice.
  • Best Fit: Search the entire free list and use the smallest block that is large enough. This minimizes wasted space within the chosen block but is slower (must examine every free block) and can leave behind many tiny, unusable fragments.

Each strategy involves tradeoffs between allocation speed (throughput) and memory utilization. No single strategy is optimal for all workloads.

Fragmentation

Fragmentation is wasted memory that reduces the effective capacity of the heap. There are two types:

Internal Fragmentation

Internal fragmentation is wasted space inside an allocated block. It occurs because:

  • The allocator rounds up the requested size to satisfy alignment constraints (e.g., requesting 20 bytes but getting a 32-byte block).
  • There is a minimum block size (the block must be large enough to hold the header and free-list pointers).
  • The header itself takes up space that the user did not request.
  User requests 20 bytes. Allocator gives a 32-byte block:

  +--------+--------------------+----------+
  | Header | Payload (20 bytes) | Padding  |
  | 4 bytes|                    | (8 bytes)|
  +--------+--------------------+----------+
  |<------------- 32 bytes --------------->|

  Internal fragmentation = 32 - 4 (header) - 20 (requested) = 8 bytes wasted

External Fragmentation

External fragmentation is when there is enough total free memory on the heap to satisfy a request, but no single free block is large enough. The free memory is scattered in small chunks between allocated blocks.

  Heap state:  [alloc 16] [free 8] [alloc 32] [free 8] [alloc 16] [free 8]

  Total free memory: 24 bytes
  Request: malloc(20)  --  FAILS! No single free block has 20 bytes.

External fragmentation is the more serious problem and is difficult to eliminate entirely. Unlike languages with garbage collection (such as Java), C cannot move allocated blocks to compact free memory, because any pointer to the moved block would become invalid.

Coalescing

When a block is freed, the allocator checks whether the adjacent blocks (immediately before and after in memory) are also free. If so, it coalesces (merges) them into a single larger free block. This reduces external fragmentation.

  Before freeing the middle block:
  [free 16] [alloc 32] [free 16]

  After free() is called on the middle block:
  [free 16] [free 32] [free 16]

  After coalescing:
  [free 64]    <-- one large block instead of three small ones

To coalesce with the previous block efficiently, many implementations use boundary tags: a copy of the header is placed at the end of each block (a footer). This allows the allocator to quickly find the size and allocation status of the previous block by looking at the footer just before the current block's header.

Common malloc Errors

Dynamic memory allocation is a major source of bugs in C programs. Here are the most common errors:

Memory Leaks

A memory leak occurs when allocated memory is never freed. The memory remains allocated for the lifetime of the process, even though the program no longer needs it. Over time, memory leaks can consume all available memory.

/* MEMORY LEAK: allocated memory is never freed */
void memory_leak_example() {
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
        int *p = (int *)malloc(1000 * sizeof(int));
        // use p for something...
        // OOPS: forgot to call free(p)!
    }
    // 1000 blocks are now leaked -- 4 MB of wasted memory
}

Dangling Pointers (Use After Free)

A dangling pointer is a pointer that refers to memory that has already been freed. Using a dangling pointer is undefined behavior: the memory may have been reallocated for a different purpose, so reading or writing through the pointer can corrupt other data or crash the program.

/* DANGLING POINTER: using memory after it has been freed */
void dangling_pointer_example() {
    int *p = (int *)malloc(sizeof(int));
    *p = 42;
    free(p);

    // BAD: p now points to freed memory
    printf("%d\n", *p);  // undefined behavior!
    *p = 99;             // undefined behavior -- may corrupt other data!
}

Double Free

Calling free() on the same pointer twice is undefined behavior. It can corrupt the free list data structure, leading to crashes or exploitable security vulnerabilities.

/* DOUBLE FREE: freeing the same pointer twice */
void double_free_example() {
    int *p = (int *)malloc(sizeof(int));
    *p = 42;
    free(p);
    free(p);   // BAD: double free -- undefined behavior!
}

Buffer Overflow (Heap Overflow)

Writing past the end of an allocated block overwrites the header of the next block or other heap metadata. This can corrupt the free list and cause malloc or free to crash later — often far from the line of code that caused the problem, making these bugs very difficult to find.

/* BUFFER OVERFLOW: writing past the end of an allocated block */
void buffer_overflow_example() {
    int *arr = (int *)malloc(5 * sizeof(int));  // 5 ints = 20 bytes

    for (int i = 0; i <= 5; i++) {  // BUG: should be i < 5, not i <= 5
        arr[i] = i;  // when i == 5, writes past the allocated block!
    }

    free(arr);  // may crash here because the heap metadata is corrupted
}

Correct Usage

Here is an example that demonstrates proper dynamic memory management:

/* CORRECT: proper malloc/free usage */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

char *duplicate_string(const char *src) {
    // Allocate enough space for the string plus the null terminator
    size_t len = strlen(src) + 1;
    char *copy = (char *)malloc(len);
    if (copy == NULL) {
        return NULL;  // allocation failed
    }
    memcpy(copy, src, len);
    return copy;   // caller is responsible for freeing this
}

int main() {
    char *greeting = duplicate_string("Hello, world!");
    if (greeting == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        return 1;
    }

    printf("%s\n", greeting);

    free(greeting);       // free when done
    greeting = NULL;      // prevent accidental reuse

    return 0;
}

Detecting Memory Errors with Valgrind

Valgrind is a tool that monitors every memory access your program makes and reports errors such as:

  • Reading uninitialized memory
  • Reading or writing freed memory (dangling pointers)
  • Reading or writing past the end of allocated blocks (buffer overflows)
  • Memory leaks (allocated memory that was never freed)
  • Double frees
  • Mismatched malloc/free (e.g., using delete on memory from malloc)

To use valgrind, compile your program with the -g flag (for debug symbols) and then run:

gcc -g -o myprogram myprogram.c
valgrind --leak-check=full ./myprogram

Valgrind will print detailed reports of any memory errors it detects, including the line numbers in your source code where the errors occurred. You should run valgrind on all of your C programs that use dynamic memory allocation. A clean valgrind report (no errors, no leaks) is a strong sign that your program manages memory correctly.

Module 9: Virtual Memory, Linking, and Dynamic Memory

Lesson 4: Debugging Memory Errors with Valgrind

Introduction

In Lesson 3, we saw the common memory errors that plague C programs: leaks, dangling pointers, double frees, and buffer overflows. We also saw that these bugs can be subtle and hard to find — a heap buffer overflow might not crash until much later, when malloc or free tries to use corrupted metadata. The symptoms often appear far from the actual bug, making manual debugging extremely frustrating.

Valgrind is the tool that finds these bugs for you. It monitors every memory access your program makes and reports errors at the exact instruction that causes them — not when the symptoms appear later. In this lesson, we will learn how to use Valgrind systematically to detect and fix every major category of dynamic memory error.

What Valgrind Is

Valgrind is a dynamic analysis framework that runs your program on a synthetic CPU. Rather than executing your program directly on the hardware, Valgrind translates each machine instruction and executes it in a controlled environment where every memory access can be monitored.

Valgrind's default tool, Memcheck, monitors every memory access and tracks which bytes are allocated, freed, and initialized. For each byte of memory, Memcheck maintains two pieces of metadata:

  • Addressability: Is this byte part of a currently allocated block? Or has it been freed, or was it never allocated?
  • Definedness: Has this byte been written to with a known value, or does it still contain uninitialized data?

This lets Memcheck detect errors at the exact instruction that causes them. When your program reads from freed memory, writes past the end of an array, or branches based on an uninitialized value, Valgrind reports it immediately — with the exact line number and a full stack trace.

Compiling for Valgrind

Valgrind works on compiled binaries, but it gives much better output when your program is compiled with the right flags:

  • -g — Include debug symbols so that Valgrind can report source file names and line numbers instead of raw addresses.
  • -O0 — Disable optimization so that the compiled code structure matches what you wrote. With optimization enabled, the compiler may reorder, inline, or eliminate code, making Valgrind's reports harder to map back to your source.

Example:

gcc -g -O0 -o myprogram myprogram.c

You should always compile with -g. The -O0 flag is strongly recommended during development and debugging. Without it, Valgrind still works, but some error reports may point to unexpected lines due to compiler transformations.

Running Valgrind

The basic syntax is:

valgrind ./myprogram

This runs your program under Memcheck and reports any memory errors. For more detailed output, use additional flags:

valgrind --leak-check=full ./myprogram

The --leak-check=full flag gives detailed information about each memory leak, including the exact location where the leaked memory was allocated.

valgrind --leak-check=full --show-leak-kinds=all ./myprogram

The --show-leak-kinds=all flag reports all types of leaks, including "still reachable" blocks (memory that was not freed but was still pointed to at program exit). By default, Valgrind only reports "definitely lost" and "possibly lost" blocks.

If your program takes command-line arguments, just add them after the program name:

valgrind --leak-check=full ./myprogram arg1 arg2

Reading Valgrind Output

Valgrind's output has a distinctive format. Every line is prefixed with ==PID==, where PID is the process ID of your program. This makes it easy to distinguish Valgrind's messages from your program's own output.

A typical error report looks like this:

==12345== Invalid write of size 4
==12345==    at 0x4005A3: main (example.c:6)
==12345==  Address 0x5204054 is 0 bytes after a block of size 20 alloc'd
==12345==    at 0x4C2AB80: malloc (vg_replace_malloc.c:299)
==12345==    by 0x400593: main (example.c:4)

Each error report has several parts:

  • Error description: The first line describes what went wrong (e.g., "Invalid write of size 4").
  • Stack trace: The indented lines show where the error occurred, from the most recent function call down to the caller. With -g, these show file names and line numbers.
  • Additional context: Valgrind often provides extra information, such as where the relevant memory block was allocated or freed.

At the end of the run, Valgrind prints a heap summary and a leak summary:

==12345== HEAP SUMMARY:
==12345==     in use at exit: 400 bytes in 1 blocks
==12345==   total heap usage: 3 allocs, 2 frees, 1,424 bytes allocated
==12345==
==12345== LEAK SUMMARY:
==12345==    definitely lost: 400 bytes in 1 blocks
==12345==    indirectly lost: 0 bytes in 0 blocks
==12345==      possibly lost: 0 bytes in 0 blocks
==12345==    still reachable: 0 bytes in 0 blocks
==12345==         suppressed: 0 bytes in 0 blocks

The leak categories mean:

  • Definitely lost: Memory that is not pointed to by anything — a definite leak. This is the most important category.
  • Indirectly lost: Memory that is only reachable through a "definitely lost" block. For example, if a linked list's head node is leaked, all the subsequent nodes are "indirectly lost."
  • Possibly lost: Memory that is pointed to by an interior pointer (a pointer to the middle of a block rather than the beginning). This sometimes indicates a leak and sometimes does not.
  • Still reachable: Memory that was not freed but is still pointed to at program exit. This is usually not a serious problem, but it indicates a missing free.

Detecting Invalid Reads and Writes

An invalid write occurs when your program writes to memory it does not own — for example, writing past the end of a heap-allocated array. An invalid read is the same for reading. These are the heap buffer overflows and underflows we discussed in Lesson 3.

Consider this program with an off-by-one error:

#include <stdlib.h>

int main() {
    int *arr = (int *)malloc(5 * sizeof(int));
    for (int i = 0; i <= 5; i++) {  // off-by-one: writes past end
        arr[i] = i * 10;
    }
    free(arr);
    return 0;
}

When i is 5, the loop writes to arr[5], which is one element past the end of the allocated block (which only has indices 0 through 4). This might not crash — it might silently corrupt the heap metadata stored after the block — but Valgrind catches it immediately:

==12345== Invalid write of size 4
==12345==    at 0x4005B3: main (overflow.c:5)
==12345==  Address 0x5204054 is 0 bytes after a block of size 20 alloc'd
==12345==    at 0x4C2AB80: malloc (vg_replace_malloc.c:299)
==12345==    by 0x400593: main (overflow.c:4)

The message tells us:

  • The error is an "Invalid write of size 4" (writing a 4-byte int).
  • It happened at line 5 of overflow.c (the arr[i] = i * 10; line).
  • The address being written to is "0 bytes after a block of size 20" — meaning it is immediately past the end of a 20-byte block (which is 5 ints of 4 bytes each).
  • That block was allocated at line 4 of overflow.c (the malloc call).

The fix is straightforward: change the loop condition from i <= 5 to i < 5.

Detecting Use of Uninitialized Memory

Memory returned by malloc is not initialized — it contains whatever data was previously stored at that location. Reading this data before writing to it is undefined behavior, and bugs of this kind can produce different results on different runs.

Consider this program:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

int main() {
    int *p = (int *)malloc(sizeof(int));
    if (*p > 0) {       // reading uninitialized memory
        printf("positive\n");
    }
    free(p);
    return 0;
}

The variable *p was never assigned a value, so the if condition reads uninitialized memory. Valgrind reports:

==12345== Conditional jump or move depends on uninitialised value(s)
==12345==    at 0x4005A3: main (uninit.c:6)

This error means that a branch decision (the if) depends on a value that was never initialized. The fix is to assign a value to *p before reading it, or use calloc instead of malloc to get zero-initialized memory.

By default, Valgrind tells you where the uninitialized value was used but not where it came from. To trace it back to its origin, use the --track-origins=yes flag:

valgrind --track-origins=yes ./uninit

This adds an extra message showing that the uninitialized value was created by the malloc at a specific line, which is especially useful in larger programs where the allocation and the use are far apart.

Detecting Use After Free

A use-after-free error occurs when your program accesses memory through a pointer after that memory has been freed. The pointer becomes a dangling pointer — it still holds the old address, but that address is no longer valid.

Consider this program:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

int main() {
    int *p = (int *)malloc(sizeof(int));
    *p = 42;
    free(p);
    printf("%d\n", *p);  // use after free
    return 0;
}

After free(p), the memory at p has been returned to the heap. Reading *p on the next line is undefined behavior. It might print 42, or it might print garbage, or it might crash — depending on whether the freed block has been reused. Valgrind catches it reliably:

==12345== Invalid read of size 4
==12345==    at 0x4005C3: main (useafterfree.c:8)
==12345==  Address 0x5204040 is 0 bytes inside a block of size 4 free'd
==12345==    at 0x4C2BDEC: free (vg_replace_malloc.c:530)
==12345==    by 0x4005B3: main (useafterfree.c:7)
==12345==  Block was alloc'd at
==12345==    at 0x4C2AB80: malloc (vg_replace_malloc.c:299)
==12345==    by 0x400593: main (useafterfree.c:5)

Valgrind's report gives you three critical pieces of information:

  • What happened: An "Invalid read of size 4" at line 8 — the printf that reads *p.
  • Where the block was freed: At line 7 — the free(p) call.
  • Where the block was originally allocated: At line 5 — the malloc call.

The fix is to not access memory after freeing it. A common defensive practice is to set the pointer to NULL after freeing: free(p); p = NULL;. This way, any subsequent dereference will cause an immediate segfault rather than silently reading stale data.

Detecting Memory Leaks

A memory leak occurs when your program allocates memory but never frees it. The memory remains allocated until the program exits, wasting resources. In a long-running program (a server, for example), leaks accumulate and can eventually exhaust available memory.

Consider this program:

#include <stdlib.h>

int main() {
    int *arr = (int *)malloc(100 * sizeof(int));
    arr[0] = 42;
    // forgot to free arr
    return 0;
}

Running with --leak-check=full:

valgrind --leak-check=full ./leak

Valgrind reports:

==12345== HEAP SUMMARY:
==12345==     in use at exit: 400 bytes in 1 blocks
==12345==   total heap usage: 1 allocs, 0 frees, 400 bytes allocated
==12345==
==12345== 400 bytes in 1 blocks are definitely lost in loss record 1 of 1
==12345==    at 0x4C2AB80: malloc (vg_replace_malloc.c:299)
==12345==    by 0x400553: main (leak.c:4)
==12345==
==12345== LEAK SUMMARY:
==12345==    definitely lost: 400 bytes in 1 blocks
==12345==    indirectly lost: 0 bytes in 0 blocks
==12345==      possibly lost: 0 bytes in 0 blocks
==12345==    still reachable: 0 bytes in 0 blocks
==12345==         suppressed: 0 bytes in 0 blocks

The report tells us that 400 bytes (100 ints times 4 bytes each) are "definitely lost," and it shows the exact line where the leaked block was allocated (line 4 of leak.c). The "1 allocs, 0 frees" in the heap summary is a quick way to see that something was allocated and never freed.

The fix is to add free(arr); before return 0;.

Detecting Double Frees

A double free occurs when your program frees the same block of memory twice. This corrupts the heap's internal data structures and can lead to crashes, incorrect behavior, or security vulnerabilities.

Consider this program:

#include <stdlib.h>

int main() {
    int *p = (int *)malloc(sizeof(int));
    *p = 42;
    free(p);
    free(p);  // double free
    return 0;
}

Valgrind reports:

==12345== Invalid free() / delete / delete[] / realloc()
==12345==    at 0x4C2BDEC: free (vg_replace_malloc.c:530)
==12345==    by 0x4005A3: main (doublefree.c:7)
==12345==  Address 0x5204040 is 0 bytes inside a block of size 4 free'd
==12345==    at 0x4C2BDEC: free (vg_replace_malloc.c:530)
==12345==    by 0x400593: main (doublefree.c:6)
==12345==  Block was alloc'd at
==12345==    at 0x4C2AB80: malloc (vg_replace_malloc.c:299)
==12345==    by 0x400573: main (doublefree.c:4)

The report shows:

  • An "Invalid free()" at line 7 — the second free(p).
  • The block was previously freed at line 6 — the first free(p).
  • The block was originally allocated at line 4 — the malloc call.

The fix is to remove the second free(p). As with use-after-free, setting the pointer to NULL after freeing (free(p); p = NULL;) is a good defensive practice. Calling free(NULL) is defined by the C standard to do nothing, so a second free(p) after p = NULL is harmless.

A Complete Debugging Example

Let us look at a more realistic example: a function that builds a dynamically allocated array of strings. This program has several bugs.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

char **make_names(int count) {
    char **names = (char **)malloc(count * sizeof(char *));

    for (int i = 0; i <= count; i++) {     // Bug 1: off-by-one
        names[i] = (char *)malloc(20);
        sprintf(names[i], "name_%d", i);
    }

    return names;
}

void print_and_free(char **names, int count) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%s\n", names[i]);
        free(names[i]);
    }
    // Bug 2: forgot to free names itself
    // Bug 3: also leaked names[count] from the off-by-one
}

int main() {
    char **names = make_names(3);
    print_and_free(names, 3);
    return 0;
}

Running under Valgrind with --leak-check=full reveals all three bugs:

==12345== Invalid write of size 8
==12345==    at 0x400623: make_names (example.c:9)
==12345==  Address 0x5204048 is 0 bytes after a block of size 24 alloc'd
==12345==    at 0x4C2AB80: malloc (vg_replace_malloc.c:299)
==12345==    by 0x4005F3: make_names (example.c:6)
==12345==
==12345== LEAK SUMMARY:
==12345==    definitely lost: 24 bytes in 1 blocks
==12345==    indirectly lost: 20 bytes in 1 blocks
==12345==      possibly lost: 0 bytes in 0 blocks
==12345==    still reachable: 0 bytes in 0 blocks

Bug 1 (off-by-one): The loop condition i <= count should be i < count. When count is 3, the array names has space for 3 pointers (indices 0, 1, 2), but the loop writes to names[3], which is past the end. Fix: Change the loop condition to i < count.

Bug 2 (leaked array): The function print_and_free frees each string but not the array of pointers itself. Fix: Add free(names); at the end of print_and_free.

Bug 3 (leaked extra string): Because of the off-by-one, an extra string names[count] was allocated but is never freed by print_and_free (which only iterates up to count - 1). Fixing Bug 1 eliminates this bug as well, since the extra allocation never happens.

Here is the corrected code:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

char **make_names(int count) {
    char **names = (char **)malloc(count * sizeof(char *));

    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {       // Fixed: i < count
        names[i] = (char *)malloc(20);
        sprintf(names[i], "name_%d", i);
    }

    return names;
}

void print_and_free(char **names, int count) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%s\n", names[i]);
        free(names[i]);
    }
    free(names);                             // Fixed: free the array itself
}

int main() {
    char **names = make_names(3);
    print_and_free(names, 3);
    return 0;
}

Running the corrected program under Valgrind:

==12345== HEAP SUMMARY:
==12345==     in use at exit: 0 bytes in 0 blocks
==12345==   total heap usage: 4 allocs, 4 frees, 84 bytes allocated
==12345==
==12345== All heap blocks were freed -- no leaks are possible
==12345==
==12345== ERROR SUMMARY: 0 errors from 0 contexts

A clean report: zero errors, zero leaks.

Tips for Using Valgrind

  • Always compile with -g and preferably -O0. Without debug symbols, Valgrind's reports show raw addresses instead of file names and line numbers, making them much harder to interpret.
  • Run with --leak-check=full as a habit. This should be your default Valgrind invocation. Without it, Valgrind reports the total bytes leaked but not where the leaks originated.
  • Fix errors in order. The first memory error can cause cascading effects. An invalid write might corrupt data that leads to additional errors later. Fix the first reported error, re-run Valgrind, and repeat.
  • Valgrind slows your program down roughly 10–50x. This is normal and expected. Valgrind is instrumenting every memory access, so this overhead is unavoidable. If your program normally takes a few seconds, it will take a minute or two under Valgrind. For programs with very large inputs, consider testing under Valgrind with a smaller input first.
  • A clean Valgrind report should be the standard. For any C program that uses dynamic memory, you should aim for 0 errors and 0 leaks. If Valgrind reports no issues, you can be confident that your program has no heap memory errors — at least on the execution path you tested.
  • Use --track-origins=yes to trace uninitialized values back to their source. This flag makes Valgrind slower but produces more informative reports for "uninitialised value" errors, showing where the problematic memory was allocated rather than just where it was used.
Practical tip: Make Valgrind a routine part of your development workflow, not something you run only when something goes wrong. A good practice is to run your program under Valgrind every time you test — especially after making changes to code that allocates or frees memory. Many professional C development teams run Valgrind as part of their automated test suite, failing the build if any memory errors are detected. The few extra seconds of Valgrind runtime can save you hours of debugging mysterious crashes.

Module 9: Virtual Memory, Linking, and Dynamic Memory

Lesson 5: Garbage Collection

The Problem: Manual Memory Management is Hard

In Lesson 3, we saw the malloc/free API and the many ways it can go wrong: memory leaks, dangling pointers, double frees, and heap buffer overflows. These bugs are difficult to find, difficult to reproduce, and often lead to security vulnerabilities.

The root cause is that the programmer is responsible for deciding when to free every block of memory. In a large program with complex data structures — linked lists, trees, graphs, objects pointing to other objects — tracking which memory is still in use becomes extremely error-prone.

Garbage collection (GC) is an automatic solution: the runtime system itself determines which memory is still reachable (could be accessed by the program) and frees everything else. Most modern languages — Java, Python, Go, JavaScript, C#, Ruby — use garbage collection.

Reachability

The key idea behind all garbage collectors is reachability. A block of memory is reachable if the program could possibly access it by following a chain of pointers starting from a root. Roots include:

  • Local variables on the stack
  • Global/static variables
  • CPU registers

If no chain of pointers from any root leads to a block, the program has no way to access it, and the memory can safely be reclaimed. This is the same criterion you use mentally when deciding whether to call free() — the garbage collector just automates it.

Reference Counting

Reference counting is the simplest form of garbage collection. Each object maintains a reference count — the number of pointers currently pointing to it. When a pointer is assigned to point to an object, the count increases; when a pointer is reassigned or goes out of scope, the count decreases. When the count reaches zero, the object is immediately freed.

  a = new Object()    # Object refcount = 1
  b = a               # Object refcount = 2
  a = null            # Object refcount = 1
  b = null            # Object refcount = 0 --> freed immediately

The Cycle Problem

Reference counting has a fundamental flaw: it cannot reclaim cycles. If object A points to object B and object B points back to object A, both have a reference count of at least 1 — even if nothing else in the program can reach either of them.

  A.next = B          # B refcount = 1
  B.prev = A          # A refcount = 1
  (remove all other references to A and B)

  # A refcount = 1 (from B.prev), B refcount = 1 (from A.next)
  # Neither will ever reach 0 --> MEMORY LEAK

Languages that rely on reference counting deal with cycles in different ways:

  • Python uses reference counting as the primary mechanism but runs a separate cycle detector periodically to find and reclaim cyclic garbage.
  • Swift uses reference counting and requires the programmer to break cycles manually using weak references.
  • Rust uses Rc (reference counted pointers) and Weak for the same purpose, though Rust's ownership model avoids most GC needs entirely.

Mark-and-Sweep

Mark-and-sweep is a tracing garbage collector that handles cycles correctly. It works in two phases:

  1. Mark phase: Starting from the roots (stack, globals, registers), follow every pointer and mark each reachable object. This is essentially a graph traversal (DFS or BFS) over the object graph.
  2. Sweep phase: Walk through the entire heap. Any object that was not marked is unreachable — free it. Clear all marks for the next collection cycle.
  Roots: [stack] [globals]
           |        |
           v        v
          [A] ---> [B] ---> [C]
                    |
                    v
                   [D]

          [E] ---> [F]    (E and F are not reachable from any root)

  Mark phase:  A, B, C, D are marked (reachable from roots)
  Sweep phase: E and F are not marked --> freed

Mark-and-sweep handles cycles naturally: if A and B point to each other but neither is reachable from a root, neither gets marked, and both are freed in the sweep phase.

The main downside is that the program must pause while the collector runs (a "stop-the-world" pause). For most applications this pause is imperceptibly short, but it can be a problem for real-time systems. Mark-and-sweep is used by Java, Go, and JavaScript (among others), though usually with optimizations that reduce pause times.

Generational GC

Empirically, most objects die young — they are allocated, used briefly, and become garbage. This observation is called the generational hypothesis, and it motivates an important optimization.

A generational collector divides the heap into two or more generations:

  • The young generation (or "nursery") holds recently allocated objects. It is collected frequently, which is fast because most young objects are already dead.
  • The old generation holds objects that have survived several young collections. It is collected rarely, which amortizes the higher cost of scanning long-lived objects.

Objects that survive enough young-generation collections are promoted to the old generation. This optimization dramatically reduces the average cost of garbage collection. It is used by Java (the HotSpot JVM) and .NET.

Compacting and Copying Collectors

Recall from Lesson 3 that external fragmentation is when free memory is scattered in small chunks between allocated blocks, and no single chunk is large enough to satisfy a request. We noted that C cannot solve this problem because moving an allocated block would invalidate every pointer to it.

Garbage-collected languages can solve this problem. Since the GC knows where every pointer is, it can move objects to new locations and update all pointers that refer to them. Two common approaches:

  • Compacting collector: After mark-and-sweep, slide all surviving objects to one end of the heap, eliminating all gaps. The free space becomes one large contiguous block.
  • Copying collector: Divide memory into two halves. Allocate from one half; when it fills up, copy all reachable objects to the other half (packed tightly), then swap the roles of the two halves.

Both eliminate external fragmentation entirely. The tradeoff is the cost of copying objects and updating pointers.

Why C Doesn't Have Garbage Collection

C allows raw pointer arithmetic: you can cast integers to pointers, store pointers in integers, compute pointer offsets, and so on. This means the runtime cannot reliably determine what is a pointer and what is not. Consider:

int *p = (int *)malloc(sizeof(int));
*p = 42;
uintptr_t secret = (uintptr_t)p;     // pointer stored as an integer
p = NULL;                             // the only "visible" pointer is gone
// ... later ...
int *q = (int *)secret;              // recover the pointer from the integer
printf("%d\n", *q);                  // still works -- the block is still needed!

If a garbage collector were managing this memory, it would see that no pointer variable currently refers to the block (only the integer secret does, and the GC cannot tell that an integer holds an address). The collector might reclaim the block, and then dereferencing q would be a dangling-pointer bug — even though the program legitimately still needs that memory.

Furthermore, since C pointers are raw addresses, a collector cannot move objects — there is no way to find and update every copy of a pointer. This is exactly what Lesson 5 noted: "Unlike languages with garbage collection, C cannot move allocated blocks to compact free memory."

Conservative GC: Boehm GC

There is one exception: the Boehm-Demers-Weiser conservative garbage collector is a drop-in replacement for malloc/free in C and C++ programs. It works by treating every value in memory that looks like it could be a pointer (i.e., falls within the heap address range) as if it were one.

This is "conservative" because it may keep objects alive that are not actually reachable — a random integer that happens to look like a heap address will prevent that block from being collected. But it will never incorrectly free memory that is still in use. The Boehm GC is used in practice by several language runtimes and as a leak-prevention measure in some C/C++ applications.

Tradeoffs Summary

Manual (C)Reference CountingTracing GC (Mark-and-Sweep)
Who frees memory?Programmer (free)Runtime (when refcount = 0)Runtime (periodically)
Handles cycles?N/ANo (needs extra mechanism)Yes
Pauses?NoneUsually none (but cascading frees can cause bursts)Yes (stop-the-world)
Can compact?No (raw pointers)Not typicallyYes (if moving/copying)
OverheadNo GC overhead (malloc/free have their own cost)Count updates on every assignmentPeriodic tracing of all reachable objects
SafetyError-prone (leaks, dangling ptrs)Mostly safe (cycles can leak)Safe
Used byC, C++Python, Swift, Rust (Arc, opt-in)Java, Go, JavaScript, C#

Module 9: Virtual Memory, Linking, and Dynamic Memory

Module 9 Summary

Wrap Up

In this module, we studied how the operating system manages memory and how programs are loaded, linked, and given access to the heap. We began with virtual memory — the abstraction that gives each process a private address space while sharing physical memory. We then examined linking: how the linker resolves symbols, combines object files, and supports shared libraries through position-independent code. From there, we studied dynamic memory allocation with malloc and free, including the internal data structures that manage the heap. We concluded with garbage collection, the automatic alternative to manual memory management used by most modern languages.

Key Takeaways

  • Virtual memory is an abstraction provided by the OS and hardware together. Each process sees a private, contiguous virtual address space. The MMU translates virtual addresses to physical addresses using page tables. The TLB caches recent translations to make this fast. Page faults handle the case when a virtual page is not in physical memory, loading it from disk on demand.
  • Linking is the process of combining object files into an executable. The static linker resolves symbol references, handles strong vs. weak symbols, and produces a self-contained binary. The dynamic linker defers library loading until runtime, using the PLT and GOT to resolve function addresses lazily. Dynamic linking saves disk space and memory when multiple programs share the same libraries.
  • Position-independent code (PIC) allows shared libraries to be loaded at any virtual address. This is essential for ASLR and for sharing physical pages of library code between processes.
  • Dynamic memory allocation with malloc/free gives the programmer explicit control over heap memory. Internally, malloc maintains a free list of available blocks, uses allocation strategies (first fit, best fit, next fit) to choose blocks, and coalesces adjacent free blocks to fight fragmentation.
  • Common memory errors in C — memory leaks, dangling pointers, double frees, and buffer overflows — are a major source of bugs and security vulnerabilities. Tools like valgrind can detect these errors and should be used routinely on any C program that uses dynamic memory allocation.
  • Valgrind is a dynamic analysis tool that detects memory errors at the exact instruction that causes them. Running programs under Valgrind with --leak-check=full catches leaks, invalid reads and writes, use of uninitialized memory, and double frees. A clean Valgrind report should be the standard for any C program that uses dynamic memory.
  • Garbage collection automates memory management. Mark-and-sweep traces reachable objects from the roots and frees everything else. Reference counting is simpler but cannot handle cycles. Generational collectors exploit the observation that most objects die young, collecting the nursery frequently and the old generation rarely.

Additional Resources
