ModuleLayerConnection to Kernel Organization
Module 1Data representationThe kernel and all its data structures are built from the same integer and memory representations you learned first
Module 2Floating pointHardware representation of data, including the tradeoffs designers must make at every level of a system
Modules 3-4Assembly and machine codeSystem calls use specific instructions (syscall) and register conventions that are defined at the assembly level; hardware privilege levels (ring 0 vs. ring 3) are enforced by the CPU itself
Module 5Processes and signalsProcess creation, scheduling, and signal delivery are core kernel responsibilities
Module 6ThreadsThread management and synchronization primitives are implemented by the kernel
Module 7File I/O and networkingThe file system and networking stack are kernel subsystems (in monolithic kernels) or user-space servers (in microkernels)
Module 8Memory hierarchy and optimizationCaches exploit locality to bridge the CPU-memory speed gap; understanding the memory hierarchy is essential for writing performant code and for understanding how the kernel manages memory
Module 9Virtual memory, linking, and dynamic memoryVirtual memory, page tables, and the TLB are managed by the kernel's memory subsystem; linking determines how programs are loaded into the virtual address space; malloc/free operate within the heap region of that address space
Module 10Kernel organizationHow all of these subsystems are structured and how they interact

Understanding kernel organization gives you the architectural context for everything else you have learned. When you know how the kernel is structured, you can better understand why system calls have the performance characteristics they do, why context switches are expensive, why a segmentation fault kills your process, and why operating system design involves fundamental engineering tradeoffs that have been debated for over 30 years.

Additional Resources

The Linux Kernel Archives — the official source of the Linux kernel, where you can browse the actual source code of a monolithic kernel

The seL4 Microkernel — the homepage of the world's first formally verified general-purpose OS kernel

L4 Microkernel Family — overview of the L4 family of microkernels, from Liedtke's original to modern descendants like seL4, Fiasco.OC, and NOVA

MINIX 3 — Andrew Tanenbaum's reliable microkernel OS, with documentation on its fault-tolerant design

QNX Developer Documentation — technical documentation for the QNX real-time microkernel OS

The Tanenbaum-Torvalds Debate (1992) — the original Usenet thread where Andrew Tanenbaum and Linus Torvalds debated monolithic vs. microkernel design

eBPF.io — an introduction to eBPF, the technology bringing sandboxed extensibility to the Linux kernel

Unikraft — a modular unikernel development framework

Reference: Systems Programming Guides

_start Assembly Syntax Reference

This reference matches the style used in this course: GNU assembler (as), GNU linker (ld), hand-written x86-64 assembly, and direct entry at _start (no C runtime).

Minimal Program Skeleton

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        mov $60, %rax      # syscall: exit
        xor %rdi, %rdi     # status 0
        syscall

Build and Run

$ as -o prog.o prog.s
$ ld -o prog prog.o
$ ./prog
$ echo $?

Multi-file link example:

$ as -o main.o main.s
$ as -o readInt.o readInt.s
$ as -o writeInt.o writeInt.s
$ ld -o app main.o readInt.o writeInt.o

Core Syntax Rules (AT&T)

  • Order is source, destination (not destination, source).
  • Immediates use $ (example: $42).
  • Registers use % (example: %rax).
  • Instruction size suffixes: b (1 byte), w (2), l (4), q (8).
  • 32-bit register writes (example: movl ... , %eax) zero-extend into the upper 32 bits of the 64-bit register.
  • # starts a comment.

Sections and Directives

DirectivePurpose
.textExecutable code section.
.dataWritable initialized data.
.rodataRead-only constants (strings, tables).
.bssZero-initialized/uninitialized storage.
.global nameExport label for linker visibility.
.extern nameDeclare symbol defined in another file.
.byte/.long/.quadDefine 1/4/8-byte data values.
.asciz "..."NUL-terminated string.
.equ NAME, valueSymbolic constant.

Addressing Forms

General memory operand form:

displacement(base, index, scale)
  • Computed address = displacement + base + index*scale.
  • scale must be 1, 2, 4, or 8.
  • RIP-relative form for static data: label(%rip).
movq 16(%rsp), %rax
movq (%rbx,%rcx,8), %rdx
lea arr(%rip), %r8

Data Movement and Arithmetic

  • mov does not allow memory-to-memory operands in one instruction.
  • lea computes addresses/arithmetic; it does not read memory contents.
  • idiv uses the pair %rdx:%rax; run cqto before signed 64-bit division.
movq %rax, %rbx
movq $123, %rax
movq (%rsi), %rax
lea (%rdx,%rdx,4), %rdx      # rdx = rdx*5
addq %rbx, %rax
subq $8, %rsp
imulq $3, %rax, %rax
cqto
idivq %rcx

Compare, Test, and Jumps

cmpq %rbx, %rax      # flags from (rax - rbx)
testq %rax, %rax     # flags from (rax & rax)
TypeCommon Jumps
Equalityje, jne
Signedjl, jle, jg, jge
Unsignedjb, jbe, ja, jae
Zero/nonzerojz, jnz

Stack and Calls

pushq %rax
popq %rbx
call readInt
ret
  • pushq is equivalent to subq $8,%rsp then store at (%rsp).
  • popq loads from (%rsp) then adds 8 to %rsp.
  • Keep stack alignment consistent before call sites when interoperating with ABI-compliant routines.

Linux x86-64 Syscall Convention

FieldRegister
Syscall number%rax
Arg 1..6%rdi, %rsi, %rdx, %r10, %r8, %r9
Return value%rax
Clobbered by syscall%rcx, %r11

Common syscall numbers used in this course:

  • read = 0
  • write = 1
  • exit = 60

Common Patterns

Write a string to stdout

        .section .rodata
msg:    .asciz "Hello\n"
len = . - msg - 1

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        mov $1, %rax
        mov $1, %rdi
        lea msg(%rip), %rsi
        mov $len, %rdx
        syscall

        mov $60, %rax
        xor %rdi, %rdi
        syscall

Read bytes from stdin into a buffer

        .section .bss
buf:    .skip 64

        .text
        .global _start
_start:
        mov $0, %rax
        mov $0, %rdi
        lea buf(%rip), %rsi
        mov $64, %rdx
        syscall                # %rax = bytes read

        mov $60, %rax
        xor %rdi, %rdi
        syscall

On return, %rax holds the number of bytes actually read. A return value of 0 means EOF; a negative value indicates an error.

Exit with computed status

        mov $60, %rax
        mov %r12, %rdi
        syscall

echo $? reports the low 8 bits (0-255).

Common Mistakes Checklist

  • Using main instead of _start when linking directly with ld.
  • Forgetting .global _start.
  • Reversing operand order (AT&T is source then destination).
  • Forgetting $ on immediates.
  • Using invalid memory-to-memory arithmetic/move forms.
  • Using signed jump for unsigned compare (or vice versa).
  • Forgetting that syscall overwrites %rax with return value.
  • Failing to preserve needed registers/values across calls and syscalls.

Useful Commands

$ objdump -d prog.o
$ gdb ./prog
(gdb) break _start
(gdb) stepi
(gdb) info registers
(gdb) x/8xg $rsp

Scope note: This page is a syntax and convention reference for the course's `_start` workflow. It is not a full x86-64 instruction manual.

Reference: Systems Programming Guides

Processes, Signals, and Exceptions Reference

Quick reference for Module 5 topics: exceptional control flow, process control, and signal handling on Linux/x86-64.

Exception Classes

ClassSourceTypical Return BehaviorExample
InterruptAsynchronous external eventResume next instructionTimer interrupt, device I/O
TrapSynchronous intentional exceptionResume next instructionsyscall
FaultSynchronous potentially recoverable exceptionRetry faulting instruction if fixedPage fault
AbortSynchronous unrecoverable exceptionTerminate processSerious hardware/internal failure

Process Lifecycle Syscalls

pid_t pid = fork();
if (pid == 0) {
    execl("/bin/ls", "ls", "-l", (char *)0);
    _exit(127);    // only runs if exec fails
}
int status;
waitpid(pid, &status, 0);
  • fork(): returns 0 in child, child PID in parent, -1 on error.
  • execve() family: replaces current process image, does not return on success.
  • waitpid(): reaps child and prevents zombies.
  • Use _exit() in child error paths after fork() if needed.

Zombies and Orphans

  • Zombie: child has exited but parent has not reaped it yet.
  • Orphan: parent exits first; child is re-parented (typically to PID 1/systemd).
  • Install SIGCHLD handling or call waitpid() reliably to avoid zombie buildup.

Signal Basics

SignalDefault ActionTypical Source
SIGINTTerminateCtrl+C
SIGTSTPStopCtrl+Z
SIGKILLTerminateAdministrative kill, cannot catch/block/ignore
SIGSTOPStopCannot catch/block/ignore
SIGCHLDIgnore (commonly)Child state change
SIGALRMTerminateTimer expiration

Installing Handlers (Recommended: sigaction)

volatile sig_atomic_t got_sigint = 0;

void on_sigint(int signo) {
    got_sigint = 1;
}

struct sigaction sa;
sa.sa_handler = on_sigint;
sigemptyset(&sa.sa_mask);
sa.sa_flags = 0;
sigaction(SIGINT, &sa, NULL);
  • signal() is simple but less precise across platforms; prefer sigaction().
  • Keep handler work minimal; set a flag and return.
  • Use volatile sig_atomic_t for shared handler flags.

Async-Signal Safety

  • Safe in handlers: low-level async-signal-safe functions such as write().
  • Unsafe in handlers: printf(), malloc(), most stdio and non-reentrant library code.
  • If output is needed inside a handler, prefer write(STDOUT_FILENO,...).

Blocking and Unblocking Signals

sigset_t mask, prev;
sigemptyset(&mask);
sigaddset(&mask, SIGINT);
sigprocmask(SIG_BLOCK, &mask, &prev);

// critical section

sigprocmask(SIG_SETMASK, &prev, NULL);
  • SIG_BLOCK: add to blocked set.
  • SIG_UNBLOCK: remove from blocked set.
  • SIG_SETMASK: replace blocked set exactly.

Process Groups and kill

  • kill(pid, sig): signal one process if pid > 0.
  • kill(0, sig): signal all processes in caller's process group.
  • kill(-pgid, sig): signal all processes in process group pgid.
$ kill -9 12345      # process 12345
$ kill -9 -15111     # process group 15111

Common Wait Macros

int status;
waitpid(pid, &status, 0);
if (WIFEXITED(status)) {
    int code = WEXITSTATUS(status);
}
if (WIFSIGNALED(status)) {
    int sig = WTERMSIG(status);
}

Reliable SIGCHLD Reaping Loop

void on_sigchld(int signo) {
    int saved = errno;
    while (waitpid(-1, NULL, WNOHANG) > 0) {
    }
    errno = saved;
}

This pattern reaps all available terminated children and avoids leaving zombies.

Common Mistakes Checklist

  • Forgetting to reap children, causing zombies.
  • Calling non-async-signal-safe functions inside signal handlers.
  • Assuming blocked standard signals queue multiple times (they do not).
  • Ignoring return values and errno from fork/exec/waitpid/sigaction.
  • Using exit() in a post-fork child error path when _exit() is required.

Reference: Systems Programming Guides

Concurrency and Threads Reference

Quick reference for Module 6 topics: pthreads, race conditions, mutexes, condition variables, semaphores, and deadlock patterns.

Thread Model: Shared vs Private

Per-Thread (Private)Per-Process (Shared by Threads)
Registers, program counter, stackCode segment, heap, globals, open file descriptors

Compile/Link Flags

$ gcc -pthread -O2 -g program.c -o program

Use -pthread for correct compile + link behavior with pthreads.

Create and Join Threads

void *worker(void *arg) {
    return NULL;
}

pthread_t tid;
pthread_create(&tid, NULL, worker, arg_ptr);
pthread_join(tid, NULL);
  • Start routine signature: void *fn(void *arg).
  • Passing pointer to loop variable is a common race bug; pass stable per-thread data.

Race Condition Pattern

// not atomic:
counter++;
// often compiles to load, increment, store

Two threads interleaving these steps can lose updates.

Mutex Basics

pthread_mutex_t m = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;

pthread_mutex_lock(&m);
// critical section
pthread_mutex_unlock(&m);
  • Always unlock on all return/error paths.
  • pthread_mutex_trylock() tests lock availability without blocking.

Condition Variables

pthread_mutex_lock(&m);
while (!condition_is_true) {
    pthread_cond_wait(&cv, &m);
}
// condition holds
pthread_mutex_unlock(&m);
  • Use while, not if, because of spurious wakeups.
  • pthread_cond_wait atomically releases the mutex and sleeps, then re-locks on wake.
  • Use pthread_cond_signal (wake one) or pthread_cond_broadcast (wake all).

Semaphores

sem_t s;
sem_init(&s, 0, initial_value);
sem_wait(&s);   // P operation (decrement/block)
sem_post(&s);   // V operation (increment/wake)
sem_destroy(&s);
  • Binary semaphore (initial_value=1) can enforce mutual exclusion.
  • Counting semaphore tracks available units/resources.

Producer/Consumer Semaphore Pattern

sem_t empty, full, mutex;
// empty = N, full = 0, mutex = 1

// producer
sem_wait(∅);
sem_wait(&mutex);
// insert item
sem_post(&mutex);
sem_post(&full);

// consumer
sem_wait(&full);
sem_wait(&mutex);
// remove item
sem_post(&mutex);
sem_post(∅);

Deadlock: Four Conditions

  • Mutual exclusion
  • Hold and wait
  • No preemption
  • Circular wait

Most practical prevention in systems code: enforce a global lock acquisition order.

Reader-Writer Lock

pthread_rwlock_t rw = PTHREAD_RWLOCK_INITIALIZER;

pthread_rwlock_rdlock(&rw);  // many readers can hold concurrently
pthread_rwlock_unlock(&rw);

pthread_rwlock_wrlock(&rw);  // writer is exclusive
pthread_rwlock_unlock(&rw);

Common Pthreads APIs

TaskAPI
Create threadpthread_create
Join threadpthread_join
Detach threadpthread_detach
Initialize mutexpthread_mutex_init
Lock/unlock mutexpthread_mutex_lock/pthread_mutex_unlock
Condition wait/signalpthread_cond_wait/pthread_cond_signal
RW lockpthread_rwlock_rdlock/pthread_rwlock_wrlock

Common Mistakes Checklist

  • Sharing stack addresses that go out of scope with worker threads.
  • Returning with a mutex still locked.
  • Using if around pthread_cond_wait instead of while.
  • Assuming operation order without synchronization.
  • Inconsistent lock ordering across code paths (deadlock risk).
  • Using volatile as a replacement for mutex/atomic synchronization.

Debugging Tips

$ gdb ./app
(gdb) info threads
(gdb) thread apply all bt

$ valgrind --tool=helgrind ./app      # thread error detector
$ valgrind --tool=drd ./app           # alternative thread checker

Reference: Systems Programming Guides

File I/O and Sockets Reference

Quick reference for Module 7 topics: Unix file descriptors, buffered I/O, directories, and TCP socket programming.

Standard File Descriptors

FDName
0stdin
1stdout
2stderr

Low-Level File I/O

int fd = open(path, O_RDONLY);
ssize_t n = read(fd, buf, sizeof(buf));
ssize_t m = write(fd2, buf, n);
close(fd);
  • open returns -1 on error.
  • read returns 0 at EOF.
  • write may perform partial writes; loop until all bytes are written.

Open Flags

open("out.txt", O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC, 0644);
FlagMeaning
O_RDONLYOpen for reading only
O_WRONLYOpen for writing only
O_RDWROpen for read/write
O_CREATCreate if missing (requires mode)
O_TRUNCTruncate existing file
O_APPENDAppend writes at end

Buffered FILE* I/O

FILE *fp = fopen("in.txt", "r");
int c = fgetc(fp);
fclose(fp);
  • FILE* is buffered in user space; usually faster than byte-at-a-time read.
  • Use fflush(fp) to force buffered output to be written.

Directory Iteration

DIR *d = opendir(".");
struct dirent *ent;
while ((ent = readdir(d)) != NULL) {
    // ent->d_name
}
closedir(d);

TCP Socket Lifecycle (Server)

int listenfd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
setsockopt(listenfd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEADDR, &opt, sizeof(opt));
bind(listenfd, (struct sockaddr *)&addr, sizeof(addr));
listen(listenfd, backlog);
int connfd = accept(listenfd, (struct sockaddr *)&client, &clen);

Order is important: socket -> bind -> listen -> accept.

TCP Client Lifecycle

int fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
connect(fd, (struct sockaddr *)&server, sizeof(server));
write(fd, req, req_len);
read(fd, buf, sizeof(buf));
close(fd);

Address Conversion

struct sockaddr_in a;
memset(&a, 0, sizeof(a));
a.sin_family = AF_INET;
a.sin_port = htons(8080);
inet_pton(AF_INET, "127.0.0.1", &a.sin_addr);
  • htons/htonl: host -> network byte order.
  • ntohs/ntohl: network -> host byte order.
  • inet_pton: parse text IP to binary form.

Partial Read/Write Rules

  • TCP is a byte stream; message boundaries are not preserved.
  • One write() can be observed as multiple read() calls.
  • Loop until protocol-level message is complete.

Threaded Server FD Handoff Pattern

int client_fd = accept(...);
int *arg = malloc(sizeof(*arg));
*arg = client_fd;
pthread_create(&tid, NULL, handle_client, arg);
pthread_detach(tid);

Passing &client_fd directly from loop stack variable can race and hand wrong FD to threads.

HTTP Mini-Server Essentials

  • Request line: method, path, version.
  • Response starts with status line, then headers, blank line, then body.
  • Set at least Content-Length and Content-Type.
  • Path sanitization: reject .. to prevent directory traversal.

Useful Headers

#include <fcntl.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <sys/stat.h>
#include <dirent.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <netinet/in.h>
#include <arpa/inet.h>

Common Mistakes Checklist

  • Ignoring partial writes/reads on sockets.
  • Forgetting to close both connection FDs and listening FDs where appropriate.
  • Calling bind without SO_REUSEADDR and hitting restart delays.
  • Using host byte order directly in sin_port.
  • Not checking return values (-1) and errno.

Reference: Systems Programming Guides

Memory Hierarchy and Optimization Reference

Quick reference for Module 8 topics: RAM/caches, locality, compiler optimizations, and measurement-driven tuning.

Hierarchy at a Glance

LevelTypical Property
RegistersSmallest, fastest
L1/L2/L3 cache (SRAM)Fast, limited capacity
Main memory (DRAM)Larger, slower
Disk/SSDPersistent, much slower

Locality Rules

  • Temporal locality: recently used data tends to be reused soon.
  • Spatial locality: nearby addresses tend to be accessed together.
  • Smaller stride generally improves spatial locality.
  • In C row-major arrays, varying the last index in inner loops often gives stride-1 access.

Cache Concepts

  • Hit: data found in cache; miss: fetch from lower level.
  • Common cache line size is 64 bytes.
  • Miss types: compulsory (cold), conflict, capacity.
  • Write policies: write-through vs write-back (dirty bit tracking).

Struct Layout and Padding

struct A {
    char  a;
    int   b;
    char  c;
    double d;
};
  • Compiler inserts padding to satisfy alignment constraints.
  • Ordering fields from larger to smaller often reduces padding.

Amdahl's Law

overall_speedup = 1 / ((1 - p) + p/s)
  • p: fraction of runtime affected.
  • s: speedup of optimized part.
  • If p is small, max whole-program speedup is limited.

GCC Optimization Levels

FlagUse
-O0No optimization; easiest debug mapping
-OgDebug-friendly optimizations
-O1Basic optimization
-O2Common production baseline
-O3More aggressive, may increase code size

Useful companions: -g for debug symbols, -pg for gprof instrumentation.

Optimization Workflow

  1. Get correct output first.
  2. Measure baseline.
  3. Profile hotspots.
  4. Optimize the hotspot.
  5. Re-measure and verify correctness.

Measuring Performance

$ /usr/bin/time -p ./app
real 1.23
user 1.18
sys  0.04
  • real: wall-clock elapsed time.
  • user: CPU time in user mode.
  • sys: CPU time in kernel mode.

gprof Quick Start

$ gcc -pg -O2 app.c -o app
$ ./app
$ gprof ./app gmon.out | less

Classic Loop Pitfalls and Fixes

// pitfall
for (int i = 0; i < strlen(s); i++) { ... }

// fix
size_t n = strlen(s);
for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) { ... }

Cache-Friendly Matrix Tips

  • Prefer loop orders with stride-1 access in innermost loops.
  • Use blocking/tiling so working submatrices fit cache.
  • Avoid unnecessary temporary arrays and scattered access patterns.

Pointer Aliasing Reminder

Compiler must assume pointers may alias unless it can prove otherwise. This can block optimizations that would otherwise be legal.

Common Mistakes Checklist

  • Optimizing before profiling.
  • Comparing only single-run timings.
  • Ignoring cache behavior and memory access patterns.
  • Changing algorithms for tiny gains that hurt readability without measured value.
  • Assuming source-level simplification always maps to faster machine code.

Reference: Systems Programming Guides

Virtual Memory, Linking, and Heap Reference

Quick reference for Module 9 topics: address translation, linking, heap allocation, Valgrind, and garbage collection concepts.

Virtual Memory Basics

  • User processes use virtual addresses; MMU translates to physical addresses.
  • TLB caches recent translations.
  • With 4 KB pages, offset uses 12 low-order bits.
  • PTE fields commonly include valid bit, physical page number, and permissions.

Page Fault Flow

  1. Access hits invalid or non-resident PTE.
  2. CPU raises page fault exception.
  3. Kernel handler validates access and resolves mapping/load.
  4. Instruction is retried or process is signaled (for invalid access).

Static vs Dynamic Linking

ModeTrait
StaticLibrary code copied into executable (larger binary)
DynamicLibraries resolved at load/runtime (smaller binary, shared libs)
 
$ gcc main.c -o dyn_app
$ gcc -static main.c -o static_app
$ ldd dyn_app

PLT and GOT (Dynamic Linking)

  • PLT: call stubs for external functions.
  • GOT: runtime-resolved addresses used by those stubs.
  • First call may trigger resolver; later calls usually jump directly via GOT.

Symbol Strength (Common Rules)

  • Strong symbols: functions, initialized globals.
  • Weak/common behavior for tentative globals is toolchain-dependent (historically common with -fcommon).
  • If one strong and one weak/common definition collide, the strong definition is selected.

Heap Allocation APIs

void *p = malloc(n);
void *q = calloc(count, size);
void *r = realloc(p, new_n);
free(p);
  • malloc returns NULL on failure.
  • calloc allocates and zero-initializes.
  • realloc may move block; always use returned pointer carefully.
  • Double-free and use-after-free are undefined behavior.

Fragmentation Terms

  • Internal fragmentation: wasted bytes inside allocated blocks.
  • External fragmentation: free memory exists but split into unusable pieces.
  • Coalescing: merging adjacent free blocks.

Valgrind Quick Commands

$ gcc -g app.c -o app
$ valgrind --leak-check=full ./app
$ valgrind --track-origins=yes ./app
ReportMeaning
Invalid read/writeOut-of-bounds or bad pointer access
Definitely lostLeaked block with no remaining pointers
Indirectly lostReachable only through definitely lost blocks

Garbage Collection Concepts

  • Reference counting fails on cycles unless cycle detection is added.
  • Mark-and-sweep: mark reachable from roots, then sweep unreachable.
  • Generational GC collects young objects frequently and old objects less often.
  • C's unrestricted pointer arithmetic makes moving GC difficult.

Common Mistakes Checklist

  • Forgetting to free on all paths.
  • Using pointers after free.
  • Writing one byte past array bounds.
  • Assuming linking errors are compiler errors; often missing objects/libraries.
  • Ignoring page-fault/performance effects of access patterns.

Reference: Systems Programming Guides

Kernel Organization Reference

Quick reference for Module 10 topics: kernel responsibilities, privilege transitions, architecture styles, and practical design tradeoffs.

What the Kernel Does

  • Manages CPU scheduling and context switches.
  • Manages virtual memory, page tables, and protection.
  • Provides file systems, networking, and device access.
  • Exposes services via system calls.
  • Enforces isolation between processes and between user/kernel mode.

Privilege Levels

ModeTypical Capabilities
User mode (ring 3)No direct privileged instructions or device control
Kernel mode (ring 0)Full privileged access to CPU/MMU/devices

System Call Path (x86-64 Linux)

  1. User code places syscall number in %rax and args in syscall registers.
  2. CPU executes syscall and switches to kernel mode.
  3. Kernel dispatches through syscall table to handler.
  4. Kernel returns result in %rax and resumes user mode.

Common user-space wrapper path: libc wrapper -> syscall instruction -> kernel handler -> return.

Context Switch Essentials

  • Save current thread/process register state.
  • Select next runnable task.
  • Restore next state and memory mapping context.
  • Switching tasks incurs overhead (cache/TLB disruption + scheduler work).

Kernel Architecture Styles

StyleCore IdeaStrengthTradeoff
MonolithicMost services run in kernel spaceHigh performance via direct callsLarge trusted code base; faults can be catastrophic
MicrokernelMinimal kernel, services in user spaceFault isolation and smaller trusted coreMore IPC/mode-switch overhead
HybridMix of both approachesPragmatic performance/reliability balanceArchitectural complexity

Monolithic Kernel Notes

  • Linux is monolithic with loadable kernel modules.
  • Drivers, file systems, scheduler, networking, and VM all run in privileged space.
  • Module loading improves deployability, not protection isolation.

Microkernel Notes

  • Kernel keeps only essentials: low-level scheduling, memory primitives, IPC.
  • Drivers and services run as user-space servers.
  • If a server crashes, system can often recover without full kernel panic.

IPC and Message Passing

  • Microkernels rely heavily on IPC for service composition.
  • Fast IPC design is central to microkernel performance.
  • Copying and context switches can dominate if IPC path is inefficient.

Scheduling Terms

TermMeaning
PreemptionOS interrupts running task to run another
Time slice (quantum)CPU time budget before potential switch
LatencyTime from ready-to-run until execution
ThroughputAmount of work completed per unit time

Reliability and Security Design Points

  • Smaller trusted computing base can simplify auditing and formal verification.
  • Compartmentalization limits blast radius of component bugs.
  • Monolithic kernels reduce boundary crossings but increase privileged attack surface.

Modern Practical Directions

  • Containers: process isolation using kernel namespaces/cgroups.
  • eBPF: verified bytecode executed in-kernel for observability/networking.
  • Rust in kernel components: memory-safety improvements for new code.
  • Specialized kernels (e.g., RTOS/microkernels) in safety-critical systems.

Common Mistakes Checklist

  • Assuming loadable modules are isolated like user-space processes.
  • Treating all context switch costs as constant; cache/TLB effects matter.
  • Assuming microkernels are always too slow for real systems.
  • Assuming monolithic kernels are inherently insecure; engineering quality still dominates outcomes.
  • Ignoring workload: architecture choice depends on goals (latency, throughput, isolation, certifiability).
